name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico jury finds Facebook at fault over data collection
description: A New Mexico jury on Friday found Facebook willfully violated state law and engaged in unfair and deceptive trade practices regarding collection of user data, misinformation and hate speech on the platform and preferential treatment for government figures.
text:
Judge Francis Mathew, left, listens to the closing statements made by Dane Butswinkas, an attorney representing Meta, on September 23, 2026, in the First Judicial District Court in Santa Fe. The jury found Facebook willfully committed 43 million violations regarding unfair and deceptive trade practices over collection of user data and misinformation on the platform. (Nathan Burton/New Mexican file photo)A New Mexico jury on Friday found Facebook willfully violated state law and engaged in unfair and deceptive trade practices regarding collection of user data. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In total, the jury found that Facebook committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act. First Judicial District Judge Francis Mathew will now decide how much the company will pay; attorneys representing the state have asked for the maximum $5,000 penalty per violation.
“What this jury has said is that after 16 years of Facebook lying to New Mexicans and telling them their data was safe when they were taking all of their private thoughts and selling it to other people. Somebody finally stood up to them and said ‘we are not going to put up with that,’” attorney Randi McGinn,  who represented the State of New Mexico, told reporters following the announcement of the jury’s decision.
The state initially filed its case against Facebook in 2021, following news reports of the Cambridge Analytica data breach in which users’ personal information was used for political advertisements leading up to the 2016 election. The trial follows two high-profile courtroom victories for the state in unrelated cases against Meta, Facebook’s parent company.
In a statement provided to Source NM, a Meta spokesperson said, “We disagree with the verdict and will continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record. Meta’s platforms are forums for free expression. We have a First Amendment right to manage those platforms in a way we believe best serves the interests of our community. This means prioritizing free speech, protecting our users’ information and giving them control over their data.” 
This is a developing story and will be updated as needed.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico AG Torrez urges Congress for AI regulation after attempted OpenAI hack on UNM
description: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez urged top congressional leaders in a letter sent Thursday for immediate regulation of the artificial intelligence industry after an OpenAI program went rogue and attempted to hack into the University of New Mexico’s digital library.
text:
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez and 25 other attorneys general urged top congressional leaders for immediate artificial intelligence regulation in a letter sent on Sept. 24, 2026. Above: Torrez and state Rep. Linda Serrato (D-Santa Fe) introduced proposed legislation regulating the use of AI during the 2026 legislative session. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez urged top congressional leaders in a letter sent Thursday for immediate regulation of the artificial intelligence industry after an OpenAI program went rogue and attempted to hack into the University of New Mexico’s digital library.
Autonomous OpenAI agents unsuccessfully attacked a UNM digital attack on May 25 and 26, according to a report published on Wednesday by Transluce, an A.I. research lab. The rogue AI agents repeatedly tried to retrieve an archival photograph of a historic tuberculosis treatment center in UNM’s Valmora digital collection.
The Transluce report also found that the same OpenAI programs hacked an Australian government website in June and acquired health data.
“Across the country, we’re seeing undeniable evidence that the newest generation of AI systems can behave unpredictably and operate outside the boundaries developers intended,” New Mexico AG Raúl Torrez said in a statement on Thursday. “Congress must take action now, and here in New Mexico we’re preparing legislation to ensure these technologies are subject to meaningful safeguards before they put our communities at risk.”
UNM spokesperson Steven Carr said in an email that the university is aware of the incident reported and found no evidence of compromised systems or data.
New Mexico Democrats propose revamped consumer protection, digital safety laws

“Our internal investigation to date, which included outreach to the service provider for the digital collection management service hosting the data that was targeted, found no evidence that UNM systems or data were compromised,” Carr wrote. “UNM takes cybersecurity very seriously. Our systems and staff monitor potential threats and modify the University’s cyber-defenses as necessary to address evolving risks.”
Source NM requested, but had not received a comment from OpenAI by publication.
An OpenAI spokeswoman told The New York Times on Wednesday that the company had reached out to UNM regarding the incident. 
“In our broader review, we’re continuing to prioritize the most serious incidents while expanding our work to power-severity activity, including agents spamming websites,” she told the NYT.
Torrez, part of a coalition of 25 attorneys general, sent a letter on Thursday addressed to Speaker Mike Johnson, Majority Leader John Thune, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, and Majority Leader Chuck Schumer urging federal oversight on AI safety testing, incident response measures and state authority to enforce federal protections.
The letter said the unsuccessful UNM hack is an example of several incidents of rogue AI attacks this year. Hugging Face, an online repository, reported it was being attacked in July. A week later, OpenAI admitted its agents escaped a testing environment and infiltrated Hugging Face systems using stolen credentials.
“OpenAI was aware of the agents’ capabilities but failed to adequately monitor their activity or stop their exploits,” the letter said. “When humans engage in such activity, they violate criminal law.”
Torrez also requested Duane Arruti, chief information officer at UNM, provide a complete account on what systems, or data, was put at risk and confirmation of whether UNM was directly contacted by OpenAI.
“These events pose an extraordinary and growing danger to critical infrastructure, government institutions, private businesses, and the public, and the fact that one of them reportedly reached a University of New Mexico system brings that danger home to our state,” Torrez said in the letter.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Former Capitol Police officers testify in their manslaughter trial
description: An ex-Capitol Police officer's testimony in his manslaughter trial varies from the original statement he gave after the fatal shooting of Jaylen Lewis in 2022.
text:
Two former Capitol Police officers faced cross-examination Friday regarding their contention that they were forced to shoot a Jackson man in self-defense after he tried to run them over. 
Friday marked the third day of testimony in the manslaughter trial of Michael Rhinewalt and Steven Frederick Jr., who served on the crime suppression Flex Unit of the Capitol Police.
Friday also marked the fourth anniversary of the day, Sept. 25, 2022, when officers fired into the Jeep Grand Cherokee of 25-year-old Jaylen Lewis and killed him.
Rhinewalt testified that they stopped the Jeep Grand Cherokee because it matched the general description of a car suspected in auto burglaries.
When Lewis backed up his Cherokee and rammed into another law enforcement car behind him, he and Frederick drew their guns, Rhinewalt said.
Both of them called out for Lewis to show his hands, he said. He quoted himself as telling Frederick, “Watch his hands. I think he has a gun.”
When Lewis pulled forward, he said he and Frederick yelled for him to stop, and so did his female passenger.
Rhinewalt said he made eye contact with Lewis. “It’s like he looks up, takes a deep breath and says, ‘F— you and gasses it.’”
He said nothing blocked Lewis from going to the left, but “he turned his vehicle toward us, trying to run us over.”
He feared for his life, he said. “I thought of my wife and kids. I didn’t want to do what he made me do.”
He fired two shots into the front windshield, including the fatal shot to Lewis’ head, and a third shot hit the frame between the front windshield and side window.
He said he actually put his hand on the hood of Lewis’ the car when he fired the third shot and that the car lifted him off the ground.
The impact of the car prompted him to roll on the ground, he said.
Special Assistant Attorney General Luke Williamson asked Rhinewalt if his testimony that he told Frederick about Lewis may have a gun was in his original statement to investigators.
Rhinewalt said no.
Williamson asked him about his statement that the car lifted him up. “That’s not in the recording, is it?”
Rhinewalt said no.
Williamson asked him about his statement about rolling on the ground.
“Actually I was struck,” he said. “I lost my balance from coming off the hood.”
“That’s not in the recording?” Williamson said.
“No, it’s not,” Rhinewalt replied.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: An unexpected clue leads to family for an Alaska Native student who died at the Carlisle school
description: This story was originally published by ICT. WARNING: This story contains disturbing details about boarding schools. If you are feeling triggered, here is a resource list from the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition. While everyone else in the household was asleep, Nyché Andrew worked late into the night at the computer. An Indigenous [[...]
text:
Tummassak, at right, an Alaska Native student who died on April 8, 1900, while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania, is being repatriated to her homeland as part of the return of the remains of 12 students from Carlisle in 2026. She and six other youths boarded the USS Revenue Cutter Bear (in background) to make the two-month trip from Alaska. (Credit: Photo illustration by Charles Fox/Historical photos courtesy of the Presbyterian Historical Society)This story was originally published by ICT.
WARNING: This story contains disturbing details about boarding schools. If you are feeling triggered, here is a resource list from the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition.
While everyone else in the household was asleep, Nyché Andrew worked late into the night at the computer.
An Indigenous research specialist with the Alaska Native Heritage Center, she’d been assigned the task of finding the origins and descendants of the Alaska Native students still buried at the former site of the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania.
Historical archives and the Carlisle school records were often a labyrinth of frustrations, with numerous dead ends. Then she stumbled across a photo of one of the Alaska students, Tummassak, in the Sheldon Jackson Collection at the Presbyterian Historical Society.
“I stared in awe at her photograph because it instantly reminded me of the only photo of my great-great-grandmother, Mary Agugaq Avessuk,” Andrew, Skavaq Sivulliuqti (Yup’ik/Iñupiaq), originally from Anchorage but now living in New Jersey, told ICT.
What caught her attention was not simply the family resemblance or the way they both fixed their eyes away from the camera, but the tavluġun, a tattoo on her chin signifying a young woman’s transition into maturity. It was the same tavluġun she had seen in photos of her great-great-grandmother.
Then came the sudden realization that the young woman she’d been researching was actually a relative.
“Tummassak was a very special find,” she said. “As a researcher, I never anticipated finding my family members.”
Side-by-side photos show the same chin tattoos on Tummassak, at left, an Alaska Native student who died while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, and Mary Agugaq Avessuk, the great-great-grandmother of Indigenous researcher Nyché Andrew who realized the tattoo linked Tummassak to her own family. (Credit: Photos courtesy of Nyché Andrew and Presbyterian Historical Society)
The next morning, Andrew showed the photo to her mother, Jacqueline Agugaq Walluk.
“She softened at the sight of an Iñupiaq girl with a tattoo like Mary’s and remarked on how beautiful Tummassak was,” Andrew said. “We agreed that she looked incredibly similar to my sister, Farrell Agathluk Asiaq Stoudt.”
Tummassak is among more than 100 Native students still buried at the Carlisle cemetery, including 11 from Alaska, but she will soon be headed home.
Final Journey: Carlisle begins its ninth repatriation of students who never made it home

Family members and community leaders from Alaska are set to arrive in Carlisle on Thursday, Sept. 24, for the disinterment and later a ceremonial transfer of the remains of Tummassak and three other Alaska Native students whose remains will be repatriated this year – Mabel Booth, whose last name is listed as Stack or Stock in school records; Edward Angalook; and Lucy Spaulding.
The repatriations are among 12 this year from the Carlisle cemetery. The remains of three students from the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes were returned home to Montana in early September, and the remains of another five students from five different tribes are set to be repatriated by mid-October.
Officials with the Office of Army Cemeteries, which oversees the Carlisle Barracks Post Cemetery where the children are buried, have not released details about which of the remaining five students have been repatriated so far.
Twenty-two graves in the cemetery remain marked, however, as “unknown” because the children’s remains cannot be identified, the result of a mix-up that likely occurred when the cemetery was moved in 1927.
Benjamin Jacuk, Dena’ina/Sugpiaq, the director of research at the Alaska Native Heritage Center, said the Office of Army Cemeteries reached out to the center in 2024 for help identifying family members of the children buried there.
“A lot of the times really the best places to look are more local,” Jacuk told ICT. “What research is, at the end of the day, is making sure that we’re uncovering every stone to figure out how to be able to bring our families back.”
‘Another death’
Tummassak was 12 years old when she arrived at the Carlisle school on Nov. 14, 1897, and died of tuberculosis less than three years later on April 8, 1900. She is listed as Tomicock on her gravestone and as Tomiclock in Carlisle archives.
The school newspaper, The Indian Helper, recorded the details of Tummassak’s final moments in the April 13, 1900, issue.
“We are grieved to record the death of another of our Alaska pupils — Tomicock (Tummassak),” the article stated.
“She was patient, gentle and brave. She bore her illness in silence. Her smile was ready even when too weak to talk. She was conscious to the end,” the newspaper reported. “She asked Miss Barr to hold her and breathed her last while resting in those kindly arms, ever ready to help one in distress. Annebuck was her chosen friend and close companion, and the bereft child has the sympathy of all who knew the tender and sisterly feeling between the two.”
The grave of Tummassak (spelled Tomicock on the gravestone) is among more than a dozen Alaska Native students buried at the Carlisle Barracks Post Cemetery in Pennsylvania after dying while attending the school. Tummassak is set to be repatriated starting Sept. 25, 2026. (Credit: Photo by Charles Fox/Special to ICT)
The Carlisle Indian Industrial School operated from 1879 to 1918. Established on a vacant military base, hundreds of miles from the influences and traditions of most tribes, it was the first federally funded, off-reservation Native American boarding school in the United States and served as a model for schools across the U.S. and Canada.
Almost 8,000 Native American and Alaska Native students attended the school, part of an oppressive government attempt at forcefully assimilating Native students into White civilization. Its aim was to change them forever by cutting links to their family, language and culture.
Records indicate that 232 students died while enrolled at the school, and many did not return home. Prior to 2017, when repatriations began at Carlisle, there were 186 students buried in the cemetery. Another 37 were returned to their homes for burial, nine died while on the school’s outing program and were buried near those locations, and three died while enroute home from the school, according to Jim Gerencser, associate dean for archives and special collections at Dickinson College and the Carlisle Indian School Digital Resource Center.
Of all the students who were shipped to Carlisle, none had to travel as long and as far to get there as the Alaska Native students.
The first two Alaska Native students were brought to Carlisle by Sheldon Jackson, who managed the western states and Alaska for the Presbyterian Board of Home Missions. He was also named the general agent of education for Alaska.
He took Fred Harris (Ko-woot-ke-ish) and Henry Phillips (Ka-ka-ish), to Carlisle in December 1887 to learn the trades of tin smithing and printing.
On Sept. 20, 1897, a group of six Iñupiat youths, including Tummassak, boarded the US Revenue Cutter Bear, an early version of an ice breaker, at the Teller Reindeer Station in Port Clarence for transport to Seattle in Puget Sound after a side trip to Siberia. Following a 2,700-mile, cross-country train ride, they arrived in Carlisle almost two months later on Nov. 14, 1897, where they were photographed in their parkas.
Though they escaped the “Great Deaths” in Alaska when flu and other illnesses wiped out entire villages, they were not as lucky in Carlisle. Laublock, or Lablok, the only male in the group, died on Sept. 15, 1899, and Tummassak died the following year. Student Cooki Glook, also known as Kokiglook or Cookiglook, died on Jan. 4, 1904.  All died of tuberculosis, known as “consumption” at the time, though Cooki Glook also suffered from rheumatism of the heart, according to school records.
Laublock and Cooki Glook remain buried in the school cemetery and, according to Jacuk, are expected to be returned home in 2027.
A group of Inupiat children from Alaska arrive at Carlisle Indian Industrial School on Nov. 18, 1897, in traditional clothing with fur-lined hoods. (Credit: Photo courtesy of the Presbyterian Historical Society.)
Over the years, 127 Alaskan students attended the Carlisle school, and 14 died and were buried in the school cemetery, according to records.
Three Alaska Native students have been returned home during the Carlisle repatriation efforts prior to this year. And at least one student, Ephraim Alexander, Yup’ik, died from tuberculosis while spending his final days with Moravian missionaries in Lititz, Pennsylvania, where he remains buried in a Moravian cemetery, according to the research of Lucy Rath while at Franklin and Marshall College.
One of his best friends, Henry Rose, who was at Alexander’s bedside when he died, lies in an unknown grave in the school cemetery.
 Finding the families
Jacuk said the Office of Army Cemeteries reached out for help identifying students because they felt they’d “exhausted the documentation in the primary source material that’s useful in trying to return home these children buried at Carlisle.”
The Office of Army Cemeteries had initially refused to repatriate children unless descendants could be found, rejecting requests from tribes that their members be released to them under the federal Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, or NAGPRA.
The dispute prompted a federal lawsuit in 2024 from the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska, asking the court to order the government to honor the tribe’s request to return two boys who died at the school more than 100 years ago. A judge ruled in favor of the government and dismissed the case, but an appellate court in May 2026 overturned the lower court’s decision and ruled that NAGPRA regulations would apply to the repatriation of children.The ruling allows the Winnebago lawsuit to proceed against the government.
The Office of Army Cemeteries has declined to comment on whether it is honoring tribal authority to obtain repatriation of their children while the case is reconsidered. But the need to find a specific family member for each child had created additional pressure on Andrew.
“A big part in doing this research is not just looking at the places that everyone else has looked at, it’s making sure that we are looking at the places that they might not think to look at,” Jacuk said. “And so, that’s when we really went to looking at things like baptismal records, finding names and correspondence.”
Jacuk stressed the importance of being connected to communities to weed through inaccuracies in the school records and cemetery gravestones.
“We’re here to represent all peoples of Alaska,” he said. “And so, as a result, it becomes really easy to find connections very quickly within our communities. Because if someone doesn’t know what family to talk to … they know someone who can do that for us very easily.”
Native Alaska students enjoy a laugh on the grounds of the Carlisle Indian Industrial School. From left are Tummassak, Cooki Glook, Annie Coodlalook, and Annebuck. Tummassak’s relative, Nyché Andrew, says it is the only photo she has seen of the young woman smiling. The man is not identified. (Credit: Photo courtesy of Dickinson College Special Collections)

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: On ‘9 to 5’ day, North Carolinians celebrate Dolly Parton and her love of literacy
description: Nick Blanchard tumbled out of bed and poured himself a cup of ambition Friday morning, then headed straight to a table in front of the Wake County Express Library in downtown Raleigh. Blanchard and his friend Kelly Forbes were presiding over a children’s book drive to honor the late music icon and philanthropist Dolly Parton. […]
text:
Donated children's books in honor of Dolly Parton will be placed in little libraries across Raleigh. Nick Blanchard came up with the idea to honor the late singer on "9 to 5" day. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)Nick Blanchard tumbled out of bed and poured himself a cup of ambition Friday morning, then headed straight to a table in front of the Wake County Express Library in downtown Raleigh.
Blanchard and his friend Kelly Forbes were presiding over a children’s book drive to honor the late music icon and philanthropist Dolly Parton.
Gov. Josh Stein declared September 25th, or 9/25, officially “Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library Day of Reading” across North Carolina in memory of the Tennessee musician, her hit song “9 to 5,” and her philanthropic generosity to Helene victims as well as young readers.
Parton’s Imagination Library, launched in 1995, has delivered more than 300 million free books to children around the globe. In North Carolina, the initiative has delivered 25 million free books to children in all 100 counties.
“I had an idea of just doing something in Dolly’s honor,” said Blanchard. “She was so entrenched with children’s literacy. And I thought this would be a good opportunity for us to all get together and give books.”
On this day, all the books collected by Blanchard and Forbes will end up in little box libraries in five neighborhoods across the city.
“You can’t get along with this world without reading,” said Blanchard. “Dolly really wanted to get people involved in reading from birth. And that’s why we’re collecting so many different kinds of books.”
Forbes said she welcomed the chance to be a part of the inaugural event, getting her employer Team Triangle Realty to donate books, and even sponsoring one of the little libraries.
“I do absolutely love [Dolly] and everything that she stands for,” said Forbes. “What a good person she was! And we love to honor her memory this way.”
Forbes said a beautifully illustrated, physical book can open the world of reading to a young person at a time when too many people are fixated on screens.
“I think that it’s sad that people use screen time to babysit their children,” said Forbes. “Picking up a book for a kid is fabulous.”
While Parton died at age 80 on Aug. 25, her dream of sending a free book every month to children from birth until they reach 5 years old is still alive through The Dollywood Foundation. Here’s where parents can subscribe at no cost.
Kelly Forbes and Nick Blanchard sift through a box of donated books that will be shared with young readers across Raleigh. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Czech President Petr Pavel visits Nebraska
description: The Czech president Petr Pavel visited Nebraska to highlight the state’s ties and partnership with the Czech Republic.
text:
Czech President Petr Pavel speaks in the Nebraska Capitol in Lincoln on Sept. 24, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Czech President Petr Pavel visited Nebraska Thursday to highlight the state’s ties and partnership with the Czech Republic. 
The day’s affair included multiple stops. Pavel visited the University of Nebraska-Lincoln to talk with students about the state’s deep connections with the Czech Republic. He had a work lunch with Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen. The former president also visited the Nebraska National Guard. Then he went to Wilber, dubbed “the Czech Capital of the USA.” The trip to the Cornhusker State ended with a short press conference at the Nebraska Capitol with Pillen. 
Pavel said he was emotional about meeting so many people in Wilber who identify with Czech “ancestry, tradition and history.” 
“I was simply moved by how devoted they are to promote this heritage for next generations, because quite often, even in my own country, we are not that enthusiastic about traditions as they were,” Pavel said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Poll: 2 out of 3 North Carolinians get political news from local TV or social media
description: No other source reached more than 17%, according to the poll.
text:
The entrance to the Durham County Main Library, where voters cast their primary ballots on Feb. 12, 2026, the first day of early voting. (Photo: Brandon Kingdollar/NC Newsline)Local television and social media are where most North Carolina voters get their political and government news, according to a poll released Friday. 
Common Cause NC found that the two sources each reach about a third of voters, with 36% of respondents saying they rely on local TV news for their state political news and 35% saying social media.
Voters could name up to two sources — 8% named both — so together local TV news and social media reach 63% of voters. 
No other source reached more than 17%, according to the poll. Cable news, radio, a North Carolina newspaper (print or online), and national news networks each reach 17% of voters. 
The survey found partisan differences. Democrats are more likely than Republicans to name a North Carolina newspaper, 21% to 12%, while 17% of unaffiliated voters said they get their news from a North Carolina newspaper. 
Nearly half of Democrats said they get their state political news from local TV, at 45%, compared to 32% for both Republicans and unaffiliated voters.
Unaffiliated voters rely heavily on social media for state political news, at 42%. Meanwhile, 34% of Democrats and 28% of Republicans say they get their news from social media. 
New poll shows NC voters across party lines see childcare as workforce, affordability issue

Cable news leans Republican at 22%, while 15% of both Democrats and unaffiliated voters named that source. Radio tends to be most popular with unaffiliated voters, reaching 21% of independents, 18% of Republicans, and 13% of Democrats. cable n
Six percent of respondents say they don’t follow North Carolina politics. That breaks down to 10% of Republicans, 5% of unaffiliated voters, and 4% of Democrats.
The poll is part of a survey ahead of the 2025 U.S. Senate race. It also shows Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper maintaining a sizable lead over former Republican National Committee and North Carolina GOP chair Michael Whatley, 51% to 41%. 
Common Cause NC conducted a statewide survey of 857 likely 2026 general election North Carolina voters between Sept. 17 and 20. The margin of error was plus or minus 3.3 percentage points.

Caldwell has also been deeply committed to addressing the long-standing challenges facing Black communities across our state,” Sherrill told reporters in Trenton Friday.

name: WyoFile
title: After ICE arrest, Jackson restaurant worker’s community springs into action
description:
Federal agents detained Feride Bardakci at a bus stop Sept. 15 for allegedly overstaying her student visa. After learning of Wyoming community’s support, she plans to contest her removal.
The post After ICE arrest, Jackson restaurant worker’s community springs into action appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
JACKSON—When Feride Bardakci called her roommate from immigration custody in Casper, the 26-year-old restaurant worker tried to make a joke.
“Honey, I guess you know why I’m calling right now,” her roommate recalled Bardakci saying.
Hours earlier, federal immigration officers restrained Bardakci’s hands behind her back and took her from a START bus stop as she traveled between shifts at two Jackson restaurants. Her alleged violation was overstaying her authorized time in the United States — a civil immigration matter.
Federal agents traveled roughly 270 miles from Casper to Jackson that day, arrested Bardakci and drove her back to the Natrona County Detention Center, according to her roommate.
Federal officials have not accused Bardakci of committing a crime. They described her arrest as a “targeted enforcement operation” but have not explained why she was selected or how agents located her.
Even from custody, Bardakci’s immediate concern was not herself. She worried about missing work and leaving her roommate to cover their rent alone.
“She is the strongest girl I’ve ever met,” said the roommate, who asked not to be named.
Bardakci’s Sept. 15 arrest has raised questions about why agents selected her and why federal officials provided conflicting explanations about whether she posed a concern to the community.
Conflicting information
Federal officials have provided conflicting accounts of why Bardakci was targeted and how agents carried out the arrest.
In a written statement attributed only to a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, the agency said Bardakci legally entered the United States in June 2023 but remained after her authorized stay expired in April 2024. DHS identified the alleged overstay as the basis for her arrest and did not accuse her of criminal conduct.
Federal representatives who declined to publicly provide their names told the Jackson Hole News&Guide that hundreds of people are arrested under similar circumstances every day across the country.
Federal officials also gave Teton County Sheriff Matt Carr a different explanation for the arrest. Carr said one official described Bardakci as “somebody that warrants great concern for having them in your community” and suggested undisclosed information made her a priority.
“For whatever reason, this person was significant enough that they came for what they call a targeted individual,” Carr said. “They were after one individual person, and they took that person and they left.”
Carr acknowledged that he has not seen the information to which the official alluded and does not know why Bardakci was targeted or whether the characterization was justified. ICE told the News&Guide only that the operation was targeted because Bardakci had violated immigration law by overstaying her authorized time in the country.
Asked in a follow-up email what made Bardakci a significant community concern, ICE public affairs said Carr had received information that conflicted with DHS’s official account.
“Whoever talked to the sheriff directly contradicts the statement that DHS provided,” the response said.
ICE then offered broader statistics about the people it arrests.
“Nearly 70% of ICE arrests are of criminal illegal aliens who have been convicted or have pending charges,” the agency wrote. “This statistic doesn’t account for those wanted for violent crimes in their home country or another country, INTERPOL notices, human rights abusers, gang members, terrorists, etc. The list goes on.”
The agency did not say whether any of those descriptions applied to Bardakci.
DHS’s original statement also referred to Tren de Aragua, MS-13, criminal rings, murderers and rapists while explaining why immigration officers sometimes wear masks. Asked whether Bardakci had any connection to a gang or violent crime, the agency replied, “They do not.”
ICE twice declined the News&Guide’s request for a copy of Bardakci’s arrest warrant, saying the agency does not release warrants to the public.
Attorney Elisabeth Trefonas, who is representing Bardakci, said the government’s statement made an alleged civil visa violation sound connected to criminal activity.
“If they had something on her, like she was a terrorist or she had a criminal record, wouldn’t they have put that in the statement?” Trefonas said. 
“That’s not there.”
Why the arrest differs
Bardakci’s arrest differed from cases covered by the Teton County Sheriff’s Office’s 48-hour immigration hold policy.
Those holds allow the Sheriff’s Office to keep people arrested on state or municipal allegations for up to 48 hours beyond their scheduled release so federal immigration officers can assume custody.
Bardakci, however, was not arrested on a local charge or booked into the county jail. Federal agents instead sought her directly in the community, restrained her at a public bus stop and transported her to Casper based on an alleged visa overstay.
Carr has defended his office’s policy by noting that detainees first enter local custody over alleged crimes, though ICE holds may be honored regardless of the charge’s severity or outcome.
Carr said this week that the bus stop arrest did not change his support for the policy.
Carr said federal officials acknowledged that agents failed to notify local dispatch before the arrest despite instructions to do so, calling the omission an internal personnel issue.
Not first street arrest
Bardakci’s arrest was not the first time ICE agents have sought people directly in Jackson rather than taking custody of them through the county jail.
During a multiday operation in July 2025, agents detained at least nine people across Teton County and western Wyoming. The detainees were initially taken to the Sweetwater County Detention Center in Rock Springs before being transferred to federal facilities elsewhere.
Among them was Juan Barranco Castro, then 56, whom agents stopped in the parking lot of Jackson’s Community Bible Church as he drove to work. Friends said agents had been looking for someone else who drove a similar vehicle.
“He was just in the wrong place at the wrong time,” one friend said. “It happened by accident.”
The 2025 operation also included people with misdemeanor DUI convictions and others for whom reporters found only traffic citations or no criminal record. Agents acknowledged during a recorded briefing that some of their information might be incomplete, at one point saying they might not have the correct address for a target.
Bardakci’s arrest nevertheless stands apart because federal officials publicly named her, issued a statement about her detention and identified only an alleged visa overstay as the basis for targeting her.
Trefonas said she could not recall ICE issuing a comparable public statement about a local detainee.
Federal data track visa overstays
Federal immigration officials use arrival, departure and immigration-benefit records to identify people who may have remained in the United States beyond their authorized stay.
A U.S. Customs and Border Protection report says the government generates daily lists of potential overstays and checks them against documented departures, visa extensions and changes in immigration status. ICE then applies screening criteria to determine which cases receive further investigation or enforcement.
DHS said Bardakci entered the United States in June 2023 with permission to remain until April 1, 2024. Her roommate said Bardakci initially arrived through the J-1 exchange visitor program and later obtained tourist status, though the News&Guide has not independently verified that visa history.
In fiscal year 2024, CBP classified 34,540 of roughly 1.4 million students and exchange visitors from countries other than Canada and Mexico as suspected in-country overstays, a rate of 2.45%. Among Turkish citizens in the combined visa categories, 618 of 23,533 expected departures were classified as suspected in-country overstays, or 2.63%.
The figures do not show how many overstays live in Jackson or explain why agents selected Bardakci.
Bardakci’s roommate said she also first came to the United States drawn by the opportunity to improve her English, earn money and experience life outside of Turkey. She moved to Jackson a few years ago and created a community that she fell in love with, her roommate said.
Friends rally after arrest
Bardakci’s arrest set off a chain of calls through Jackson’s restaurant and immigrant communities, beginning with a passerby who stopped when she saw two men placing Bardakci into an SUV.
Bardakci called out for the witness to contact a manager at one of her workplaces. The witness did not know Bardakci, but she knew about a local immigration-response hotline through a recent fundraiser held by her employer.
“I didn’t even think to record the situation or take any photos,” the witness said. “It happened very fast.”
After the agents drove away, she called the hotline and relayed what she had seen. She also helped alert Bardakci’s employer. Word reached Bardakci’s roommate around 4:30 p.m. Sept. 15 — nearly three hours before Bardakci called him from Casper.
The witness said she initially felt unprepared, despite knowing enough to connect Bardakci with help. She hopes other residents learn that the hotline exists and understand that immigration arrests are happening locally.
“It’s not just in other places that it’s happening,” she said. “It’s happening in our town.”
Friends immediately began contacting attorneys, gathering documents and raising money for Bardakci’s legal expenses. They also helped her roommate cover the next month’s rent and communicate with Bardakci’s family in Turkey.
Support extended beyond financial assistance. Friends brought meals, offered the roommate places to stay so he would not be alone and took over phone calls when he became too emotional to explain what had happened.
“Every time I was talking, I was crying,” the roommate said. “My friends helped me a lot.”
Bardakci’s roommate has remained her primary connection to Jackson, keeping his phone nearby in case Bardakci calls and coordinating with her attorney and family. The two have spoken every day since the arrest.
Bardakci initially considered leaving the country voluntarily if doing so would secure her immediate release, her roommate said.
She ultimately decided to contest her removal after learning how strongly the community had rallied around her.
“I probably wouldn’t stay if I didn’t feel that support,” her roommate recalled Bardakci saying. “She says thank you to everyone.”
The response has also expanded interest in the Teton Area Rapid Response Network, which distributes verified information about immigration activity. Emily Gomez of the Wyoming Immigrant Advocacy Project said the network now has 66 trained volunteers.
Gomez said the arrest should prompt employers, elected officials and residents to consider how they can support immigrant workers, including by connecting them with legal resources and learning how to respond when federal enforcement occurs in public.
“Are we okay with that type of enforcement?” Gomez said. “And if we’re not okay with that, then what are we going to do about this? Because I think all of us have a role to play.”
Bardakci has since been transferred from Casper to an immigration detention center in Aurora, Colorado. Her roommate said she is being held in a unit for detainees without criminal histories.
Most of the women housed with her speak Spanish, he said, so Bardakci asked him to send her a Spanish-language dictionary.
Even in detention, she has held on to her sense of humor. She has joked with her roommate that she is spending Jackson’s offseason in Denver and will return home “famous.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Dozens rally in Lewiston after landslide union vote, call for fired nurses to be reinstated
description: Roughly 80 people rallied across the street from Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston on Friday to support the facility’s newly unionized nurses and call on the hospital to reinstate nurses that were fired and suspended.  The crowd held signs while passing cars honked in support. Several staff members inside the hospital could be seen […]
text:
Katie Grinnell, a registered nurse at Central Maine Medical Center who was suspended and then fired, spoke across the street from the hospital after nurses overwhelmingly voted to unionize. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)Roughly 80 people rallied across the street from Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston on Friday to support the facility’s newly unionized nurses and call on the hospital to reinstate nurses that were fired and suspended. 
The crowd held signs while passing cars honked in support. Several staff members inside the hospital could be seen watching the crowd through the windows. 
Kelli Brennan, co-president of the Maine State Nurses Association, said she knew the nurses began to organize for one reason: to save their hospital. 
“Because nurses know what happens when your patient loads increase,” she said. “What happens when you don’t have enough clean bed linens to take care of your patients. And what happens when the hospital you have loved and you have given your lives to is captured by soulless, profit-hungry clowns who care nothing for you, your patients or your community.”
The CMMC nurses voted to join the Maine State Nurses Association Thursday, with 91% in support of joining. 
The union said the hospital has fired 15 nurses and suspended 5 more in the last several weeks. A spokesperson for CMMC did not respond to a request for comment, but previously told the Lewiston Sun Journal that the disciplinary action was not because of union activity, but were due to violations of hospital policy, such as patient abandonment and disruption of care. 
Katie Grinnell, a registered nurse at CMMC who was suspended and then fired, said at the rally Friday that the disciplinary action did not slow down the unionization efforts. 
“Our nurses who remained at the bedside were angry, and what was meant to scare them only fueled their fire,” Grinnell said. “Because we were all fighting for what our nurses and our patients need, the level of care our community deserves.”



Quotation







Our nurses who remained at the bedside were angry, and what was meant to scare them only fueled their fire. Because we were all fighting for what our nurses and our patients need, the level of care our community deserves.


– Katie Grinnell, a registered nurse at CNNC who was suspended and then fired


She said the nurses and the broader community will not sit quietly while hospital administration puts profits over patients. 
“I think I can speak on behalf of us all when I say you can suspend us, you can fire us, but you will not put out our flames,” she said. “You can retaliate against us and continue to lie to our community, but we are smart, and we all see that your actions do not match your words.”
Jesse Buck, a registered nurse at CMMC, called the decision to suspend and fire nurses “unprecedented” union-busting from the hospital, and clear retaliation for organizing. Buck and other speakers made it clear that the union’s next objective is getting the fired and suspended nurses reinstated.
“Now, having fought with you, we want to return the favor by fighting for you,” Buck said. “Our highest priority going forward is getting our nurses reinstated. We need you. Our community needs you. You deserve to be here, reaping the harvest of your hard work and sacrifice.”
Ruth Fitzgerald, a registered nurse at CMMC, said the hospital wasn’t perfect before it was acquired by California-based Prime Healthcare Foundation last year. But the new leadership made the existing issues much worse. And that has consequences for patients, she said. 
“Every closed unit, that’s a patient who waits longer,” Fitzgerald said. “Every unsafe assignment, that’s a patient who gets less. Every missing linen cart, every eliminated roll — that is not a line item on Prime’s budget. However, in our community, that is someone’s mother, that is someone’s father and that is someone’s child.”
Many state legislators and local political candidates joined the crowd while organizations across the state voiced their support for the union efforts. 
Maine Democratic Party Executive Director Devon Murphy-Anderson congratulated the nurses on the vote in a statement Friday.
“At a time when Maine’s health care system is already under enormous strain, we should be supporting the nurses who keep our hospitals running and care for Mainers every day,” Murphy-Anderson said. “Protecting quality healthcare in Maine starts with listening to and respecting the people who provide it.”
Gov. Mills criticizes CMMC leadership after firings
The suspension and firings of CMMC nurses has drawn attention and criticism from around the state. 
In a letter to CMMC President Allen Stefanek Wednesday, Gov. Janet Mills said it is “unconscionable” that the hospital would fire or suspend nurses at a time when the state is in desperate need of healthcare workers. 
“While Prime Healthcare insists that no employee was disciplined because of union activity, taking this action amid a critical statewide nursing shortage — and just days before nurses are set to exercise their right to make their voices heard in a union election — raises serious questions about retaliation,” Mills said. 
Last year, Mills’ administration issued a Certificate of Need approving Prime Healthcare’s acquisition of CMMC. And after complaints of staff shortages and quality-of-care issues, the Maine Department of Health and Human Services began reviewing the hospital’s compliance with the certificate. 
These terminations and suspensions heighten concerns that the hospital is not meeting the certificate’s criteria, Mills said. She strongly urged the hospital to reinstate every nurse that has been “wrongfully” fired or suspended.
“Failure to do so will make clear to Maine people that Prime Healthcare is prioritizing corporate interests over the commitments it made to the State of Maine to deliver the quality healthcare which Maine people expect and deserve,” Mills said. 
U.S. Reps. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) and Robin Kelly (D-Illinois) led a group of congressional Democrats in a letter to Prime Healthcare CEO Dr. Prem Reddy, to demand an end to the alleged intimidation and retaliation against nurses at hospitals around the country. 
In addition to the termination of nurses at CMMC, the lawmakers highlighted the firing of nurses at Prime Healthcare hospitals in Illinois and Nevada. U.S. Rep. Jared Golden was among the lawmakers that signed the letter. 
“Registered nurses at these Prime facilities are fighting to ensure they can provide the very best care to the communities they serve, including concerns about cuts to vital services that patients rely on,” the lawmakers wrote. 
The nurses at the Prime facility in Illinois, Olympia Fields Hospital, also voted overwhelmingly to unionize earlier this week.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island braces for early season nor’easter
description: Charge your phones and tablets, stay away from the water, and use extra caution if you must be on the roads. That’s Gov. Dan McKee’s advice as the state prepares for an early season nor’easter expected to bring strong winds, heavy rain, potential power outages and flooding to Rhode Island between Friday night and Sunday. […]
text:
Gov. Dan McKee, right, addresses the media at the Rhode Island Emergency Management Agency's Cranston headquarters on Friday Sept. 25, 2026. At center is EMA Director Mark Pappas. Far left is interim Department of Transportation Director Robert Rocchio. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Charge your phones and tablets, stay away from the water, and use extra caution if you must be on the roads.
That’s Gov. Dan McKee’s advice as the state prepares for an early season nor’easter expected to bring strong winds, heavy rain, potential power outages and flooding to Rhode Island between Friday night and Sunday.
“We’ve been through this exercise many times before,” McKee told reporters gathered at the Rhode Island Emergency Management Agency’s Cranston headquarters Friday morning. “Conditions will be dangerous, and I think that as we need to really reinforce the fact that there’s no need to take any levels of risk with your safety.”
The National Weather Service forecasts wind gusts of up to 50 to 60 mph, with the strongest winds expected along Narragansett Bay and the southern coast of the state, along with Block Island. 
Leaves still covering many trees this early in autumn could catch the wind and increase the risk of tree damage and power outages, Torry Dooley, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Norton, Massachusetts, said 
“That will kind of pull the branches and stuff like that and especially if there are trees that are maybe not the healthiest,” Dooley said in an interview.
A high wind warning is in effect Friday through 8 a.m. Sunday. A coastal flood warning is in effect from 5 p.m. Friday through 8 p.m. Sunday.
Rhode Island Energy President Greg Cornett told reporters at the Emergency Management Agency headquarters that the utility provider is fully staffed and prepared to respond throughout the storm. Cornett said the utility company secured about 215 crews to work throughout the weekend. Though he noted sustained winds above 35 mph will prevent crews from working from their trucks.
“We will be working throughout the course of the event to try to ensure that we can restore in real time as quickly as possible,” Cornett said.
Rhode Island Energy expects to know almost immediately when customers lose power since most have smart meters connected to their homes. Cornett advised residents to have to ensure their devices and backup batteries are fully charged in preparation for potential outages. 
The State Fire Marshal’s Office urged Rhode Islanders to use caution with portable generators in case of loss of power.
“Portable generators emit carbon monoxide, a toxic and deadly gas that is impossible to detect without proper equipment since it is colorless and odorless,” State Fire Marshal Timothy P. McLaughlin said in a statement.
Conditions offshore will be particularly dangerous as the storm strengthens, Dooley said. Winds over the water could reach 45 to 60 knots, with offshore seas building to 15 to 25 feet.
“Very large dangerous waves for the mariners,” Dooley said.
The storm is expected to drop 1.5 to 3 inches of rain in Providence, with most areas seeing between 1.5 and 2.5 inches, according to the National Weather Service. The rain will be spread out throughout the weekend rather than falling in one heavy burst, though Dooley said heavier downpours are possible.
Rain could still cause localized flooding, particularly in areas with poor drainage. McKee told reporters the Rhode Island Department of Transportation has assigned crews to clean drains ahead of the storm and will have equipment ready to respond to any resulting flooded roadways.
AAA Northeast urged drivers to slow down on wet roads, leave extra space between vehicles, and move over when approaching roadside assistance vehicles, first responders or maintenance crews.
Despite the potential for power outages, flooding and tree damage, McKee said he does not expect the storm to cause enough damage to qualify for a federal emergency. The state was denied federal aid for the February blizzard, which caused about $19 million in damage and cleanup costs after the state was buried under more than 3 feet of snow.
Rhode Island’s all-Democratic congressional delegation is now seeking answers about why the Federal Emergency Management Agency denied the state’s request for blizzard aid after McKee’s appeal was denied earlier this month.
“We’ve done what we can,” McKee told Rhode Island Current after his press conference. “Now we have to rely on the Trump administration to do the right thing.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Windsor leaders say ‘hate is not welcome’ following vandalism
description: Officials say a Pride flag was torn down from the town’s First Church and a plaque honoring Black veterans was stolen from a cemetery.
text:
Community leaders in the Hartford suburb of Windsor are speaking out against recent acts of potentially hate-motivated vandalism.
Officials say a Pride flag was torn down from the town’s First Church, a plaque honoring Black veterans was stolen from a cemetery, and a bench honoring two Black community leaders was stolen from another cemetery.
“Hate is not welcome here in Windsor, Connecticut,” Mayor Nuchette Black-Burke said at a Friday morning press conference at Windsor Town Hall. “It will not be tolerated.”
Black-Burke said the Windsor police are investigating the incidents. Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz said the Connecticut State Police had been made aware of the vandalism and stand ready to assist in the investigation.
The acts are “despicable and reprehensible,” Bysiewicz said.
“When we see acts of hate, we must stand up and call them out,” she said.
Corrie Betts, president of the Greater Hartford branch of the NAACP, called for the events to be investigated as hate crimes.
“Some may choose to call these acts of vandalism, but when our history, our sacred spaces and symbols of inclusion and human dignity are targeted, we must be willing to confront the possibility of something much deeper,” Betts said. “I call it hate.”
Pastor Adrienne Armes of First Church read a letter from senior minister Rev. Ned Parker.
“We have replaced the Pride flag. We will keep welcoming. We will keep praying for the people who did this,” Armes said. “We will stand with our LGBTQIA+ neighbors.”
“We will continue to insist that the gospel is larger and more inclusive than fearmongering, and we will keep believing that even those who act out of hate are not beyond the reach of God’s grace,” Armes said.
This story was first published Sept. 25, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: National
title: K-12 spending, absenteeism programs face risks as feds stop key monitoring, watchdog says
description: The U.S. Department of Education’s suspension this year of a comprehensive monitoring process puts billions of K-12 dollars at heightened risk of undetected waste, fraud and abuse, according to a new report by the nonpartisan U.S. Government Accountability Office. The congressional watchdog’s report also raised concerns about the reliability of federal absen[...]
text:
Fourth graders sit at their classroom tables in Oklahoma City. A new government watchdog report raises concerns about oversight of education spending and absenteeism data. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)The U.S. Department of Education’s suspension this year of a comprehensive monitoring process puts billions of K-12 dollars at heightened risk of undetected waste, fraud and abuse, according to a new report by the nonpartisan U.S. Government Accountability Office.
The congressional watchdog’s report also raised concerns about the reliability of federal absenteeism data, noting that absenteeism rates were reported above 100% in some schools.
Officials from the Department of Education told GAO the department suspended its consolidated monitoring of Elementary and Secondary Education Act requirements while it develops a new approach. But as of August, the department had not provided a timeline for resuming the reviews or details on an alternative for making sure states comply with federal requirements.
The change heightens the risk for Title 1 funding, which is about two-thirds of the nearly $27 billion in total Elementary and Secondary Education Act funding in 2025, the report said.  Under Title 1, states receive grants and use the money to support schools and districts with high concentrations of students from low-income families.
Education Department hands more states flexibility with federal dollars

States receiving Title I funding are required to develop statewide accountability systems, and all states had to report certain chronic absenteeism data. The Education Department defines chronic absenteeism as missing 10% or more of school days. Consolidated monitoring was fully implemented in 2019 but the Education Department suspended the process this year. 
“As a result of suspending consolidated monitoring, Education will not be able to systematically assess whether states are complying with ESEA requirements and following their approved state plans,” the report said.
On chronic absenteeism, half the states remain unmonitored for reporting requirements that apply to all states, the report said.
The Education Department directs states to report the number of chronically absent students over a school year, but to report total enrollment based on a single date. “Calculating rates using mismatched timeframes has resulted in unreliable and implausible chronic absenteeism rates (e.g., rates over 100 percent),” the GAO said.
That was especially true in low-performing schools and for those housing career and technical education programs, the report said.
“Absent quality chronic absenteeism data, this nationwide data source cannot be used to reliably track trends or evaluate the effectiveness of accountability efforts and interventions to address chronic absenteeism,” it concluded.
States try new measures to get chronically absent students back to class

Chronic absenteeism, which has been linked with declining academic performance, has remained elevated following the COVID-19 pandemic. At least one-quarter of K-12 students were estimated to be chronically absent in recent years, the report noted. 
But discrepancies in absentee rates, GAO found, were notable in low-performing schools where enrollment fluctuates more often and in shared-time schools, where students split their day between schools, often for career and technical education or other specialized programs.
More than 30% of shared-time schools had “implausible” chronic absenteeism rates, compared with under 2% of other schools. Among schools designated for Comprehensive Support and Improvement, a federal category for low-performing schools, nearly 13% had implausible rates over 100%, compared with about 2% of schools not in that category.
In Pennsylvania, GAO found 98% of shared-time schools there had implausible chronic absenteeism rates. By contrast, Delaware, Idaho, Maryland, Missouri, North Carolina and Rhode Island had no shared-time schools with implausible rates in GAO’s analysis.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas attorney general’s campaign amends finance report to address donation-limit controversy
description: Attorney General Kris Kobach revises campaign finance report to account for donations exceeding Kansas limits, but critics seek formal investigation.
text:
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach appears at a Sept. 14, 2026, rally by Vice President JD Vance at Webco Manufacturing in Olathe. Kobach's July finance report showed contributions from two donors that exceeded legal limits. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Attorney General Kris Kobach revised his July reelection campaign finance report after questions were raised about individual donations that appeared to violate the maximum contribution limit under Kansas law.
Requests for a formal inquiry by the Kansas Public Disclosure Commission, which is responsible for monitoring, investigating and regulating campaign finance statutes in Kansas, centered on the July report submitted by Kobach. The first point of contention was tied to two donations of $8,328 each on the same day in June by Steve Noller of Kansas. The second red flag was in regard to a pair of donations May 5 totaling $10,000 from Christopher Ruddy of Florida.
In 2025, the Legislature doubled the individual donation cap on candidates for statewide office to $4,000 for the primary and $4,000 for the general election. The manner in which Kobach originally documented donations by Noller and Ruddy exceeded those amounts.
“Kris Kobach’s own campaign filings appear to show that he either violated Kansas’ campaign finance laws numerous times this election cycle or he submitted inaccurate reports. He should be investigated either way,” said Tiffany Muller, president of End Citizens United.
End Citizens United is an organization dedicated to nullifying the 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision enabling corporations to spend unlimited amounts on campaigns.
In response to issues raised by Muller, Kobach’s campaign filed an amendment report in September covering the primary election cycle. It attributed portions of contributions initially credited to Noller and Ruddy to members of their respective families. Half of Noller’s donations were transferred to Virginia Noller of West Palm Beach, Florida. In addition, $2,000 of Ruddy’s donation was assigned to Sonja Ruddy, also of West Palm Beach, Florida.
Danedri Herbert, a spokesperson for Kobach and chair of the Kansas Republican Party, said the documents were amended in early September.
“The donations are from married couples,” Herbert said.
Muller’s complaint to the state Public Disclosure Commission also pointed to the Kobach campaign’s depiction of Noller paying donation processing fees of $656. Under Kansas law, the fees could be interpreted as contributions to Kobach in excess of the state cap.
A spokesperson for Chris Mann, the Democratic candidate for attorney general seeking to oust Kobach in November, said there was no excuse for shortcomings in Kobach’s campaign finance report.
“After running for nearly every major office in Kansas and currently serving as the state’s chief law enforcement officer, there is no excuse for not knowing or following the rules,” said Leah Rymer, a spokesperson for Mann. “Kris Kobach either doesn’t understand Kansas campaign finance laws or he is flouting the rules to improve his campaign’s financial standing.”
Before elected attorney general in 2022, Kobach served from 2011 to 2019 as Kansas secretary of state, a job making him the state’s top elections officer. He ran unsuccessfully for Kansas Senate in 2000, U.S. House in 2004, governor in 2018 and U.S. Senate in 2020.
Steve Noller is part of a prominent Kansas automobile dealership empire, while Christopher Ruddy is CEO of the cable news channel Newsmax.
In addition to the End Citizens United complaint about Kobach exceeding the aggregate donation cap, the Kansas Coalition for Common Sense said Kobach’s shortcomings in terms of campaign reporting should be considered in light of his previous role in fundraising controversy.
“Kris Kobach has a long history of ethics complaints and questionable dealings, including his work for a nonprofit whose founder pled guilty to wire fraud and was accused of money laundering. Another ethics complaint comes as no surprise,” said Ashley All, spokesperson for the coalition.
Muller, of End Citizens United, asked the state Public Disclosure Commission to investigate potential recordkeeping violations by Kobach that were reflected in his January and July reports. She said Kobach categorized contributions to his reelection campaign as donations for the primary election. The attorney general didn’t submit a last-minute contribution report, she said.
Muller said it was odd Kobach reported no in-kind contributions during the 19 months covered by finance reports associated with his reelection bid. Kobach didn’t note, for example, his campaign kickoff at Sedgwick County Republican Party headquarters that was promoted by the state party.
“Kobach’s filings are littered with apparent violations that raise serious red flags, and he owes Kansans a full accounting of what happened,” Muller said.
The predecessor of the Kansas Public Disclosure Commission in 2011 ordered Kobach to pay a $5,000 fine for inaccurate reporting of $75,000 in contributions and expenditures during his initial campaign for secretary of state in 2010.
Kobach was chairman of the Kansas Republican Party from 2007 to 2009. After leaving that position, a Federal Election Commission audit found the Kansas GOP had accepted unlawful contributions while under his leadership.
In 2022, the FEC said Kobach’s 2020 campaign for U.S. Senate accepted unlawful in-kind corporate support from We Build the Wall. Kobach, who worked as general counsel to the organization, failed to report his under-market rental of We Build the Wall’s 295,000-person donor list while striving to raise money for his U.S. Senate race.
The FEC ordered We Build the Wall and Kobach to pay a $30,000 civil fine. Four other leaders of We Build the Wall were found guilty of fraud by diverting donations for personal benefit.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ACLU-WV files lawsuit over West Virginia school aid formula
description: The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia on Friday filed a lawsuit with the state’s highest court in an attempt to require state lawmakers to “correct the school funding formula,” the organization said Friday.
text:
A child eats a free breakfast through the county’s summer feeding program at Elk Center Elementary in Charleston, West Virginia, on June 10, 2026. (Photo by Marcus Constantino for West Virginia Watch)The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia on Friday filed a lawsuit with the state’s highest court in an attempt to require state lawmakers to “correct the school funding formula,” the organization said Friday.  
The 52-page petition to the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals follows a notice of intent to sue that the ACLU sent state officials on Aug. 17, the news release said. 
“In West Virginia, each and every child is guaranteed the right to a thorough and efficient education, a promise enshrined in our Constitution since the State’s founding,” the petition says. “West Virginia made this promise concrete by defining what a thorough and efficient education requires, and what falls short. 
“Today, despite the passage of nearly half a century since this Court first recognized this right,  Lincoln County students are receiving a lower quality education than what their parents, and their grandparents, received before them,” it says. “The West Virginia Constitution does not, and should not, allow this profoundly important constitutional right to wither on the vine as the result of ongoing  financial neglect by the Respondents.”
The petition lists as respondents House of Delegates Speaker Roger Hanshaw, R-Clay; Senate President Randy Smith; Auditor Mark Hunt; Tax Commissioner Matthew Irby; Treasurer Larry Pack; the state Department of Education; the state Board of Education, the School Building Authority, State School Superintendent Michelle Blatt, as as well as Lincoln County school board officials and county officials.
It is filed on behalf of “M.D.,” a sixth grader in Lincoln County Schools, and Lakin Patten, the student’s parent.
The legal action asks the court to answer whether or not the educational conditions in Lincoln County, the county that receives the least amount of funding per pupil through the school aid formula, meet the constitutional obligation that the “Legislature shall provide, by general law, for a thorough and efficient system of free schools.” 
West Virginia has seen an accelerated wave of school closures in the last few years mostly due to the state’s declining population. During this past school year alone, 19 schools were proposed for closure. Since 2011, 139 West Virginia public schools have closed and 71% of those have been elementary schools. 
West Virginia uses a seven-step formula to determine how much state funding goes to county school systems based on factors including the number of students enrolled. 
While the state’s population is declining, the number of special education students is increasing, leading to tight budgets for many districts. Required special education costs, like providing one-on-one aides to help with feeding or toileting, have forced districts into millions of dollars of debt.
West Virginia schools are 2,685.92 school personnel positions over formula, according to the state education department, and the state has seen another year of widespread teacher and staff cuts. Counties will use local funds, if available, to avoid making job cuts. 
A recent $114,000 study from the RAND Corporation, paid for by the House of Delegates, suggested that the state give more money to special education services to improve school budgets. 
While lawmakers came into the 2026 legislative session with plans to revamp the formula, the session ended in March without any of those measures making it to the governor’s desk for consideration. 
Attorneys for the ACLU argue that, in every measure, the state’s schools fail to meet established measures of adequacy and that the failures are a result of persistent under funding. 
The state has closed 40 schools since 2017, the ACLU said in the complaint, and the difference in counties that close schools is funding. The state spends less on counties with high child poverty rates and counts contributions to the Teachers Retirement System debt as per-pupil funding, the organization says. 
The schools funding gap is widened by a rule that counts only 85 percent of each county’s school levy toward its local share of school funding formula costs, the organization said. 
According to the lawsuit, data from school assessments shows “a statewide, systematic failure to meet academic achievement benchmarks,” and the effects are even more pronounced in Lincoln County, where 71.43% of students were not proficient in mathematics during the 2024-2025 school year, compared to 62.01% statewide.
The lawsuit comes decades after the 1982 Recht decision found that state public schools were “woefully inadequate” and the funding system was unconstitutional because a child’s education depended on the property wealth of a county.   
“More than 40 years later, the same problems exist in schools across the state and particularly in Lincoln County,” ACLU-WV Legal Director Aubrey Sparks said in a news release. “In many respects, the school funding formula is yielding results that are even less fair, and raise more constitutional concerns, than the system previously declared unconstitutional.”
In the news release, ACLU-WV Director Eli Baumwell said the lawsuit could prove to be the “most important case” the organization has filed in Baumwell’s 10 years with the organization.  
“Access to a quality education is part of the bedrock of our democracy, and the decision by the Legislature to turn their back on their constitutional obligation to fund schools will have cascading effects on students, and on our communities, unless the Court intervenes,” he said in the release.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia receives $7.2 million grant to expand childcare in Southwest, Southside Virginia
description: Virginia has received a $7.2 million federal disaster-recovery grant from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to expand childcare in communities across Southwest and Southside Virginia, the governor’s office announced Friday. The award comes as Virginia continues to recover from Hurricane Helene, which caused catastrophic damage when it swept th[...]
text:
A supporter for early childhood and child care access wears a "gotta have child care" pin in Richmond on Jan. 21, 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Virginia has received a $7.2 million federal disaster-recovery grant from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to expand childcare in communities across Southwest and Southside Virginia, the governor’s office announced Friday.
The award comes as Virginia continues to recover from Hurricane Helene, which caused catastrophic damage when it swept through the state in 2024, with extreme rainfall washing out roads and bridges and destroying homes and businesses. Two Virginians were killed in the disaster. 
Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s office said the grant will increase childcare capacity and support workforce participation and economic development in Danville and in Pittsylvania, Tazewell and Washington counties. 
“Our future depends on our ability to support working families and prepare the next generation for success,” Spanberger said in a statement. “These investments will expand access to high-quality childcare in communities experiencing both workforce growth and childcare shortages — particularly in the aftermath of Hurricane Helene.” 
The funding, along with $10.5 million in other investments, will support three childcare projects: a new $8.3 million center in Danville and Pittsylvania County, that will use $2.7 million in federal funding; a $5.8 million center in Tazewell County, including $2.5 million from the grant; and a $615,000 expansion in Washington County. Another $1.2 million will support coordination and workforce development across the projects. 
EO Companies, the Virginia Department of Education’s designated regional early childhood partner for Ready Region Southwest, will implement the projects, which are expected to create more than 55 new jobs while expanding access to care for nearly 450 children.
EO’s core mission is to support education, workforce, and economic development initiatives that strengthen communities, state leaders said in the announcement.
“Strong childcare systems are essential to educational success, workforce participation, and economic prosperity,” said Virginia Secretary of Education Jeffery Smith. “This investment will help ensure more Virginia families have access to safe, affordable, and high-quality care while creating new opportunities for children to learn, grow, and thrive. We are proud to partner with EO Companies and local communities to advance this important work.”
Travis Staton, president and CEO of EO Companies, said that access to affordable, high-quality childcare remains one of the most pressing workforce and economic development challenges facing communities across Virginia. 
“This historic investment demonstrates what is possible when federal, state, local, philanthropic, and community partners come together around a common goal,” Staton said in a statement. “These projects will not only expand access to early childhood education and out-of-school programming, but they will also strengthen local economies, support working families, and help communities remain competitive in attracting and retaining talent.”
Approximately 65% of Virginia employers said their workers struggle to find open child care slots and more than 85% cited cost as a major burden in a survey earlier this year conducted by the Virginia Early Childhood Foundation, the Richmond Fed and the Virginia Chamber Foundation.



 Projects

City of Danville/Pittsylvania County Regional Childcare Center: $2.7 million grant to construct a new approximately 20,000-square-foot childcare facility serving the City of Danville and Pittsylvania County. The project represents an estimated $8.3 million investment, combining federal grant resources with additional investments from regional stakeholders and partners. The center is expected to create approximately 30 new jobs and will have licensed capacity to serve approximately 200 children.
Tazewell County Childcare Center: $2.5 million grant to construct a new approximately 10,000-square-foot childcare center in Tazewell County. The project represents a total investment of approximately $5.8 million and will create an estimated 25 new jobs. Upon completion, the center will have licensed capacity to serve approximately 148 children. Project partners and investors include EO, VDOE, Tazewell County, and the Thompson Charitable Foundation.
Washington County Expansion: $615,000 for the expansion of EO’s Regional Workforce and Child Development Hub in Washington County. The expansion will add new outdoor recreational space and interior classroom facilities to establish a comprehensive after-school and summer enrichment program serving children ages 5 to 12. The program will have licensed capacity to serve approximately 100 students, providing critical after-school care, summer programming, and workforce support services for working families throughout the region. 
Project Coordination and Workforce Development: $1.2 million will support project coordination and workforce development across the three childcare projects. Funding will help recruit, train, and prepare the workforce needed to staff the new and expanded childcare centers.
