name: Michigan Advance
title: Head Start opens a door for millions of young Michiganders. Don’t close it.
description: In 1969, when I was just four years old, my parents enrolled me in Head Start at Annunciation Catholic Church on Detroit’s East Side. The teachers there fed me lunch, cared for me, and sparked a love of learning that catapulted me into kindergarten and well beyond. And because that free, federally-funded program existed, my […]
text:
Preschool children line up to go outside at the Ralph Hawley Head Start Center in Emeryville, Calif., in December. The Trump administration has proposed major changes to the Head Start program. (Photo by Florence Middleton for CalMatters)In 1969, when I was just four years old, my parents enrolled me in Head Start at Annunciation Catholic Church on Detroit’s East Side. The teachers there fed me lunch, cared for me, and sparked a love of learning that catapulted me into kindergarten and well beyond. And because that free, federally-funded program existed, my mother and father could both go to work, knowing their youngest child was in good hands.
My time in Head Start left an immeasurable impact on my life. It fostered curiosity. It taught me valuable life skills. And it prepared me for so many of the challenges and opportunities that lay ahead. Now, I’m proud to be a military veteran and leader of a nationally recognized research center.
I wouldn’t have had access to this formative education without Head Start. And I’m far from alone. In Michigan, Head Start serves more than 26,000 children every year at nearly 600 program sites. The state receives more than $416 million in federal investments that fund local jobs and comprehensive services — such as home visits and disability accommodations — in communities across the state, from Detroit to the Upper Peninsula.
But now, the White House is aiming to dismantle this marquee anti-poverty program. The Administration claims it is working to return the program “back to its roots” by “removing” bureaucracy and saving the taxpayer a couple of bucks, all in the name of purportedly opening “Head Start to hundreds of thousands more children.”
If this sounds too good to be true, you are correct.
What the White House is proposing is nothing short of a wolf in sheep’s clothing, a proposal that would remove mandates that regulate staff-to-child ratios, take away support from children who are not English speakers, and eliminate certain wage and benefit requirements for Head Start staff. In short, the White House has no interest in “improving” Head Start. Instead, it seeks to dilute its impact through funding cuts or by abandoning its core functions. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That’s a colossal mistake. For over 60 years, Head Start has nurtured young learners and supported parents and caregivers in urban, suburban, and rural communities. Through our research at the Center for the Study of Social Policy, we’ve spoken to parents who have highlighted how important Head Start is to their families, as it not only teaches children their ABCs but also builds their socio-emotional skills to better prepare them for kindergarten – and life.
Here’s what parents told our researchers: they value how Head Start supports children’s developmental needs through developmental screenings and inclusive learning services, which is particularly critical in areas where other child care programs often turn children with disabilities away. One mother, whose son had a speech delay, told us “they had all the services that [were] needed” and that “I wish he would’ve started earlier.” Parents also appreciate the small class sizes, nutritious meals, home visits, and other core features that make Head Start so important.
Meanwhile, thousands of Michiganders—teachers, home visitors, and child care providers—work at Head Start locations across the state. Local businesses benefit from increased food purchases, and schools benefit when young minds are better prepared to start kindergarten. Head Start also connects parents to community resources and brings people together, helping build community connections.
Experts and Michigan leaders have had plenty to say about the White House’s approach to Head Start in recent days. Ruth Friedman, one of the authors of the bipartisan 2007 Head Start reauthorization, warns that deregulating Head Start would gut the program’s “science-backed standards” and keep the youngest learners from obtaining the instruction they need to “arrive at kindergarten ready to succeed.”
MaDonna Princer, executive director of Kent County Head Start, recently told the Free Press that she worries the White House is “spinning” its intentions without putting “more actual dollars into programs’ hands.” And, speaking to WLNS, Tricia Grifka, a Michigan Head Start Association board member, said any attempt to tackle Head Start bureaucracy should not come at the expense of “children’s safety and well-being and learning.”
There is nothing inherently wrong with examining government regulations, including those of Head Start. But what is being proposed as an opportunity to “expand” Head Start would lead many families already served by the program, especially those in rural areas, to scramble to find alternative childcare, bear additional costs, and ultimately lose or reduce work in an already challenging economy.
We should strive to serve more children, and those children deserve to benefit from the best of Head Start, not a program asked to do more with less.
There is no doubt that there are leaders across the country who share that connection to Head Start with me. More importantly, countless future leaders are sitting in a Head Start classroom right now, or could be in one in the future. I will be fighting for Head Start for them. I hope you’ll join me.
Whether you are a parent, a community member who cares about early-childhood education, or a business owner who partners with Head Start to serve kids in your community, you have until October 6, 2026, to submit comments to the Federal Register and protect one of the most important investments we make for young children, the Head Start program.

name: VTDigger
title: Latest poll shows Gov. Phil Scott and Amanda Janoo in tightest race in a decade
description:
Scott and Janoo in “statistical tie” in the state’s gubernatorial race. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Latest poll shows Gov. Phil Scott and Amanda Janoo in tightest race in a decade.
text:
Democratic nominee for governor Amanda Janoo, left, and Republican Gov. Phil Scott. Photos by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
A Vermont election poll on the upcoming governor’s race suggests it might be the closest in a decade.
The most recent University of New Hampshire Green Mountain State Poll released this week reported that 49% of Vermonters support Amanda Janoo in the November election, while 43% support incumbent Gov. Phil Scott.
The 6% margin led UNH pollsters to declare the Governor’s race a “statistical tie.” In a July poll released by the same group, Scott led Janoo by 15% meaning the recent numbers account for a 21-point swing.
The poll also reported former Democratic Lieutenant Governor Molly Gray leading Republican incumbent John Rodgers 54% to 35% in the lieutenant governor race. U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., comfortably leads the state’s one congressional race with a 35% margin against Republican nominee Gerald Mallo. 
Scott’s approval rating, according to the poll, has fallen 5% since July, sitting at 47%. In the October 2025 Green Mountain State Poll, the incumbent’s approval rating was 61% with a majority of Vermonters supporting a reelection bid. 
In a press release Thursday, Scott’s campaign manager Dustin Degree criticized UNH’s polling methods, specifically its partisan split. Some 60% of those surveyed self-identified as Democrats, 31% as Republicans and 9% as Independent.
Scott has historically held significant bipartisan support, but after a series of vetos on progressive bills, some Vermonters have said they’re looking for change.
Degree cited UNH’s 2024 poll, which predicted a 28% margin of victory for Scott, who went on to win reelection by more than 50%. He called Thursday’s poll “statistical malpractice.”
“The good news is, besides exciting headlines and political posturing, outlier polls don’t matter,” the press release reads. “Election Day does.”
Janoo’s grassroots campaign was successful in the primary election. She defeated Aly Richards by just over 3%. Janoo, an economist and first-time political candidate, described her democratic primary election victory as a “long-shot.”  In a press release, Janoo’s team wrote that the poll’s results reflected what they had heard “on the ground every day.”
“Vermonters are tired of a status quo that’s failing us,” the press release said. “We’re tired of managed decline for our state. We’re looking for hope and leadership that believes in Vermont. Together, we can not only win this election, but build a better future.”
Thursday’s poll teed up November’s general election, based on 882 survey responses collected last week. The data were weighted based on demographic information from the U.S. Census and 2024 election results, according to the survey. 
This story will be updated.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: After state warning, NJ panel approves 34% health premium hike for teachers
description: The vote to hike teachers’ health benefit rates came after a warning from state officials that benefits may be halted in the new year without an agreement.
text:
State officials last week told school districts they would be unable to offer health benefits to schools come January unless new rates were approved. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The School Employees Health Benefits Commission approved stark rate increases for public health plans serving school workers on Friday after deadlocking on rate hikes for nearly two months.
The panel’s 4-2 vote to increase premiums by as much as 34% for active workers in 2027 forestalls, at least for now, the collapse of a plan that insures hundreds of thousands of school employees, but commissioners who oversee the program warned its future would remain in question absent sweeping changes.
Michael Salerno, an official with statewide teachers union the New Jersey Education Association, was among those who sounded the alarm.
“Either way we vote, the way the system is right now, we’re killing the SEHBP,” Salerno said.
The commission’s vote comes after state officials last week told school districts they would be unable to offer health benefits to schools come January unless rates were approved, said Commissioner Daniel Holub.
Though the panel approved smaller rate hikes for retired school workers in late July, its membership, which is equally split between union and management due to an unfilled vacancy, has repeatedly deadlocked in recent meetings when considering much larger increases for active workers.
Holub, who represents the teachers union and who was the meeting’s interim chair, cautioned that high premiums and state officials’ warning about a potential suspension of health benefits would push more districts out of the plan, worsening its health and prompting a mid-year rate increase.
“It’s my belief that these rate increases point to larger systemic issues that will only worsen in the next plan year. It’s irresponsible for us as a commission to move forward with these rates knowing it will lead to further crises in the future,” he said. “You have to address the systemic issues that are driving this.”
Treasury officials have said New Jersey’s public worker health plans for school and local government workers are in a death spiral after years of steep premium increases that have thinned the plans’ subscriber pool.
Each successive increase prompted more units to depart the public plan for cheaper options in the private market, leaving the state program with a progressively older, sicker, and more expensive risk pool that caused more rate hikes and, in turn, more departures.
But at the same time, officials’ ability to pull many of the levers that could reduce costs is barred until 2028 as a matter of law. The prohibition on plan design changes bars alterations to copay or coinsurance or the introduction of high-deductible plans like those officials have turned to in an attempt to shore up local government workers’ plan.
“I don’t think anybody is happy with the rates, but we’re sitting here right now,” said Danielle Schimmel, who chairs the State Health Benefits Commission and who sat in Friday as the Treasurer’s representative.
She added, “The rates are what they are, and we need rates to operate a plan to be able to have enrollment, to be able to have members.”
The panel’s union members have pushed non-design changes — like changes to plan administration or procurement — as a method to lower costs, but those proposals have not gained much momentum, and legislators who could attempt their own rescue have so far moved languorously to shore up the plans.
Schimmel said state officials have indicated an openness to discuss some of those changes to the commission’s union members, but it’s unclear when such changes might materialize.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Nessel issues guidance to law enforcement on ability to enforce tribal court-issued PPOs
description: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel issued new guidance to law enforcement officers on how to enforce personal protection orders, including those issued by Michigan’s tribal governments and courts.  Those personal protection orders, or PPOs, are categorized in Michigan law as “foreign protection orders,” which are defined as “an injunction or other order i[...]
text:
The office of Attorney General Dana Nessel in the G. Mennen Williams Building in Lansing, Mich., on May 15, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel issued new guidance to law enforcement officers on how to enforce personal protection orders, including those issued by Michigan’s tribal governments and courts. 
Those personal protection orders, or PPOs, are categorized in Michigan law as “foreign protection orders,” which are defined as “an injunction or other order issued by a court of another state, Indian tribe, or United States territory for the purpose of preventing a person’s violent or threatening acts against, harassment of, contact with, communication with, or physical proximity to another person.” Foreign protection orders, including those from tribal courts, are subject to the same enforcement procedures as a protection order issued in the state of Michigan. 
Nessel’s letter also noted that “Indian tribal courts may issue and enforce civil protection orders against any person—Indian or non-Indian, tribal member or non-tribal member—in matters arising in the Indian country of an Indian tribe.”
Nessel highlighted the disproportionate rates of violence experienced by Indigenous people — and questions that persisted among law enforcement agencies about their ability to enforce orders issued by tribal courts — as among her reasons for issuing the letter clarifying the responsibilities of Michigan police officers. 
“A personal protection order may be a person’s only surety of their safety,” she said in a press release. “We want to ensure our law enforcement officers are prepared and informed on handling all valid PPOs, and for Michigan residents everywhere to know their protective orders can be faithfully upheld by public safety officers in any jurisdiction. With this letter and guidance to agencies across the State, we hope to raise awareness of the various venues that can grant and enforce PPOs and assure full enforcement of orders issued by our state courts as well as the tribal courts.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Research shows that a significant majority, nearly 85%, of Indigenous women experience violence in their lifetime, and Indigenous men experience violence at only slightly lower rates, still above 80%. Additionally, murder is the third-leading cause of death among American Indian and Alaska Native Women on Tribal lands.
The new guidance was sent as the Michigan House of Representatives passed two bills that would make personal protection orders free for survivors of domestic abuse. Currently in Michigan, while actually filing a personal protection order in court generally does not have a fee, the cost to have that order served can include a service fee plus mileage traveled, which can easily cost almost $100.
Law enforcement officers are required to serve a personal protection order if they are responding to a call alleging a violation of a PPO, if the individual who is the subject of the PPO has not been served with the order prior to that time. 
PPOs become effective and immediately enforceable anywhere in this state after being signed by a judge, and can be enforced by any law enforcement agency that has a copy of the order or has verified its existence on the state’s Law Enforcement Information Network. 
House Bills 5120 and 5121 passed on a bipartisan basis through the chamber on Tuesday, and two bills with a similar purpose, Senate Bills 611 and 612, passed the Senate in December 2025, though they remain in committee in the House. The contents of the two sets of bills must now be reconciled by the two chambers before they can be sent to Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s desk.

title: Venezuelan men shipped to brutal prison under Alien Enemies Act ask court for due process
text: WASHINGTON — An appeals panel Friday seemed inclined to agree that more than 100 Venezuelan men the Trump administration sent to a brutal prison in El Salvador are entitled to due process hearings to challenge their removal, which was made under an archaic 18th-century wartime law. Arguing on behalf of the class of men who were removed under the Alien Enemies Act of 1798, Lee Gelernt of the American Civil Liberties Union told the three-judge panel that the men, who were accused of being suspected members of the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang, were entitled to hearings to challenge those accusations. But instead, Gelernt said, the men were denied their due process rights and spent four months in a brutal Salvadoran prison. The men were eventually returned to Venezuela in a prisoner swap exchange, but many who had pending asylum cases want to challenge their removal under the Alien Enemies Act and continue their immigration proceedings.He said the Trump administration is asking for the ability to “essentially whisk people away to a foreign prison, give them no opportunity to contest the removal, even whether they're part of this gang that this proclamation applies to… and then say, ‘Because we got them out of the country into a foreign prison, that's the end of the matter.’” DOJ argues against due processThe Trump administration argued before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that the Venezuelan men are not entitled to due process hearings.Department of Justice attorney Tiberius Davis said that the United States had no custody over the 137 Venezuelan men removed to the Salvadoran mega-prison known as CECOT, and therefore the immigrants are not entitled to hearings in the U.S. He added that it would be impractical for the Trump administration to conduct more than 100 online hearings abroad. “It's a real problem with foreign sovereignty to hold hearings, and take evidentiary hearings, in foreign countries, even at our own embassies,” Davis said. “That can be a real problem. So we would have to engage in diplomacy and foreign affairs in order to even do that much.”March 2025 originsThe case began when President Donald Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act in March 2025 to rapidly deport Venezuelan immigrants. U.S. District Judge James Boasberg issued the Trump administration an order to return several deportation planes to the U.S., but instead they landed at CECOT. The U.S. paid El Salvador up to $6 million to detain the men.On Monday, there is a separate hearing where Boasberg will hear arguments as to whether several Trump officials should be held in contempt for violating his order by not returning the planes carrying men removed under the Alien Enemies Act, including possible criminal contempt charges against Attorney General Todd Blanche and an appellate judge, Emil Bove. Judge expresses doubtCircuit Judge Harry T. Edwards seemed skeptical of the Trump administration’s arguments that the U.S. had no custody over the men while at CECOT. Edwards was appointed by former President Jimmy Carter. “It seems pretty clear … that the U.S. was fully engaged and kept itself in a position of control throughout,” Edwards said.Davis disagreed and said that diplomacy was involved and pointed to how Secretary of State Marco Rubio had to engage with El Salvador's president to bring back one of the men sent to CECOT, Salvadoran national Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was unlawfully removed to his home country.“I think the district court sort of swept away those foreign affairs concerns,” Davis said.  Gelernt said it was harder to facilitate the return of Abrego Garcia because he was a citizen of El Salvador. “He's not part of our class. El Salvador clearly had an interest in their own nationals,” Gelernt said. “They have no interest in these Venezuelans, other than collecting a paycheck.”

name: VTDigger
title: Where do elections fit in the AI apocalypse?
description:
An AI agent doesn't need to want anything to threaten an election — it just needs a goal, some autonomy and the will to keep trying until it succeeds.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Where do elections fit in the AI apocalypse?.
text:
John Odum is the Montpelier city clerk and a certified ethical hacker.
I know the implications of the supposedly coming “AI apocalypse” and how it relates to elections are on people’s minds. I’ve heard it. So let’s talk about it.
Most of us have probably heard about the Hugging Face incident. During an OpenAI cybersecurity evaluation, AI agents circumvented controls designed to contain them because they were basically struggling with their homework — a cybersecurity challenge assigned to them. They took aim at the Hugging Face platform. Relentlessly seeking success and despite controls, they reached the open internet and penetrated Hugging Face’s systems. Since then, six more instances of its models behaving deceptively or working around safeguards have been discovered. 
This incident is important because the AI agents’ objective was mundane: pass a test. When solving the assigned challenge became difficult, they didn’t accept failure. The agents just inferred where the answers might be and pursued them. No human directed this attack — the agents improvised it to complete their task.
So could something like this happen to voting systems?
The first question we have to ask about the dreaded AI apocalypse we’re all being warned about is “Why?” Why would a self-directing AI mess with an election? Probably not because it cared about the election for its own sake. It would do so because a particular outcome helped it achieve another objective — perhaps one assigned by a human, or maybe one it arrived at while pursuing a broader goal. The election would not be the objective, but a means to an end.
Approaching this as a hacker rather than an AI professional, consider how things work at present. Election-management systems, databases and other pieces of networked infrastructure could be targets, and AI doesn’t have to become the full-on existential threat of an artificial sentience crafting its own agenda. Acting on somebody else’s agenda is apocalyptic enough when you’re talking about a technological threat that refuses to lose.
Project even further forward to the time of quantum computers capable of breaking many of today’s encryption systems, and the prospect becomes scarier still. 
Nobody assigned a social or political agenda, or machine consciousness, to make the Hugging Face incident happen. In the scenario everyone is concerned about, an AI could weaponize itself against free and fair elections. You need only an agent with a political objective, enough autonomy and access to pursue it, a goal — assigned or self-generated — that it keeps pursuing until it succeeds and the ability to improvise.
An empowered AI agent could pursue an assigned outcome across the election ecosystem. That means voter-registration databases, electronic pollbooks, election-night reporting, candidate-filing systems, ballot-tracking portals, municipal email, vendor-support accounts, state networks, public-information channels and election-management systems. Voting equipment can be isolated, but by necessity, elections as an administrative process are not.

READ MORE

Simple, high-profile attacks could include erasing datasets and crashing election-management systems. Those would be high-profile and obvious, designed to crush confidence in the system — again, should doing so further its goals. This effect could lead to public policy that restricts participation in the name of further securing the overall system: a political cycle that could snowball.
But what about changing a result?
That’s much, much trickier. You can theoretically alter what would have been the actual results by targeting different groups for voter suppression the way robocalls do now. In January 2024, two days before the New Hampshire presidential primary, thousands of likely Democratic voters received robocalls using an AI-generated clone of Joe Biden’s voice. The fake Biden told them essentially to stay home. An independent agent could do more of this, finding its approaches or targets for phone calls, emails or other media itself.
An autonomous AI agent might learn that you don’t beat the audit; you attack what the audit assumes are trustworthy. Perhaps it would try to mess with which ballots exist, prevent legitimate votes from becoming paper ballots in the first place, corrupt the records telling auditors where ballots are or interfere with the audit process itself.
The underlying idea would be to exploit what the audit is not designed to detect. 
A flaw in networked systems, something AI is proving to be very skilled at finding, might be weaponized. Consider Georgia’s system, where the ordering of electronic ballot records potentially exposed how individual voters cast their ballots. One researcher reports using current AI tools to reconstruct the order of 98.9% of the in-person ballots cast in a Georgia election. 
Turning these things into an outcome-changing attack would be very difficult even in the AI apocalypse everyone is imagining. If we’re doing what we should, results should continue to be recoverable in a worst-case scenario, even though it might take a little while. That doesn’t mean we should relax, just that we should avoid any dumb mistakes and keep a constant eye on making systems better. Relaxing will never be an option.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Where do elections fit in the AI apocalypse?.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Candidates for Hinds district attorney spar over corruption, dysfunction and jail crowding
description: Candidates for the Hinds County District Attorney special election listen to a moderator's question at a forum held by the Hinds County Democratic Executive Committee on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in a church auditorium in Raymond.
text:
RAYMOND – Five candidates vying to become Hinds County district attorney pondered questions about corruption, managing public money, jail crowding and persistent case backlogs at their first forum ahead of a Nov. 3 special election. 
One question raised at Thursday’s forum summed up the enormous tasks that lie ahead to restore trust in the office after former DA Jody Owens pleaded guilty to a federal conspiracy charge earlier this summer and resigned. 
Asked to describe a situation in which they had to navigate “significant operational challenges,” each candidate pledged to run an office free of mismanagement and dysfunction and to rid the county’s justice system of problems that have persisted for decades. 
Some candidates trumpeted their experience working in the Hinds DA’s office, while others took pains to emphasize their outsider status.
“I haven’t really had an opportunity to be in dysfunctional organizations,” said Marvin Sanders, a defense attorney who worked under former DA Eleanor Faye Peterson in the early 2000s. “I avoided those situations.”
In response to a later question, Sanders assured the audience he would not commit crimes as district attorney.
“You don’t have to worry about me doing something like that, ‘cause I like my freedom,” Sanders said.
As a member of the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office in 2016, he took part in the failed prosecution of former Hinds DA Robert Schuler Smith, who was accused of conspiring to hinder a criminal prosecution.
Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi Today
Owens faces up to five years in prison after pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit bribery. He awaits sentencing in November. A son of a prominent family from Terry in southern Hinds County, Owens had been caught up in a wide-ranging FBI probe that also ensnared former Jackson Mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba and City Council Member Aaron Banks, who also await sentencing.
The nearly two-hour forum hosted by the Hinds County Democratic Executive Committee in a church auditorium provided sparse details about how each candidate would handle the nonpartisan post, if elected.
Gwen Agho, a current Hinds prosecutor, said the office was in disarray when she joined in 2016. In one example, Agho said the office wasn’t tracking whether prosecutors reached out to victims, so she created her own spreadsheet to hold herself accountable. 
Agho touted this practice as contributing to the happiness of victims whose cases she’s prosecuted. She also described problems she has witnessed in the county’s grand jury process and claimed the office lacks a functioning victim’s advocate. 
“There can be a streak of laziness in some people,” she said. 
Some of the candidates floated solutions that past DAs have tried.
Agho and Greta Mack Harris, an attorney practicing in Madison and Rankin counties, advocated for returning to a caseload management system known as vertical prosecutions, which requires one prosecutor to oversee a case across each stage of the process, from grand jury to trial and sentencing. 
Noting the persistent crowding at the Hinds County Detention Center, Mack Harris, a former Hinds assistant district attorney, said she wanted to create panels that would move cases more swiftly. She did not elaborate on how the panels would work. 
“There is absolutely no excuse for the level of pretrial detainees in Raymond,” she said, referring to the jail, which is currently over capacity. “There’s absolutely no excuse for that grand jury system to be as complicated and disorganized as Mrs. Agho alluded to.” 
Less alarmed was Wendy Wilson White, a Hinds prosecutor who currently handles probable cause hearings for defendants who aren’t indicted. She pushed back against suggestions from other candidates that the DA’s office was indicting defendants without receiving investigative files from local law enforcement. She blamed the current backlog on multiple actors within the justice system, such as law enforcement. 
“The DA’s office has no real control over the speed of investigations,” she said. 
Multiple candidates promised to establish stronger accounting over the office’s self-generated funds, which are subject to patchwork accountability from other government agencies.
Mack Harris, an attorney who previously ran unsuccessfully for Hinds County youth court judge, said she would hire an independent auditor to review the audit requested by interim DA Brad McCullouch, who was appointed by Gov. Tate Reeves to replace Owens. State law bars McCullouch from the special election ballot because he is not a Hinds County resident. 
A fifth candidate, Darla Palmer, left the forum after opening remarks, saying she was double-booked. 
“Nobody is talking about violent crime,” Palmer said before departing. She is running for the post for a third time after losing to Owens in 2019 and 2023. 
Voters and supporters listen to candidates for the Hinds County District Attorney special election discuss the issues during a forum held Sept. 24, 2026, in a church auditorium in Raymond. Credit: Molly Minta/Mississippi Today
The forum, attended by a few dozen potential voters, left some like Doug Williams dissatisfied. The self-employed Jackson resident who works in real estate asked the candidates what they would do to improve the reputation of the Hinds DA’s office, which he contended does not garner the same respect as prosecutorial operations in Rankin and Madison counties.
Mack Harris said that Hinds needs to have higher standards. Sanders said such comparisons are unfair because Hinds County prosecutors handle more criminal cases than neighboring counties. Agho said she would put more pressure on prosecutors to be productive. Wilson White spoke about the no-snitch culture in Jackson in which witnesses do not want to cooperate with prosecutors. 
“It’s going to take all of us to take a stand and fish out these criminals and let them know that we mean business,” she said. 
Williams, 54, said he plans to attend another forum to ask more questions. This Sunday, local political organizations including Women for Progress of MS and the League of Women Voters will host a forum at the Mississippi Public Broadcasting Auditorium at 5 p.m.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Sierra Club report: Clean energy efforts fail to make the grade in Mississippi
description: The Sunflower Solar Station in Ruleville, Miss., which sells power to Entergy.
text:
In a new report, Sierra Club takes aim at electric utilities across the United States for their slow transition to clean energy sources. The analysis included less than flattering grades for the state’s two investor-owned power companies, Entergy Mississippi and Mississippi Power.
The marks — an “F” for Entergy and a “C” for Mississippi Power — came in the latest edition of the national environmental advocacy nonprofit’s “The Dirty Truth Report,” released Wednesday.
The report graded the country’s utilities using three criteria: the retiring of coal plants by 2030, not adding new gas-powered production and building clean energy sources to replace fossil fuel loads by 2035. For the second year in a row, the nonprofit gave the country’s utilities as a whole an “F.” 
“As artificial intelligence data centers drive demand for energy, utility companies are rushing to expensive and dangerous fossil fuels, leading to soaring electricity prices and worsening air pollution,” said Sierra Club Chief Program Officer Holly Bender. 
The nonprofit highlighted the large amount of planned new gas generation this year, which was more than in any of the previous five years.  
The report gave Entergy a failing grade largely because it plans to add nearly 3,500 megawatts of gas-powered energy to its system by 2035. The utility is growing its power capacity, in part, to meet the needs of Amazon data centers across central Mississippi. It’s unclear, though, how much those plans were fueled by Amazon’s arrival because of limited oversight over the companies’ agreement. 

Sierra Club gave the utility a poor grade despite its plans to retire all of its coal units by 2030 and Entergy’s recent investments in renewable sources, which includes a 100-megawatt solar power plant that came online in 2022.
The utility is building three new, 754-megawatt gas plants: one in Greenville, set to be ready in 2028, which will replace an existing plant and is designed to use hydrogen in the future; another plant in Ridgeland, expected to be in service in 2029; and one in Vicksburg, which will open in 2028.
Entergy said in a response to the Sierra Club report that it aims to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. 
“We continue to invest in renewable power and storage projects, with approximately 3 gigawatts either already approved or pending regulatory review,” the company said Thursday in a statement to Mississippi Today. “Driven by strong economic growth and rising customer demand, we are developing new baseload generation capacity to power these exciting opportunities while continuing to make meaningful progress toward a net‑zero future. Changes to available tax credits for carbon‑free resources are also shaping how we optimize our clean energy investments.”
Mississippi Power, which received an “F” in last year’s edition, improved to a “C” this year. It plans to retire all of its coal power units by 2030 and is planning for 548 megawatts of new gas production by 2035.
The utility received the best grade of any subsidiary of Southern Company. The report panned the energy giant for extending the lives of its coal units. Last year, Mississippi Power received approval from the state to push back the retirement of its coal units at Plant Victor J. Daniel in Jackson County. But the utility later proposed to convert the units to gas in 2029, the Sierra Club report said.   
The report, though, gave the company a “0%” in its plans to replace fossil fuel generation and load growth with clean energy. The company’s power supply has included roughly 160 megawatts of solar power for nearly the last decade. 

In a Thursday statement, Mississippi Power pointed to those projects as well as its low rates, 22% below the national average. 
“The company continues to reliably meet our customers’ ever-evolving energy needs and is in a strong position to ensure adequate capacity and the ability to serve our customers as the state experiences robust economic growth,” the utility said. 
The company also mentioned the potential benefits from a solar power battery storage project in Walnut Grove, which it called “one of the nation’s most advanced green microgrids.”
“Lessons learned from the project are helping inform how renewable energy and battery storage may be integrated into our system in the future,” Mississippi Power said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Most intriguing RI race to watch? New UNH poll shows LG Matos in tight race with Loughlin
description: One of the least powerful state offices could end up being the headline of Rhode Island’s general election: Democrat Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos is neck-and-neck with her Republican challenger, John Loughlin, according to a University of New Hampshire poll published Thursday. The poll of 598 likely general election voters, conducted online from Sept. 17 to […]
text:
Rhode Island Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos, left, makes a point during the taping of a televised debate with her Republican challenger John Loughlin, right, on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, at WPRI 12 in East Providence. The debate airs on Fox Providence Friday at 6:30 p.m. and Sunday at 10 a.m. (Photo by James Bartone/WPRI 12)One of the least powerful state offices could end up being the headline of Rhode Island’s general election: Democrat Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos is neck-and-neck with her Republican challenger, John Loughlin, according to a University of New Hampshire poll published Thursday.
The poll of 598 likely general election voters, conducted online from Sept. 17 to 21, shows 48% support for Matos compared with 44% for Loughlin — essentially a statistical tie given the 4% margin of error for the survey. Another 7% of voters were undecided.
The razor-thin margin separating the two contrasts with the gubernatorial race. Democratic nominee Helena Buonanno Foulkes held a commanding lead with 44% support from likely voters, the survey said. Independent Ken Block trailed Foulkes by 19 points, with GOP nominee Aaron Guckian coming in third with 17% support. Ten percent of voters were still undecided, with the remainder split between independents C.D. Reynolds, Jay Gotra or “another candidate,” the poll said.
Foulkes, who trounced Gov. Dan McKee in the September primary, pointed to the latest survey results — the first conducted since she secured the party nomination — as evidence that voters want change.
“Helena is running to be a governor who works every day to lower costs, build homes and apartments people can afford, grow our economy, strengthen our public schools, and create a healthcare system that works for people,” Angelika Pellegrino, a campaign spokesperson, said in a statement. “Over the next 39 days, Helena will continue to campaign in communities all across the Ocean State to earn the support of every Rhode Islander.”
But Block and Guckian weren’t backing down. Block noted that the poll shows nearly 4 in 10 voters viewed Foulkes unfavorably, compared to the 1 in 4 who had a favorable opinion of her. Block’s favorability rating was only slightly higher, at 29%, but with a much smaller share who viewed him unfavorability, 17%. 
“I’m the only candidate in this race with a positive favorability rating, and I’m gaining momentum,” Block said in an email. “This poll demonstrates that a majority of Rhode Islanders don’t want Helena Foulkes as their next governor. My mission is to unify that majority, and as an independent, I’m the only candidate who can.” 
But nearly one in three voters said they didn’t know or weren’t sure what to think of Block, suggesting he lacked name recognition. Just 9% of survey respondents were unsure what to think of Foulkes. 
An even larger share of respondents, nearly 4 in 10, didn’t know or were unsure what to think of Guckian. But Guckian maintained that the poll was the problem, noting that pre-primary polls by UNH showed him trailing his primary rival, Elaine Pelino, by 20 points. Guckian defeated Pelino by 259 votes.
“I know we have a lot of work ahead of us, but I’ve been underestimated before,” Guckian said in a statement. “I’m going to keep doing what I’ve been doing from the beginning, showing up listening to Rhode Islanders, and talking about how we make this state more affordable and make government work better for the people it serves.”
All three main gubernatorial contenders have emphasized affordability, economic development and government efficiency in their campaigns, with Block and Guckian each releasing similar plans to cut “unnecessary” taxes and fees. Foulkes has honed in on the housing crisis, with a promise to build 20,000 homes with funding from the millionaire’s tax and enact a tenant’s bill of rights.
While politically moderate, Foulkes drew the most support from socialist, progressive and liberal voters in the survey, as well as younger voters. Block, who has run for governor twice before, once as a moderate and then as a Republican, was backed by ideological moderates and libertarians, voters 65 and older, and people who voted for Trump in the 2024 election. Guckian, who describes himself as a “compassionate conservative,” was most popular among conservative voters. He was the only candidate whose support skewed heavily toward voters with a high school-level education or less.
Democratic Lieutenant Governor Sabina Matos and her Republican challenger, John Loughlin, were tied among voters overall, with Loughlin leading among independents. (Courtesy of University of New Hampshire Survey Center)
Independents favor Loughlin 
In the lieutenant governor’s race, Matos had strong support from registered Democrats and younger voters. But Loughlin, a former state representative, captured the bulk of the independent voters’ support, along with conservative voters and those 65 and older, according to the survey.
Matos, who beat back four primary challengers, bested Loughlin among respondents from every geographic area of the state except for Kent County and Blackstone Valley — both more conservative areas. She also had higher support in every education level except for voters with a technical school background or “some college” — but no degree.
Mark Gray, Matos’ campaign manager, remained confident.
“The real poll is the one that happens on Election Day,” Gray said in a statement Friday. “At a time when Trump and the Republican party’s agenda has resulted in a skyrocketing cost of living, the Matos campaign is looking forward to comparing his dangerous record with the Lieutenant Governor’s work to lower food costs and create more affordable housing.”
Loughlin acknowledged a request for comment but did not provide a response to the survey, citing preparations for his debate against Matos. The two will face off for the first time in a televised debate hosted by WPRI-TV 12 and airing on Fox Providence tonight at 6:30, and already available online.
The survey also took the temperature in the U.S. Senate race, where more than half of likely voters backed incumbent Democrat Jack Reed in his reelection bid. Republican Ray McKay had support from 1 in 3 likely voters, while 5% backed independent Michael Bahry. 
Meanwhile, McKee’s approval rating sank even lower following his defeat in the primary. More than 8 in 10 survey respondents disapprove of the governor’s handling of the job, including two-thirds of registered Democrats. His net favorability rating of minus 68 marks a new low, and continues his dubious distinction as the least popular governor of any New England state. 
McKee’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Gov. Dan McKee’s approval rating dipped to its lowest point following his defeat in the Sept. 9 primary. (Courtesy of University of New Hampshire Survey Center)
The survey did not ask voters to link their opinions about McKee to the Washington Bridge, though past polls showed a direct connection between the governor’s poor approval ratings and his handling of the closure and rebuild of the westbound highway.
More than 6 in 10 voters remained doubtful that the replacement bridge will open by Nov. 3, 2028, despite repeated assurances from McKee’s administration that the project is on-time, or even ahead of schedule. 
Half of survey respondents said they take detours rather than contend with traffic on the bridge since its closure, with those still using the highway across the Seekonk River reporting their trips take longer. Most said their trips take an extra 10 to 29 minutes. Nearly 1 in 5 respondents said it took them 30 to 44 extra minutes.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont AG takes anti-ICE protest cases to trial after Chittenden County prosecutor declines
description:
The move reverses months of Chittenden County State's Attorney declining to prosecute numerous cases.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont AG takes anti-ICE protest cases to trial after Chittenden County prosecutor declines.
text:
Protesters block the exterior entrance to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center in Williston on Friday, July 24, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
In Chittenden County, State’s Attorney Sarah George has repeatedly declined to prosecute demonstrators arrested while protesting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, arguing that pursuing the cases did not serve justice.
This week, matters were taken out of George’s hands.
Rather than bringing to George’s office criminal cases against 13 protesters cited in July for trespassing at ICE’s National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center in Williston, state police routed the citations directly to Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark’s office. Twelve protesters charged with trespassing in adult criminal court were arraigned Thursday.
Clark’s office also initially charged an 18-year-old protester in criminal court even though state law requires 18-year-olds to be processed through family court for most offenses. Vermont’s Raise the Age law dictates that many minor crimes committed by someone under the age of 19 are charged in juvenile court. The attorney general’s office eventually changed course to charge the person as a juvenile.
 The 12 defendants being prosecuted in criminal court this week pleaded not guilty.
Sarah George declined to comment on the case due to a busy schedule.
Senate Majority Leader Kesha Ram Hinsdale, D-Chittenden Southeast, said in a statement that she was “deeply disappointed” by the attorney general’s office for taking on the case.
“At a moment when the federal government is escalating attacks on immigrants and our civil liberties, Vermont should not be using its prosecutorial power in ways that chill free speech and peaceful dissent,” Hinsdale said.
The case appears to signal a shift in the way anti-ICE protests are handled in Chittenden County. George, the county’s state’s attorney, had previously declined to prosecute more than 20 ICE protesters in multiple different cases this year. 
Moving forward, however, Vermont State Police will go directly to the attorney general to handle cases of trespassing in anti-ICE protests in Chittenden County, according to Vermont State Police Col. Shawn Loan.
Vermont law allows the attorney general to take on cases before they are viewed by local prosecutors, Clark said in an interview. Cases sometimes come straight to her rather than first being prosecuted on a county level, she added.
“The 14 county state’s attorneys have jurisdiction to prosecute crimes in their counties, and the attorney general has jurisdiction statewide,” Clark said. “And it isn’t necessarily a delineated approach to who takes what case.”
Clark used the example of Addison County, where the elected State’s Attorney, Eva Vekos, recently had her law license suspended. Earlier this year, Clark took on all Addison County cases concerning homicide, sexual assault or child abuse.
“There was no lawyer in the office to handle the cases, so that is why we took over the rest of the cases,” Clark said. She said the attorney general’s office has stepped in in other counties as well when county prosecutors were overstretched or other issues arose.
Loan said the charges in the Whitecap Business Park protest were related to trespassing, rather than the protest itself, which is protected by the First Amendment.

A person is led to a vehicle by two Vermont State Troopers after being arrested for blocking the entrance to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center in Williston on Friday, July 24, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

“The issue is the violation of the state statute when you refuse to leave a private property,” Loan said. “Because at that point you’re violating that property owner’s rights.”
When asked about the initial decision to charge the 18-year-old protester as an adult, Clark told VTDigger in an interview that she was unable to comment on the specifics of the ongoing case. But Matthew Bernstein, Vermont’s child, youth and family advocate, said that while the court eventually decided to move the teen’s case to juvenile court, some damage had already been done.
One of the major reasons for Vermont’s Raise the Age law, which designates 19 as the cut-off age for family court rather than adult criminal court, is to protect 18-year-olds’ identities in court proceedings, Bernstein said. In the trespassing case, the defendant’s name was published in multiple news sources.
“Once that’s happened, then it’s too late to reverse it,” Bernstein said.
 VTDigger is not disclosing the name of the 18 year old.
Bernstein added that the decision to try a young protester for a nonviolent crime in adult court could discourage young people from other forms of civic engagement.
“They’re finding their voice, and raising that voice when they feel like it’s time to raise it is a crucial part of being a young person,” Bernstein said. 
George has previously declined to prosecute 13 demonstrators involved in a February protest, declined to prosecute six cases in April, and refused four more cases in May. She wrote in a statement reported by VTDigger that prosecuting the six individuals involved in the March 11 Dorset Street ICE standoff would not serve the community’s best interests, and that police escalation contributed to the situation in question.
“To charge these six individuals with no criminal records, and expect that they bear the burden of all the harm caused that day — is not something I was interested in our office being a part of,” George wrote.
Loan said the Vermont State Police still saw a case for conviction in the cases that George dropped.
“I can’t get into the details as to why she declined, but she did choose to decline them,” Loan said. “We felt these still met criteria, and that’s the decision to bring it to the AG for prosecution.”
When asked whether the attorney general’s office will seek to prosecute seven clergy members arrested in a separate anti-ICE protest, Clark declined to comment. 
Clark said her duty is to uphold the Constitution, which sometimes requires her to make unpopular decisions. She added that she cannot allow her personal opinions to influence her court cases.
“Whether I agree or disagree with what a protest is about cannot determine whether someone is held accountable under the law,” Clark said.
Hinsdale, the senate majority leader, cautioned Clark against continuing the prosecution.
“Our courts are already backlogged with real threats to public safety, and this is not what our top prosecutor should be prioritizing,” Hinsdale said. “There is still time to change course, and I urge the Attorney General’s Office to dismiss these charges.” 
Gov. Phil Scott said in a press conference Thursday that he knew Clark’s decision was a hard one to make. He said prosecution “doesn’t mean that they’re all going to be thrown in jail, but they’re going to be held accountable for violating the law.”
“So I applaud her for making that decision, and we’ll see where it goes from here,” Scott said.
Amanda Janoo, who is running for governor against Scott, in a statement condemned the actions of Clark’s office. Janoo said Vermont may not be able to influence the federal government’s decisions, but Vermont officials do have the power to decide what they would like to enforce within the state.
“The question for every institution and every elected official right now is not simply: What are we allowed to do?” Janoo said. “It is: What does this moment require of us?”

title: Trump set to rally GOP voters, hold midterm election event in Oklahoma
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — In what would be his first official visit to Oklahoma in six years, President Donald Trump is set to attend a rally Thursday in Durant, the Republican National Committee announced.  The “midterm rally” featuring Trump is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. at the Choctaw Event Center. The rally will be hosted […]
text:
President Donald Trump gives a speech at the World Economic Forum on Jan. 21, 2026 in Davos, Switzerland. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)(Getty Images cannot be republished without a subscription)OKLAHOMA CITY — In what would be his first official visit to Oklahoma in six years, President Donald Trump is set to attend a rally Thursday in Durant, the Republican National Committee announced. 
The “midterm rally” featuring Trump is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. at the Choctaw Event Center. The rally will be hosted by the Trump 47 Committee, a fundraising arm that links the 47th president’s campaign, the Republican National Committee and state GOP chapters. 
It wasn’t clear Friday morning if anyone else would share the stage with Trump at the rally, though the president has endorsed several Oklahoma politicians seeking both state and congressional seats. 
Trump has endorsed Republican Mike Mazzei in his bid to be Oklahoma’s next governor but it was not immediately clear if Mazzei would be attending. Mazzei won the statewide GOP primary last month by just over 2,000 votes.
As recently as Thursday morning, Mazzei posted confirmation that he would be participating at 7 p.m. in an hour-long debate with Democratic gubernatorial candidate Cyndi Munson. The debate, which will be hosted by PBS television affiliate OETA, is expected to overlap with Trump’s visit. Durant is 2.5 hours south of Oklahoma City, where the television station is located.
Mazzei’s campaign has not said whether he would attend the rally. 
Trump’s approval rating in Oklahoma has dropped since he won all 77 counties in the 2024 election, according to polling by the Economist and YouGov. Americans cited inflation and the economy as their biggest concerns.
Durant, located in Bryan County, is deeply Republican. During the 2024 general election, Trump carried more than 78% of the county’s vote. Mazzei also won the county during the most recent primary runoff election with 62% of the vote. 
Registration is free for tickets to the event, but limited to four tickets per person. Doors will open at 2 p.m. 
This is the third time a sitting U.S. president has visited the Choctaw Nation, said Chief Gary Batton.
“We hope his visit provides an opportunity to learn more about what we do as a sovereign nation for our members and for all people in southeast Oklahoma,” he said in a statement. 
Democratic President Barack Obama visited Durant in 2015 to meet with tribal leaders and announce a pilot program to increase high-speed internet access. Theodore Roosevelt also visited in 1905 to give a speech urging the Oklahomans to prepare for statehood.
U.S. Sen. James Lankford, R-OK, said on social media that Oklahoma is “honored” to host Trump in Durant. 
U.S. Rep. Kevin Hern, R-OK, who is running as a Republican for U.S. Senate, also wrote that he was glad to be hosting Trump in Oklahoma and said he would be attending. 
“He won all 77 Oklahoma counties three times, and I’m proud to fight alongside him to secure our borders, strengthen our economy, and restore the American Dream,” Hern posted on social media. 
Trump’s last Oklahoma visit was in June 2020, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic. He hosted a rally at the BOK Center in Tulsa. The event drew thousands of protesters and was poorly attended, despite his campaign claiming a million tickets had been requested. 
Former presidential candidate Herman Cain died of coronavirus shortly after attending the Tulsa rally. 
The Republican National Committee also announced Trump would attend a separate rally Oct. 2 in Mobile, Alabama, a state where Trump’s popularity is also said to be waning.

Southern Delaware event moves because of incoming storm; Wilmington’s Walk to End Alzheimer’s remains scheduled for Oct. 31
REHOBOTH BEACH, Del. — The Southern Delaware Walk to End Alzheimer’s has been postponed to Saturday, Nov. 14, because of the incoming storm, organizers announced Friday.
The walk had been scheduled for Saturday, Sept. 26.
The Alzheimer’s Association Delaware Chapter made the decision to move the event as potentially disruptive weather approaches the region.
The Southern Delaware event is one of two Walk to End Alzheimer’s events planned in Delaware this fall. The Wilmington walk remains scheduled for Saturday, Oct. 31.
The annual walks bring together people living with Alzheimer’s and other dementias, caregivers, families, friends and supporters while raising money for Alzheimer’s research and the association’s care and support programs.
Participants can walk individually or as part of a team and raise money in support of the Alzheimer’s Association’s mission.
A signature part of the event is the Promise Garden ceremony. Participants carry different-colored flowers representing their personal connection to Alzheimer’s and dementia, including those living with the disease, caregivers and people walking in memory of someone they have lost.
The Delaware walks are part of the nationwide Walk to End Alzheimer’s program, which the Alzheimer’s Association describes as the world’s largest fundraiser for Alzheimer’s care, support and research.
The organization provides education and support for Delaware families dealing with Alzheimer’s and other forms of dementia. Its 24/7 Helpline also connects families and caregivers with information, local resources and support.
The postponement gives Southern Delaware participants several additional weeks to register, organize teams and raise money before gathering Nov. 14.
The Wilmington event is not affected by the Southern Delaware postponement and remains scheduled for Oct. 31.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana Supreme Court vacates decision to put Butte data center issue to voters
description: The Montana Supreme Court on Thursday vacated an earlier ruling that the Butte-Silver Bow elections office print a citizen’s initiative question on the ballots after learning the department had already mailed ballots to voters.  Thursday’s ruling overturned a Tuesday order that required an initiative seeking to regulate data center construction by requiring[...]
text:
A view of downtown Butte is seen through a car window on July 6, 2017 in Butte, Montana. (Photo by Janie Osborne/Getty Images)The Montana Supreme Court on Thursday vacated an earlier ruling that the Butte-Silver Bow elections office print a citizen’s initiative question on the ballots after learning the department had already mailed ballots to voters. 
Thursday’s ruling overturned a Tuesday order that required an initiative seeking to regulate data center construction by requiring voter approval to appear on the November ballots. 
But less than 48 hours later, the court reversed its ruling, stating it was unaware that voters had already received — and in some cases returned — absentee and mail ballots, according to the county. Sherman told the court that “absentee/mail ballots had been issued” but the Secretary of State’s Office maintains an Oct 9 timeline for general election ballots to be sent, with the exception for overseas ballots which go out Sept. 18.
The initiative was engaged in a legal battle after the organizers — Denise Kelly and citizens’ group 406 People First — submitted signatures to qualify for the ballot in early August. While Cynthia Sherman, the county’s clerk and recorder overseeing elections, initially accepted and certified the signatures — more than the 3,652 required — it later told the organizers that a new Montana law had bumped the deadline for turning in signatures by more than a week, invalidating the measure. 
The proponents of the measure took the issue to district court to prevent the elections office from using the new statutory deadline, and after the district court ruled against them, appealed directly to the Montana Supreme Court. 
In a five-page order, the high court said it stood by its reasoning in granting the injunction that would have required the initiative be printed. 
If the initiative were left off the ballot, and later found to have met legal requirements, there would be no remedy, the court had argued on Tuesday. But if it were included — and approved by voters — there would have been an avenue to revoke the initiative if found legally insufficient. 
Now, the court said there is “no remedy” under state law. 
After Tuesday’s ruling, the city-county filed a notice asking how it was expected to comply with the order with ballots already mailed to voters. 
State statute has provisions for correcting ballots if there are errors in some office, but does not spell out a method for correcting issues with ballot initiatives — including if they are left off. 
The city-county asked whether it should send out new, corrected ballots or send out supplemental ballots with the initiative question, and whether they should include all registered voters, including those who had already turned in ballots. 
“Montana’s ballot statutes do not contemplate this decision and we have no good answers for the city-county’s very good questions as to how Sherman can implement our order,” and comply with state law, the order states. 
The court also points out that the situation was “entirely avoidable,” if the city-county had filed a notice that ballots had already gone out while the court was deliberating, and if the proponents of the ballot measure had also indicated a timeline for printing. 
In addition, the court also said that due to a “clerical error” there was a multi-week delay before the court learned that an appeal had been filed, which also added to the issue. 
Representatives for 406 People First told the Daily Montanan Thursday night they are speaking with counsel and considering next possible steps. Lawyers for the group filed an additional emergency petition asking the court to reconsider the issue, determine the timeline for ballots being sent out, and ensure the county complied with a previous temporary restraining order.

title: Commission open to sculpture idea for Cameron, Nebraska’s ‘Capitol Cat’
description: LINCOLN — A commission expressed openness Friday to a revised proposal for a sculpture to honor the Nebraska State Capitol’s longtime unofficial feline mascot. Multiple members of the seven-person Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission said they might be able to support the scaled-back idea to honor 11-year-old Cameron the “Capitol Cat.” For nearly a decade, t[...]
text:
An AI-rendered image of what a proposed sculpture honoring Cameron the Capitol Cat outside the Nebraska State Capitol could look like is projected during a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Sept. 25, 2026. The artificial intelligence image is not the final design. The supporters and  sculptor Benjamin Victor would design the final work. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A commission expressed openness Friday to a revised proposal for a sculpture to honor the Nebraska State Capitol’s longtime unofficial feline mascot.
Multiple members of the seven-person Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission said they might be able to support the scaled-back idea to honor 11-year-old Cameron the “Capitol Cat.” For nearly a decade, the tabby regularly trotted to the Capitol, where he would greet legislators, staffers and the public. In May, Cameron and his owner, Dianna McGinnis, moved into assisted living.
The proposed location for a sculpture honoring Cameron the Capitol Cat outside the Nebraska State Capitol is projected during a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The revised proposal calls for a life-size bronze statue of Cameron on the south side of the Capitol atop a bench, the final materials of which — limestone, granite or otherwise — are still being ironed out. A final vote could come as soon as next month.
“In no way do we want to compete against the historical figures that are at the Capitol,” former state Sen. Anna Wishart of Lincoln, a project leader, told the commission Friday. “Instead, we want to have just his presence there in a way that reflects the joy and the nonpartisanship that he brought to those who know him and to future people through the statue.”
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward is also assisting the project. Speaker John Arch of La Vista has also endorsed the idea.
‘I like this a lot better’
Commissioners generally thanked Wishart and her team for listening to commission feedback at an August meeting and scaling back what was originally a taller, more monumentlike proposal. The sculpture would move slightly closer to the state parking lot at the intersection of Goodhue Boulevard and H Street. It would also be lower to the ground, intended to be more interactive.
Commissioner Eileen Bergt at a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“I do like this site … and having it down lower and being able to sit next to it I think is great,” said Commissioner Eileen Bergt. “I think it’s more whimsical that way, rather than trying to elevate it more and more.”
“Generally, I like this a lot better than what we saw last month,” added Commissioner Andrea Gebhart. “I appreciate the feedback that you heard and actually incorporated into this.”
Among the additional feedback commissioners gave Friday was whether to add a plaza near the sculpture for students and visitors to relax in.
Bergt also suggested that when Cameron dies, his ashes could be incorporated into the area. Wishart said her team would talk with McGinnis and her family.
“Then his spirit lives on there,” Bergt said.
Commissioner Andrea Gebhart at a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Commission Chair Kile Johnson said he believes it would be good to have public art along Goodhue Boulevard, the street running south of the Capitol, if it’s “high quality.” A portion of Goodhue is included in the Capitol Environs District, which the commission oversees to preserve the impact and quality in the cardinal directions leading to the Capitol.
“And this, to me, is high quality,” Johnson said of the proposed Cameron sculpture.
Collin Christopher, a staff planner for the Lincoln-Lancaster County Planning Department, which assists the committee, said commission staff are generally comfortable with the idea and would recommend approval if it comes up for a final vote.
‘Be careful what you approve’
Benjamin Victor, an Idaho-based sculptor, is poised to sculpt Cameron’s bronze statue and pedestal, assuming enough private funds are raised. Johnson praised Victor’s past work, which is also displayed in the Capitol Environs District, including bronze statues for Ponca Chief Standing Bear and Dr. Susan La Flesche Picotte on Lincoln Mall north of the Capitol.
Victor has also sculpted four statues in Statuary Hall in the U.S. Capitol, including a Chief Standing Bear statue for Nebraska.
Former Nebraska State Capitol Administrator Bob Ripley during a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Aug. 28, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Bob Ripley, who was the State Capitol administrator from 1975 until 2023, again raised hesitation about the sculpture idea, as he did last month. He said he didn’t know how anyone could argue with the idea but worried what precedent it could set.
As an example, Ripley said he approved many activities on the north side of the Capitol in his former role, including rallies for the American Nazi Party. He said he didn’t support the event, but organizers had met requirements for hosting.
“I’m just saying: Be careful what you approve, because you may get someone coming along asking for approval that you may not want to stand up and make a campaign speech for,” Ripley said.
‘More than a charming story’
Courtney Wittstruck of Lincoln, a registered lobbyist at the Capitol, again testified in favor of the idea in her private capacity. She said honoring Cameron would be in line with the symbolism of the Capitol, similar to the Sower, bison and pioneer families found in and around the building.
She said Cameron is more than a “beloved cat” and proved people could “remember that the person on the other side of a political argument was still a neighbor and a fellow Nebraskan.”
“That is more than a charming story about a Capitol mascot,” Wittstruck said. “It is a simple, accessible expression of values this building was deliberately designed to teach.”
Courtney Wittstruck of Lincoln after speaking to the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission in support of a sculpture for Cameron the Capitol Cat on Sept. 25, 2026. She wears a shirt that bears a photo of Cameron. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Among the virtues of Nebraska which Cameron represents, Wittstruck said, she listed magnanimity, charity, temperance, justice and hope. Wittstruck said a child doesn’t need to understand constitutional theory to understand kindness.
“Cameron made those abstract ideals tangible and approachable by giving them four legs and a face people could recognize, and that I believe is why the fact that Cameron is a cat is not a weakness in this proposal,” Wittstruck said. “It may be precisely what makes this symbol work.”
Wishart told reporters after the meeting that her team has a “little more homework,” such as determining ongoing maintenance, selecting final materials and considering additional landscaping, but she hopes to be back next month seeking final approval. She said supporters are confident they’ll raise enough private funds and will take all feedback into account.
“We’re doing everything possible to make this a sculpture that everybody embraces,” Wishart said.
The next Capitol Environs Commission meeting is scheduled for 8:30 a.m. Oct. 23 in Lincoln.

description: A Tennessee law preventing adults from giving information to minors about legal out-of-state abortions will remain blocked, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit ruled Thursday. ​A three-judge panel agreed with a federal district judge that barring adults from giving out information about abortions violates the First Amendment. ​Senior United States[...]
text:
A three-judge panel U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit agreed with a federal district judge that barring adults from giving out information about abortions violates the First Amendment. Photo from a 2022 Nashville protest following the Dobbs v. Jackson ruling. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennnessee Lookout)
A Tennessee law preventing adults from giving information to minors about legal out-of-state abortions will remain blocked, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit ruled Thursday.
​A three-judge panel agreed with a federal district judge that barring adults from giving out information about abortions violates the First Amendment.
​Senior United States Judge Jane Stranch said in her ruling the Tennessee law had “no compelling interest in shielding its citizens from information about activities outside its borders.”
​Stranch added in the ruling, the state “criminalizes speech that encourages a minor to get an abortion yet is silent on speech encouraging a minor to carry a pregnancy to term with or without parental involvement.”
​Tennessee lawmakers passed the law in 2024, two years after the state’s near-total abortion ban went into effect following the Supreme Court decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization.
​State. Rep. Aftyn Behn, a Nashville Democrat, and attorney Rachel Welty filed a lawsuit against the law shortly after its passage, and a federal district judge prevented it from taking effect.
​Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti then appealed the ruling.
​The blocked law made it a misdemeanor for any adult who “recruits, harbors, or transports a pregnant un-emancipated minor” to obtain an abortion, including drug-induced abortion, without consent from the minor’s legal guardian.
​The law came in response to abortion advocates providing information and resources to those wanting the procedure in states where it remains legal.
