name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Diesel fuel prices in Connecticut hit record high
description: The head of the Connecticut Energy Marketers Association said consumers likely will face shortages and more price increases in coming months.
text:
Despite diesel prices hitting a record high this week and home heating oil up 50% in just three months, the state’s fuel distributors warn the problems are far from over.
The head of the Connecticut Energy Marketers Association said consumers likely will face shortages and additional price increases this fall and winter.
“There’s no limit to how high [prices] could go if these wars continue,” Chris Herb, the association’s president and CEO, said Wednesday, referring to ongoing conflicts between the U.S. and Iran and between Russian and Ukraine, both of which interfere with petroleum production and exports. “I am immensely concerned.”
The average retail diesel price hit a record high Wednesday in Connecticut, approaching $6.48 per gallon, then ticked another 3/10ths of a penny over that mark on Thursday, according to AAA. That’s up 71% from the $3.78 average price recorded here one year ago.
The national average hit a record Tuesday at $6.53 per gallon and stood at $6.51 on Thursday, AAA reported. One year ago, the national average stood at $3.69 per gallon.
Besides the ongoing wars, diesel prices also often surge each autumn as farmers in the U.S. and other Northern Hemisphere nations need fuel to run equipment for harvest, said Herb. “We have two events colliding at the same time,” he added. “Unfortunately, it’s beyond our control on how we would attract supply.”
The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported this week that diesel and other related fuel stocks were about 12% below the seasonal average, and Herb warned that could mean tight supply conditions for months to come, depending on whether President Donald Trump’s administration restricts fuel exports to preserve domestic supplies.
Further complicating matters, the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection reported an average price of $5.91 per gallon this week for home heating oil. That’s up 50% from the $3.95 price noted the week of June 22, but still below the $6.37 cost the department listed in early May of 2022, two-and-a-half months after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine began.
Home heating oil is very similar in chemical structure to diesel fuel. Both are distillates, produced by boiling crude oil and then cooling it back into liquid form. And because of their similarities, both are subject to the same political and market pressures.
The heating oil situation is particularly troublesome here for low-to-moderate residents who rely on the Connecticut Energy Assistance Program to keep warm.
While the demand for aid has grown steadily in recent years, demand for the federal Low-Income Household Energy Assistance Program funds that the state doles out via the CEAP program has not.
The state Department of Social Services projects the poorest and most vulnerable households that qualify for the program would receive $1,995 this winter, down 33% from the $2,980 maximum grant provided in 2019-20.
Members of a state energy advisory board, including Connecticut AARP Director Nora Duncan, have urged Gov. Ned Lamont and the General Assembly in recent years to add state dollars to the program to bolster grant levels.
Many legislators from both parties also have endorsed the use of state funds to expand energy assistance.
Lamont and lawmakers have set aside $550 million from past state budget surpluses to mitigate federal human service programs cuts. About $260 million remains in the response fund, which already has been tapped to bolster healthcare and nutrition programs and to assist immigrants whose legal status has been challenged by the Trump administration.
A spokesman for Lamont’s reelection campaign, Rob Blanchard, said, “Trump’s war in Iran [is] driving up gas, home heating oil and diesel prices on everything we buy, and instead of helping, the White House keeps trying to gut LIHEAP, the program families need most right now. Connecticut deserves a partner in Washington, not more chaos.”
But minority Republicans in the state House and Senate say local Democrats’ policies have done plenty to make Connecticut unaffordable. The GOP released a tax relief plan that includes repealing a highway mileage-based levy on large commercial non-farm trucks.
“Connecticut didn’t become one of the most expensive states in the country the day President Trump took office,” House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford, said two weeks ago when Republicans rolled out their tax-cutting options.
According to state analysts, that truck tax will generate $62 million in revenue this fiscal year for the state’s transportation program, which holds more than $640 million in reserves and projected surplus.
But that $62 million cost, along with spiking fuel expenses, is passed onto shoppers at supermarkets, department stores and other retail outlets that rely on deliveries from diesel-powered trucks, said John Blair, president of the Motor Transport Association of Connecticut.
Blair, whose association represents more than 500 trucking and related businesses, called the rising diesel prices “a grave concern” for his industry, predicting consumers would benefit from any repeal of the highway tax.
“Any cost that we can reduce,” he said, “we can pass along.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: The cowardice of masked law enforcement: Recent Kansas immigration raids remind us why faces matter
description: “Disgusting,” a voice on the Facebook video says. Captured in Kansas City, Kansas, this summer, the footage shows a handful of law enforcement officers — most of them masked — detaining a man. Their black SUVs surround his white pickup at the intersection of 6th Street and Central Avenue. After two minutes and 16 seconds, […]
text:
A masked ICE agent stands guard outside as ICE and other law enforcement agents raid a restaurant in Minneapolis, Minnesota, last year. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)“Disgusting,” a voice on the Facebook video says.
Captured in Kansas City, Kansas, this summer, the footage shows a handful of law enforcement officers — most of them masked — detaining a man. Their black SUVs surround his white pickup at the intersection of 6th Street and Central Avenue. After two minutes and 16 seconds, the officers have the handcuffed man in a back seat and drive him away.
The most common face covering among the officers is a black elastic cloth pulled up to cover their chin, mouth, cheeks and nose. As they mill around the intersection and inspect the truck, the thin fabric keeps each of them anonymous.
“They can’t even show their faces,” the bystander’s voice continues, before using an expletive to describe the agents.
As unprecedented immigration enforcement continues this week in Kansas and nationwide, the masks worn by law enforcement create a looming, yet cowardly, specter: law-enforcement officers so morally compromised by their work that they can’t show their faces, whether in Liberal or Garden City. Their work is so counter to the wishes of the community that they must hide themselves.
For the sake of this column, please reserve all of the other political and moral objections to the immigration raids — and there are many: separation of nuclear families, coordination with local law enforcement and insistence that you not record their public actions, because of a Kansas statute.
For a moment, let’s focus on the anonymity of the mask.
I could have written this column about masked agents in Kansas this summer or this spring or last year (as my Kansas Reflector colleague Max McCoy did). Choose your month and week. Federal immigration raids persist.
This week, local news outlets along with Kansas Public Radio reported that “ICE agents with masks covering their faces” were “stopping cars and questioning passengers” in Liberal. During a Kansas City, Missouri, raid this summer, another operation “involved at least six unmarked vehicles with Kansas and Missouri license plates,” as reported by KCUR. Immigration officers in Kansas are faceless and nameless, stripped of even the most basic identity, back story or credentials. 
Chilling photos by KCUR news intern Cassandra Isobelle Flores give us a clear look at the standard faux-military costumes the agents prefer: a backward baseball hat, a T-shirt, a tactical vest bulging with hidden gadgets, jeans and boots — every face covered in a mask.
If you had shown me these photos in 2010, I would have assumed they were from a country gripped by paramilitary violence. In 2015, I would have assumed they were actors on the set of “Homeland” or “24,” taking on the role of a CIA operative spiriting terrorists away to a black site for questioning.
We would all be terrified at being confronted by beefy men with badge numbers hidden, intent to stuff you into an unmarked car while refusing to identify themselves. Given the civic instability that their anonymous presence causes, it’s a stretch to even call them law enforcement. 
The federal agency alphabet soup decorating their vests is another matter. While they might claim that it helps to identify them as federal agents, it only makes them more mysterious because the acronyms are esoteric.
Most Americans and immigrants know the meaning of “POLICE” and “ICE.” 
But test yourself. I am going to give you three acronyms. Which two are actual immigration enforcement agencies? And which one is not? Your options: HSI, USIC and ERO.
Two of these acronyms appear on the tactical vests of agents in Kansas. Did you guess ERO, which stands for Enforcement and Removal Operations? What about HSI, Homeland Security Investigations?
(If someone is wearing a USIC vest, they are likely coming to locate underground utilities in your backyard.)
A law enforcement uniform is supposed to be exactly that: uniform. The crisp blues and badge of a traffic cop. The brown-on-brown of a sheriff’s deputy. The full range of military uniforms that designate: “This is who I am. This is my authority.”
The gear of today’s masked immigration officer as he walks main streets in southwest Kansas is intentional sartorial anarchy, saying: “I might look like this. Or like this. But regardless, you must obey.”
While I now live far from small-town Kansas, I once lived in a midwestern town smaller than Liberal, Dodge City and Garden City. I can imagine how residents would have reacted with alarm at seeing strangers dressed for insurrection. After all, the wonder (and claustrophobia) of rural life is how familiar you are with everyone. In the small towns of Kansas even more than big cities, masked strangers — especially a pack of swaggering and largely untrained strangers — creates outsized chaos.
The counterarguments from the Department of Homeland Security are shot through with hyperventilation, falsehood and distraction.
Why must their agents use masks?
Without masks, their identities could be revealed through doxing online.
Without masks, they would be “targeted by highly sophisticated gangs like Tren de Aragua and MS-13, criminal rings, murderers, and rapists.”
Officers are “flanked by vehicles marked with the name of the department,” a ludicrous claim that I needed to re-read three times.
This is normally the part of my column that I reserve for pointing at the prospect of change through state legislation. However, legislation in other states that aimed to unmask federal immigration agents has fallen flat. In New Jersey and New York, judges have paused state laws. In New Jersey, the Department of Justice argued in a court filing that the “supremacy” clause means that federal authority holds more power than a state law about masks. In New York, a judge cited the federal government’s designated role to police immigration as reason to defer to their masking policy.
In Washington state, a law has proven essentially toothless. Federal officers simply continue to wear the masks.
An executive decision by President Donald Trump has trickled down to small-town Kansas through Homeland Security instructions and policies with no recourse for normal citizens. This federal department and this careening president are aligned in wanting agents with masks on American streets.
But why?
I agree that one key reason for the masks is to create fear, of course. But another is shame.
Consider the pride of other civil servants and law enforcement: municipal police, firefighters and the military. The holiday parades. The public adulation. The local heroes. Compare that with the shameful image of an immigration agent — claiming to simply be doing his job — while hiding behind a scrim of facial obscurity.
Among the wash of jarring visuals from the Trump era, masked agents will be one of the most enduring. We will remember the sinister image: eyes perched above an anonymous male face tightly and darkly wrapped.
We will also remember the message of that image: one of impunity, cruelty and xenophobia, cloaked in the reassuring, condescending lie of “law and order.”
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Underly says it’s urgent to fix the school funding formula but timing will depend on the election
description: Wisconsin State Superintendent Jill Underly called for the state to overhaul the school funding formula in her sixth State of Education address Thursday, saying that the state “simply cannot afford to wait any longer.”  Underly delivered the address less than six weeks before the November election, when Wisconsin voters will decide who she will be […]
text:
“The formula used for funding our schools, for years, has failed our children, schools and entire communities,” Underly said during her address. Underly speaks to reporters after delivering her sixth State of Education address.  (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner) Wisconsin State Superintendent Jill Underly called for the state to overhaul the school funding formula in her sixth State of Education address Thursday, saying that the state “simply cannot afford to wait any longer.” 
Underly delivered the address less than six weeks before the November election, when Wisconsin voters will decide who she will be working with in the governor’s office and in the state Legislature on the next state budget. She will need their support to get the funding for the budget proposals she has begun to formulate.
The Department of Public Instruction so far has only submitted the first part of its budget request, which covered funding for libraries, support for children who are deaf and blind, public libraries, cybersecurity, technology modernization and the investigation of alleged educator misconduct. The agency said last week that it would release the second part of its request, for “categorical aid programs and other critical supports” for Wisconsin’s public schools, in November. The election is scheduled for Nov. 3. 
“The formula used for funding our schools, for years, has failed our children, schools and entire communities,” Underly said during her address. “The reasons are varied and complex, but you don’t need to be familiar with every detail of the funding formula to know that it’s simply not working. The evidence is all around us.” 
More than 75 school referendum requests carrying a total cost of $1.5 billion will go before voters in November. It’s just the latest round in a now-familiar ritual as school districts across the state  seek approval to raise property taxes to make up for a shrinking pool of  state aid. School districts that can’t pass a referendum have had to cut costs including by eliminating programs, staff and in some cases closing or consolidating schools. Districts on a streak of failed referendum requests have faced dissolution. 
Underly noted that the classrooms of the Hustisford School District “sat empty” on the first day of school this year. The district started the dissolution process after its referendum failed in April.
“Every kid felt the impact,” Underly said. “Kindergarteners, who should have been walking through the doors of the school their family chose when they made this beautiful community home, instead traveled to a neighboring town. Meanwhile, seniors who spent the past 12 years as Hustisford Falcons started their last year of school in an unfamiliar building,” Underly continued. “This is what happens when we turn our back on our schools. And when schools close, the impact doesn’t stop with students. It ripples through entire communities.”
Underly said the state funding formula “places value on the wrong things,” including enrollment, district spending and property value, instead of on student needs. 
“It fails to ask the most essential question: How much does it actually cost to educate the students who live in a district so that they have an equal opportunity to succeed? A student’s opportunity for success should not depend on their zip code,” she said. 
School funding will depend on who’s in office. Republican candidate Tom Tiffany and Democratic candidate David Crowley are running to be governor and control of the state Senate and Assembly are up for grabs. 
Some lawmakers have argued that rather than increase funding for schools the state needs to explore more school consolidation given declining enrollment. Asked about when school closure is the appropriate answer to declining enrollment, Underly told reporters she thinks “it deserves some study and conversation to figure out what’s best for kids.”
Underly pointed to the 2019 bipartisan Blue Ribbon Commission while speaking to reporters. The commission, which was created by Assembly Speaker Robin Vos and then-Senate Majority Leader Scott Fitzgerald in 2017, developed a report offering ideas to address school funding issues, as a guiding document for what the state should be doing. She said that the reports showed that there are kids who need additional support including those in poverty and who have special needs. She said money also needs to be invested in career and technical education, mental health supports and speech and language pathology.
“All these things have been in my past budget requests, and that’s what we will be able to expect in the next one, too,” Underly said. The agency’s 2024 state budget request totaled over  $4 billion. 
Urgent, but possibly not very fast
While Underly delivered her message with urgency, the timeline for changes could look vastly different depending on who wins in November.
Senate Minority Leader Dianne Hesselbein (D-Middleton), who could become the Senate Majority leader depending on the results of the November elections, has said Democrats will increase school funding in the next state budget, but changing the state’s school funding formula could be a “multi-year” process. 
“We’re also looking at a long-term goal of seeing what other states are doing and how they are funding their public schools, but that’s going to take probably a multi-year task to try to figure that all out and talking to our friends in Minnesota, Michigan, Illinois,” Hesselbein said. 
Crowley has been supportive of increasing school funding, including moving the state toward reimbursing districts for 90% of the cost of special education, instead of the current rate of 38% , but he has also suggested throughout his campaign for governor that there may need to be another Blue Ribbon Commission to study tax issues including school and local government funding. The last Blue Ribbon Commission on school funding took two years to complete. 
Tiffany has said he wants some increases to school funding, but also promises to freeze property taxes if elected. He hasn’t provided clarity on how much he would invest or how he would balance the two issues. Tiffany has focused on issues of accountability and ensuring “high standards” as opposed to school funding when discussing education issues.
Underly has had a strained relationship with Republicans on the Joint Finance Committee, who have declined to invite her to testify in front of the committee, and it’s unclear whether a working relationship between her and Tiffany would be an improvement. Tiffany recently described the state superintendent’s position as a constitutional office as a “problem” at a Moms For Liberty Town Hall in Richfield. He said he would use the state budget, which determines the state’s spending for a two-year period, to try to steer the superintendent  to make the decisions he wants her to make.
Underly said responding to the comments that independence is positive.  
“When you think about my office, my office is nonpartisan. It’s independent. It is not at the whim of any governor and I think that actually strengthens public education,” Underly said. “I think his comments stand on their own.”
In her speech, Underly called for people to look at the candidates’ records on school issues, not their talking points, when making their decisions at the ballot box this November. 
“We have people running for office who have spent a decade or more in government, in positions to make school funding decisions — or who have left state government for another level and now want to return — whose records include repeatedly voting against investments in Wisconsin’s children,” Underly said, apparently referring to Tiffany, who as a state lawmaker served on the budget committee before he was elected to Congress. “Past actions are the best evidence we have of what someone will do when given power again. Wisconsin does not need more people who tell us they support children while their votes tell a different story. We need people in positions of decision-making power who are pro-public school, pro-child and pro-Wisconsin.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: A battle brews over Maine’s salmon farms
description: Glenda Beal’s roots in lobstering run nearly as deep as her roots in the town that shares her name: Beals Island, Maine. Her husband and two sons are lobstermen, as were her father and uncle, both grandfathers and a few generations before that. “Our economy runs on lobster fishing, predominantly,” said Beal, 60, a descendant […]
text:
There are around 215 aquaculture operations in Maine, such as this seaweed bed. (Photo by Justin Smulski via Inside Climate News) 
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News,  a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.

Glenda Beal’s roots in lobstering run nearly as deep as her roots in the town that shares her name: Beals Island, Maine. Her husband and two sons are lobstermen, as were her father and uncle, both grandfathers and a few generations before that.
“Our economy runs on lobster fishing, predominantly,” said Beal, 60, a descendant of one of the island’s original settlers.
It’s a tough industry in which to make a living, Beal said, and the three salmon farming operations in nearby Eastern Bay only make it tougher. She said her community’s lobstermen have noticed barren and polluted waters, damaged gear, floating trash and, on one occasion, dead salmon washed up on their shorelines, and they believe aquaculture is to blame.
The corporation that owns these operations, Cooke Aquaculture, a Canadian multinational based in Saint John, New Brunswick, is being sued for business practices alleged to harm the environment, local fisheries and tourism.
“Having areas taken up by [a] large acreage of pens prevents fishermen from fishing in these traditional waters that they’ve always been able to use,” Beal said. “There isn’t a fisherman out there that likes it.”
That’s why Beals Island and a few other Maine towns have recently tried to exert more local control over whether and how aquaculture facilities operate in their waters.
The growing industry
Maine’s aquaculture industry contributed more than $200 million to the state’s economy in 2023, according to the Maine Aquaculture Association.
A young Atlantic salmon at a Maine hatchery that breeds the endangered fish to boost wild populations, which currently number less than 2,000 in the state. (Photo courtesy of Downeast Salmon Federation)
The largest company is Cooke Aquaculture, which has 24 active lease sites along Maine’s coastline, plus inland hatcheries and a processing facility, according to records on the state’s Department of Marine Resources website.
Cooke operates in 16 countries. Its Maine facilities primarily grow Atlantic salmon in open net pens, floating cages within a larger body of water. Each lease site has multiple pens that hold tens of thousands of salmon during their growth from juvenile to adult size.
The company’s net-pen facilities dot sheltered bays along the Maine coast, places that also sustain ecosystems of lobster, periwinkles, oysters, clams and juvenile fish, including the endangered wild Atlantic salmon. Many of those species form the basis for Maine’s commercial fisheries.
According to state regulations, aquaculture sites aren’t allowed to harm these sensitive ecosystems or interfere with active fisheries. Yet, Beal said that’s exactly what she sees happening. The Conservation Law Foundation agrees—and filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine in January 2025 alleging ongoing Clean Water Act violations at Cooke facilities and harm to area fishing and tourism
 Dead in the water
The daily upkeep of salmon aquaculture—feedings, pen maintenance, treatments for disease and pests when needed—all occurs in the open water and influences the ecosystem far beyond the pen’s boundaries.
Beal said local fishers have reported that former harvest sites near the pens are no longer viable and the seabed is unusually empty of life.
Waste from the pens, including excess food, excrement and sometimes bits of dead fish, rots and can upset the balance of nutrients like nitrogen and sulfide, Beal said. The resulting low-oxygen conditions suffocate life on the seabed below, including the eelgrass beds that protect young fish and crustaceans.
“That’s the nursery bed of all our sea creatures,” Beal said. “They are critically important.”
The CLF lawsuit against Cooke described a “thick layer of toxic sediment on the ocean floor” and a “foul-smelling black sludge” on lobster traps near the net-pen sites.
According to the CLF, Cooke has repeatedly reported toxic sulfide levels at multiple sites. The lawsuit also alleges the company has failed to meet state monitoring requirements on several occasions, exceeded pollutant discharge limits and reported sediment samples “indicative of poor ecological quality.”
Salmon aquaculture formerly used chemicals to treat sea lice in the pens, which were toxic to other marine life. Today, Maine Aquaculture Association Executive Director Sebastian Belle said the industry instead relies on hot-water baths to kill the lice and letting sites fallow to stop disease and parasite spread.
The CLF lawsuit, however, claims that Cooke boats have been witnessed dumping water with blood and a “chemical odor” after delousing activity.

Dead Atlantic salmon washed ashore after a 2021 die-off of farmed salmon stock at a Cooke Aquaculture facility in Maine. (Photo courtesy of Crystal Canney)
Cooke facilities had major die-offs of their stock at one Maine site in 2021 and two others in 2024. Disease or pests can cause these mass deaths to occur, as can high temperatures or low oxygen.
Beal said dead salmon floated in the water and washed up on beaches around Beals Island after the 2024 die-off. Though the state cleared Cooke of wrongdoing, Beal said there was “very little satisfactory explanation” about what happened, and she believes pollution from the pens played a role.
Past infractions
Cooke has received six letters of warning and 20 notices of violation from the Maine Department of Environmental Protection in the past decade, as well as a 2019 consent agreement to pay $190,000 in fines for improper sulfide sampling and exceeding the allowed number of fish per pen.
The company has previously been sanctioned in Chile and fined in Canada and Washington state for other violations. Cooke was accused of animal rights abuses and neglecting sanitary standards at Maine facilities in 2019 and again earlier this year.
The latest undercover video, published in May by an animal rights group, prompted state and third-party investigations.
Cooke did not respond to interview requests, but it previously put out a statement declaring that the CLF’s claims are false. Cooke has also filed a motion to dismiss the suit, which is currently awaiting a judicial decision.
Belle and the Maine Aquaculture Association have also repeatedly called the lawsuit’s claims false and misleading. Belle asserted that modern management practices have reduced the input of excess feed, antibiotics and chemicals into the water and have made salmon aquaculture safe and sustainable.
Dwayne Shaw, the executive director of the Downeast Salmon Federation, a nonprofit focused on wild salmon restoration, cast doubt on the effectiveness of those practices: “Even with that, they’ve not been able to prevent the pollution and the impacts.”
A sensitive species
The proximity of farmed salmon to wild salmon concerns Shaw. Net pens can fail and allow escapes due to storms, seal attacks, employee error or equipment degradation, as happened at Cooke sites in Maine in 2020 and 2023.
This can be a big problem for wild Atlantic salmon, which Shaw said are a “very sensitive species.”
Federal and state agencies and groups like the Downeast Salmon Federation have put years of work into breeding efforts and habitat restoration to keep them from extinction.
Hatchery-raised wild Atlantic salmon are eventually released into existing populations of the endangered fish, in hopes of boosting their numbers. The Downeast Salmon Federation says nearby salmon farms are a risk to the health and genetic fitness of wild salmon. (Photo courtesy of Downeast Salmon Federation)
Right now, there are less than 2,000 wild Atlantic salmon living in Maine, Shaw said, well below restoration goals.
Escaped farm salmon are additional competitors for food and other resources, and they can spread disease and parasites, Shaw said. Researchers have found that farmed salmon in Norway have repeatedly spread sea lice that killed wild Atlantic salmon. The CLF lawsuit attributes at least one disease outbreak among wild salmon to Cooke fish.
Farmed salmon are bred to produce better meat, but those traits make wild survival more difficult. “If those genes mix, then you’ve got an inferior creature in terms of its fitness in the wild,” Shaw said.
He worries about the possibility of interbreeding between escaped domestic salmon and wild salmon. Two Cooke facilities are “immediately adjacent” to Downeast Salmon Federation sites, he said.
There are some protective measures in place. Companies must put identifying marks on their salmon and create an annual containment plan to prevent escapes. Belle said escaped fish are lost profits, so the industry is incentivized to create protections.
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service does genetic screenings to make sure its wild salmon hatcheries don’t use fish with domesticated DNA.
DMR staff also do testing to prevent farm-raised salmon from entering spawning areas. Since aquaculture companies keep genetic records of their stock, the DMR can attempt to find a match and trace an escapee back to its source.
So far, there are no known instances of interbreeding in Maine. However, it has occurred in several Norwegian rivers after farmed salmon escapes, and Scotland and Ireland have also found escaped salmon traveling and spawning with wild salmon.
Washington decided to ban net-pen farming of non-native fish after a 2017 net failure at a Cooke facility released 250,000 fish into Puget Sound. California, Alaska and British Columbia have similar restrictions in place or planned for the near future.
“On the West Coast they’ve been banned, so why are we having them on the East Coast?” Beal asked
The coastal economy
Even if aquaculture lease sites don’t overlap with seafood harvest areas on paper, Beal said they still impact local fishers. “I don’t believe there’s a fisherman around who would think having Cooke in our waters is a good thing,” she said.
The CLF lawsuit states that some of the foundation’s members have had to relocate lobster traps and other fishing gear farther away from “dead zones” near the net pens. Floating trash, such as feed bags, tubes, ropes and nets, appears in the water and on the shoreline around the island, and Beal said Cooke appears to be the most likely source.
Tubes and ropes are a danger to fishing boats, Beal said, and “could cost them a day’s work, could cost them major repairs.”
Boats traveling to and from the Cooke sites have damaged lobster traps or accidentally cut their lines. In Lubec, a coastal Maine town northeast of Beals Island, a Cooke boat damaged the town’s commercial pier earlier this year. The CLF lawsuit alleges that Cooke’s presence has also harmed tourism industries like whale watching.
At Severine von Tscharner Welcome’s farm on Cobscook Bay, near another Cooke net-pen facility, she sometimes sees “acres of foam floating off of those sites that are closest to me” while working in her seaweed and oyster beds.

A seaweed harvest at Severine von Tscharner Welcome’s farm on Cobscook Bay, Maine. Welcome said she worries about the impact of nearby salmon farms on the quality of her crop and the health of her workers. (Photo by Lauri Churchill)
Welcome, 45, said she worries about how the unidentified foam and other pollutants will affect her crop and the people who help her harvest it. “They’re violating the principles of sustainable practice and they’re making a bad impact on the bay at large,” said Welcome, who is also the director of Greenhorns, a nonprofit for new farmers.
She said Cooke lease sites “monopolize the whole space” in Cobscook Bay. “Our economy is not Cooke. Our economy is diverse fisheries, recreation, tourism, ‘Vacationland,’” Welcome said, referencing the state’s nickname.
Cooke does pay wharf and property taxes and other fees at each of its facilities, and Belle said salmon farming employs about 200 Mainers.
But according to Beal, those revenues don’t come close to the costs her town has experienced.
“They’re really not compensating the towns enough for that use to make up for the pollution and the lack of fishing waters,” she said.
Crystal Canney, the executive director of the Protect Maine’s Fishing Heritage Foundation, said she’s heard seafood harvesters along Maine’s coast complain about large-scale aquaculture and how the state regulates it.  “A lot of the lobstermen are just ticked off,” Canney said.
An oversight problem
Maine’s Department of Marine Resources and Department of Environmental Protection set the standards for aquaculture operations and environmental impact. However, most of the compliance data is monitored and reported by the facilities themselves.
The DMR conducts an initial site review for proposed facilities and annual inspections of existing facilities and fish health. The DEP also conducts annual site visits.
Everything else—feed reports, sediment and water quality tests, pollution discharge monitoring, fish health reports, biosecurity audits and annual containment management plans—is documented by the company and submitted to the state for review. These reports are considered proprietary and aren’t made public.
“There’s no transparency there,” Canney said. “I would like to see the state take the responsibility it should in the oversight of these net pens instead of abdicating it to the very businesses they’re supposed to be overseeing.”

Aquaculture companies must report major incidents like fish escapes, disease outbreaks or excessive pollutant discharge to the state, along with a plan to address the problem.
This prompts a site visit by the DMR or DEP to investigate the cause and solutions. Belle said aquaculture facilities are also subject to third-party audits when these incidents occur.
However, Beal believes that DMR and DEP scientists are too far away to respond quickly to reported problems, and that the state is essentially “rubber-stamping” lease applications and renewals because it wants the industry to grow.
In 2025, the state Legislature removed the option of public hearings for aquaculture lease renewals, though the DMR must still notify adjacent landowners, publish a local newspaper notice and accept public comments for 30 days. The stated goal was to reduce administrative burdens for the DMR and lease applicants.
For towns like Beals Island, the loss of public hearings feels like being shut out of the process. “It’s pretty egregious that the government would lease state waters to a known violator for 20 years and remove public comment from that process,” Welcome said.
Local control
Beals Island is one of nine Maine communities that have passed ordinances restricting aquaculture operations in their waters.
“Basically, we felt that the state was not doing enough to protect our waters,” said Beal, who was chair of her town’s selectboard during the ordinance’s year-long drafting process.
The Protect Maine’s Fishing Heritage Foundation has helped several of these towns in drafting their ordinances, though Canney said the final decisions are always up to community members. A few towns have ultimately decided against the proposed ordinances.
Beal said residents at her town’s public meetings were overwhelmingly in favor of establishing an aquaculture review committee, with violation enforcement by the harbormaster.
The ordinance also sets a limit on the total acreage of aquaculture in Beals Island waters and how much space any single company can lease. Cooke’s upcoming lease renewals would exceed that limit.
Since the ordinance passed in October 2025, Beal said the town has already issued a notice of violation to Cooke for a navigational hazard, which was then corrected.
“I do think the ordinance keeps them on their toes,” she said. “I feel like that is affirmation that what we have done was necessary.”
These ordinances are on shaky ground, however. Municipalities have limited control over intertidal zones, but only the state DMR commissioner can decide on aquaculture siting and lease applications. The DMR has already publicly objected to these municipal ordinances, which it said lacks legal standing.
But since the DMR has not expressed interest in going to court over these ordinances, it’s unclear what will happen when state and local decisions conflict.
Beal said large-scale aquaculture has its place on Maine’s coast, as long as there’s enough regulation, independent monitoring and enforcement. She also wants to see the state deny leases when there are repeated violations or a lack of community support.
“Aquaculture has a right to be there, but not at the expense of these traditional fisheries,” Beal said.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Justices sound skeptical of Georgia agency’s decision to remove children from their home
description: Warning: This story involves the subject of suicide. If you or someone you know may be experiencing a mental health crisis, contact the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline by dialing or texting “988.” Georgia Supreme Court justices had pointed questions this week for representatives of the Georgia Department of Human Services’ Division of Family and […]
text:
Georgia Supreme Court Justice Charlie J. Bethel asks questions during a hearing in this 2023 file photo. Jill Nolin/Georgia RecorderWarning: This story involves the subject of suicide. If you or someone you know may be experiencing a mental health crisis, contact the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline by dialing or texting “988.”
Georgia Supreme Court justices had pointed questions this week for representatives of the Georgia Department of Human Services’ Division of Family and Children Services.
A case working its way through Georgia’s highest court has to do with the government’s power to remove a child from his or her home.
Lawyers for the state argue that government officials should have the right to temporarily remove children from a home without a hearing in some cases, even if there is no immediate danger.
One Fulton County mom says the state exceeded its authority in taking her two kids shortly after a family tragedy, and questions from justices asked during oral arguments this week indicated they might agree.
Facts of the case
In 2024, Dayshundra Wilson lived in Atlanta with her five children. On June 8, her 13-year-old son was taken to the hospital with a self-inflicted gunshot wound that would claim his life three days later. The medical examiner ruled the death a suicide.
On July 9, a month after the shooting at the family home, the Georgia Department of Human Services’ Division of Family and Children Services filed paperwork with the juvenile court arguing that two of Wilson’s minor children were “dependent,” which in this context means they had been abused or neglected and were in need of protection. The division filed an emergency order to take two of the kids into protective custody. The other two children were living with their father.
In the order, the state indicated the children were not in immediate danger, that their placement in shelter care was not necessary to protect people or property, that the agency did not have a good faith belief that the children were likely to run away and that they were not without a parent or guardian.
The judge rejected the order because the children were not in immediate danger and because Wilson had been cooperating with caseworkers.
On July 11, the state filed another emergency order, again indicating that the children were not in immediate danger but this time emphasizing the 13-year-old child’s suicide and stating that Wilson knew about an unsecured weapon in her home and that the department had severe concerns about inadequate supervision.
The same judge approved the second order, citing the suicide and claims that the mother and children knew about the unsecured weapon. The children were removed to foster care.
In a July 15 juvenile court hearing, a caseworker testified that the gun that the child used did not belong to Wilson and that no other guns were found in the apartment. One of the siblings said he knew his brother had a gun but was keeping it a secret. The sibling said he thought his brother had likely gotten the gun from a local kid who Wilson had warned him to stay away from. No evidence that Wilson knew about the gun was presented, and she was not charged with any crime in relation to the shooting.
The caseworker also said there was no evidence that the siblings were abused or neglected either before or after their brother’s death and that the children wanted to be with their mother.
The caseworker testified that “upper leadership” at the agency wanted the children removed.
The juvenile court ordered the state to immediately return the children and scolded the agency for compounding the children’s trauma by unnecessarily removing them from their home after their brother’s death.
But the juvenile court denied a separate challenge under the 14th Amendment, reasoning that the agency had followed the proper procedures, and the state Court of Appeals affirmed the decision. The case is now before the Georgia Supreme Court, which heard oral arguments this week.
Arguments
In the Georgia Supreme Court, Wilson’s attorneys argued that because caseworkers took her children without a hearing while acknowledging that the children were not in immediate danger, the state violated the Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment, which says that governments cannot deprive people of life, liberty or property without due process of law.
“Had DFCS sought ex parte removal of Ms. Wilson’s surviving children in the immediate aftermath of their brother’s tragic suicide – amidst a chaotic, unfolding scene – this would be a different case, because that is an emergency,” said Emma Brown-Bernstein, an attorney representing Wilson, during oral arguments Tuesday. “And in an emergency, the state may act first to protect children and provide a hearing after, but this case is not about an emergency. It’s about an unusual circumstance.”
Attorneys for the state agency argue that Wilson’s rights were not violated because they followed the state’s juvenile code, which balances the right to due process with the need to protect children, and that they promptly scheduled the hearing in which Wilson’s parental rights were restored.
“My colleague appeals to the flexible concept of due process, but she demands a rigid rule that strips juvenile courts of their discretion to remove children in all but the most extreme situations of acute harm,” said Deputy Solicitor General Sven Henningson with the state. “A rigid rule here would harm children, and the Constitution does not require it.”
Henningson argued that the case should be considered moot because it was resolved in Wilson’s favor and she got the relief she was seeking, the return of her children.
Justices forcefully questioned Henningson.
“So the state’s position is that the department, the state, can go in, without a parent present, affirmatively say, ‘There is no emergency here, but I would like to take these children,’ and due process permits that?” asked Justice Charlie Bethel.
“In exceptional circumstances –” Henningson began.
“– No emergency — the state is on record: ‘There is no emergent risk to this child, but I would like to take them anyway,’” Bethel said.
“Yes, your honor, in exceptional circumstances short of emergency,” said Henningson.
“What exceptional circumstances were present here?” Bethel asked.
“Particularly after a month had passed,” added Justice Verda Colvin.
“The exceptional circumstances were that a child died in the house, and there was conflicting information from a minor child about whether or not there was an unsecured weapon in the home,” Henningson said. “That would be exceptional.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Tom Tiffany blocks reporters, taking a page from Donald Trump
description: The Republican candidate for governor of Wisconsin, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, has been a reliable ally of President Donald Trump in Congress. He objected to the certification of Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 presidential election, voted repeatedly against reining in Trump’s war in Iran, supported the massive healthcare cuts that are hitting rural Wisconsin […[...]
text:
GOP gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany speaks to supporters at a campaign event in Oconomowoc on Wednesday evening. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)The Republican candidate for governor of Wisconsin, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, has been a reliable ally of President Donald Trump in Congress. He objected to the certification of Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 presidential election, voted repeatedly against reining in Trump’s war in Iran, supported the massive healthcare cuts that are hitting rural Wisconsin particularly hard, and cast the deciding vote in the House for a measure that, had it not stalled in the Senate, would have banned all AI regulation by the states for the next 10 years.
But recently Tiffany has softened his tone, distancing himself from some of Trump’s most unpopular positions. Just this month he conceded that Biden won the 2020 presidential election and said it’s time to wind down the war in Iran. He also claims he wants to “preserve Medicaid for our most vulnerable” and is campaigning on preventing AI data centers from eating up Wisconsin’s farmland. 
A recent text to voters from the Tiffany campaign strikes a friendly, moderate tone, declaring “it’s time to fix problems.”
“When I’m governor, we’ll raise academic standards. We’ll make health care more transparent, stop Wall Street from buying our homes, and lower property taxes. Kids who can read, prices you can see, and a home you can own. That’s a Wisconsin that works for everyone, and that’s the commonsense governor I’ll be.”
But this week, the mask slipped. 
On Thursday, Tiffany’s campaign blocked two reporters from the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel from covering a campaign event. Taking a page from Trump, who yanked White House press credentials from CNN, POLITICO and MS NOW this week because he doesn’t like their reporting, Tiffany and his campaign staff called the Journal-Sentinel’s coverage “slanted” and said only journalists who produce what the campaign deems “balanced” coverage will be allowed to report on his candidacy. 
Tiffany’s effort to keep out journalists whose reporting he doesn’t like violates the same constitutional principle protecting the free press that a federal judge cited when he ordered the White House to restore press passes to the three news outlets Trump banned.
When he was asked about Trump’s White House press ban earlier this week, Tiffany claimed to be a believer in an “open, free press” and said he was not planning to restrict journalists’ access. But, as Henry Redman reports, his campaign not only blocked Journal-Sentinel  reporters Mary Spicuzza and David Clarey from covering Tiffany’s event Thursday, it followed up with a personal attack on Spicuzza from the campaign’s official  social media account, calling her a “liberal activist” and doubling down on the Trump-like threat to ban journalists whose stories Tiffany doesn’t consider “balanced.”
Those stories likely include Spicuzza’s report this week on campaign finance records showing that three billionaires are responsible for about two-thirds of the campaign cash Tiffany has raised so far. 
Spicuzza’s serious, factual journalism raises real questions about whose interests Tiffany would represent as governor — the millions of ordinary Wisconsinites whose problems he says he wants to solve, or his three ultra-rich donors, Diane Hendricks and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein — two of whom live in Illinois —who have given him close to $10 million. Richard Uihlein’s Restoration of America PAC has separately spent another $11.3 million to boost Tiffany, Spicuzza and her colleague Eva Wen report. All that money has given Tiffany a massive financial advantage in the governor’s race, they point out.
By banning journalists and ducking multiple debates, Tiffany reinforces the impression that he prefers to remain in a bubble with like-minded Republicans and high-dollar donors, instead of making himself available to the public and the reporters whose job it is to shine a light on public officials and keep voters informed. That does not bode well for a potential Tiffany administration.
In addition to Tiffany’s Trump-like aversion to criticism and his attacks on a widely respected reporter, his coziness with the conspiracy-minded fringe elements of the Republican party are cause for concern. 
This week, Examiner reporters Redman and Baylor Spears published an investigative report on Tiffany supporter Leonard Boltz, the pilot who crashed while flying Tiffany in a private plane earlier this month. Boltz, the chair of the Langlade County Republican Party and a retired major in the U.S. Air Force, has spent a lot of time flying Tiffany around the state in his small, private plane during the current campaign season. He is also deeply involved in promulgating election-related conspiracy theories and, Spears and Redman report, has said that if Tiffany loses in November it will be because of “cheating” by Democrats. 
Unlike Tiffany, Boltz does not present as a friendly, folksy rural Wisconsinite. Nor has he backed away from the more paranoid edges of MAGA world. In a video of a speech he gave to the Langlade Republican Party in June, linked in Redman and Spears’ story,  he paces and rants, spewing dark warnings about cheating Democrats whom he says are engaged in rampant voter fraud. He gave that speech in front of a poster proclaiming the heroism of Harry Wait, the Racine County election conspiracy theorist who was convicted of breaking the law by impersonating Assembly Speaker Robin Vos and Racine Mayor Cory Mason to request absentee ballots in their names. Boltz, like Wait, wanted to drive Vos out of office for not doing enough to overturn the 2020 election results. 
It’s sobering to contemplate the possibility of a governor of Wisconsin who is close to the most out-there conspiracy theorists in the state party and who has championed their preposterous claims. 
It’s even more concerning if that governor considers himself above scrutiny by the press. When Spears and Redman traveled to a Tiffany campaign event this week to try to get a comment from Tiffany for their story about Boltz, a campaign staffer intervened physically to block the question and adopted an aggressive posture that appeared to be designed to intimidate them. 
That’s not an atmosphere consistent with press freedom, democracy, or a healthy Wisconsin.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Husted took gifts from JobsOhio while he was Ohio lieutenant governor, financial disclosures show
description: Financial disclosures filed by Ohio Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted with the Ohio Ethics Commission show that the quasi-private economic development entity JobsOhio gave gifts to Husted in 2021, 2022, and 2023 when he was lieutenant governor. The gifts could have been as paltry as a meal at a local restaurant or they could have […]
text:
Then-Lt. Gov. Jon Husted (right) welcomes President and CEO of JobsOhio J.P. Nauseef to the podium at a groundbreaking ceremony for Intel’s new semiconductor manufacturing site on Sept. 9, 2022, in Licking County, Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for the Ohio Capital Journal / Republish photo only with original story)Financial disclosures filed by Ohio Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted with the Ohio Ethics Commission show that the quasi-private economic development entity JobsOhio gave gifts to Husted in 2021, 2022, and 2023 when he was lieutenant governor.
The gifts could have been as paltry as a meal at a local restaurant or they could have been trips worth thousands, but Husted’s office won’t say what gifts JobsOhio gave him or what they were worth, neither will JobsOhio, and Ohio law doesn’t require them to.
Husted approaches a close midterm election contest against former Ohio U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat.
While the financial disclosures he filed with the Ohio Ethics Commission show that JobsOhio gave Husted gifts in 2021, 2022 and 2023. In 2024, Husted’s disclosure doesn’t show any gifts from JobsOhio, but it does show one from its CEO, J.P. Nauseef.
JobsOhio was created by the legislature, its board is appointed by the governor, and it controls the state liquor franchise. As a “private” corporation, it has been exempt from most state open meetings and records laws as it has disbursed more than $2 billion in what used to be public money — profits from the state liquor franchise — to private businesses.
In its 15 years, it’s made contributions to many entities, but good government watchdogs have questioned the ones it’s made to the businesses of its board members and those of affiliated entities. 
Earlier this year, the public learned that JobsOhio paid $60,000 to a woman with whom Ohio State President Ted Carter had an “inappropriate relationship” that led to his ouster. 
The money was supposed to fund production of four episodes of a podcast, but only one was made. JobsOhio in March said it would look into trying to claw the money back, but now it won’t respond when asked if it’s attempted to do that. 
Catherine Turcer, executive director of Common Cause Ohio, said of the gifts to Husted that the public should have enough information to determine whether it could influence decision making.
“It makes sense for JobsOhio to be as transparent as possible because otherwise voters are going to really question their motives and assume the worst,” she said. “It’s not necessarily fair that the public would assume the worst, but that’s one of the reasons why transparency is essential… It’s always better to have good information than have things be super-foggy.”
State law allows for quite a bit of fogginess.
Ohio law “only requires that the filer disclose ‘the source of each gift of over seventy-five dollars,’” Paul Nick, executive director of the Ohio Ethics Commission, said in an email. “It does not require the filer to disclose the nature or value of the item.”
Nick added, however, that officials can’t take a gift “that is of such character as to manifest a substantial and improper influence upon the public official or employee with respect to that person’s duties.”
He added, “We’ve said that, in simpler terms, means you cannot accept (and no private party or entity can give) a substantial thing of value if the source of the thing of value is someone who is doing or seeking to business with, regulated by, or interested in matters before the official’s public agency.”
In one of the years Husted received gifts from JobsOhio, Gov. Mike DeWine appointed lobbyist Josh Rubin to chair the JobsOhio Board, in September 2023. Rubin was being paid by Intel at the time and continued to be at least until this year.
Rubin was registered until the end of last year to lobby JobsOhio on behalf of Intel and other businesses, the Capital Journal reported in August. 
JobsOhio has committed $150 million to the long delayed Intel chip-making project near Albany. The DeWine administration, of which Husted was a member at the time, committed more than $2 billion in taxpayer dollars.
Rubin’s lobbying disclosures show that he actively lobbied Husted and the lieutenant governor’s office for Intel until DeWine appointed Husted to fill the U.S. Senate seat at the start of 2025 that was vacated by now-Vice President JD Vance.
Though the substance and value of the gifts remain unknown, Husted received gifts from JobOhio and its CEO while he was still lieutenant governor and the chairman of JobsOhio’s board was being paid to lobby him on behalf of a company that had already gotten more than $600 million from the state and stood to get much more.
Was the gift “a substantial thing of value” and was its source “someone who (was) doing or seeking to business with, regulated by, or interested in matters before the official’s public agency,” we asked.
“I can’t draw any direct conclusions in response to your questions without investigating all of the facts,” Paul Nick of the Ethics Commission said.
He referred to a written explanation of how the law relates to gifts to public officials from nonprofits (JobsOhio is a 501(c)(4) nonprofit organization).
The law “prohibits a person or nonprofit organization from promising, offering, or giving ‘things of value’ to a public official or employee if the things of value could have a ‘substantial’ and ‘improper’ influence on the public official or employee,” it says.
“’Substantial’ gifts could include jewelry, the promise of future employment, meals at expensive restaurants, entertainment activities, such as exclusive golf outings or season tickets for a professional sports team, or travel, meal and lodging expenses,” it says.  
The document defines as an “improper source” entities seeking to do business with a public agency, that are regulated by a public agency, or that have matters before the public agency. 
For a follow-up question on whether the Ethics Commission had any way of knowing what JobsOhio had given Husted short of mounting an investigation — and whether such a probe would be undertaken, Nick was out of the office and not immediately available for comment.
Turcer of Common Cause said that in the context of recent controversies, state laws regarding gifts and political contributions need to be updated — and Husted and JobsOhio need to be more transparent.
In those recent controversies, Husted controversially joined the board of a private bank in 2022, saying he was doing it for the experience, not the money. The bank contributed nearly $500,000 to his political committee. Husted and the DeWine administration also were part of an energy bailout that blew up into one of the biggest corruption scandals in state history. 
“We’re living in a time period when what’s legal and what’s ethical are clearly being bent and broken,” Turcer said.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio lawmakers turn their backs on public schools again
description: The Heights Coalition for Public Education is a grassroots organization formed in 2014 by public education activists in the Cleveland Heights-University Heights (CHUH) school district. Like most taxpayers across Ohio, we want our public schools to excel so that our children, economy, and democracy can thrive. Our focus is state policies that impact the abili[...]
text:
Students work in a classroom. (Photo by Spenser Heaps, States Newsroom.)The Heights Coalition for Public Education is a grassroots organization formed in 2014 by public education activists in the Cleveland Heights-University Heights (CHUH) school district. 
Like most taxpayers across Ohio, we want our public schools to excel so that our children, economy, and democracy can thrive. Our focus is state policies that impact the ability of communities to provide students the quality of education they seek for their children.
The current financial crisis facing Ohio public schools and the legislature’s continued indifference is the latest case in point. 
Communities across Ohio are facing new school levy requests and/or deep cuts to education opportunities. The Cleveland Heights-University Heights schools have done both. 
More than 20% of Ohio school districts will run out of funds in FY2029. 
The Ohio Legislature triggered this crisis when the current state budget abandoned the final phase of the Fair School Funding plan. 
According to Policy Matters, the state appropriated $2.75 billion less for FY26 and FY27 than what the plan required. Like more than 400 districts, our district received less funding than in the previous two-year budget.
By failing to fulfill its constitutional obligation to adequately fund public education, the Legislature shifted even more of the funding burden to local communities. 
This year the state share dropped to 32.2% compared to 43.3% in FY24. In a fair system, the state share would reduce not increase reliance on local property taxes.
Ohio ended its fiscal year in June with more than $2.428 billion in unencumbered funds in part because tax revenue was higher than predicted (estimated $1.237 million) while expenses were about $778 million less than planned. 
Instead of directing this substantial surplus to fill the public education funding gap, lawmakers passed Ohio House Bill 479 and committed more than $1.2 billion to the rainy-day fund and one-time rebates. 
None of the money benefited public education — the only expenditure mandated by the Ohio Constitution.   
As students head back to school, their public schools are hurting. The state could provide them some immediate relief. About $536 million of the surplus is still sitting in the General Revenue Fund. 
Lawmakers should use this remaining surplus to increase state funding for Ohio’s most vulnerable students: children with disabilities and children from low-wage families. 
This investment would give school districts across the state short-term financial relief and improve education opportunities for students whose unique costs have been studied for the Fair School Funding Plan but not addressed in the state budget. 
Over the last four years the number of children with disabilities and the number of children from homes with limited income have increased.
These higher cost students now make up a larger share of public-school enrollment. Their needs are real and extra resources matter, but per pupil spending has been stagnant and shamefully inadequate.
An infusion of funds would enable resource starved school districts to better meet student needs during this school year. 
It would not remove the need for local levies or the need for the legislature that is elected in November to bring forward a budget for the next biennium that adequately funds public education. 
What can we do? 

State lawmakers can commit any remaining surplus funds to the education of our neediest students for this school year. 
Make sure public education is lawmakers’ priority in the next state budget.
Sustain our local public schools. 

The next state budget is the real opportunity to ensure that state policy makers support our aspirations for the 1.2 million children who rely on public education. We need leaders who share that goal and understand that it’s essential to a state budget that helps public schools thrive.

name: Maryland Matters
title: State revenues get modest bump despite ‘mixed’ economic indicators
description: The Board of Revenue Estimates added $320 million to its revenues forecast from March, but the report also highlighted concerns about growing inflation and a sharp drop in tax withholdings in the first half of the coming year compared to a year earlier.
text:
Comptroller Brooke Lierman, left, and Treasurer Dereck Davis, members of the Maryland Board of Revenue Estimates, in a file photo. The panel adopted a new forecast that ads $320 million to the state's revenue projections, but also raises some concerns. (File photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Maryland’s revenue forecast for the current year has improved and a first look at the coming fiscal year shows some modest improvement despite a “mixed picture” of economic indicators.
Those projections, released Thursday by the Board of Revenue Estimates, added $320 million to the board’s revenue forecast from March. But it also highlighted concerns about growing inflation and a projection that tax withholdings in the first half of the year would grow at half the rate of the same period a year ago.
“Overall, this forecast does reflect continued resilience despite real economic uncertainty and real challenges on a day-to-day basis for Marylanders, Maryland families, and small businesses,” said Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D).
“Taken together, these numbers show a mixed picture,” Lierman said. “Our revenues are stronger than expected, but paycheck-related growth is slowing while prices continue to rise, and we certainly cannot examine these numbers in a vacuum.”
Despite the upward revision, to more than $27.4 billion, the new outlook represents a decline of a little less than 1% “on an ongoing basis” compared to fiscal 2026, according to board Director Robert Rehrmann.
“It’s important to note that’s not because we’re forecasting a recession that’s pushing our major revenues down, but it’s a collection of unusual events,” Rehrmann said.
Budget officials ask agencies to tighten belts, including a 10% cut scenario

Last fiscal year, the state benefited from much larger than expected estate taxes, including one payment of $260 million. The unexpected increase is not likely to be repeated in the coming year.
Also not to be counted on is the increase in capital gains taxes in fiscal 2026 that allowed the state to end the year $550 million over the board’s estimate. The tax is considered one of the “most volatile and difficult to predict” revenue sources, Rehrmann said.
The board also revised revenue estimates from an IT and Data tax down. That tax, passed in 2025, has woefully underperformed the $500 million in revenues projected by legislative analysts. In March, the state collected just $35 million in the first half of fiscal 2026. After a full year, the state had collected $100 million.
“In addition to decreasing the board year estimates, we’re also decreasing the out-year estimates as well, and waiting for additional data in this fiscal year on that tax,” Rehrmann said.
The reason for the less-than-expected revenue from the digital tax remains unclear. Opponents of the tax claim the result is proof that businesses shifted operations outside the state. Supporters say businesses may not be fully aware of how the tax applies and others may simply be avoiding payments.
Additionally, the state will have to refund $280 million to Potomac Edison. In July, the Supreme Court of Maryland ruled the state overcharged the company on production of electricity. Ongoing, the decision reduces state revenues by about $15 million per year.
“That, combined with some modest growth rates, is what ultimately ends up in a slight decline” compared to the previous year, Rehrmann said.
The board estimates released Thursday also provided a first look at expectations for fiscal 2028.
There, the board projected general fund revenues of nearly $28.4 billion. The estimated 3.3% growth year over year is still under the state’s trend growth rate of 4%.
Overall, the report is a mixed bag for state fiscal leaders, said Budget Secretary Yaakov “Jake” Weissmann.
