name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC inmate guilty in stabbing death of 3 during prison riot, jury decides
description: Larry White performed a rap for the judge just before receiving three life sentences for joining a mob that killed three.
text:
Inmate Larry White was found guilty at the Lee County Courthouse in Bishopville, S.C., pictured on Dec. 5, 2023. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)A Lee County jury found an inmate guilty Thursday of participating in a mob that killed three people during the nation’s bloodiest prison riot in a quarter-century.
Larry White, now 30, was found guilty of criminal conspiracy and three counts of assault and battery in the first degree. White was one of 47 inmates indicted in connection with the 2018 riot that killed seven and injured 20.
White was the third inmate to go to trial and the third to be found guilty on all counts. Two dozen of those charged have pleaded guilty, and two have died in prison while awaiting trial, according to the Department of Corrections.
The jury handed down its verdict after about two hours of deliberations, ending a four-day trial.
Larry White, 30, was convicted Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, of joining a mob that killed three in a 2018 prison riot. (Photo courtesy of SC Department of Corrections)
White will serve three life sentences, one for each of the assault and battery charges he faced, decided Judge Ferrell Cothran. When the riot began, White was serving 15 years for attempted murder and burglary, with a projected release date in 2031. His lengthy disciplinary record dates to 2017, soon after his sentence began, according to the state prison system.
Just before Cothran handed down his sentence, White gave a statement in the form of a rap. Calling the prison system “crooked and manipulative,” White said he gets to talk to his 13-year-old daughter just once a week and called himself “a decent person.”
“Justice is never served because our stories are never heard,” White said.
Prosecutors argued White was part of a group that killed three men: 28-year-old Raymond “Twin” Scott, 38-year-old Corey Scott and 33-year-old Joshua Jenkins. Video showed White repeatedly stabbing one of the men, whose identity was unclear, as he laid on the ground outside the fence.
“Every time someone dies, the world is less,” prosecutor Barney Giese said during his closing statement. “That includes people in the Department of Corrections who have a right to live and go home.”
White and his attorney contended the violence arose as part of a fight among gang members, not as part of a premeditated plan.
Violence broke out at the maximum security Lee County prison around 7 p.m. on April 15, 2018, after a group of inmates attacked Michael Milledge, a well-liked fellow prisoner, in his cell. A rival gang retaliated, killing the inmate who stabbed Milledge to death.
Word of the attack spread using contraband cellphones, and rival gangs went head to head across the prison’s seven units.
White, a member of the Crips gang, lived in the only unit where other gang members outnumbered the Bloods. After 9 p.m., as tensions rose, White joined gathering gang members, security video played during the trial showed.
The Crips and Gangster Disciples, who wore jackets and other clothing made out of plastic from mattresses meant to protect them from blades, met outside the dorm’s showers. There, they hatched a plan to kill the dorm’s Bloods, prosecutors said.
But White testified Wednesday he only knew the Bloods had to leave.
A group of Crips and Gangster Disciples chased the dorm’s Bloods outside, into the rain. They cornered the rival gang members against a 12-foot razor-wire fence with a locked gate. Some of the men climbed over the fence to escape, many injuring themselves on the razor wire or in jumping to the other side, prosecutors said.
The attacking inmates repeatedly stabbed the four inmates who didn’t make it over, killing three and severely injuring another, prosecutors said.
White joined the attackers for four minutes before returning to his dorm room, where he retrieved a second shank before running back to join his fellow gang members, White said when prosecutors questioned him. He admitted to standing over and stabbing at least one of the men left behind, though he said he didn’t remember who.
The three men killed had a combined 163 stab wounds, prosecutors said. Investigators said White inflicted at least 16 of those wounds, though White said he did half that.
Under state law, any single person in a mob is responsible for the group’s actions, making White responsible for every wound, prosecutors said.
Attorneys recall chaos, bloodshed of Lee County prison riot at trial of inmate

Before inmates chased the Bloods outside, White knew the gate was locked, prosecutors said. White agreed.
After tensions first began to boil in his dorm, White went outside to check the gate and discovered he couldn’t get through, he testified.
That knowledge of the gate was key in showing White and his fellow gang members planned to attack the Bloods, said Giese, a special prosecutor for the attorney general’s office who works with the Department of Corrections. If they really had wanted to let the gang members leave peacefully, they wouldn’t have led them into an ambush, Giese said.
“They had a plan, and when they executed it, they executed three people,” Giese said. “They had no chance down there. They had no chance.”
White’s return to the action after going to his cell for another weapon also showed his intent, prosecutors said. White could have removed himself from the fighting then and hid out there, but instead he decided to return to continue attacking, Giese said.
White rejoined the attack because it seemed “worth doing at that time,” he testified. When Giese asked White if he found the attack enjoyable, White said he did.
“He admits to chopping people up,” Giese told the jury during closing arguments. “He admitted enjoying it.”
Although White didn’t dispute joining in on the attack, he called it a fight that broke out after one of the Bloods threatened a fellow inmate.
White carried a shank because everyone did, he said. He joined the group of gang members because he worried about being alone in his cell and because he knew he’d be asked to answer for himself if he didn’t defend them.
“My purpose was to assemble for self-defense and to defend them if anything were to happen,” White said.
White returned to his cell to check on his cousin, who was still in the dorm, he said. He saw blood on his face when he looked in the mirror. Believing someone had hit him, he ran back outside for retribution, he said.
“When you left your cell, you’re coming all the way back down, and you were going to stab some Bloods, weren’t you?” Giese asked him.
Inmate in deadly SC prison riot guilty of murder, jury decides

“Yes,” White replied.
Much of White’s defense focused on issues in the prison the night of the riot.
Just one guard was responsible for more than 200 inmates in his dorm, and she barricaded herself in a guards’ station after fighting began. Contraband cellphones and weapons were rampant, many doors didn’t lock, and attacks happened often, said defense attorney Christopher Thompson.
“That environment created what happened to these poor victims here,” Thompson said.
The Department of Corrections agreed in 2021 to pay $6 million to settle 81 lawsuits over the riot.
Regardless of the culture at the prison, White should have known it was wrong to stab fellow inmates to death, prosecutors said.
“The buck stops here,” said prosecuting attorney Margaret Scott. “Larry White’s excuses need to stop. Today is the day that Larry White will finally be held accountable for his actions.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Medicaid Fraud Control Unit highlights efficiency; critics call for more funding
description: Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said Thursday that recommendations about increased staffing and funding for existing Medicaid fraud elimination efforts will come at later meetings of the state Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force. The task force was established by executive order July 1 by Gov. Kim Reynolds. It is charged with submitting a final report […[...]
text:
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, joined by Jeremy Ingrim, director of the state Medicaid Fraud Control Unit and other members of the state Medicaid fraud task force for a meeting Sep. 24, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said Thursday that recommendations about increased staffing and funding for existing Medicaid fraud elimination efforts will come at later meetings of the state Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force.
The task force was established by executive order July 1 by Gov. Kim Reynolds. It is charged with submitting a final report by Oct. 29, 2026 for the governor and lawmakers with recommendations on how to reduce and prevent incidents of Medicaid fraud. While the members did not deliberate on any specific planned recommendations, leaders gave updates from work groups about their efforts to find areas for improvement.
Members also got an update on work currently underway by the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit to address fraud within Iowa’s taxpayer-funded healthcare program. Jeremy Ingrim, the director of the unit, said federal evaluations and data have shown Iowa’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit is more efficient than those in other states, “despite being one of the smallest units based on staffing and funding.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ingrim said in federal fiscal year 2025, Iowa’s unit was ranked 10th highest in total convictions with 37 total convictions, above the national average among all 53 units of 22. With total operating expenses for the Iowa MFCU at $1.3 million in FY 2025, he said the approximate government cost for the unit was $36,700 for each conviction, the lowest conviction cost among all units nationwide.
“In other words, the government got the most bang for its buck in Iowa for criminal convictions in federal fiscal year 2025, and the unit remains on track in the current federal fiscal year for similar results,” Ingrim said.
Iowa’s fraud control unit was created in the 1970s and exists within the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals, and Licensing (DIAL).
Dean Lerner, who served as director of Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals under former Democratic Gov. Chet Culver, told reporters after the task force meeting the funding for Iowa MFCU was “woefully inadequate compared to other states with similar budgets.”
Lerner, as well as Kevin Techau, another former Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals director, held a news conference in July calling the task force a “sham.”
Lerner said hiring additional staff and providing more funding for the MFCU would be the most effective way to tackle Medicaid fraud in the state, because 75 cents per dollar spent comes from federal funding, and he said between $4 and $5 are recovered by the unit for each dollar spent.
According to Ingrim, the Iowa MCFU has nine staff members — five investigators, an assistant attorney general, a data analyst who also serves as an auditor, a paralegal, as well as a director. The unit is authorized to have 11 total staff and currently has two vacancies.
Bird said the task force has not yet made funding or staffing recommendations for the MCFU, but said, “that would be something that would be in a final report.” She praised the Iowa MCFU is “a very efficient unit,” but said the task force’s goal was to provide new avenues to find instances of fraud.
“It’s important that we are not just reactive, but we are proactive when it comes to fighting fraud,” Bird said. “And so it is very important that we get those tips from people, and that those are investigated and followed up on — but we also need to be more proactive, looking at where the fraud may be occurring, rather than waiting for someone to discover it and report it. … Even though we have a great and efficient unit, which I do appreciate, we should take a look at everything. Everything’s on the table to make sure that we are doing what we can as a state to eliminate fraud in our state, especially when it comes to taxpayer dollars.”
Working group leaders shared ideas and discussions they had since the August task force meeting on finding ways to allow Iowans to report instances of fraud, as well as to use data and analytics to identify cases where fraud may be occurring by flagging issues like overlapping claims or unusual billing.
Ingrim also told the task force increasing enforcement of the state’s Civil False Claims Act “could increase Medicaid fraud recoveries” in Iowa. The MCFU already has an assistant attorney general who works to ensure Iowa’s participation in nationwide civil cases involving Medicaid programs in multiple states, he said, but said there could be increased efforts to expand enforcement of Iowa Code on actors attempting to present false or fraudulent claims for payment to the state of Iowa.
“Establishing procedures and coordinating available DIAL and Attorney General’s office resources to pursue violations of Iowa Code Chapter 685 may serve as a force multiplier to increase Medicaid fraud recoveries and assist in deterring healthcare fraud in Iowa,” Ingrim said.
Lerner said the Iowa AG’s office is responsible for investigating Iowa Civil False Claims Act cases. He said Bird should increase a focus on pursuing cases against care facilities that do not provide services Medicaid pays for under this law.
“There are numerous opportunities to file those cases against nursing homes that are providing woefully inadequate care to people and killing people,” Lerner said. “Those dollars that are spent on those nursing homes for Medicaid residents should be sought from the nursing homes and put back into the state coffers, and they’re not being done, and that would be one area that should be a big focus.”
Bird said while the task force will create a report on ways to reduce Medicaid fraud, it will be up to state lawmakers and the governor whether to implement their recommendations.
“This is the first step in the process, but a very important one, because we want to make sure that the solutions that we’re proposing, the ideas that task force members have about how to make things better, are things that will work and be effective, and that we are doing everything we can to eliminate fraud in Iowa,” Bird said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma can’t deny Jewish charter school from opening, federal judge decides
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — In a decision that could enable the nation’s first religious charter school to open, an Oklahoma City federal judge has ruled in favor of a Jewish school seeking to operate with taxpayer funds. Oklahoma Western District Judge David L. Russell decided Thursday that the Statewide Charter School Board violated the First Amendment […]
text:
Oklahoma Western District Judge David L. Russell decided Thursday the state cannot exclude religious applicants from accessing charter school funding. Russell heard arguments in the case on Aug. 5 at the William J. Holloway Jr. United States Courthouse in Oklahoma City, pictured Dec. 4, 2023. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/ Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — In a decision that could enable the nation’s first religious charter school to open, an Oklahoma City federal judge has ruled in favor of a Jewish school seeking to operate with taxpayer funds.
Oklahoma Western District Judge David L. Russell decided Thursday that the Statewide Charter School Board violated the First Amendment when it voted against establishing Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School solely because the school would teach a particular religion. 
The board had denied opening Ben Gamla in light of a 2024 Oklahoma Supreme Court ruling that rejected taxpayer-funded, faith-based charter schools.
“The Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board wanted to follow the First Amendment, but regretfully, they were bound by Oklahoma law when reviewing Ben Gamla’s application,” the board’s attorney, A.J. Ferate, said Thursday. “The court’s ruling today affirms that religious charter school applicants should not be excluded from consideration simply because of their religiosity.”
Attorney A.J. Ferate speaks to news reporters after a hearing Aug. 5 in Oklahoma City federal court over a Jewish charter school. Ferate represents the Statewide Charter School Board, which denied the school. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The board will review the court order at its next meeting and take the appropriate next steps, according to a statement from its hired legal firm, the First Liberty Institute.
The decision allows the school to proceed toward opening. However, attorneys on all sides of the case have said the matter could be caught in a string of appeals ultimately leading to the U.S. Supreme Court, which deadlocked on a previous attempt to open a Catholic charter school in Oklahoma.
Two groups of state residents intervened in the Ben Gamla case to oppose the school’s creation. One, mostly made up of Jewish Oklahomans, is represented by local and national legal organizations, including the American Civil Liberties Union and Americans United for Separation of Church and State. 
The judge’s conclusion “opens the door to a dangerous sea change for our democracy,” the group’s legal team said in a statement.
“Forcing taxpayers to fund religious public schools violates state and federal law,” the attorneys said. “Ben Gamla will not only indoctrinate students into a particular religion — it will discriminate against families that don’t share the school’s beliefs. We will continue to fight for all Oklahomans, who deserve public schools that are secular and open to all students.”
Charter schools have long been considered to be public schools because they primarily rely on taxpayer funding, though they’re run by non-elected boards and are exempt from certain regulations.
Attorneys supporting Ben Gamla contend charter schools more closely resemble private entities that should be free to espouse a religion.
Former Democratic U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch, of Florida, applied to open Ben Gamla as a free online charter school. Ben Gamla would teach the tenets of the Jewish faith along with typical school subjects.
Former U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch speaks to the Statewide Charter School Board on Jan. 12 in Oklahoma City to present an application to open an online Jewish charter school in Oklahoma. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Deutsch, a plaintiff in the lawsuit, said Thursday the court decision is a “victory for educational freedom, religious equality, and families in Oklahoma.”
“The state cannot single out religious schools for exclusion while welcoming everyone else into the charter school program,” he said in a statement. “We’re eager to open wide the doors of educational opportunity in Oklahoma.”
The federal judge agreed after listening to arguments from all sides of the case in an Aug. 5 hearing. Excluding private applicants from opening a state-funded school just because of their religious character violates the free exercise of religion, Russell decided.
Unlike the state Supreme Court, the federal judge determined charter schools are not government actors who must remain secular.
An Oklahoma law that requires charter schools to be nonsectarian “expressly discriminates” against religious schools that would otherwise be eligible for state funding, he decided.
However, Attorney General Gentner Drummond contended in a separate lawsuit that the board intentionally excluded other concerns raised about Ben Gamla’s viability outside of the religious element when voting to reject its application. Drummond alleged the board did so to benefit the school’s chances to succeed in court. 
That lawsuit, filed in Oklahoma County District Court, hasn’t had any movement in months, records show. The Attorney General’s Office confirmed Thursday that the case is still active.
Drummond, who led the legal fight against the Catholic charter school, originally was listed as a defendant in the federal lawsuit over Ben Gamla, but he had himself removed from the case.
“In 2024, the Oklahoma Supreme Court ruled that a religious charter school violates the Oklahoma Constitution, state law and the U.S. Constitution,” Drummond said in a statement Thursday. “The U.S. Supreme Court left that decision in place last year.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana nabs $175M from feds to fix regional electricity ‘choke point’
description: The project will unlock 2,000 to 4,000 megawatts of transfer capacity for an Indiana grid interconnection that Gov. Mike Braun dubbed a "choke point."
text:
U.S. Department of Energy General Counsel Jonathan Brightbill announces $1.9 billion in transmission grants, while Indiana Energy and Natural Resources Secretary Suzanne Jaworowski looks on, at the Statehouse in Indianapolis on  Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana has won $175 million in federal funding to upgrade a critical “choke point” between two regional electricity grid operators, officials announced Thursday.
“The challenge isn’t simply generating more electricity,” U.S. Department of Energy General Counsel Jonathan Brightbill said. “It’s making the grid so that it can move power where it is needed quickly, affordably, and reliably across one of the most important regional seams in the country — and that comes and lands right here in Indiana.”
The “seam” is where the Midcontinent Independent System Operator’s service territory meets that of the PJM Interconnection. The border between the two regional transmission organizations runs through Illinois, Indiana, Michigan and Kentucky.
Gov. Mike Braun speaks on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026 at the Statehouse in Indianapolis. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Brightbill said the project will unlock 2,000 to 4,000 megawatts of transfer capacity for an interconnection in the Hoosier state that Gov. Mike Braun dubbed a “pinch point” and a “choke point” in comments to reporters.
The work is expected to save ratepayers in and outside of Indiana between $50 million and $150 million annually by relieving congestion at that interconnection point.
“Congestion, that may cut off access to generation that’s available,” Brightbill said. “The way the bulk power system works, you end up with pockets. And then with dynamic pricing … you can end up with prices spiking in localized areas that then will cost those local ratepayers a lot of money.”
The four-year project will include:

Replacing old power lines with new ones with materials that carry electricity more efficiently.
Implementing dynamic assessment of the lines, allowing them to carry more electricity under ideal weather conditions. Static lines are set more conservatively, for the worst-case scenario.
Adding topographic software so grid operators can direct electricity from cheaper sources along more efficient routes to where it’s needed.

The project’s sponsors will put up an additional $150 million for a total price tag of $325 million.
Brightbill was in Indiana to announce the selection of 31 projects nationwide worth more than $5 billion. The $1.9 billion in federal investments are set to leverage an additional nearly $3.4 billion.
“Selected projects will reconduct or rebuild more than 1,500 miles of transmission infrastructure. They will deploy cutting-edge, grid-enhancing technologies across nearly 21,000 miles of transmission lines,” Brightbill said. “And, together, we are expected to unlock more than 23 gigawatts of additional grid capacity. That’s a lot.”
Money for the initiative was authorized under the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law during former President Joe Biden’s administration.
Originally called Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships, President Donald Trump’s administration has renamed the program to SPARK, which stands for Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades.
Nuclear regulation deal inked
Also on Thursday, Indiana became the 41st state to take over responsibility of non-energy nuclear and radioactive materials used in medical, industrial, academic and fusion technologies from the federal government.
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission can hand down oversight under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954. Kentucky became the first “agreement state” in 1962. Dozens of states have followed in its stead, with Indiana the latest.
The announcement has been in the works for years. Then-Gov. Eric Holcomb in 2021 submitted a letter of intent to pursue a deal.
“Agreement state status gives us better customer service, faster permit review times — which was always an issue — faster incident responses, and lower regulatory fees,” Braun said.
Gov. Mike Braun, front left, and U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission Chair Ho Nieh sign an agreement giving Indiana control over nuclear permitting and inspections within the state, on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026 at the Statehouse in Indianapolis. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
The Indiana Department of Homeland Security will manage the program.
Spokeswoman Ashley Morgan said the agency will have five health physicists responsible for handling licensing and inspections.
The work will be largely funded by licensing fees. An eight-page fee schedule shows costs, mostly in the thousands, for each type of license.
The state Department of Homeland Security also houses a dedicated radiation team managing nuclear emergency response and risk, and works with communities exploring nuclear — in collaboration with the Indiana Office of Energy Development.
“Making more licensing and permitting decisions here in Indiana rather than in Washington means Hoosiers have more control over Indiana’s energy future,” Braun said, calling the deal a “necessary step for Indiana to meet our nuclear energy generation goals.”

CONTACT US




Federal officials, however, maintain regulatory authority over all commercial nuclear power reactors, research reactors and nuclear fuel cycle facilities, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s website.
Indiana currently has no nuclear plants in operation. But Braun and other state leaders hope to “lead” the nation in nuclear energy.
Commission Chair Ho Nieh said permissions for nuclear-fueled energy production will come faster under Trump’s “new NRC.”
“If Indiana and companies in Indiana want to pursue nuclear energy, I can assure you that the NRC will not be an impediment,” he said. “We will perform our safety responsibilities with efficiency, with credibility, and predictability … There’s a new NRC that has been created here, one that is going to safely enable and accelerate the deployment of nuclear technologies in America.”
The federal agency plans to approve applications for first-of-its-kind reactors in 18 months or less, and repeat reactor types in a year or less, Nieh said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Senate candidate Scott Colom calls for temporary ban on data centers in Mississippi
description: Mississippi Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom speaks with Madison County resident Carol Mann at a press conference in Jackson on Thursday, Sep. 24, 2026
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom on Thursday called for a temporary ban on new data centers in Mississippi. 
“The reality is, the consequences of data centers in Mississippi are already here. We’re seeing it in our power bills. We’re seeing it where we live. We’re seeing it where we pray,” Colom said at a press conference.
Colom, who is challenging incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith has a list of conditions that he would want met before proceeding with any new data center construction in the state. It includes having data centers pay their own way and more transparency about the deals. He said this would give the state a chance to study the impacts of data centers and come up with regulations. 

While artificial intelligence and data centers have come up in midterm elections in other states, and have already become an issue for Mississippi’s statewide elections next year, they have not been a driving issues in Mississippi’s congressional races to date. Data center development decisions have been made at the state and local levels, with Republican Gov. Tate Reeves being a leading advocate for them. A recent poll from Pew Research Center found that over half of Americans believe data centers are mostly bad for the environment. 
Data centers in Mississippi have come under increasing scrutiny. In the small town of Walls, hundreds of people showed up to a planning meeting this week in opposition to rezoning for a potential data center. Since 2024, the state has seen an influx of projects, part of the historic investment building data centers nationwide to power artificial intelligence. Mississippi has seven data center projects under construction and local leaders are interested in bringing more. 
A few states have passed temporary bans on data centers. New York announced a one year moratorium on data centers and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott paused new data center approvals until the state completes audits of the state’s power grid. 
Colom said Hyde-Smith has not signed on to the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill designed to protect customers from paying for upgrades to the grid that data centers need.
“She refuses to provide any oversight,” Colom said, “And then last week we learned why she has refused to do it. The AI data center Super PAC is running ads on her behalf.”
Leading the Future, a super PAC funded by Greg Brockman, president of OpenAI, and prominent venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, is spending $2 million to support Hyde-Smith and three other Republican Senate candidates. The group has cautioned that too much government regulation of AI will slow down innovation and adoption, as has President Donald Trump. 
“The senator’s campaign has no involvement in the outside group’s ads. Senator Hyde-Smith shares the concerns of Mississippians and wants to make sure that families come first, that local resources are protected, and that data centers are only built once those standards are met,” said Jake Monssen, Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager.

title: Lawsuit alleges companies collected $30 million in ‘illegal wager on human life’
description: Another Iowa lawsuit has been filed based on claims of illegal wagering on people’s life expectancy through insurance policies. The lawsuit involves the late George A. Neukom Jr. of Florida and two multimillion-dollar insurance policies that were allegedly taken out on Neukom’s life by people unknown to him. After Neukom died three years ago, a […]
text:
(Photo by Mohamad Faizal Bin Ramli/iStock/Getty Images Plus)Another Iowa lawsuit has been filed based on claims of illegal wagering on people’s life expectancy through insurance policies.
The lawsuit involves the late George A. Neukom Jr. of Florida and two multimillion-dollar insurance policies that were allegedly taken out on Neukom’s life by people unknown to him. After Neukom died three years ago, a bank and two companies collected the policies’ death benefits. The lawsuit claims the estate is legally entitled to recover those benefits.
The lawsuit claims Neukom bore no financial risk from the policies’ purchase since it was strangers who paid the premiums on the policy, expecting to collect a profit either by receiving the policy’s proceeds when he died or by selling the policy to yet another group of investors who also were strangers to Neukom.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While the practice of wagering on the life expectancy of strangers through insurance policies dates back to the 16th century, the spread of stranger-originated life insurance, or STOLI, policies originated in the early 2000s. The policies are designed to serve the interests of institutional investors who hope to profit on people’s death through high-value policies that serve no traditional insurance-related need.
STOLI polices are widely considered to be illegal, and under the state law of Delaware, where many insurance companies are incorporated, a decedent’s estate can recover from the investors any proceeds that were paid out through a STOLI policy. Because of those laws, civil lawsuits seeking recovery of death benefits are on the rise.
In the newly filed Iowa lawsuit, Neukom’s estate is suing U.S. Bank, Wilmington Trust and two companies identified in court records only as “Company A” and “Company B.”
According to the lawsuit, Neukom was a resident of Florida when he died on Sept. 5, 2023. The lawsuit over his life insurance is filed in Iowa due to the involvement of Principal Life Insurance Company, which is based in Des Moines and which allegedly collected the premiums on Neukom’s life-insurance policies from U.S. Bank and Wilmington Trust.
According to the lawsuit, from 2011 until Neukom’s death in 2023,  U.S. Bank was the owner of, and the beneficiary under, a $20 million insurance policy on Neukom’s life that was issued by Principal in 2008. After Neukom died, U.S. Bank claimed and received that policy’s $20 million death benefit, the lawsuit alleges.
After collecting the death benefit, U.S. Bank allegedly transferred the money to Company A, which had hired U.S. Bank to serve on its behalf as its agent, according to the lawsuit.
Separate from that policy, the lawsuit claims, Wilmington Trust was the owner and beneficiary of a $10 million life insurance policy on Neukom. After Neukom’s death, the lawsuit alleges, Wilmington Trust collected that policy’s death benefit and then transferred the money to Company B, which had hired Wilmington Trust to act on its behalf.
The lawsuit asserts that although U.S. Bank knows Company A’s true identity, and Wilmington Trust knows Company B’s true identity, the Neukom estate has not been able to ascertain that information.
The lawsuit notes that “virtually all jurisdictions” in the United States prohibit third parties from creating life insurance policies for the benefit of those who have no relationship to the insured. The policies, the lawsuit claims, “lack an insurable interest and are thus an illegal wager on human life.”
According to the Neukom estate, although human-life speculators have operated for hundreds of years, it has only been in the past 20 years that STOLI policies have been issued on a massive, multibillion-dollar scale. As part of that alleged scheme, STOLI promoters worked with a nationwide network of insurance producers, who, acting as agents for those promoters, identified senior citizens who met the promoters’ investment criteria.
“Not only do these STOLI policies violate public policy against wagering and insurable-interest laws, but they take advantage of senior citizens and otherwise convert a legitimate life insurance product into an illegitimate cash machine whereby a stranger to the insured is more interested in seeing the insured dead than alive,” the lawsuit claims.
In Neukom’s case, the lawsuit asserts, a STOLI promoter by the name of Oceanus, a Wisconsin-based company, procured the two policies at issue, along with 160 similar policies on other seniors.
The lawsuit alleges civil conspiracy, aiding and abetting, and violations of state insurance laws. The defendants in the case, which do not include Principal, have yet to file a response to the lawsuit.
Separate lawsuit names Cedar Rapids company
In March, the estate of the late Evelyn Zeman of Michigan sued a Cedar Rapids company called ULI Funding, alleging a group of individuals who had no ties to Zeman took out a $1.1 million life insurance policy on her in 2006 when she was 79 years old.
The lawsuit claims Zeman had no need for the policy and bore no financial risk as these strangers paid the premiums on the policy, expecting to collect a profit either by receiving the policy’s proceeds when she died or by selling the policy to yet another group of investors who also were strangers to Zeman.
The lawsuit alleges ULI Funding is the owner of the policy and collected its proceeds from the insurance company Transamerica Occidental Life Insurance Company. ULI Funding has denied any wrongdoing in the matter and the case is still pending, with discovery and depositions now taking place.

title: Democrats gain 4 in US Senate GOP on Iran war resolution, but vote falls short
text: WASHINGTON — Despite skyrocketing fuel prices and sinking approval ratings for President Donald Trump’s conflict in Iran ahead of the November midterms, Senate Republicans blocked Democrats’ efforts Thursday to check the president’s unfettered military action in the Middle East.Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, Rand Paul, R-Ky., and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., joined Democrats in supporting the House-approved Iran War Powers Resolution. But the number of Republicans who wanted to curb Trump’s prolonged military action in the Islamic Republic fell short in the final tally of 49-50.While Collins, Murkowski and Paul have supported Iran War Powers Resolutions over the past several months, Thursday’s vote marked the first time the retiring Tillis crossed the aisle on the issue. The North Carolina Republican announced he would not seek reelection after Trump publicly harangued him for voting against the “big beautiful bill” in July 2025. Sen. John Fetterman, a Pennsylvania Democrat, voted against the resolution, as he has on more than a dozen occasions. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., did not vote.Senate Republicans locked in tight races, including one who spoke out about the war just one day ago, voted against the measure.Sen. Jon Husted, who is facing a heated challenge in Ohio from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, said Wednesday, “The war needs to come to an end as quickly as possible so that we can lower gas prices,” according to Politico.Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who’s facing a challenge from Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, and Sen. Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican facing an increasingly tight race, also voted no.House passes resolutionThe block in the Senate comes after seven House Republicans, including two vulnerable Iowa incumbents who for the first time supported halting the Iran conflict via a War Powers Resolution, jumped on board with Democrats Sept. 15 to pass the measure 220-204.Iowa Republicans Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks both face tough reelection bids rated as “toss-ups” by the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter.The war has dragged on since late February, ricocheting through the Middle East and disrupting global oil supplies. Americans are paying on average $1.30 more per gallon of gasoline than they were a year ago, according to AAA. Diesel hit a record high national average of $6.52 Tuesday.Trump mulls war optionsTrump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signaled this week neither were ready to settle the conflict when they addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York City. Trump contemplated aloud whether he would “annihilate” Iran’s population “with no chance of survival” if the Islamic Republic leaders refused to make a deal. Trump has made similar comments as far back as April, when he was still promising a swift end to the conflict.Thursday’s vote marks the 15th time Senate Democrats have forced an Iran War Powers Resolution on the floor. Thursday’s vote was on Washington state Democrat Rep. Pramila Jayapal’s resolution that passed the House on July 23.  A similar measure squeaked through the Senate 50-48 on June 23, when Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., joined Collins, Murkowski and Paul in support – though two Republicans, Kentucky’s Mitch McConnell and Pennsylvania’s Dave McCormick, were absent.Cassidy lost the Senate Republican primary recently after Trump endorsed another candidate. But Cassidy voted against the latest War Powers Resolution Thursday.Diesel export banIowa’s longtime Sen. Chuck Grassley urged the White House as recently as Wednesday to ban diesel oil exports.Trump administration officials have so far tiptoed around the issue of halting diesel exports. The White House denied a Politico report Wednesday claiming the administration was preparing for a 90-day embargo. Energy Secretary Chris Wright reportedly told Reuters Wednesday that an export ban would put “upward pressure” on the oil market and increase prices.A White House official denied the Politico report in an email to States Newsroom Thursday.But Trump signaled Tuesday that he’s “been talking about it” and supports the idea, according to reporters who traveled with him to New York.Global petroleum supply is backlogged as Iran maintains its stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen gain more control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Both narrow passageways on either side of the Arabian Peninsula are major transit points for crude oil and liquid natural gas exports, among other commodities like fertilizer. Ukraine’s recent strikes on Russian oil refineries are also contributing to rising fuel prices. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sharply criticized Russia during his address at the U.N. Wednesday.

name: VTDigger
title: Restoring the river’s memory: Bringing back the banks of the Batten Kill
description:
Recent efforts have established natural structures, stabilized eroding banks, reestablished more natural floodplains, and created narrowed channels that cool the water.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Restoring the river’s memory: Bringing back the banks of the Batten Kill.
text:
The Sunderland River Project, led in part by Trout Unlimited’s Jacob Fetterman, aims to restore a damaged floodplain, stabilize eroding banks, and bring back a more beneficial habitat for trout and other wildlife. Here, Fetterman stands at the edge of the eroded bank and indicates where and when the excavation work and plantings will begin. Photo by Danielle M. Crosier/Bennington Banner

This story by Danielle M. Crosier was first published in the Bennington Banner on Sept. 15, 2026.
SUNDERLAND — On a quiet stretch of the Batten Kill River, located between Arlington and Manchester, conservationists are working to help the river remember how it once moved, how it flooded, and how it cooled itself. The Sunderland River Project, led in part by Trout Unlimited’s Jacob Fetterman, aims to restore a damaged floodplain, stabilize eroding banks, and bring back a more beneficial habitat for trout and other wildlife.
On a warm morning in early fall, and standing at the edge of the north bank, Fetterman described a river that has been constrained for decades by agriculture, as well as the practice of mowing right up to the water’s edge.
The result is a sheer, unstable drop and a river that runs too straight and too warm to support the kinds of fish and floodplain life that it once held.
Along portions of this stretch of the river, the north bank is an eight‑foot drop to a channel that’s about three feet deep – with the river “cut in, left a little bit high” where the bank has repeatedly collapsed and eroded.
On the opposite bank, the south bank, the Batten Kill still has “pretty good floodplain access,” allowing water to spread out during higher flows and recede back into its channel during drier events. That natural access helps mitigate downstream flooding.
The goal on the north side is to recreate some of that function – once again allowing the river to spill out, to slow down, and to rebuild its own richly populated habitat.
A river cut too deep and running too straight
Beginning in the 1990s, the Batten Kill River began experiencing a major decline in wild trout populations due to human-induced habitat loss, rising water temperatures, and other contributing factors.
Recent efforts by groups like Trout Unlimited and the Battenkill Conservancy, both of which have launched relatively aggressive restoration projects, have established natural wood and rock structures, stabilized eroding banks, ensured that the river can properly aerate, reestablished more natural floodplains, and created narrowed channels that cool the water.
These efforts have measurably increased the populations of brown and brook trout.
Explaining that, in this reach, the Batten Kill has been forced into a shape that serves neither people nor wildlife particularly well, Fetterman pointed to the drawbacks of the current channel. It runs straight, relatively deep, and is slow‑moving; it is largely devoid of woody debris that would normally break up the flow; and it is unshaded by trees, which allows the water to warm.
That combination is difficult on cold‑water species like trout. Fetterman notes that in this section, you might see an occasional trout move through, but would most likely not see fish “holding” in place to feed and rest the way they historically did in the past.
Without structure, cooler water, and varied depths, the river becomes a long uniform run rather than a string of riffles, pools, and cool shady hiding spots.
The bank itself is evidence of years of stress. The field above was rather consistently mowed to within about four feet of the edge, removing deep‑rooted trees that could hold the soil together. As floods hit this unnaturally steep and unvegetated face, “massive amounts of sediment” began to slough off the bank and into the river.
The river has been trying to correct that by cutting and collapsing but, without room and without rooted vegetation, each correction simply results in greater damage.
Rebuilding the floodplain and grading back the bank
The heart of the Sunderland River Project is a careful reshaping of the north bank so that the river can reconnect with its floodplain.
Fetterman describes a phased cut where an excavator will be brought in to taper the bank. The new slope will run from the current water elevation back about 10 feet on a two‑to‑one slope, softening the eight‑foot drop. Beyond that, workers will create a roughly 20‑foot “bankfull bench” – a flat or gently sloped terrace at the level of the river’s typical annual high flow.
“Bankfull” flows, Fetterman explained, are those regular high‑water events that do most of the work of forming and maintaining the channel. Larger floods do occur, but it’s that recurring bankfull stage that shapes the river’s curves, bars, and banks over time.

The Sunderland River Project, led in part by Trout Unlimited’s Jacob Fetterman, aims to restore a damaged floodplain, stabilize eroding banks, and bring back a more beneficial habitat for trout and other wildlife. Here, Fetterman stands at the edge of the eroded bank and looks down at the river below. Photo by Danielle M. Crosier/Bennington Banner

By giving the Batten Kill a bench at bankfull level, the project allows water to spread out horizontally instead of just cutting down vertically. When flows rise, the water will be better able to move across this new surface. The results will be a slower velocity and the dropping of sediment – and the river will once again begin to build a healthier floodplain rather than simply scouring a deeper trench.
Fetterman is clear that the river will always have the final say. The project’s role is to set up conditions – gradual slopes, deep roots, room to move – to ensure that, over years and decades, the channel can shift in a way that is safer for downstream communities and more supportive of aquatic life.
Planting shade, structure, and stability
Regrading alone would leave the soil highly vulnerable to erosion. To stabilize it, the project team is moving quickly to establish vegetation.
Immediately after excavation, the newly shaped surfaces will be seeded and mulched with a mix of grasses, wildflowers, and wetland species and designed to form a sod layer and early root network that will hold the soil in place. Next, the group will help to establish a diverse planting of trees and shrubs this fall. Fetterman listed species that include red osier dogwood, willows (such as native pussy willow), sycamore, cottonwood, black cherry, river birch, maples, and oaks.
These plantings will initially extend just 30–40 feet back from the river’s edge, creating a corridor of riparian vegetation. Ducks Unlimited will later extend that planting an additional 160 feet into the field, for a total of roughly 200 feet of restored buffer.
This living edge is designed to serve multiple roles – specifically to provide shade, structure, stability, and habitat.
Overhanging branches will help to provide shade and will in turn cool the water during the summer months, a critical factor for trout establishment. Fallen limbs and trees will create the woody debris that slows the velocity of the current, help to establish and form pools, and protect fish. Deep roots will bind soil and slow erosion, so that flooding events remove less sediment. Shrubs and trees will support insects, birds, amphibians, and mammals in the riparian zone.
Over time, those plantings will turn what is now an exposed, collapsing edge into a layered riverside forest that both protects the bank and enriches the river.
Ducks Unlimited, Trout Unlimited, and a coalition of interested partners
The Sunderland River Project emerged when Ducks Unlimited purchased the former agricultural field with the explicit intent of restoring wetland habitat. That acquisition opened possibilities beyond crop production – a mosaic of wetlands, riparian forest, and an improved river corridor.
Recognizing the Batten Kill as a major cold-water resource, Trout Unlimited joined as a partner to focus on the in-river and tributary components. The site also includes Tanner Brook, a cold-water tributary that flows in through the woods. Tanner Brook has also become a key part of the work.
The overall project has drawn in a broad coalition that includes the Bennington County Conservation District, the Batten Kill Watershed Alliance, the Vermont Department of Fish and Wildlife, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), and Watersheds United Vermont (which administers the grant funding).
Funding comes through the Vermont DEC Clean Water Project program, which supports efforts to improve water quality, reduce erosion, and restore natural processes in rivers and wetlands statewide.
As a part of “permitting and due diligence,” Fetterman also noted that an archaeological study was completed along the strip to be excavated, ensuring that no significant historic resources would be disturbed.
Mimicking the effect of beavers in Tanner Brook
While excavators reshape the Batten Kill’s north bank, a quieter form of engineering will unfold in the Tanner Brook tributary. In Tanner Brook, crews plan to install approximately ten Beaver Dam Analogs (BDAs) over about a half‑mile stretch.
BDAs are human‑built structures that mimic natural beaver dams. Fetterman described them as rows of wooden stakes driven across the channel, perpendicular to the flow of the water. These stakes are then interwoven with branches and plant material, much like a beaver will weave a lattice of sticks.

An excavator at the site of the Sunderland River Project has been brought in to taper the bank, creating a new gradual slope. Beyond that, workers will create a roughly 20‑foot “bankfull bench” – a flat or gently sloped terrace at the level of the river’s typical annual high flow. Photo by Danielle M. Crosier/Bennington Banner.

The low leaky dams are intended to raise water levels slightly and slow the current, spread water out over the floodplain, reconnect side channels and wetlands, and create deeper pools and varied habitat for trout and other species.
In winter, trout seek out deeper, somewhat warmer water – “warmer” in a relative sense, in comparison with the shallow fast‑flowing sections that can freeze more solidly. By building pools and improving groundwater interactions, BDAs can provide fish with more options, enabling them to endure the more harsh winter conditions.
Fetterman noted that BDAs are well suited to small tributaries like Tanner Brook, where flows are lower and structures can persist.
In the mainstem Batten Kill, however, the larger forces at work would likely blow out such small dams in a single high‑water event – so the river restoration there relies instead on felled large trees that are placed along the margins to form cover and complexity within the flow.
Letting the river do the work
Taken together, the bank grading, the floodplain reconnection, the riparian planting, and the beaver-mimicking structures, form a single philosophy – give water more space and better tools, and then step back and allow the river to adapt.
Fetterman emphasized that some erosion in the early years will be expected. Spring run‑off, for example, will test the new slopes and the vegetation. The river will nibble at the edges, deposit gravel and sand where it slows, and carve pockets where woody material deflects the flow.
The project team is not trying to force the Batten Kill into a fixed design. Instead, they are restoring the ingredients – the room, the shade, the roots, the wood, and the wetlands – so that the natural processes can rebuild a more resilient system.
In the long term, that will translate to reduced impacts downstream during flood events, as floodwaters have space to spread and slow. It also translates to cleaner water, with less sediment and nutrient-laden runoff entering the channel.
Additionally, there will be a healthier trout habitat – with cooler temperatures, deeper pools, and sheltering structures. And, richer wetlands and riparian corridors will develop – supporting birds, amphibians, invertebrates, and plants.
For the communities along this stretch of the Batten Kill, the Sunderland River Project is both “practical infrastructure” and “ecological healing.”
It recognizes that a river is not just the water between its banks, but it is also the floodplain, the wetlands, the forests, and that tributaries that breathe with it.
In Fetterman’s work – and in the partnerships behind this effort – there is an understanding that restoring a river is less about imposing a new shape and more about giving it back the space and the conditions it needs to remember its own shape and path.
Implementation timeline
According to Fetterman, construction on the regrading and floodplain work should soon begin nearing its conclusion. The tree and shrub planting will follow at a later date in the fall.
The Ducks Unlimited wetland restoration will continue into next summer, extending the vegetated buffer and expanding habitat in the field beyond the newly graded bank.
As the machinery leaves and the first roots take hold, the Batten Kill and Tanner Brook will begin – slowly and quietly – to rewrite their own courses, guided by the work of partners intent on helping these rivers function once again as healthy rivers must.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Restoring the river’s memory: Bringing back the banks of the Batten Kill.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: RI Energy bills are going up, then down, then up again. What to expect starting Oct. 1.
description: The seasonal spike in electricity bills won’t burn as big a hole as usual in Rhode Island Energy customers’ wallets. At least, not this year. The Oct. 1 start date for the six-month period of higher electricity pricing coincides with the beginning of a separate set of company-issued refunds, mandated under the 2022 sale of […]
text:
Seasonal electric price increases for Rhode Island Energy customers take effect Oct. 1. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)The seasonal spike in electricity bills won’t burn as big a hole as usual in Rhode Island Energy customers’ wallets.
At least, not this year.
The Oct. 1 start date for the six-month period of higher electricity pricing coincides with the beginning of a separate set of company-issued refunds, mandated under the 2022 sale of the state’s poles, wires and gas lines. 
The net impact for the average residential electric customer is a monthly increase of $16.42 starting Oct. 1.
Starting in January, a second set of customer discounts from the state’s regional gas cap-and-trade program revenue will reduce bills by another $20.45 for each of the first three months of 2027.
Buckle up! The energy bill roller coaster is about to begin.

Increased demand and limited availability cause natural gas prices to rise during the colder months, returning to a lower cost in the summer. Rhode Island Energy by law cannot profit off of electricity purchased from third-party suppliers, instead passing the prices directly onto its customers, following review by state regulators.
While the Public Utilities Commission has heavily scrutinized and at times forced Rhode Island Energy to temper service fee hikes, the panel cannot reject or alter the seasonal supply pricing unless there is proof that the company failed to meet procurement standards.
Chairman Ronald Gerwatowski acknowledged the cut-and-dry nature of its review of seasonal electricity price hikes during the commission’s meeting on Thursday.
“I think there was a lot of attention on it,” he said of the higher supply pricing, which has promoted mounting criticism from ratepayer advocates for years. “In the end, it was not complicated.”
The commission unanimously approved the seasonal electric rates almost immediately, without discussion. There was also no discussion on its stamp of approval for the winter bill credits, drawn from the state’s Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative program.
Gov. Dan McKee, who pushed for winter bill discounts in conjunction with an emergency declaration over rising energy costs in July, praised the commission for backing his proposal. 
“I’ve said for years that energy affordability is one of my top priorities, and that I will use every tool available to lower costs for Rhode Islanders,” McKee said in a statement Thursday. “This summer, we took unprecedented emergency action because families needed relief, and today we are delivering on that commitment. Together with the other relief we have secured, Rhode Island households are now seeing historic support on their energy bills at a time when they need it most.”  
Rhode Island Energy acknowledged ongoing affordability concerns in an emailed response to Rhode Island Current.
“Together, these credits will help offset bill impacts while we continue to deliver safe, reliable service,” said Michael Dalo, a company spokesperson.
Winter 2027 is coming 
The combination of bill credits and customer refunds will continue to provide relief on energy bills through next fall. But market-driven prices are forecasted to keep rising, hitting customers just as the final credits end.
Electric pricing could surge to 19.2 cents per-kilowatt-hour starting in October 2027, according to mandated forecasts submitted by Rhode Island Energy to state regulators. If the forecast proves correct, this would be the highest electricity supply pricing in state history, more than 7% above the last record high, during the 2022-2023 winter season. On the lower side, base pricing could be 17.81 cents per-kilowatt-hour, which is slightly below the record from four years ago, but higher than the price for the upcoming winter.
Asked about its future forecasting, Dalo reiterated that supply costs are out of the company’s control, and several procurement cycles away.
“At this time, we are focused on supporting our customers through the current winter,” he said.
Energy costs dominated Rhode Island’s election cycle, with candidates from federal, state and local offices and both political parties centering their campaigns on cost-of-living concerns.
McKee, who lost his reelection bid to Democratic challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes in the Sept. 9 primary, sought unsuccessfully to change state decarbonization mandates and energy efficiency programs to cut customers’ bills. McKee’s plan was stricken from the final fiscal 2027 state budget approved by lawmakers.
Foulkes has not said specifically how she will defray rising energy costs, but insisted that climate change goals and cost concerns are not mutually exclusive.
Ken Block, an independent gubernatorial candidate, has also targeted “hidden fees” in energy bills as part of a broader plan to relieve residential cost pressures. In an interview on Thursday, Block suggested replacing the fees associated with renewable energy projects, some of which are charged to every customer regardless of their use of solar panels or other renewable options, with money from the state’s general revenue fund as a “fairer” solution.
Republican gubernatorial nominee Aaron Guckian has also called for reexamination of the state’s renewable energy mandates, using “innovation competition and technology” to incentivize green energy rather than customer charges. 
Customers in seven municipalities — Barrington, Central Falls, Narragansett, Newport, Portsmouth, Providence, and South Kingstown — can also opt out of the Rhode Island Energy prices, instead participating in a community aggregation plan that leverages bulk buying power to secure lower-priced electricity for its residents. Winter electricity prices through the Community Electricity Aggregation plan, which begin Nov. 1, have not been announced.
About 30% of 780,0000 Rhode Island Energy customers already opt out of the company’s default electric prices.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis, Uthmeier announce arrests of 20 people in Florida for voter fraud
description: Gov. Ron DeSantis and Attorney General James Uthmeier told reporters Thursday in Palm Beach County that state agents have arrested 20 people for voter fraud in Florida. Sixteen of them, they said, were non-citizens who claimed U.S. citizenship and four others had felony convictions but registered and voted while still on probation. The announcement came […]
text:
Floridians began early voting in most Florida counties on Oct. 21, 2024. The Florida Capitol stands in the background of an early voting sign at the Leon County Courthouse. (Photo: by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Gov. Ron DeSantis and Attorney General James Uthmeier told reporters Thursday in Palm Beach County that state agents have arrested 20 people for voter fraud in Florida.
Sixteen of them, they said, were non-citizens who claimed U.S. citizenship and four others had felony convictions but registered and voted while still on probation.
The announcement came 40 days before the midterm elections.
Each charged offense is a third-degree felony. If convicted as charged, 18 of those arrested could face up to 10 years in a state prison. Two other defendants face slightly longer sentences.
“I view these election crimes as some of the most dangerous in our country. Because when you vote illegally, it cancels out the votes of others. It challenges our very American sovereignty,” said Uthmeier.
He added that more than 100 people have been arrested for voter fraud in Florida since the Office of Election Crimes was created to review alleged violations in 2022.
David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research and a former senior trial attorney in the U.S. Department of Justice, said he was troubled at the timing.
“It’s always been the practice of the DOJ that you do not bring these kinds of claims close to an election, because of the possibility that it could influence an election,” he said on a remote conference call with Florida reporters when asked about the expected announcement. “So, you wait until usually odd years, for instance — certainly not 40 days before an election — to bring these claims.”
Florida Democratic House Leader Fentrice Driskell echoed those sentiments.
“While we all want free and fair elections, I think the timing of this announcement reeks of voter intimidation, especially now that mail-in ballots are going out,” she said in a statement released after this story was initially posted. “The Governor talked about ‘showing some accountability’ to uphold election integrity. How about some accountability for state officials at the highest levels who abused 10 million of taxpayer dollars for political purposes? When will Floridians see some accountability for Hope Florida?   I am all for holding people who break the law responsible. Let’s make sure we are consistent.”
The DeSantis administration has done this before, however.
It was five days before the 2022 August primary elections when the governor held a press conference at the Broward County Courthouse to announce that 20 individuals were being arrested for voter fraud. Some of those charges were later dismissed.
The Trump administration earlier this week said its effort to find and prosecute noncitizens voting illegally had resulted in 160 arrests. As the Associated Press reported, that falls far short of the hundreds of thousands of noncitizen voters that President Donald Trump had previously suggested were on the rolls.
Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections Wendy Sartory Link said earlier Thursday that she had not been informed about the press conference. She did say that officials with the Office of Election Crimes regularly inquire about certain voters.
According to the Office of Election Crimes and Security’s 2025 annual report, the agency received more than 3,400 complaints last year but just 44 individuals were arrested “and/or” convicted of election-related crimes.
Brad McVay, the Florida statewide prosecutor, said the investigation took place over the past two months.  He said that 12 of the 20 people named were already in custody.
One of those individuals, Giorgio Dominique Mucelli, a Canadian citizen and lawful permanent resident, was charged with one count of voting by a non-citizen and one count of false affirmation. Uthmeier had announced that matter during a press conference in July.
McVay promised “many more arrests” for voter fraud in the future.
Proof of citizenship 
Florida lawmakers have passed legislation nearly every year since the 2020 presidential election to tighten state election laws. The latest bill, HB 991, requires proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote but will not go into effect until next year.
It is similar to federal legislation called the SAVE Act that passed the U.S. House but has stalled in the U.S. Senate, despite the protestations by Trump. That measure also would require voters to show identification at the polls, something that has been the law in Florida for decades.
Florida Secretary of State Cord Byrd used the press conference to announce that, after the November elections, he will leave his office to head a new national organization called the Association of State and Local Election Officials.
“We want to take the Florida blueprint, we want to take the model that has been so successful in the third largest state in the country and take it nationwide,” he said.
In DeSantis’ first year as governor, the state joined a national organization that shared voter election data with other states called the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC), but abruptly withdrew from the consortium in 2023. Florida was one of several mostly conservative-led states to withdraw on the same day Trump called on all Republican governors to leave the organization.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma energy secretary steps down, deputy to take over
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma’s energy secretary will be stepping down effective Oct. 3 and replaced with the deputy secretary, Gov. Kevin Stitt announced on Thursday.  Jeff Starling, who has served as energy secretary since 2024, told Oklahoma Voice that he will have more information next week on what’s next for him.  Starling said in a […]
text:
Oklahoma Secretary of Energy and Environment Jeff Starling speaks at an about Oklahoma's role in the biotechnology industry at Innovation Hall in Oklahoma City on Aug. 19, 2025. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma’s energy secretary will be stepping down effective Oct. 3 and replaced with the deputy secretary, Gov. Kevin Stitt announced on Thursday. 
Jeff Starling, who has served as energy secretary since 2024, told Oklahoma Voice that he will have more information next week on what’s next for him. 
Starling said in a statement that he’s glad to have had the opportunity to serve in the role and is excited to continue advocating for Oklahoma’s energy industry. He recently made an unsuccessful bid for Oklahoma Attorney General. 
Chris Schinnerer is pictured. (Photo provided by the Office of the Secretary of Energy & Environment)
Stitt said he’s tapped deputy secretary Chris Schinnerer to step into the role for the remainder of his term as governor. 
“Chris is well-known in Oklahoma’s energy circles,” Stitt said in a statement. “He has long championed our oil and gas industry, and has helped lead the charge to explore new areas of energy development, including the state’s effort to secure a U.S. Department of Energy grant for one of three Nuclear Energy Lifecycle Campuses.”
Schinnerer previously worked in the private sector for Devon Energy and Lagoon Midstream as well as in the public sector at the National Security Council under former President George W. Bush. 
He lives in Edmond and has a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from Oklahoma State University as well as a master’s degree in energy and finance policy from Columbia University, according to his bio. 
“It is an honor to continue to serve my state in this capacity,” Schinnerer said in a statement. “Oklahoma has led the world in energy development for over a century, and we are on the cusp of the next generation of energy innovation. I’m proud to continue to support Gov. Stitt and his administration through these opportunities and set Oklahoma up to continue to lead.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia Power, Google announce deal to pay for nuclear upgrades
description: This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Google would help pay for upgrades to Georgia’s nuclear reactors under an agreement recently announced by Georgia Power.  Georgia Power wants to upgrade four of the state’s older nuclear reactors at Plant Vogtle, near Augusta, and Plant[...]
text:
Plant Vogtle near Augusta, Georgia. Emily Jones / WABEThis coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.
Google would help pay for upgrades to Georgia’s nuclear reactors under an agreement recently announced by Georgia Power. 
Georgia Power wants to upgrade four of the state’s older nuclear reactors at Plant Vogtle, near Augusta, and Plant Hatch, near Baxley, so they produce more energy. State regulators approved the Vogtle upgrades last year, but the specifics of how to pay for the work weren’t hashed out.
Now, the utility is asking the Georgia Public Service Commission for permission to move ahead with the updates at Plant Hatch too — as well as approval to create a new subscription program so large customers like Google can pay for both.
“We appreciate Google’s continued leadership in this space and partnership in developing this program, which we see as the latest example of how large-load growth can benefit all electric customers,” said Aaron Mitchell, senior vice president of strategic growth for Georgia Power, in a statement. 
The tech giant needs energy to power its data centers, and has set a target of using only carbon-free energy by 2030. Since nuclear plants don’t use fossil fuel, the power they generate qualifies. Google has long operated a data center in Douglas County, and is also building new facilities in LaGrange and Columbia County.
Under the proposed program, a large customer like Google would pay a subscription fee on top of its electricity bill to help cover the cost of the nuclear upgrades. In exchange, Google would get credit toward its clean energy target. It’s modeled on similar programs that the utility offers for renewable energy like solar. 
Precise details of the agreement between Google and Georgia Power haven’t been made public. It’s expected to add 96 megawatts of nuclear capacity to the grid and provide “approximately $900 million in projected benefits to customers over the life of the units,” according to the utility.
“This collaboration with Georgia Power ensures that digital infrastructure growth goes hand-in-hand with positive local impact, helping to deliver hundreds of millions of dollars in direct customer benefits and supporting a more affordable, clean, and reliable energy system for all Georgia residents,” said Lucia Tian, director of advanced energy technologies for Google, in a statement.
Georgia Power recently completed its expansion at Plant Vogtle, adding the first two new nuclear reactors to be built in the United States in decades. That project ended up running years behind schedule and came in billions over budget. The upgrade work covered under this program is for the two older reactors at Vogtle, which went into operation in the late-1980s.
The proposal still needs approval from the Public Service Commission.
