title: Iowa Veterans Home sued for alleged workplace discrimination
description: A pharmacist fired from the state-run Iowa Veterans Home is now suing the state, alleging discrimination based on age, gender and disability. Kimberly Helmbrecht, who was hired at the Iowa Veterans Home in early April 2020 during the initial stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, is suing the facility as well as Commandant Tom Jacobus, Operations […]
text:
The courtyard at the Iowa Veterans Home in Marshalltown. (Photo and logo courtesy of the State of Iowa)A pharmacist fired from the state-run Iowa Veterans Home is now suing the state, alleging discrimination based on age, gender and disability.
Kimberly Helmbrecht, who was hired at the Iowa Veterans Home in early April 2020 during the initial stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, is suing the facility as well as Commandant Tom Jacobus, Operations Executive Nathan Wilson, manager Melissa Sienknecht, and pharmacy supervisor Doni Keeling in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa.
In her lawsuit, Helmbrecht alleges that in 2023, the Iowa Veterans Home’s planned rollout of a new pharmaceutical dispensing system was “delayed multiple times due to software and hardware failures, ineffective leadership by the defendants and poor project management by the IVH executives.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
According to the lawsuit, the new system would have required Helmbrecht to handle the after-hours processing of medication orders on an on-call basis, and so she sought accommodations for a modified work schedule that would take into account her sleep disorder and mental health issues.
The lawsuit alleges that in December 2023, Helmbrecht met with Sienknecht and Keeling who terminated her employment at the home, citing an inability to agree to Helmbrecht’s request for accommodations.
Prior to her termination, the lawsuit claims, Helmbrecht’s performance reviews had been positive, with her superiors stating that she had met or exceeded the state’s expectations. In the months leading up to her firing, Helmbrecht alleges, she suffered panic attacks and possibly a heart attack as a result of the stress associated with her working conditions.
The lawsuit asserts the conduct of the defendants in the case was “calculated” and deliberate, and was designed to push Helmbrecht “past her breaking point, such that manifestations of physical harm overcame her.”
The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages for alleged violations of the federal Americans with Disabilities Act and the state and federal civil rights acts, as well as alleged retaliation and defamation.
The state, which does not comment on pending litigation, has yet to file a response to the lawsuit. A trial date has not yet been scheduled.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Deaths of students at the University of Mississippi cast spotlight on kratom
description: Kratom capsules are seen on Sept. 27, 2017, in Albany, N.Y.
text:
A drug task force in Mississippi is urging people to avoid kratom after authorities found packages of the substance while investigating the deaths of two University of Mississippi students.
The warning Tuesday came despite no “confirmed information” that kratom contributed to either death, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics said in a news release. The students were found Monday afternoon in different locations, one on campus and the other off campus, a university spokesperson said.
The university on Thursday identified the students as Aidan Hamilton, a freshman from Englewood, Colorado, and Robert Strang, a junior from Atlanta. The school said in a statement that their families “have asked for privacy as they grieve.”
U.S. health officials and states have increasingly scrutinized kratom, an herbal extract that acts as a stimulant at low doses and a sedative at high doses, over the past decade. Kratom is legal at the federal level, but some state and local governments have banned the substance and federal authorities have issued warnings about its risks.
Toxicology reports aren’t yet available
Two state agencies were working to expedite toxicology reports for the students, Gov. Tate Reeves said in a statement Wednesday.
“Mississippi is praying for the families and friends of the two Ole Miss students during this incredibly difficult time,“ Reeves said.
Authorities said they had no evidence the deaths were connected but noted the kratom found at the scenes was sold at a retail store. Officials did not name the store or say whether any criminal charges would be filed.
“Out of an abundance of caution, we encourage everyone to avoid kratom and any other medication or substance that was not prescribed to you or obtained from a trusted, regulated source,” the task force’s news release said.
Kratom is extracted from a tree native to Southeast Asia
It is used in capsules, powders and liquids that are often sold in gas stations or smoke shops. Proponents say that in its pure form, kratom is a safe, natural herbal supplement that can help manage pain, anxiety and depression and ease the effects of opioid withdrawal.
Doctors who treat addiction, however, say people can quickly become dependent on it, leading to withdrawal symptoms. A U.S. Food and Drug Administration webpage is blunt: Don’t use it.
The agency says it carries the risk of serious adverse effects, including liver toxicity, seizures and substance use disorder.
In rare cases, it’s been associated with deaths, though kratom was usually used in combination with other drugs in those cases, and the contribution of kratom in the deaths is unclear, the agency says on its website.
A trade organization has pushed back
Mac Haddow, with the American Kratom Association, said the FDA and states that have banned kratom are conflating the natural product with synthetic and chemically manipulated ones, which are associated with adverse effects and even deaths.
Haddow, a senior fellow on public policy with the association, said he’s heard numerous people tell lawmakers over the years how kratom has improved their lives.
“Some believe it saved their lives because it allowed them to get off of opioids,” he said.
Podcast host Joe Rogan and Cindy Crawford’s late son, Presley Gerber, have talked about their experiences using kratom.
Last year, the FDA recommended a ban on products with concentrated levels of 7-hydroxymitragynine, a chemical found in only trace amounts in natural kratom.
Mallory Pullman, managing director at Mississippi Poison Control, said she’s seen an increase in such concentrated products in recent years, and consumers may not be able to distinguish them from natural kratom.
“Until you know what product you’re working with, whether it’s kratom or some of these highly concentrated derivatives, you really have to be careful about buying a product and just taking it arbitrarily,” she said in a phone interview with The Associated Press.
Eleven states have banned kratom
Others, including Mississippi, have regulated it, in part by requiring people to be 21 or older to buy it. Both the city of Oxford and Lafayette County, where the University of Mississippi is located, have bans in place.
North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong signed a bill this month restricting the sale of kratom products after declaring kratom a public health crisis this summer and calling a special legislative session to address it. The state has had 50 deaths associated with kratom since 2019, according to the governor’s office.
Despite the bans and restrictions, use of kratom in the U.S. has increased, according to researchers at the University of Michigan and Texas State University.
In a paper published this year, they found kratom use in the U.S. was at an all-time high, with more than 5 million people saying they had used it in their lifetime. The group includes more than 100,000 young people ages 12-17.
“Policy changes regarding kratom and 7-OH products are needed in all states if we are serious about protecting our children,” the study’s main researcher, Sean McCabe, said in a statement in the University of Michigan News.
___
Associated Press writer Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ utilities board votes to keep electricity rates level
description: The Board of Public Utilities on Thursday pledged no net increase in electricity rates for New Jersey’s four regulated utilities.
text:
The Board of Public Utilities on Thursday pledged no net increase in electricity rates for New Jersey’s four regulated utilities. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)The Board of Public Utilities approved a series of rate changes Thursday that will keep rates roughly level for residential electric ratepayers while shaving dollars off most residential gas customers’ monthly bills.
Thursday’s votes come months after Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed an executive order that directed New Jersey’s energy regulator to modify components of ratepayers’ monthly bills in an effort to keep costs from soaring amid steep increases in electricity demand. Sherrill signed the order during her inauguration as governor in January.
“Taken together with the items on the agenda earlier this month, these actions will result in no net increase in electricity rates and a slight decrease in gas rates,” said Ben Hertz-Shargel, the board’s president.
Among the state’s four electric distribution companies, Rockland Electric Company will see the largest monthly decrease, though overall bills will remain roughly unchanged at each of the utilities.
The average Rockland customer using about 650 kilowatt-hours within a billing cycle can expect their bill to decrease by 67 cents, board staff said, and ratepayers with Atlantic City Electric will pay 5 cents less each month.
The average Jersey Central Power and Light customer will see their bill drop by 8 cents.
Average monthly electric bills with PSE&G were expected to rise by 2 cents as a result of transmission rates flowing from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, but board staff said state offsets would eliminate the increase.
Gas rates will decline further. The average monthly bill with Elizabethtown will fall $18.16 as a result of Thursday’s votes, with a $17.03 decrease for New Jersey Natural Gas customers.
PSE&G gas customers’ average monthly bills will drop by a more conservative $5.85, the board’s staff said, and South Jersey Gas customers’ bills will stay roughly level after a 2-cent monthly decrease.
“The board continues to prioritize energy affordability,” Hertz-Shargel said.
The commission’s votes come amid a worldwide spike in electricity prices driven by data centers’ mammoth energy demands and supply disruptions stemming from the Iran war and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Some customers will see individual components of their bills increase, but those will be offset by drops to other components.
Atlantic City Electric’s average monthly bills, for example, will rise by $4.09 because of changes to its Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative charges, certain infrastructure investments, and shifts in transmission charges set federally. But those same bills will fall by $4.14 due to changes to some Societal Benefits Charge components and lost sales related to energy efficiency and conservation programs, leaving the average monthly bill 5 cents cheaper than before.
In New Jersey, electric utilities sell electricity at cost and profit at rates negotiated with regulators on infrastructure investments needed to distribute power.
Though regulators and other officials have limited control over some bill components like wholesale electricity prices, they can make offsetting reductions on other utility charges.
Board of Public Utilities Commissioner Michael Bange warned of other affordability issues on the horizon. He said investments in water infrastructure over the coming years could blindside ratepayers focused on their rising electricity bills, and he urged utilities to warn their customers before those increases hit home.
“We’re talking billions of dollars,” Bange said. “For all the water utilities that are out there, I ask you: Please, communicate and educate your customers on the changes that are coming.”

title: Inside Indiana’s new downtown archives, where state history gets a new home
description: Indiana’s centuries-old paper trail — from the state’s original constitutions to governors’ correspondence and millions of agency records — is back downtown after a quarter-century in a temporary warehouse. State officials marked the opening of the new Indiana State Archives with a ribbon-cutting Thursday, celebrating a long-awaited home designed to better p[...]
text:
Shelves of records fill one of four storage floors at the new Indiana State Archives in downtown Indianapolis. Staff moved about 90,000 cubic feet of boxes into the building. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana’s centuries-old paper trail — from the state’s original constitutions to governors’ correspondence and millions of agency records — is back downtown after a quarter-century in a temporary warehouse.
State officials marked the opening of the new Indiana State Archives with a ribbon-cutting Thursday, celebrating a long-awaited home designed to better protect the records and make them easier for Hoosiers to explore.
The building at 350 W. Ohio St., alongside Indianapolis’ Central Canal, brings together archival storage, conservation and imaging workspaces, exhibits and a public reading room near the Statehouse. With the Indiana Historical Society and Indiana State Museum across the canal and the Indiana State Library nearby, the archives adds to a cluster of institutions where visitors can explore the state’s history within a few downtown blocks.
Behind the new public spaces are four floors of records storage. Staff moved in about 90,000 cubic feet of boxes, said Chandler Lighty, executive director of the Indiana Archives and Records Administration.
State officials cut the ribbon at the new Indiana State Archives in downtown Indianapolis on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Some contain the paperwork of state government. Others hold evidence of family members’ military service, ancestors’ naturalization or court fights that helped define Hoosiers’ rights.
Gov. Mike Braun pointed to his own experience with historical records, recalling a map that helped him trace property he owns in Dubois County to an original land transaction.
“I look up on that map and see 320 acres, half of which I now own, was part of that original land transaction,” Braun said at Thursday’s ribbon-cutting ceremony. “It gave me the chills. And that’s what you’re going to find here.”
During a behind-the-scenes tour earlier this week, Lighty described three priorities for the building: proper climate controls, bringing staff together and improving public access.
“We’re one of the smaller agencies, but up until this point, we were in four different locations,” he said. “Having everybody in one location allows us to work more cross departmentally.”
The public reading room at the new Indiana State Archives provides space for visitors to examine historic records. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Preservation advocates had raised concerns about the former facility at 6440 E. 30th St., a former RCA record-stamping warehouse. Along with extreme climate fluctuations, they cited vulnerability to tornadoes and roof leaks caused in part by gunfire.
Elizabeth Hague, who works in the archives’ conservation lab, recalled watching an old book’s cover warp as conditions changed at the previous building. Climate fluctuations caused materials to expand and contract — and dry conditions damaged leather bindings.
“In the winter, the humidity would go down to like 12% in the lab, or up to 73% in the summer,” she said, noting that the humidity should stay between 35% and 50%, with temperatures around 68 degrees. “The leather dries out, and then you get red rot, and spines fall off.”
The new building’s storage areas, however, are designed to maintain the temperature and humidity needed for long-term preservation.
A ‘temporary move’ — 25 years later
The archives moved out of the Indiana State Library’s basement during a 2001 renovation and into a warehouse on East 30th Street. The arrangement was supposed to be temporary. But finding and financing a replacement took years.
An earlier proposal under then-Gov. Mike Pence was tied to Indiana’s bicentennial celebration. His plan to help pay for construction through a public-private partnership involving state-owned cellphone towers was scrapped by his successor, Eric Holcomb, in 2017.
Indiana’s new State Archives building stands alongside the Central Canal in downtown Indianapolis. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Lawmakers authorized a new building in the 2021 budget and provided funding in 2023. The State Budget Committee approved work on the project that June, with a $102 million budget, despite criticism from lawmakers over both the price and the state’s delay in moving forward.
Holcomb joined officials for the groundbreaking in August 2023. Plans called for a five-story, 133,000-square-foot building on the narrow site between the canal and the Senate Avenue Parking Garage.
“We take a while maybe to get from here to there,” Braun said Thursday. “We’re understated on the way, but we always overperform.”
Completed offices now look out toward the canal and the Indiana History Center across the water. The public reading room has long tables, individual lamps and tall windows shaded by an architectural design Lighty said draws on a paper motif. Visitors also can use computers to access digital collections and equipment to read records preserved on microfilm.
A rooftop terrace provides space for gatherings, with views across downtown.
Architect Bill Browne of RATIO Design said the narrow site offered an advantage for storing fragile records: the space against the parking garage could accommodate storage areas that needed no daylight, leaving the canal frontage for offices and public rooms.
Connecting the building to an existing tunnel also allowed the archives to use the state office building’s loading dock rather than construct its own.
Putting pieces back together
In the conservation lab, the work can come down to a few fragile scraps of paper.
Among Hague’s current projects is a survey map of Porter County that had broken into pieces. She uses tinted mending tissue to reassemble the fragile document without making the repairs more conspicuous than necessary.
“It is so, so brittle that it just shattered,” she said of the deterioration.
Presses, tools and work surfaces fill the conservation lab at the new Indiana State Archives. Staff can clean, flatten and mend fragile records so researchers can use them and clearer digital images can be made. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
She estimated the restoration would take four to six weeks.
The repairs require drying time, so Hague works on several projects at once, switching tasks while a mend dries before returning to the map.
Other records require cleaning, humidifying and flattening before researchers can safely use them.
Some old court papers arrived folded and covered in soot after being stored near a coal furnace, said Jill Weiss Simins, the agency’s historian and director of special projects.
The results can be difficult to distinguish from a document that never needed repair.
“Some of the people that visited the other day thought they were replicas,” Hague said of materials prepared for display. “The idea is to make it very subtle and not noticeable.”
Conservation also improves the images staff can make when documents are digitized, Lighty said.
“Obviously, we do that to make them available for patrons to use,” he continued. “But also, anytime we digitize something, the better conserved it is, the better the scan we’re going to get of it.”
Four floors of Indiana history
Upstairs, rows of boxes and bound volumes show the scale of the collection.
On the shelves holding governors’ papers, the amount of correspondence grows from one era to the next. Materials from Indiana’s early decades occupy relatively little shelving, Lighty said, while later administrations generated far more correspondence.
More recently, that work has shifted to electronic records. Lighty said the gubernatorial records received from the Pence and Holcomb administrations were electronic.
An open safe reveals boxes and volumes at the new Indiana State Archives. Its holdings include unusual pieces of Indiana history, such as Jim Jones’ church incorporation papers and photographic negatives from the Beatles’ Indiana State Fair appearance. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Elsewhere, an old combination-lock safe holds some of the collection’s more unusual and recognizable materials: Jim Jones’ church incorporation papers, Donald Trump’s casino application for Gary and photographic negatives from the Beatles’ Indiana State Fair appearance.
Indiana’s original constitutions are kept in the safe when they are not on exhibit, Lighty said.
Even staff who work with the records regularly find surprises.
“As we were getting ready to move and we had our hands on everything, I found a book with little wheels on the bottom so it would roll on and off the shelf,” Hague said. “That was awesome.”
The new storage areas also include room for the collection to grow. Lighty estimated the move left capacity for another 30,000 to 40,000 cubic feet, although some existing materials will take up more space as archivists unfold and process them.
Movable shelving uses hand cranks, a choice Lighty said should require less maintenance than the aging electronic system at the previous building.
State history on display
The opening additionally introduces a small ground-floor exhibit, “Indiana’s Foundations of Independence, 1776–1851,” connecting the nation’s founding ideas with the records of Indiana’s government.
The display on Thursday included the state’s 1816 and 1851 constitutions, legislative acts and Indiana Supreme Court decisions. Lighty told attendees that both original constitutions were on display together for the opening day only. The exhibit coincides with the nation’s 250th anniversary and the 175th anniversary of the 1851 Constitution.
That second constitution remains Indiana’s governing charter. The exhibit pairs it with the state’s most recent constitutional amendment, approved in 2024, Weiss Simins said.
The Indiana Historical Society is visible across the Central Canal from a seating area inside the new Indiana State Archives. The archives’ downtown location puts researchers near the Indiana Historical Society, Indiana State Library and the Indiana State Museum. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Other documents show how individual Hoosiers made their cases to government.
An 1803 petition tells the story of Sarah Lusk, a widow who sought permission to operate an Ohio River ferry after a man seized it following her husband’s death.
Lusk argued that the ferry was her means of supporting herself and her children. Fourteen men signed in support of her account, and the court agreed to let her run it.
Nearby materials from the Vincennes Library Company, established in 1806, document what early Hoosiers read. A lending record tracks books donated and borrowed, while a selection of volumes includes works by classical and Enlightenment thinkers.
The records help show the ideas available to people building the state’s institutions, Weiss Simins said.
The archives will continue that focus with a public symposium on the Indiana Constitution on Nov. 5. The program includes a keynote address by Indiana Chief Justice Loretta Rush.
Beyond online searches
On site, visitors can research family histories and other subjects in records that aren’t necessarily available online.
The sheer volume makes it impossible to describe every document individually, Lighty said. An archivist can help identify a promising set of records, but a researcher may still need to work through boxes to find a particular person, letter or event.
“Sometimes, you have to dig and find the history that’s related to your ancestor — your ancestry,” Light said. “It takes a little work to find the bit of history you’re looking for.”


Visitors can visit the archives from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Monday through Saturday. The reading room is open Tuesday through Saturday. Appointments are strongly encouraged so staff can retrieve materials ahead of time. The building closes on state holidays and selected Saturdays.
Free parking with validation is available in the adjoining Senate Avenue Parking Garage. Research appointments can be arranged by calling 317-591-5222 or emailing arc@iara.in.gov.


The agency is expanding digital access, too.
Partnerships with FamilySearch have helped make records with genealogical value available online, Lighty said. Staff also are working with new digital collections software to make frequently used materials easier to access.
An online index can help a researcher determine whether the archives has a relevant record even when an image of that document is not available.
“We do work hard to index some of those records so people can do a quick search for their family member and see, ‘Oh, they do have something,'” Weiss Simins said. “It might not be digitized. They can’t click and see it. They might have to order a scan or make an appointment. But they can see that we do have the records up there.”
That work has uses beyond historical research, too. Archives staff are indexing military discharge records, for example, to help veterans locate documents they may need for benefits. The archives provides those records to veterans free of charge.
The agency also has two electronic records archivists working on the growing challenge of preserving records created digitally.
Lighty described the archives as a forum rather than a temple — a place for people to use historical records, not simply admire them from a distance.
“Ultimately, this building belongs to you because the records preserved inside are for you,” he said. “Any Hoosier can come here and look at the exact documents that they live under.”

name: National
title: CDC’s latest youth behavior report offers a narrower look at teen health
description: For more than 35 years, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has surveyed American high school students every two years about their health and behavior. The Youth Risk Behavior Survey, established in 1991, draws a nationally representative sample of students in grades 9 through 12 at public and private schools. Over the years, […]
text:
Students leave William H. Wells Community High School at the end of the school day in Chicago. The federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s latest national survey of high school students focuses on diet, physical activity, sleep, digital behavior and mental health. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)For more than 35 years, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has surveyed American high school students every two years about their health and behavior.
The Youth Risk Behavior Survey, established in 1991, draws a nationally representative sample of students in grades 9 through 12 at public and private schools. Over the years, it has tracked a broad range of issues affecting teenagers, from substance use and sexual behavior to violence, mental health and other health risks.
But the CDC’s latest national report, a full-color publication with photos, graphics and high school success stories, offers a markedly different portrait of adolescent health than the one it published two years ago.
The 2025 Youth Risk Behavior Survey report focuses on five areas — diet, physical activity, sleep, digital behavior, and mental health and suicide risk — while largely leaving out national findings on substance use, sexual behavior, violence and disparities among student groups that were prominent in previous reports. 
Meta to pay 47 states up to $17.1B in landmark child safety settlement

The underlying survey data on the CDC’s website still contains many of those measures, including trends in alcohol and drug use, and sexual activity, but they are not part of the national report’s key findings.
The shift comes as Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the Trump administration have made preventing childhood chronic disease and promoting nutrition, physical activity and other health behaviors central to their “Make America Healthy Again,” or MAHA, agenda. Kennedy also chairs the presidential MAHA Commission, which has focused on the root causes of childhood chronic disease.
The 2025 report is also substantially shorter than the CDC’s previous national Youth Risk Behavior Survey report. It runs 36 pages, including the title page, table of contents and references, compared with 88 pages for the 2023 report, which also included some technical notes, references and appendices.
Dr. Jennifer Shuford, CDC’s deputy director and chief medical officer, touted changes in student attitudes toward nutrition, physical activity and mental health. 
“These are meaningful improvements, and they show that progress is possible when schools, families, and communities work together to support young people,” she said in a news release. 
“At the same time, too many students are still struggling with daily health behaviors that can negatively affect their long-term health,” Shuford said.
A focus on health and wellness
The 2025 report provides a snapshot of high school students’ health in 2025 and compares changes over the previous two and 10 years. Its five focus areas reflect behaviors and experiences the CDC says affect adolescent health now and into adulthood.
Some of the findings are encouraging. Thirty-nine percent of high school students said they ate fruit daily in 2025, up from 33% in 2023 and 34% in 2015. Sixty-three percent ate vegetables daily, compared with 58% in 2023 and 61% in 2015.
The share who said they drank plain water at least three times a day rose to 58% in 2025, up from 56% in 2021 and 49% in 2015, while daily soda consumption fell to 17% from 20% in 2015.
State lawmakers embrace RFK Jr.’s health policies

The share of students who played on a sports team also increased, reaching 58% in 2025 compared with 52% in 2023 and 49% in 2021.
Several measures of mental health and suicide risk improved as well. The share of students who reported persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness fell to 33% in 2025, from 40% in 2023 and 42% in 2021. It was 30% in 2015.
The share who seriously considered attempting suicide fell from 22% in 2021 to 14% in 2025, while the share who made a suicide plan fell from a high of 18% in 2021 to 12% in 2025.
Female students continued to report higher rates of mental health and suicide risk than male students. In 2025, 43% of female students reported persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness, compared with 24% of male students.
But the report also shows that several measures of youth health have worsened over the longer term.
Just 25% of high school students were physically active for at least 60 minutes a day in 2025, unchanged from 2023 and down from 27% in 2015. Twenty-four percent got at least eight hours of sleep on an average school night, compared with 27% in 2015.
Daily breakfast consumption fell from 36% in 2015 to 27% in 2025. The report also found long-term declines in daily physical activity, muscle-strengthening activity and daily physical education.
About 36% of students said they used social media every hour or more in 2025, little changed from 37% in 2023.
A different look at adolescent health
The latest report’s focus marks a significant change from the CDC’s 2023 national Youth Risk Behavior Survey report.
That report, published during the Biden administration and as the country was recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, was organized around sexual behavior, substance use, experiences of violence, mental health and suicidal thoughts and behaviors. It also examined emerging issues including parental monitoring, social media use, racism in schools, unfair school discipline, school connectedness and unstable housing.
Cities, towns nationwide revive teen curfews amid summer crowds

The 2023 report included more student demographic data broken down by sex, race and ethnicity, and sexual and gender identity. For the first time, the national survey asked students whether they identified as transgender, and the report highlighted disparities affecting LGBTQ+ students and marginalized racial and ethnic groups.
The 2025 report does not mention LGBTQ+ students or sexual and gender identity. It also provides fewer detailed demographic comparisons. The CDC says the new report includes only selected statistically significant demographic differences, while the underlying survey data remain available through the agency’s data system.
The new public-facing report does not mean the CDC stopped collecting underlying information about many of the issues featured in previous youth risk behavior reports. The agency continues to make the national dataset available publicly, including demographic information, through its online data tools.
Instead, the change is in how the CDC presents the findings nationally. That produces a different portrait of the nation’s high school students — one that captures some notable improvements while giving considerably less attention to several categories of health and risk that have been prominent in the CDC’s national youth surveillance reports for years.
Declines in substance use
For example, the decline in teen substance use that has unfolded over decades is absent from this year’s report, despite the 2025 data showing alcohol and marijuana use at or near historic lows.
About 20% of high school students reported current alcohol use in 2025, down from 22% in 2023 and nearly 52% in 1995. Current marijuana use also fell to about 13% in 2025, from 17% in 2023, while the share who had ever used marijuana dropped to about 25% in 2025 from 42% in 1995.
The share of students who had ever used other illicit drugs, including cocaine, inhalants, heroin, methamphetamines, ecstasy or hallucinogens, was 9.7% in 2025, essentially unchanged from 9.9% in 2023 and about 13% in 2015.
Vaping also continued its long-term decline. Current e-cigarette or vape use fell to 16% in 2025 from a high of nearly 33% in 2019. The share of students who had ever used these products also fell to 30% in 2025 from about 34% in 2023 and about 45% in 2015.
Sexual activity and school violence
The new report also gives little attention to several measures that have long been part of the CDC’s youth survey, including sexual activity and violence at school.
The share of high school students who reported being currently sexually active fell to about 19% in 2025, down from nearly 21% in 2023 and nearly 40% in 1995.
Other measures show longer-term declines but less consistent changes. The share of students who reported carrying a weapon on school property fell to about 3% in 2025, from more than 4% in 2023 and almost 10% in 1995.
The share who said they had been threatened or injured with a weapon, such as a gun or knife, at school was about 8% in 2025, compared with 9% in 2023 and about 8% in 1995. Bullying on school property was reported by 19.7% of students in 2025, roughly unchanged from 19.2% in 2023 and about 20% in 2015. Reported bullying hit a low of 15% in 2021.
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.

description: TOPEKA — Kansas politicians urged federal immigration enforcement officials to coordinate with local law enforcement following reports of indiscriminate stops on southwest Kansas streets, causing business delays and warnings from schools. Republican U.S. Sens. Jerry Moran and Roger Marshall said Wednesday they both were in contact with Department of Homeland[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kansas, joined federal politicians and candidates in urging federal immigration officials to coordinate with local law enforcement while conducting arrests in southwest Kansas. He appears in July 2025 at the KU Cancer Center facilities in Kansas City, Kansas. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas politicians urged federal immigration enforcement officials to coordinate with local law enforcement following reports of indiscriminate stops on southwest Kansas streets, causing business delays and warnings from schools.
Republican U.S. Sens. Jerry Moran and Roger Marshall said Wednesday they both were in contact with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin after southwest Kansas law enforcement agencies said they didn’t know about Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity and residents reported people being stopped at random.
“When ICE operates in Kansas, it needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement,” Marshall said in a post on X. “Our sheriffs and police know these communities better than anyone, and working together keeps officers and residents safe.” 
ICE activity reportedly began around 5 a.m. Tuesday, according to the Kansas News Service. In response, a meatpacking plant in Liberal delayed its starting hours, the school district in Dodge City encouraged parents to ensure their children’s emergency contacts were up-to-date, and area residents scheduled demonstrations to protest the raid. 
“Secretary Mullin assured me these warrants are only for the purpose of arresting individuals who have been charged with criminal activities,” Moran said in a post to X.
The Rev. Adam Hamilton, a Kansas City-area pastor who is running as a Democrat against Marshall, said on social media that immigration agents “should focus on serious criminals in coordination with local officials and Kansas families shouldn’t live in fear.”
“Something has gone very wrong when schools are warning about children going uncared for and businesses are closing in fear,” he said.
U.S. Rep. Tracey Mann, a Republican whose district encompasses the cities where ICE has executed enforcement actions, declined to comment Thursday. As of midday Thursday, he had not posted about the ICE activity on his Twitter or Facebook accounts.
Lauren Reinhold, a Lawrence Democrat running for Mann’s seat, said in a Facebook post ICE was “snatching Kansans from the street.”
“This is an extreme overstep for an agency whose jurisdiction only extends a few miles from the border,” she said. “This is the pattern of attacking Americans my campaign is running to halt.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Rokita lawsuit against IHSAA alleges racial discrimination
description: Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita filed a lawsuit against the Indiana High School Athletic Association in a bid to eliminate a race-based quota for the association’s board of directors, which reserves two of its 19 seats for minorities. The lawsuit, filed in Marion County Superior Court Wednesday, alleges the IHSAA is engaging in racial discrimination […]
text:
Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita filed a lawsuit against the Indiana High School Athletic Association in a bid to eliminate a race-based quota for the association’s board of directors, which reserves two of its 19 seats for minorities.
The lawsuit, filed in Marion County Superior Court Wednesday, alleges the IHSAA is engaging in racial discrimination in how it selects board leadership in violation of its nonprofit status.
IHSAA bylaws reserve two seats for “qualified minorities,” defined as “an individual other than a white male or female,” according to the lawsuit.
“This is an overt racial classification that treats individuals differently solely based on race for the purpose of allocating positions of institutional authority,” state attorneys wrote in the suit.
Story continues below.
c2c9a07b-a49d-45e6-86a3-03b40ffc5160
 
The IHSAA did not immediately return emails seeking comment.
Earlier iterations of IHSAA bylaws reserved several board seats for what it termed minority directors, though the definition periodically changed since the practice started in 1993.
One version reserved the seats for “an individual other than a white male,” another for “urban school representatives,” according to the lawsuit.
“In all its iterations over the last 33 years it has been maintained, IHSAA’s minority quota has operated as an express, discriminatory racial classification,” state attorneys wrote in the suit. “It categorizes all individuals into two groups — those who are ‘white’ and those who are not — for the sole purpose of allocating seats on IHSAA’s governing Board. It excludes white males and white females from eligibility for the reserved minority seats solely because of their race.”
The lawsuit marks an escalation in the attorney general’s fight with the IHSAA.
Rokita asked the nonprofit organization to eliminate the quota in April, but the board declined. Instead, the IHSAA suggested it might consider changing its bylaws in 2027, according to a news release Thursday.
The office filed the lawsuit this week after sending additional notice to the IHSAA, which held an executive committee meeting in August.
“Hoosier students should not be governed by a sports association that picks its leaders based on race,” Rokita said in the release. “IHSAA’s quota tells kids that skin color, rather than merit, is an appropriate way to judge people.”
“That lesson has no place in Indiana’s education system, and, regardless, the law does not permit it,” he said. “The IHSAA exists to build character. A racial litmus test for choosing leadership on the IHSAA’s board does the opposite, and after months of delay, the Association left us no choice but to take legal action.”
The state is seeking a permanent injunction for the IHSAA to eliminate the “qualified minorities” provision from its bylaws, and permanently enjoin the organization from using race as a criteria for allocating board leadership in future bylaws or policy. The lawsuit also asks the court to declare IHSAA’s existing bylaws violate state law.

name: VTDigger
title: D.K. Johnston
description:
D.K. was fun-loving, but deep when he needed to be. He strove for excellence within our imperfect world.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  D.K. Johnston.
text:
Born: 11/12/1948
Syracuse, NY
Died: 05/28/2026
Philadelphia, PA
Details of service:

David Keith (D.K.) Johnston was born near Syracuse to Katherine Bates Johnston and Robert Johnston on November 12, 1948.  He never stopped enjoying celebrating his birthday, right up until his last one, as friends gathered in his room at Stapeley Hall in Philadelphia.  He died on May 28, 2026, after spending almost five years at Stapeley, where he received compassionate care through his long illness, from both the staff there and his faithful friends and weekly visitors, Jim Wilcox and Herbert Rutledge.
D.K. was a proud alumnus of Middlebury College.  After graduating in 1970 with a degree in Art History, he went on to get Master’s Degrees in City Planning and Sociology from the University of Virginia.  He worked for the Federal Emergency Management Administration in Charlottesville before moving to Rochester, New York, where he worked as a City Planner and Historic Preservation Officer from 1973 to 1980.  During that time, he discovered his love (and talent) for rehabilitating historic houses—a passion he pursued throughout his life.
In 1980, D.K. was drawn to Philadelphia.  Initially he worked for the City Office of Housing and Community Development, facilitating the rehabilitation of affordable housing.  He then moved to a private firm where he worked on master plans for urban design studies as well as restoration of historic properties.  But it was his work with buildings that drew him away from planning and into the field of architecture.  While working with several architectural firms, he went on to get his Bachelor of Architecture degree at Drexel University in 1988.  
He brought planning and architecture together in work with the Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority, focusing on multifamily residential buildings, nursing homes, and community centers.  Next, D.K. worked for the Philadelphia Housing Authority, where one of his more dramatic projects was overseeing the demolition of the twenty-story tall Schuylkill Falls public housing projects.
D.K. continued to enjoy acquiring and rehabilitating historic houses in several Philadelphia neighborhoods—which he usually lived in.  But his love of Vermont sent him back to his beloved lakeshore house in Burlington, where he lived for several years while serving as the Zoning Administrator in Williston before returning to Philadelphia.
As well as birthday parties, D.K. threw wonderful balloon-filled New Year’s Eve parties.  He supported Democratic campaigns and progressive causes.  D.K. was of the generation of gay people who came to voice in the 1980s.  It was also the generation ravaged by AIDS, and he lost many of his friends before HIV drugs became available.  Still, he found joy and community in living in the Gayborhood and singing with the Gay Men’s Choruses of Philadelphia and Wilmington.  As his friend Bill Pelle said, “He was fun-loving, but deep when he needed to be…He strove for excellence within our imperfect world.”
D.K. was predeceased by his parents and his only sibling, Richard Johnston. He is survived by his sister-in-law Susan Johnston (of Williamsburg, VA), nephew Kevin Johnston (Doha, Qatar), niece Christy Johnston (Hawaii), and three grandnieces and a grandnephew. He was also godfather to the children of Katie Day (Cambridge, MD) and Gerard Cooney (Edenton, NC), Julian and Molly Day-Cooney (of Wellington, New Zealand and Tampa, FL respectively).

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Fired administrator sues Tama County, alleging libel and defamation
description: A former Tama County official, fired amid allegations of misusing county funds, is now suing the county’s board of supervisors for libel and defamation. Former Tama County human resources manager Tammy Wise is suing supervisors Curt Hilmer, Mark Doland, David Turner, Heather Knebel and Curt Kupka in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of […]
text:
(Stock photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)A former Tama County official, fired amid allegations of misusing county funds, is now suing the county’s board of supervisors for libel and defamation.
Former Tama County human resources manager Tammy Wise is suing supervisors Curt Hilmer, Mark Doland, David Turner, Heather Knebel and Curt Kupka in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Iowa.
Wise, who was hired by the county in February 2000, also served as the county’s insurance administrator. She alleges that in May 2022, citizens attended a county board meeting to complain about wind turbines and later formed an ad hoc group called Tama County Against Turbines, aiming to influence county policy regarding the devices.

The group also filed lawsuits against the county to pursue its goals and, as insurance administrator, Wise worked with the supervisors and the county’s insurance carrier to defend the county in those cases.
All five members of the current board of supervisors were members of TCAT or were sympathetic to its goals, the lawsuit alleges. In January 2025, soon after those supervisors were sworn in, the county hired an individual to perform an “audit” of Wise’s work.
On Feb. 3, 2025, the board allegedly went into an illegally closed meeting to discuss Wise’s performance, although Wise had not requested the meeting be closed to the public, according to the lawsuit.
After the closed session, the board voted to terminate Wise, alleging she may have benefitted financially by purchasing an a generator for her own use, with her own money, but without paying sales tax.
Wise’s termination letter alleged she had improperly accepted gifts, failed to have adequate knowledge of county policies, failed to administer the county’s Family Medical Leave, had negotiated a union agreement that violated the Fair Labor Standards Act and was not administering recruitment policies in accordance with state law.
“The allegations included in the termination letter are false,” the lawsuit alleges. “The board issued a press release that repeated the same falsehoods.”
Doland and Knebel then contacted the Office of Auditor of State and alleged Wise had received an “unwarranted discount” on her purchase of a generator and that Wise engaged in nepotism and did not properly post a vacant position later filled by her daughter.
The lawsuit claims Doland and Knebel also alleged that Wise, in her capacity as central point of coordination for Tama County, “stole personal property from clients,” including jewelry, a wallet and cash, and that she improperly used county funds to settle claims with former county employees, including her former husband, Craig Wise.
“These false statements and allegations were thereafter published in the audit conducted by (Auditor of State) Rob Sand,” the lawsuit claims.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages for alleged libel and violations of Wise’s constitutional rights. A similar lawsuit was filed by Wise in state court last year but was dropped shortly before this week’s filing of the federal lawsuit.
The county has denied any wrongdoing in the matter and stated that the supervisors “held an honest belief that (Wise’s) performance was deficient which resulted in the decision to terminate her employment.”
A trial date has yet to be scheduled.
Earlier this year, the Auditor of State published a report identifying $251,200 in questionable spending by Tama County’s human resources department, led by Wise.
The state auditor’s report cited $81,376 in “questionable disbursements” of federal American Rescue Plan Act funds intended to provide assistance related to the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as $1,183 of “improper disbursements” that included $417 paid to Wise and $526 in purchases made using the department’s credit card.
The majority of the questionable spending was tied to $168,710 in “unsupported disbursements” where there weren’t enough records kept to determine the nature of the purchases.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Rep. Mike Flood and Chris Backemeyer spar in 1st District debate
description: One of the biggest fights was over the Iran war; both campaigns declare victory.
text:
U.S. Rep. Mike Flood, R-Neb., left, and Democrat Chris Backemeyer will face off for Nebraska's 1st Congressional District in November 2026. (Candidate photos courtesy of respective campaigns | U.S. Capitol photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)LINCOLN — Nebraska Rep. Mike Flood and his Democratic challenger Chris Backemeyer squabbled Wednesday in the only debate for the 1st Congressional District. 
The Nebraska Public Media debate covered a range of topics, including the Iran war, tariffs, trade, housing and AI. Throughout the debate, Backemeyer attacked Flood over the Iran war and his votes during the secondTrump administration, as Flood tried to paint Backemeyer as an outsider while making his own case that he is an effective congressman. 
One of the biggest spats was on the topic of the Iran war. Backemeyer pointed to his experience as a diplomat; he served as a senior State Department negotiator for then-President Barack Obama’s Iran nuclear deal in 2015. He said the deal would have prevented the current war but was torn up for “partisan political purposes,” adding that the war has contributed to higher prices for gas, fertilizer and groceries. 
“I will fight to bring an end to the war in Iran, so we can use that billion dollars a day to invest here at home and put towards our national debt,” Backemeyer said during his opening remarks. 
Flood defended his votes on the Iran war while acknowledging the economic woes that the war has caused, saying he is open to diesel export bans and changes to gas taxes. Flood also attacked Backemeyer over the 2015 Iran deal, calling it a “failed” deal. 
“We are in a situation where we have a country that vows death to America; it is painful. We need to bring prices down, but we can’t do what Joe Biden did, and that is cut and run, like he did in Afghanistan,” Flood said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The two are fighting over who will represent the 1st District, which comprises 12 counties, including Lancaster County, home to heavily Democratic Lincoln, whose blue voters are often outvoted by the region’s more conservative smaller cities and rural areas. 
Despite a midterm environment that is becoming extremely favorable to Democrats, election analysts still view the 1st District as safely Republican — though national Democrats see the race as competitive. 
Flood has won his past two U.S. House elections by 20 and 16 percentage points.  
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
On trade, Flood said the Trump administration has made progress in trade relationships with countries across the globe, but “it takes time to dig out of the hole,” referring to earlier trade deals. 
“We saw in the first Trump administration, great progress was made. Under Joe Biden, no progress was made,” Flood said. “Mexico said, ‘We’re not going to accept Nebraska’s white corn.” Nobody did a thing about it. President Trump is rewriting our trade relationships.”
Backemeyer said he would end the “tax and tariff regime” and emphasized that Congress should decide whether to impose tariffs. 
Tariffs have been a key tool for the Trump administration, which has used them as a bargaining chip with other countries. Trump’s tariffs have affected Nebraska — much like the rest of the country— especially farmers. Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court dealt a major blow to Trump’s trade agenda, ruling that the tariffs he had issued under the International Economic Emergency Powers Act are illegal, but Trump still has some tariffs in place. 
Flood defended his vote for Trump’s tax and spending bill, pointing to the tax cut from the bill. Backmeyer criticized his vote, saying the tax cuts benefited the wealthy — using Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos’ families as examples. 
The tax and spending law made most tax cuts from the first Trump administration permanent, cementing most of its benefits for higher earners. Its new work requirements for Medicaid and other social safety net programs are meant to offset the costs of the tax cuts and other funding for Trump’s domestic agenda.
In addition to Flood and Backemeyer, the race includes America First Party candidate Dan Hartong and Libertarian Nik Sandman. The two others were not involved in the debate. 
After the debate, both campaigns quickly declared victory. 
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawmakers call on Michigan House to move on offshoring protections for call center workers
description: On Thursday, communications workers gathered with lawmakers from separate sides of the aisle as they continued an almost 10-year push to keep call center jobs in Michigan. In June, state Reps. James DeSana (R-Carleton) and Amos O’Neal (D-Saginaw) introduced a pair of bills to require companies with a large call center workforce to notify the […]
text:
Communications Workers of America Union Senior Campaign Lead Charles Daniels, State Reps. James DeSana (R-Carleton) and Amos O'Neal (D-Saginaw), former state Rep. Jon Hoadley and members of the Communications Workers of America Union District 4 gather on the west Capitol steps on Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)On Thursday, communications workers gathered with lawmakers from separate sides of the aisle as they continued an almost 10-year push to keep call center jobs in Michigan.
In June, state Reps. James DeSana (R-Carleton) and Amos O’Neal (D-Saginaw) introduced a pair of bills to require companies with a large call center workforce to notify the Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity of their plans to move jobs out of the country while giving the state an opportunity to recoup any funding the company is receiving through a loan, grant or tax incentive.
Now the pair of lawmakers, alongside members of the Communications Workers of America union, are calling on House leadership to put the bills to a vote.
“I cannot think of anything more offensive than taking my taxes and those of my fellow Michiganders and giving them to corporations that offshore jobs and hire foreign workers when these jobs had Americans ready and willing to fill them,” said DeSana, who was one of the two Republicans who voted in favor of previous versions of the bill which were vetoed by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. 
Rep. James DeSana (R-Carleton) speaks out against offshoring during a press conference on Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
In a divided political climate, O’Neal argued that protecting Michigan workers should not be a partisan issue.
“We all know what happens when good jobs leave our state,” O’Neal said. “People feel this at the kitchen table, an uncertainty of how to make ends meet without a steady income, the anxiety of competing for a new job against dozens of former coworkers, and the wounded pride of having to explain to your neighbors, your friends and your families of why you lost a job.”
If Michigan provides a company with a loan, grant or tax break, that is an investment of taxpayer money, O’Neal said, introducing a simple question: What are Michigan workers gaining in return?
“If a company asks Michigan taxpayers to help them grow, we should expect them to have the commitment to Michigan workers,” O’Neal said. “We should not be helping that company today only to watch those jobs move overseas tomorrow.”
Charles Daniels, a senior campaign lead with the Communications Workers of America, noted that when Whitmer vetoed the bills, she called them duplicative.
“The Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act already requires certain employers to provide written notice at least 60 days in advance of a facility closure or mass layoff,” Whitmer wrote in her veto message. “Accordingly, these bills would likely result in the unnecessary use of the department’s time and resources.”
Rep. Amos O’Neal (D-Saginaw) joined members of the Communications Workers of America Union to push for accountability for call centers that move jobs overseas at a press conference on Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
However, the WARN Act was passed in 1988, nearly 40 years ago, Daniels said. 
“We’ve had a dozen CWA call centers close during that time,” Daniels said. “And that’s thousands of workers, and that’s just CWA. Think about everything else. If the WARN Act actually saved jobs, it would have saved jobs. This will save jobs, and these are the people that are going to make it happen”
DeSana and O’Neal’s House Bills 6069 and 6070 were referred to the House Economic Competitiveness Committee, where they await a hearing.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Nolan Wells’ autopsy and cellphone raise more questions about his death
description: Attorney Ben Crump, who is representing the parents of Nolan Xavier Wells, holds a stack of printed SnapChat messages pulled from Wells' phone during a Thursday Sept. 24, 2026, news conference in Florida.
text:
Attorneys for the family of Nolan Xavier Wells on Thursday released the state’s autopsy report and recovered information from his cellphone, raising more questions about what led to his death, including evidence of deleted messages and a lack of water in his lungs, airway and stomach. 
Digital forensic experts hired by Wells’ family examined his phone, including images, videos and social media apps to create a timeline providing more information about what led to his death on Horn Island, where his body was found on July 6. 
Earlier this week, a Jackson County grand jury declined to bring criminal charges relating to the death of the Black teenager. Based on the condition of his body, location and position, the group concluded that he likely drowned. Wells’ parents said the grand jury findings did not provide clarity. 
“This mystery still needs to be investigated,” Ben Crump, the national civil rights attorney representing his parents, said in a Thursday online news conference. “We cannot simply close the chapter, wash our hands of it, put a bow on it and say, ‘Nothing to see here.’”
Garrett Discovery, the Florida firm Wells’ parents hired, extracted information to track the location of Wells’ phone and SnapChat messages sent to it between July 4, when he went to Horn Island, up to when the forensic experts collected his phone.
GPS showed how Wells, 18, went to a McDonald’s the morning of July 4 before going to a friend’s house. By 10:30 a.m., his phone showed it was on a boat that traveled to Horn Island off the Mississippi Gulf Coast, where it remained for several hours. 
Andrew Garett, CEO of the digital forensics firm, said the phone data shows Wells last used the device on the boat around 2:20 p.m. He chose to remain on the island, according to friends, and was last seen that afternoon. Around 4:30 p.m., his friends returned to the mainland with Wells’ phone on the boat. 
His parents, Christine and Elmore Wonsley, retrieved his phone from his friends the next day and had it in their possession since then. Early on, they noticed few pictures or videos from the day on his phone, even though he commonly took them. They wondered if any had been deleted. 
Andrew Garrett, CEO of Garrett Discovery, speaks during a Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, news conference in Florida about digital information pulled from the phone of Nolan Xavier Wells. Garrett guided reporters through the findings and showed a video created by his firm using GPS from Wells’ phone, showing where the phone traveled when it was in his possession and after when Wells stayed on Horn Island.  Credit: screenshot
Garrett confirmed Thursday that there was evidence some messages sent to Wells were deleted. 
He also talked about how experts worked on Wells’ phone, including having to manually extract SnapChat messages because the programs typically used to do that were not compatible with the version of the app on the phone. 
The additional amount of time that took them led the experts to prepare a preliminary report that the grand jury reviewed. Once the extraction was done, it provided a final report to the grand jury including SnapChat conversations from Wells’ phone. 
Liza Park, a member of the family’s legal team, explained the process that led to phone extraction. She and Garrett pushed back against public comments about that process by District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath. In the video statement, McIlrath said her office was the one accused of “(refusing) to cooperate and/or obstructed a mutual examination.” 
But in reality, saying that led some people to believe it was the family who walked away from an agreement, Garrett wrote in a Wednesday letter to Crump provided to reporters. During the news conference, Park clarified that Wells’ family never kept the phone away from the district attorney’s office and law enforcement. 
Conversations about holding a mutual examination of the phone began after July 15, when the family, its legal team and McIlrath met at her office in Jackson County. After that, they said the state changed its parameters, most notably by selecting the location of the phone inspection, which the legal team says would have prohibited the family being there. 
During the news conference, Crump’s team also released the state’s autopsy report, which it had not seen until Wednesday evening. They said it will be posted on his firm’s website. 
Attorney Ben Crump holds a page from the autopsy completed by the state medical examiner’s office on Nolan Xavier Wells. On the diagram, the pathologist noted two contusions found on the back of Wells’ skull. Crump’s team continues to ask what caused those injuries and whether they contributed to the teenager’s death.  Credit: screenshot
Park read from the three-page report and highlighted the finding of two contusions on the back of Wells’ head noted on a diagram. Crump’s team continues to ask what caused those injuries and whether they contributed to Wells’ death. 
Dr. Roger Mitchell, who was hired by the family to do the independent autopsy, will speak at a future news conference about findings from both of the autopsies, Crump said. 
The state’s report also showed no signs of fluid in Wells’ airway, lungs or stomach. Park said water is typically present in those areas in drownings. 
The family and legal team have called for the investigation to remain open and for officials to release the state’s autopsy and law enforcement investigative file. They are also asking for independent review by the U.S. Department of Justice. 
If additional evidence is uncovered, it can be brought before a different grand jury at a later time to decide whether criminal charges could be brought and who to indict.

name: Mississippi Today
title: State college board pays $330,000 to settle discrimination lawsuit over 2023 Jackson State presidential search
description: Eastern view of Green-Gibbs Plaza on the campus of Jackson State University.
text:
Mississippi’s college board paid $330,000 to Debra Mays-Jackson, a former Jackson State University administrator, to resolve a sex discrimination lawsuit that challenged the 2023 presidential search process and decisions trustees used to select former President Marcus Thompson. 
The college board did not admit any liability as part of the settlement, and Mays-Jackson, the former JSU vice president and chief of staff, agreed not to apply for another job at Jackson State or any other public universities governed by the college board. 
Mississippi Today obtained the six-page agreement through a public records request. 
“Dr. Mays-Jackson is pleased to have this lawsuit behind her,” her attorney Lisa M. Ross said. “There is more work to be done” to protect public employees from discrimination and retaliation, she said. 
John Sewell, a spokesperson for the Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning, said the college board authorized the settlement with Mays-Jackson in closed session at its Aug. 20 meeting. 
Mays-Jackson sued IHL for sex discrimination in 2023, the same day trustees selected Thompson as Jackson State’s president. Thompson resigned as president in May 2025 after a little more than a year in the position. 
Debra Mays-Jackson Credit: Courtesy of JSU
The Mays-Jackson agreement is the latest settlement stemming from employment disputes during Thompson’s tenure. In June, Jackson State agreed to pay Linda Rush, former interim vice president of enrollment management, $150,000 to resolve a sex discrimination lawsuit. Rush alleged that Thompson passed her over for a promotion and that she was later fired because of her age and sex. 
Rush also agreed not to seek employment at Jackson State or any other public university. Jackson State and Thompson did not admit any wrongdoing. 
The IHL board, Thompson and JSU also settled a lawsuit with former faculty senate president Dawn Bishop McLin after she was placed on leave pending termination in fall 2024. The settlement agreement returned McLin to her job as a tenured professor, restored roughly $38,000 in research grants McLin lost after her termination, and paid her $10,000 for summer school courses she would have taught while she was on leave.
Another lawsuit from Thompson’s tenure remains pending. Jerome Tinker, an alumni engagement officer in JSU’s Alumni Affairs office, sued Thompson and the university in federal court in December after he was passed over for the office’s director position. 
In his lawsuit, Tinker accuses Thompson of retaliating against him because he had reported alleged misconduct involving former JSU President Thomas Hudson, who resigned in 2023. 
Ross, who is also Tinker’s attorney, declined to comment on his lawsuit. Pope S. Mallette, Thompson’s attorney, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: As Legislature’s progressive caucus hires its own staffer, parties raise ethics concerns
description: State lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are wary of the ethics of a privately funded staffer being hired by the Maine Legislature’s progressive caucus who does not fit neatly into existing regulations. “That could be replicated left, right, and center of the political spectrum, and I suspect likely will if this precedent is […]
text:
The Hall of Flags in the Maine State House in Augusta, Maine on Feb. 25, 2025. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)State lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are wary of the ethics of a privately funded staffer being hired by the Maine Legislature’s progressive caucus who does not fit neatly into existing regulations.
“That could be replicated left, right, and center of the political spectrum, and I suspect likely will if this precedent is allowed to move forward,” Minority Leader Trey Stewart (R-Aroostook) said during a meeting of legislative leaders on Thursday. “I think this is a juncture point for us.” 
The progressive caucus, an informal group of representatives with a core team of seven, began work about a year ago to advance collaboration among the progressive members of the Maine House of Representatives, specifically to address pressing affordability issues. 
Over the summer, the caucus posted a policy and communications director job after raising $100,000 from undisclosed donors, a salary that will be routed through the 501(c)(3) arm of the Maine People’s Alliance, as first reported by the Bangor Daily News. 
“We see this position as focused primarily on communications,” Rep. Gary Friedmann, a Democrat who represents Bar Harbor and serves as the caucus chair, told legislative leaders during a Thursday meeting. “Someone who would be in the position would be supporting the entire membership of the progressive caucus in framing issues and in helping them to advance those issues in the State House.”
Friedmann and another caucus member, Rep. Dan Sayre (D-Kennebunk), said the group does not intend for the hire to be a lobbyist, but the job description sounded like a lobbyist to other lawmakers, opening up questions about disclosure requirements and limits that did not yield clear answers on Thursday. 
Because of that, legislative leaders will be sending a letter to the Maine Ethics Commission to seek clarity on the boundaries as they start to draft a related policy. Currently, the body currently lacks a policy that would govern such an arrangement, said Suzanne Gresser, executive director of the Legislature.
The caucus members said they have not yet hired someone for the role but are in the final stages of a search process. 
“We do not regard this role as a role within state government,” Sayre said. “We regard this role as someone who is an employee of a fiscal agent to this group of legislators. That said, however, if there are requirements of lobbyists around their conduct in the building, we certainly want this person to comply.”

title: Alabama commission approves compensation increases for violent crime victims
description: The Alabama Crime Victims Compensation Commission Thursday voted to increase the payouts on some claims from victims of violent crimes. Under the administrative code change approved by members at a special meeting, payouts will go up for financial losses, lost wages, and funeral and medical expenses. “I am so excited to do so because we […]
text:
The entrance to the Alabama Crime Victims Compensation Commission as seen on Sept. 24, 2026. The agency Thursday approved  increases to compensation for violent crime victims. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Crime Victims Compensation Commission Thursday voted to increase the payouts on some claims from victims of violent crimes.
Under the administrative code change approved by members at a special meeting, payouts will go up for financial losses, lost wages, and funeral and medical expenses.
“I am so excited to do so because we had needed these changes for a long time,” said Darlene Hutchinson, commissioner with ACVCC.
The board voted to approve the changes for public comment with the Legislative Services Agency during the meeting in May. The changes will take effect next week. The payouts will increase in steps based on a specified time frame the claims are filed, according to the filings on the Legislative Services Agency website.
Victims or their families who file claims beginning in October for an economic loss or lost wages may receive $600 per week up to $15,000. Currently, the limit is $400 a week for claims filed before October 2025, and $500 for claims filed after that date.
Victims may also receive benefits to offset half of their medical expenses stemming from the incident, an increase from 30%. Commissioners also increased the maximum payout from $6,000 to $10,000. Those who filed claims before October will be compensated at the previous rate.
The agency also increased the maximum payout for funeral expenses from $5,000 to $7,000, and for moving expenses from $1,000 to $2,500.
The agency also extended the window for victims to apply for claims with the commission from one year to two years in the administrative code. That change was made after lawmakers passed HB 255, sponsored by Rep. Russell Bedsole, R-Alabaster, two days before they adjourned the legislative session for the year.
The Alabama House of Representatives passed a similar version in 2025, but it was not approved in the Senate before the session ended that year.
Survivors of crime victims organized a rally in February at the state capitol to urge lawmakers to pass HB 255 and for the state to expand outreach and enhance services for victims of crime.

title: Flathead County reports potential measles exposure
description: The Flathead City-County Health Department announced this week that an individual with measles visited the county and had potential exposure sites during their visit. A suspected case of measles in the county tested negative. As of Wednesday, the county is aware of three public sites the individual visited and is warning county residents and visitors […]
text:
Diseases like measles have surged to the highest level in decades in the United States.(Photo by Getty Images Plus)The Flathead City-County Health Department announced this week that an individual with measles visited the county and had potential exposure sites during their visit.
A suspected case of measles in the county tested negative.
As of Wednesday, the county is aware of three public sites the individual visited and is warning county residents and visitors that they may have been exposed to measles if they were present in the following locations:

Glacier Highland – Gift Store & Restaurant 12555 Hwy 2E, West Glacier, (from Sept. 8 through Sept. 11)
Logan Health Primary Care 1675 Talbot Road, Columbia Falls, (Sept. 8 from noon to 5 p.m.)
Amtrak Train No.8,  traveling eastbound on Sept. 11 from West Glacier

Potentially exposed individuals should complete the Measles Exposure Self-Assessment  and monitor for symptoms for 21 days.
Measles is a very contagious disease that spreads mainly through the air. When an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks, tiny droplets containing the virus are released and can remain in the air for as long as two hours. This means someone can get measles even without direct contact with the infected person. The virus can also spread by touching contaminated surfaces and then touching the mouth, eyes or nose.
Measles usually starts with a fever, cough, runny nose, and red eyes, along with small white spots inside the cheeks. About 7 to 14 days after exposure, a red rash appears, beginning on the face and then spreading to the rest of the body.
If you have symptoms of measles, call your healthcare provider right away. Your provider will tell you how to get care safely without exposing others. If you are concerned about exposure, health officials recommend staying at home and not having guests or visitors until you are no longer contagious, or measles is ruled out. People immune through vaccination, lab-confirmed immunity or prior infection, or those born before 1957 are generally not considered at risk for infection. Unvaccinated individuals have about a 90% chance of infection if exposed.
