outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: FDA nominee faces skepticism on vaccines from Republican senators at confirmation hearing
text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration appeared to disappoint senators from both political parties Thursday with how she answered questions about medication abortion access during her confirmation hearing. Dr. Heidi Overton also faced skepticism from committee Chairman Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican, about her work on vaccine policy during the current administration, indicating she may not have the support needed to secure the job. “You're a medical doctor. Of course, that resonates with me. You've seen patients. You have a deep understanding of the healthcare system and health policy, but I have concerns,” he said. “You were behind the president in the Oval Office when he signed an executive order to break up the vaccine schedule into more doses, completely ignoring the reality of families today struggling to make life affordable.”Cassidy said that executive order was “based on zero scientific evidence” and would require parents to spend more time and more money taking their children to medical appointments to receive vaccine shots. Overton, he said, needed to convince him and others on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee that if confirmed by the full Senate, she would be “radically honest.” “You'll also need to ensure that uninformed ideologies do not influence FDA's decisions on whether to approve individual products, even if the president is pressuring you,” Casidy said. In response to a question from Cassidy about the vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella, Overton said she believed it as well as “every vaccine on the U.S. market right now” is safe and effective. She added the MMR vaccine remains “our best tool right now in the public health response to the measles outbreak” and that it is “97% effective in stopping transmission of the virus after two doses.” Questions on medication abortionIn addition to several questions about vaccine and food safety, senators pressed Overton about her personal views on mifepristone, one of two prescription pharmaceuticals used in medication abortion. Senate confirmation would place Overton as the head of the agency conducting a safety review of the drug, though she declined to say how she would handle that process.“Mifepristone was approved by the FDA as having met its safety and efficacy standard,” she said in response to a question from Washington state Democratic Sen. Patty Murray.The senator then referenced a policy brief that Overton wrote with Matias Perttula for the America First Policy Institute that was published in February 2023. The co-authors began by writing that “Abortion is corrosive to children, women, and society broadly because it devalues and extinguishes innocent human life.” They later added that medication abortion, which is approved for up to 10 weeks gestation, had become “the most common method of terminating a pregnancy” and that it “deserve(d) greater medical scrutiny.”Overton declined to answer a question from Murray about whether an IUD counts as an abortifacient, saying that if confirmed she would be “fully briefed on all their prior decisions and make determinations according to the standards of safety and efficacy.”Hawley presses on FDA positionMissouri Republican Sen. Josh Hawley also questioned Overton on her statements during the hearing about mifepristone, saying they didn’t match what the Trump administration was arguing in ongoing legal cases. “I want to get to the bottom of this. I want to be sure that the FDA is not changing its position. I think this could be news to the court,” Hawley said. “So, are you saying that the FDA's position is now that the drug is safe and effective and appropriately labeled?”Overton replied that the current Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy for mifepristone, which changed during the Biden administration to allow for it to be prescribed via telehealth appointments and shipped to patients, is under FDA review. “That safety study is ongoing and very important. Women's health and women's safety is a critical piece of this. So there is no change in position,” she said. “The FDA does need to do that safety study to look at the internal data that has not been looked at since a REMS change was made.”The FDA wrote in a statement to States Newsroom that “Due to active litigation, the FDA and HHS cannot comment” on the safety review.Murkwoski sees 'political pressure'Alaska Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski didn’t ask Overton any questions about mifepristone, but said she believes there was “political pressure” on FDA officials to “revisit the approval status of certain products.”“We're going to be in a very challenging position in a very rural state like Alaska if in fact the move to require in-person dispensing of the medication as opposed to telehealth appointments is the direction,” Murkowski said. “You have effectively taken about ... 80% of the communities in the state, and put them in a very challenging position in terms of access to providers, access to this FDA-approved drug.”Murkowski added that she didn’t ask Overton a specific question on the issue since it appeared she would “go down this same rabbit trail and probably get the exact same very specific technical responses that you have provided the committee.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: LSU struggles with multimillion-dollar athletics deficit: ‘We’ve got to stop that bleeding’
description: After years of minimal profits, LSU athletics is now tens of millions of dollars in the red.
text:
Clouds pass over Tiger Stadium on Monday, March 20, 2023, on LSU’s campus in Baton Rouge (Photo by Matthew Perschall/Louisiana Illuminator)After years of minimal profits, LSU athletics is now tens of millions of dollars in the red.
LSU President Wade Rousse told the state Board of Regents on Tuesday the school’s sports program is projected to carry a $26 million deficit this year.
The program’s shortfall for fiscal year 2025-26 was $44 million, according to LSU spokeswoman Meg Sunstrom. It was the first year in which NCAA Division I programs were allowed to directly compensate student-athletes for their name, image and likeness. Like most Power Four conference schools, LSU spent the maximum amount allowed — $21. 5 million — accounting for the biggest portion of the deficit.
LSU athletics has overspent its budget over the past six years by a total of $177.5 million, Rousse told the Regents at their annual budget hearing for all schools under their purview.
Rousse said the university would soon publicly announce details of a new revenue generation plan discussed with donors in July at a private event at the Governor’s Mansion. Following that gathering, reports circulated that the plan includes a private equity deal linked to media rights for LSU sports. It would most likely involve getting upfront cash from investors who would share profits from an entity that receives income from broadcast deals or other business arrangements.
An announcement on the plan is on hold pending a valuation of LSU’s brand, Rousse said.
“We want to make sure that our brand is valued the right way,” Rousse said. “At no point do we ever lose control of anything there.”
The plan would provide funding not only to athletics but eventually across the entire LSU System, which includes campuses in New Orleans, Shreveport, Alexandria and Eunice, according to Rousse.
“The acute need is certainly athletics, so we’ve got to stop that bleeding first,” Rousse said in an interview. “But you know, I think what we’re building is scalable. And if we do it the right way, it could have a positive effect on revenue for the entire system.”
At the same time LSU is increasing its athletics spending, it’s also trying to boost investment in its academic research in its quest to rank as one of the top 50 research universities.
To do so, Chancellor Jim Dalton said the university needs to boost its federal funding by about $150 million and hire 100 to 150 faculty over the next five years. He leads LSU’s main campus in Baton Rouge and its research-intensive campuses, which include its medical schools in Shreveport and New Orleans, the Pennington Biomedical Research Center and LSU AgCenter.
For the first year, LSU is requesting $31.7 million from the state legislature to hire 45 faculty members and provide them with startup packages to build out their research programs.
LSU is also seeking $21 million from the state to offer competitive stipends for graduate students.
Lawmakers will consider the request in their next legislative session, which begins in April.

title: Pilot for Tom Tiffany deeply involved in election conspiracy politics
description: Leonard Boltz, the 73-year-old who has flown Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany to events across the state, has long had ties with some of the state’s most prominent election deniers and said recently that if Tiffany loses in November it will be because of “cheating” by Democrats. text:
Leonard Boltz speaks about illegal voting at a Republican Party of Langlade County meeting in June, 2026. (Screenshot via Rumble)Leonard Boltz, the 73-year-old who has flown Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany to events across the state, has long had ties with some of the state’s most prominent election deniers and said recently that if Tiffany loses in November it will be because of “cheating” by Democrats.
Boltz, the chair of the Langlade County Republican Party and a retired major in the U.S. Air Force, has been a regular contributor to Republican candidates and causes, state and federal campaign finance records show, but has provided personal air travel only for Tiffany’s gubernatorial campaign.
Earlier this month, Boltz was flying Tiffany from La Crosse to Wausau when a mechanical failure forced a crash landing into Lake Wausau. Both men swam to a shallow area where they were rescued and treated for minor injuries. Boltz was lauded as a hero.
Wisconsin state campaign finance records show that Boltz flew Tiffany around the state 12 times between January and June. The total value of these in-kind contributions was claimed on campaign finance filings as $2,354.
Beyond the instances in which the Tiffany campaign reported flying with Boltz, the two men appear to have both attended the same conservative events over the past year.
Flight tracking data shows that Boltz’s Beech K35 aircraft was flown to the same area as a Tiffany campaign event on at least three other occasions in July.
On July 11, Tiffany was in Door County picking cherries the same day that Boltz’s plane flew from the Door County airport in Sturgeon Bay to Antigo. On July 25, flight records show the plane flew from Rhinelander to Waukesha the same day that Tiffany appeared at an event in Pewaukee. Two days later, on July 27, the plane flew from Rhinelander to Milwaukee on the same day Tiffany held events across the Milwaukee area.
The plane was also in Green Bay the same day that Tiffany attended a Charlie Kirk memorial event there on Oct. 14 last year and landed in Baraboo the same weekend in May that Tiffany was crowned the Republican nominee for governor at the party’s convention in Wisconsin Dells.
The flight data and campaign finance records, along with public statements Boltz has made, suggest an ongoing relationship between Tiffany and an outspoken member of the election conspiracy wing of the state Republican Party even as Tiffany works to distance himself from his previous support of the ideas Boltz espouses and their originator, President Donald Trump.
Tiffany voted against certifying the 2020 election results and in May of this year, would not say whether Biden won. This month, Tiffany told Wisconsin Watch that Biden won the 2020 election, but that he would cooperate with Trump’s ongoing federal investigations into the election. 
The Examiner approached Tiffany for comment for this story at a campaign event in Waukesha County Wednesday evening. Tiffany ducked into his car while two of Tiffany’s staff members, including Alex Walker, the son of former Gov. Scott Walker, physically blocked a reporter as he asked a question.
As of publication, the campaign had not responded to a list of questions sent by email.
The Examiner reached Boltz by email and phone Thursday morning. He said on the phone he had “no comment” and hung up before he could be asked any questions.
Boltz’s support for election conspiracy theories
An Examiner review of videos of Boltz posted to the right-wing video platform Rumble show the extent of Boltz’s support for election conspiracy theories — including his support for GOP Senate candidate Eric Hovde’s claim that, despite Trump’s 2024 victory in Wisconsin, Democrats somehow cheated Hovde out of a win over Democratic U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin on the same ballot.
At a Republican Party of Langlade County meeting in late June, video shows Boltz saying people had been asking him how Tiffany’s campaign was going. He said the November election would come down to whether or not the SAVE Act is passed to stop “cheating.” The Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act introduces a slew of proposed restrictions on voting across the country in the name of stopping noncitizens from voting. Tiffany has been supportive of the measure in Congress, which Trump strongly supports.
“What I tell people is, well, if Trump can get through some of these election integrity issues before November, I think it’s a piece of cake,” Boltz said.
“I don’t think there’s any question that Tom will win if we can stop some of the cheating. Again, we’re not going to stop it all, but if we can stop some of the cheating, I think, certainly, Tom is going to win… Cheating is all they’ve got. They’ve got to cling, they’ve gotta hang onto cheating, and they gotta get cheating. It’s the only possible way.”
At that same meeting, Boltz said he’d recently spoken with Tiffany about the party’s chances of winning this fall.
Harry Wait, a prominent Racine County election conspiracy theorist, also spoke at the county party meeting in June. Wait was convicted in May of breaking state law by impersonating voters to request absentee ballots, with the intention of trying to expose flaws in the election system. He filed the requests using the names of Assembly Speaker Robin Vos and Racine Mayor Cory Mason without their permission.
Wait, campaign finance records show, has made several donations of $1,000 to Boltz’s Langlade County Republican Party.
Ahead of the 2020 election, Boltz helped Terry Brand, the former chair of the Langlade County GOP and former mayor of Antigo, resurrect the county party, serving as vice chair and then chair.  He became involved in the state’s election conspiracy movement shortly after the 2020 election.
Video posted to Rumble shows Boltz appeared at a rally in 2021 outside of the Wisconsin State Capitol to call for a “cyber forensic audit” of the 2020 election. He spoke there about going to Maricopa County, Arizona, the Phoenix-area county that helped swing the state for President Joe Biden and became a target of Trump’s false claims the election was stolen from him. At the time, an IT firm with no election experience was running a widely derided audit of the election. 
Boltz said he went to Arizona with former Rep. Janel Brandtjen of Menomonee Falls. Brandtjen, who used her position as chair of the Assembly elections committee to spread conspiracy theories and attempt to oust Meagan Wolfe from her position as the administrator of the Wisconsin Elections Commission, was kicked out of Republican caucus meetings and then lost her seat in the Assembly in a 2024 primary election. 
“I was very fortunate to be able to get out to Maricopa County,” Boltz said at the rally outside the Capitol. “My chairman, Terry Brand, and I decided that it was high time Wisconsin get out to Maricopa County…  I was able to join the delegation. Now, that worked out awfully well, because a lot of the delegation sort of got muzzled… Robin Vos muzzled most of the people that went out there.”
Boltz went on to say the state needed to have a cyber forensic audit because “there’s so much fraud in Wisconsin.” Brandtjen and former state Rep. Timothy Ramthun made similar calls at the time.
“There’s maybe more fraud in Wisconsin than there was in Maricopa County, and they had plenty,” Boltz said. “Our legislators, for the most part, with the exception of Janel [Brandtjen] and a couple others have failed us. Our courts have certainly failed us. Who’s gonna make this happen? You are. You are. We’re gonna have to force this issue. Folks, we’re gonna have to keep the pressure on our legislators, keep the letters, the emails, the phone calls coming, but really, it’s still going to be up to you, us.”
Boltz’s work also extended to electing Republican legislators who would buck the authority of Vos — who in his tenure as speaker was known for maintaining a tight grip on the actions of his caucus. The election denial wing of the party had become hostile to Vos after he fired former state Supreme Court Justice Michael Gableman from his job investigating the 2020 election and refused to support the effort to impeach Wolfe. 
In an August 2024 video, Boltz stood alongside county party chairs and candidates for the Assembly, including now-Rep. Lindee Brill (R-Sheboygan Falls) and criticized Assembly Republicans for not helping oust Wolfe. He said not supporting Brandtjen in that effort was like “going against apple pie in America.”
“That’s why these people are here,” Boltz said. “They want to change things in the Assembly. They want to be independent thinkers and not just vote Robin Vos. That’s why we can’t always be unified with the Republicans in the Assembly because they’re not real Republicans. They’re RINOs.”
The advocacy of Brandtjen, Ramthun and their allies was crucial to the creation of Gableman’s fruitless review of the 2020 election. Gableman donated $1,000 to the Langlade County party last November.
In 2022, Boltz, then the vice chair of the county party, and Brand, then the chair, also played a role in a campaign finance scheme in which about $40,000 was funneled through the county party’s accounts to the campaign of Adam Steen, an election denier who attempted several times to unseat Vos. The state ethics commission recommended that criminal charges be filed against Boltz, Brand and Brandtjen but local prosecutors declined to charge them. 
In 2023, Boltz said in an interview that he flew to Springfield, Missouri to appear with Ramthun at the “Election Crime” summit held by Mike Lindell, the MyPillow CEO and election conspiracy theorist who this year ran a failed campaign for Minnesota governor. Boltz said he and Ramthun were taking the place of Gableman, who was supposed to deliver a report on Wisconsin at the summit but was unavailable at the last minute. 
On Jan. 6, 2025, Boltz appeared on the “Regular Joe” show’s “Red, Right & Wisconsin” podcast where he was introduced as the chair of the county party. Boltz talked about his work to grow the Langlade County Republican Party as well as Wisconsin’s 2024 U.S. Senate race.
Boltz said he didn’t believe Eric Hovde, the failed GOP Senate candidate, lost against Sen. Tammy Baldwin. In 2024, Hovde didn’t concede to Baldwin until nearly two weeks after the election as he questioned the vote counting process. There was no evidence of irregularities in the vote count.
“Why don’t you look to see if Hovde really did lose? I don’t believe he did,” Boltz said. He added that Peter Bernegger, a prominent purveyor of election conspiracy theories in Wisconsin, did not believe Hovde lost either. At Brandtjen’s invitation Bernegger made several appearances before the Assembly elections committee to give testimony containing numerous debunked claims about the 2020 election.
“You know we still have Democratic clerks in Milwaukee, Madison, Green Bay, Kenosha, Racine,” Boltz said on the Regular Joe podcast. “Those Democrat clerks are a problem and they have proven themselves to be a problem.”
This year, on May 13, Tiffany donated $475 to the Langlade County Republican Party. On the same day, records show, the party gave a “gift” of $3,000 to Bernegger. 
In April, Gableman, Bernegger and Wait all appeared as speakers or special guests at the Langlade County Republican Party’s annual Lincoln-Reagan-Trump dinner.
Since 2010, Boltz has given more than $35,000 to county chapters of the Republican Party, the state party and candidates including Scott Walker, Rebecca Kleefisch and Brad Schimel. He’s also donated to several state legislative candidates including Brandtjen, Brill and Sen. Cory Tomczyk (R-Mosinee). 
Federal campaign finance records show that Boltz has donated more than $7,000 to the national Republican Party and federal candidates for office. That includes $1,500 in donations to Tiffany’s previous congressional campaigns and a $1,000 donation this year to the campaign of Michael Alfonso, the Trump-endorsed candidate  running for Tiffany’s 7th Congressional District seat. He’s also given to the presidential campaigns of both John McCain and President Trump.

name: Daily Montanan
title: No Mollie’s Pack, Yellowstone wolves killed, Wyoming reports after hunt area’s quick close
description: EVANSTON, Wyoming—Yellowstone National Park’s last original wolf pack, Mollie’s Pack, emerged unscathed from a hunting season that opened last week and has already closed, Wyoming wildlife officials announced Monday. Dan Smith, a Wyoming Game and Fish Department interim deputy director, provided the update, allaying concern that had run rampant online and in[...]
text:
Members of the Mollie's Pack traverse a wind-blown hillside as seen from the air March 12, 2018, in Yellowstone National Park. (Douglas Smith/National Park Service)EVANSTON, Wyoming—Yellowstone National Park’s last original wolf pack, Mollie’s Pack, emerged unscathed from a hunting season that opened last week and has already closed, Wyoming wildlife officials announced Monday.
Dan Smith, a Wyoming Game and Fish Department interim deputy director, provided the update, allaying concern that had run rampant online and in circles of wolf-watching devotees. Worries centered on the Mollie’s Pack, named after the late U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Mollie Beattie, who died of cancer during the historic 1995-96 reintroduction.
Today, Mollie’s Pack is the last remaining wolf pack still intact since reintroduction three decades ago. The famous pack had been making headlines for leaving the safety of its longtime territory in Yellowstone’s Pelican Valley and mostly spending late 2025 and the first half of this year in Wyoming’s wolf hunt area one, located northwest of Cody.
“Wolf hunt areas one and two did close on Saturday, after reaching the mortality limit of four wolves,” Smith told the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission. “None of the wolves taken were from wolf packs previously assigned to Yellowstone National Park.”
Recent movements had put Mollie’s Pack in a good position to survive Wyoming’s hunt. Ahead of hunting season, the National Park Service had reported to WyoFile that the pack, which consisted of five adults and five pups in July, was “mostly” back in Yellowstone, where hunting isn’t allowed.
Wildlife advocates had been pressuring Wyoming wildlife managers to close down the hunt area where Mollie’s Pack had been spending time. Monday’s news came as a relief.
“Mollie’s Pack survived the hunt,” said Wyoming Untrapped founder Lisa Robertson, who traveled to Evanston for the commission meeting. “For more than three decades, they have taught us about resilience, family, adaptation, and the enduring nature of the wild.”
Yellowstone officials declined an interview Monday, saying the wolf hunt is a state issue. Packs crossing park boundaries, mostly into Montana, have altered the park population at times. Wolves that spend most of their time in Yellowstone are poorly suited to survive hunting because they generally lack a fear of humans, and sometimes even badly habituate to crowds.
Where wolves are managed as trophy game, Wyoming’s hunt is already tightly managed relative to Idaho and Montana. This year hunting opportunities were reduced as a result of a distemper outbreak that has dropped the population to its lowest level in two decades. The state OK’d hunting regulations that allow the killing of up to 22 wolves — half of 2025’s limit — during a season that runs through the end of December.
Game and Fish set a quota of four animals that could be killed in hunt areas one and two. Hunters reached that limit over the weekend, Smith said.
Statewide, 10 of 22 wolves that can be killed in Wyoming’s wolf trophy game area have been dispatched by hunters during the first week of the season, according to the state’s mortality database. No other hunt areas have reached their mortality limit.
Wolf hunting is a notoriously difficult pursuit. Wyoming’s hunters devote about 500 days of effort per animal they kill. Especially early in the fall, the pups of the year are the most vulnerable.
Wyoming’s trophy game area covers just 15% of the state. Across the rest of Wyoming, wolf hunting regulations are scant and wolves are managed as predators. No licenses are required in the remaining 85% of the state, and killing takes place without limit and few restrictions on method year-round.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma House lawmaker faces sexual harassment allegations. Committee recommends he resign.
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — State lawmakers recommended Thursday that a Republican colleague resign immediately and not seek reelection following allegations of repeated sexual harassment against multiple female Oklahoma House employees.  After hearing testimony behind closed doors earlier this month, the House Rules Committee on Thursday took the unusual step of recomm[...]
text:
Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, speaks to the House Rules Committee meeting Sept. 24, 2026 at the state Capitol ahead of a vote to censure him as well as recommend that he resign and end his bid for reelection following allegations of misconduct and sexual harassment. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — State lawmakers recommended Thursday that a Republican colleague resign immediately and not seek reelection following allegations of repeated sexual harassment against multiple female Oklahoma House employees. 
After hearing testimony behind closed doors earlier this month, the House Rules Committee on Thursday took the unusual step of recommending that state Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, be censured for “disorderly behavior” and face a number of other consequences.
Williams immediately called the decision “unfair.”
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, left, and Rep. Mike Osburn, R-Edmond, speak to members of the media after the House Rules Committee voted on Sept. 24, 2026 to censure and take action against Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, following allegations of misconduct and sexual harassment. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
But House Speaker Kyle Hilbert said while he said he can’t force Williams to resign or end his bid for reelection, he planned to implement the rest committee’s recommendations. Those included that Williams be permanently stripped of all committee assignments and leadership positions, that he not be assigned a legislative assistant and that he have no one-on-one contact with House staff. Williams will also be asked to complete 80 hours of “approved sexual harassment training and toxic workplace training” at his own expense, half of which need to be completed before Legislature next convenes in February, but Hilbert said he cannot enforce this. 
The committee also recommended that Williams be formally reprimanded by the full House when they next convene.
Hilbert, R-Bristow, would not discuss specifics of most of the allegations, but he said one incident involved allegations that Williams urinated in a cup after hours and then left it on his assistant’s desk. Multiple witnesses confirmed it was urine by smell, he said. 
After the meeting, Williams said he had “not broken any rule or any law” and that he maintained his innocence. 
“I was told that I was not eligible for due process,” he said. “I couldn’t challenge people that accused me. I couldn’t deal with false statements. I mean, there have been some statements made about me that I have never done in my entire life, but I have no way to deal with that and to me, that’s unfair.”
After making those brief remarks to the media, Williams, 77, did not answer questions. He attended the meeting Thursday with his attorney to listen to his colleagues vote on the series of actions designed to curtail his influence.
Williams – who Hilbert said was only one of two people present working late that night – has previously denied the allegation that he urinated in a cup. 
The committee alone does not have the power to compel Williams to resign nor not seek reelection, but the full House could vote to expel him with a two-thirds vote. 
Williams is up for reelection and faces Democrat Blake Cummings on the Nov. 3 ballot. It was not immediately clear if Williams would continue seeking reelection, but the deadline has passed to remove his name from the ballot. 
Hilbert said Thursday that he had already temporarily taken some of the actions recommended by the committee. 
Members of the House Rules Committee listen to Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, give a statement on Sept. 24, 2026, ahead of a vote to censure him following allegations of misconduct and sexual harassment. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
While Hilbert said the specific details of the allegations against Williams remain confidential to protect the anonymity of those who reported him, Hilbert said the claims were all substantiated and there were 11 witnesses who participated in the investigation, as well as electronic evidence. There were also additional witnesses who chose not to participate. 
“I think one of the most frustrating things about this is just not acknowledging what has happened, or not having remorse and just kind of doubling down,” Hilbert said. “Because I think with a lot of these things, remorse would have went a long way. But unfortunately, that was not the choice that he chose to make, and so here we are today.”
Hilbert said his office and House staff made the best decisions possible with the information they had at the time in order to “uphold the integrity of the Oklahoma House.” 
Hilbert said it’s up to the constituents of House District 28, which includes parts of Seminole and Pottawatomie counties, whether they want to reelect Williams. 
“We have made public as best as we can the conduct of Rep. Williams, and now the decision of whether or not he should be a member is in the hands of the voters of that district, and they will have that decision in a few weeks,” he said.
Hilbert said he is also encouraging both Democrats and Republicans to offer increased workplace behavior and sexual harassment trainings at their respective caucus retreats. 
“I hope if any good comes from this incident, it is that members take these situations very seriously and are aware and act appropriately in support,” Hilbert said. 
Timeline of the investigation
The first HR complaint against Williams was presented to the Speaker on May 18 and interviews with witnesses began two days later. Those revealed more instances of improper behavior and more people that needed to be interviewed, Hilbert said. Hilbert said he and Rep. Anthony Moore, R-Clinton, met with Williams on May 26. 
Rep. Mike Osburn, R-Edmond, right, speaks to Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, on Sept. 24, 2026, at the state Capitol ahead of a vote by the House Rules Committee to censure him following allegations of misconduct and sexual harassment. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
At this point, Williams would have been terminated if he were a private employee but the Oklahoma Constitution does not allow the speaker to unilaterally fire a legislator, Hilbert said. 
An outside law firm was then hired to investigate the claims against Williams in addition to the House’s internal HR investigation. The report, which Hilbert said he received July 22, prompted him to refer the situation to the House Rules Committee and inform all chamber lawmakers of the situation. 
The reports have not been made public. 
“It was clear upon reading this report that there were several substantiated claims of inappropriate behavior by multiple victims, and I will also say these were not he-said, she-said,” Hilbert said. 
The Rules Committee, led by Rep. Mike Osburn, R-Edmond, previously met behind closed doors for a total of 13 hours earlier this month to discuss the findings of investigations into Williams and what actions they would take. 
Rep. Andy Fugate, D-Del City, who sits on the committee, in a statement Thursday thanked Hilbert for his “quick action.” 
“If any business in this state had an employee face the same accusations as Rep. Danny Williams, he would be terminated,” he said. “Unfortunately, the House of Representatives is limited by its rules, procedures, and the reality of an election just weeks away. The action taken today was all we had available, but it was not enough. The House employees who came forward deserve better, and so do the people of Oklahoma.”
Another ethical investigation
Allegations of potential misuse of state resources by Williams also surfaced during the House’s internal investigation, Hilbert said. 
Hilbert said he asked a former attorney with the Oklahoma Ethics Commission to conduct an investigation into the matter. He said he received the report on the matter in July and his office referred the matter to the Ethics Commission. 
Neither the report nor the contents of the complaint have been made public, but the Ethics Commission voted Aug. 13 to open a formal investigation into Williams. The investigation is still ongoing. 
Lee Anne Bruce Boone, executive director of the Ethics Commission, said in a text to Oklahoma Voice she could not share more details about the investigation. 
“We are working diligently on a serious matter, recognizing that it is of public interest and an election is upcoming,” she said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Clerks reiterate Michigan elections are ‘safe, secure, fair’ as absentee voting begins
description: As absentee ballots for November’s general election begin to be mailed out to Michigan voters on Thursday, clerks and election advocates urged Michiganders to feel confident in the safety and security of the state’s election system and those who administer it. “I can say with complete confidence that our elections are safe, secure, fair and […]
text:
Absentee ballot | Susan J. DemasAs absentee ballots for November’s general election begin to be mailed out to Michigan voters on Thursday, clerks and election advocates urged Michiganders to feel confident in the safety and security of the state’s election system and those who administer it.
“I can say with complete confidence that our elections are safe, secure, fair and have accurate results,” said Grand Rapids City Clerk Joel Hondorp in a press conference hosted by the ACLU of Michigan on Thursday morning. 
Ingham County Clerk Barb Byrum, whose jurisdiction includes two cities — Lansing and East Lansing — that were targets of Department of Justice election monitors in the state’s August primary, said that those election monitors were treated as poll watchers, and if they return to any Ingham County polling places in November, the same will be true.
“In Michigan, local clerks and county clerks, and the Secretary of State and the Attorney General are ready to welcome them in, so long as they follow the rules and serve as poll watchers,” Byrum said, acknowledging that her whole district falls in the highly-contested 7th Congressional District.
Byrum emphasized that the reasoning provided for monitors to be present in August was not accurate, specifically referencing allegations of long lines, the non-use of provisional ballots and non-use of the qualified voter file by clerks. 
“We have not received any information of what was concerning, if they saw anything concerning, but it is important that we note that Michigan elections are transparent, and we welcome poll watchers. The more people watching, the more eyes on our election, the more faith people will have in the integrity of our elections,” Byrum said. “I think the intent was to make voters worry and make voters question the integrity of our elections, but truth be told, we have poll watchers all the time, and so the local clerks in Ingham County welcomed those DOJ watchers.”
A test ballot is submitted to a precinct tabulator in the Lansing Elections Office prior to the August primary. July 20, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Byrum’s comments come as election administrators and elected officials in Michigan and nationwide are preparing to respond in the case of federal interference, including armed federal officials at polling places, in November. 
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, for example, said in a panel on Wednesday that she is preparing her staff to station attorney general office agents in case there is a criminal incident or voting threat at polling locations, and making sure its assistant attorneys are prepared to do the same.
“We have briefs that we’ve prepared for virtually every set of circumstances we could think of, except the zombie apocalypse,” Nessel said in the event hosted by the Center for American Progress. “I don’t have that down yet.”
Mackenzie Walz, the election protection director for Promote the Vote, explained that, as a part of Michigan’s Election Protection Program, her organization is working to educate voters on their rights and on the election administration process, as well as to recruit nonpartisan challengers to observe the elections process at polling places, early voting sites and voter counting boards across the state to ensure that votes are being cast and counted properly.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
She also highlighted the election protection hotline, which allows voters to ask questions and get assistance with any part of the voting process, up through actually casting their ballot.  
“Call volume has been increasing for the Michigan call center, as we have expected, and we’ve been preparing for, by having more legal professionals prepared to staff,” Walz said. “We received several hundred calls for the August election, which is typically higher than what we’ve seen in the past, and we’ve already noticed call volume increasing now. We usually receive around a thousand calls on election day in November. We’re expecting at least that, if not more.”
Byrum also emphasized the importance of Michigan’s decentralized election system, saying, “This means that thousands and thousands and thousands of Michiganders across the state work together to carry out our elections. These dedicated folks are our neighbors. They work in bipartisan teams who are united for a single purpose: to deliver on the promise of democracy, and to do so with elections that are fair and free.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: KY Supreme Court declines to reconsider case of Fayette County judge
description: The Kentucky Supreme Court will not reconsider their decision that stopped the General Assembly from impeaching Fayette Circuit Judge Julie Goodman, according to a Thursday ruling. Last spring, the House voted to forward article of impeachment to the Senate, but the Supreme Court found the process unlawful because it violated constitutional separation of pow[...]
text:
Kentucky House Majority Whip Jason Nemes, R-Middletown, said while introducing impeachment articles against Fayette Circuit Judge Julie Goodman that judges "need not fear impeachment" if they are doing their job. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)The Kentucky Supreme Court will not reconsider their decision that stopped the General Assembly from impeaching Fayette Circuit Judge Julie Goodman, according to a Thursday ruling.
Fayette Circuit Judge Julie Muth Goodman (Kentucky Court of Justice photo)
Last spring, the House voted to forward article of impeachment to the Senate, but the Supreme Court found the process unlawful because it violated constitutional separation of powers and because her alleged wrongdoing did not rise to criminal offenses.
Republican lawmakers asked the Supreme Court to reconsider and because of a split vote without a majority, they declined.
Last year’s drama emerged out of numerous complaints surrounding Goodman’s conduct and decisions on the bench, including the judge doing her own research into a fatal hit and run case in Lexington.
However, the case was never referred to the Judicial Conduct Commission, which assesses complaints against judges.
Last May, House Speaker David Osborne and Rep. Jason Nemes, R-Louisville, asked the court to reconsider their decision with another hearing that would allow for oral arguments.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Childcare survey seeks to help reduce Omaha poverty
description: OMAHA — In a quest to reduce poverty, Omaha leaders on Thursday launched a citywide parent survey on childcare. Representatives of the state’s most populous city — which, along with Lincoln, was mandated by a 2024 state law to create a Poverty Elimination Action Plan — will use survey findings to help its mayor shape […]
text:
Toddlers at Kids Can, an early childhood education and day care, are shown here after a 2023 expansion into a new Omaha headquarters. Omaha has launched a survey to learn more about gaps that will inform potential new policy, grants and legislation. (Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
OMAHA — In a quest to reduce poverty, Omaha leaders on Thursday launched a citywide parent survey on childcare.
Representatives of the state’s most populous city — which, along with Lincoln, was mandated by a 2024 state law to create a Poverty Elimination Action Plan — will use survey findings to help its mayor shape new policy, grant or legislative recommendations.
No funding was attached to the state law, but Omaha leaders said they were taking the mandate seriously and earlier identified goals in focus areas that include affordable housing, job training and healthcare access. 
During a news conference, Mayor John Ewing Jr. noted that execution of the five-year anti-poverty plan is one of his top priorities. He said access to affordable childcare — which has been a stated goal of the Legislature as well — is key to family success. 
Ewing said Omaha’s research shows that 7% of a household’s gross salary is what should go toward child care.
“That is not happening anywhere in the City of Omaha at this point that I’m aware of, so if we can look at ways to reduce the cost, then we keep dollars in people’s pockets,” Ewing said, linking childcare with anti-poverty efforts. 
To date, the city’s working group on early childhood education and childcare has gathered data and held focus groups with providers and parents. The group of about 20, which includes representatives of nonprofits and childcare providers, wanted more feedback.
Now the survey, which is anonymous and closes Nov. 25, is open to all Omahans who are parents or guardians of kids 12 and under. Questions, offered in English and Spanish, seek insight on demographics, costs, barriers and suggested changes.
“Childcare is very important when addressing poverty, and it’s also a key economic driver,” said Cailin Daly Dejillas, Omaha’s city human rights and relations director, who is helping to lead the anti-poverty effort. “Please weigh in through the survey.” 
Omaha’s 164-page poverty elimination plan was adopted by the Omaha City Council in 2025 in response to the law introduced by state Sen. Terrell McKinney of north Omaha, whose aim was to improve economic circumstances for low-income families across the state. Lawmakers ultimately narrowed the mandate to apply only to Omaha and Lincoln.
Also helping to coordinate Omaha’s plan is the Nebraska Center for Justice Research of the University of Nebraska at Omaha.
Dejillas said UNO researchers will analyze the childcare survey results and focus group responses, and she expects those results early next year.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Source New Mexico
title: U.S. Rep. Leger Fernández calls for ‘pause’ on data centers in New Mexico, as Oracle stock falls
description: U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) on Thursday issued a call for a “pause” on data centers in New Mexico, and released a set of standards she said such developments should meet before receiving approval. Her announcement came as Oracle stock dropped amid reports it seeks to limit liability on Project Jupiter.
text:
New Mexico residents protested a pending air quality permit application for the Oracle and OpenAI data center, Project Jupiter, outside the New Mexico Environment Department in Santa Fe on Aug. 21, 2026. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) on Thursday issued a call for a “pause” on data centers in New Mexico, and released a set of standards she said such developments should meet before receiving approval.
Leger Fernández’s call follows concerns voiced by fellow Democratic New Mexico U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury last month about tech giant Oracle’s Project Jupiter, the data center under construction in southern New Mexico.
Project Jupiter has faced a variety of legal and regulatory challenges, and the New Mexico State Ethics Commission last week reported that the Oracle had spent more than $3.4 million in recent months on advertisements meant to influence the New Mexico Environment Department’s air quality permitting process for Project Jupiter.
Now, according to a Thursday report from Bloomberg, Oracle has sent Project Jupiter’s developer a notice citing “force majeure,” essentially a contract provision that would allow it to delay payments if Project Jupiter is not online by 2028. Numerous financial outlets report that Oracle stock dropped 4% following news of that notification.
Leger Fernández’s announcement also comes as state lawmakers gear up to consider a data center moratorium during next year’s legislative session, and as Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland, a recipient of Oracle campaign contributions, says she would sign an executive order instituting such a moratorium on day one of her administration if elected.
Leger Fernández, in a news release, said data centers should abide by certain provisions if elected, which she titled the No Blank Checks for Data Centers Principles. Those principles include being able to demonstrate that a data center won’t increase electricity bills or negatively impact water resources and must meet the state’s renewable energy requirements. They would also have to create union jobs that pay well; not require taxpayer subsidies and have community approval.
“The role of government is to protect us from greedy corporations,” Leger Fernández said in a statement. “Data centers want our water, our land, and our power. Communities may want the jobs they could bring to New Mexico. But we will not give them a blank check.” 
Leger Fernández also linked the concerns over data centers to the rising call for oversight of AI, saying in a statement: “We cannot let AI and data centers regulate themselves.”
Source senior reporter Joshua Bowling contributed reporting to this story.

title: Tiffany campaign blocks Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel reporter from event
description: The gubernatorial campaign of Republican Tom Tiffany blocked a reporter for the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel from entering an event in Milwaukee Thursday, preventing the state’s largest newspaper from covering the campaign.  The campaign’s decision to prevent reporter Mary Spicuzza from covering the event comes just days after Tiffany said at a news conference[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany answers questions from the press at the Wisconsin Counties Association annual conference on Sept. 22. (Screenshot/WisEye)The gubernatorial campaign of Republican Tom Tiffany blocked a reporter for the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel from entering an event in Milwaukee Thursday, preventing the state’s largest newspaper from covering the campaign. 
The campaign’s decision to prevent reporter Mary Spicuzza from covering the event comes just days after Tiffany said at a news conference that he would allow reporters, even those from “slanted” outlets such as the Journal-Sentinel, access to his campaign. Tiffany was asked about press access in the wake of President Donald Trump’s decision to revoke White House press badges for reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico. 
“As you can see, I did not deter anyone here from joining us today and I don’t plan on doing that — even you [Journal-Sentinel reporter] Laura [Schulte], I’m going to continue to allow you here,” Tiffany said at the Wisconsin Counties Association conference on Tuesday. “I believe in open, free press, that they be able to ask us questions. The principle that I live with, is I just expect all of you to be fair, and as long as you’re fair in your writing, I always welcome the press here. It’s when the press is slanted, that’s what’s frustrating.” 
At the event, Tiffany told reporters that he’ll “have to talk to his communications team” about Spicuzza’s access. 
In a post on social media after the event, Tiffany’s campaign said it had notified Spicuzza that she wouldn’t be allowed into the event because of her alleged political views, but that other staff members from the outlet would be allowed. 
“Liberal activist [Spicuzza] was notified yesterday that she would not be permitted to attend,” the Tiffany campaign wrote on X. “[The Journal-Sentinel] has a photographer at the event, and we welcome all balanced journalists across Wisconsin, including [Journal-Sentinel reporter Jessie Opoien]. That’s why WISN, CBS 58, and other outlets are in attendance.”
Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel Editor Greg Borowski said in a statement that preventing the paper’s reporters from covering events prevents information from being shared with voters.
“When our reporters cover campaigns and attend political events, they are there on behalf of the public,” Borowski said. “Blocking them blocks the public from vital information. Our aim is to help voters understand the candidates, their backgrounds and their positions. We will continue to pursue fair and unbiased coverage, despite campaigns creating unnecessary hurdles.”

description: Gov. Andy Beshear asked Kentucky’s congressional delegation in a Thursday letter to throw their support behind a bill amending the Black Lung Benefits Act to “provide adequate benefits for miners suffering from black lung disease.”  The Black Lung Benefits Act “provides monthly payments and medical benefits to coal miners totally disabled from pneumoconiosis[...]
text:
X-rays of a patient with black lung disease. (National Archives at College Park photo)Gov. Andy Beshear asked Kentucky’s congressional delegation in a Thursday letter to throw their support behind a bill amending the Black Lung Benefits Act to “provide adequate benefits for miners suffering from black lung disease.” 
The Black Lung Benefits Act “provides monthly payments and medical benefits to coal miners totally disabled from pneumoconiosis (black lung disease) arising from their employment in or around the nation’s coal mines,” according to the Office of Workers’ Compensation Programs in the U.S. Department of Labor. 
The bill Beshear is supporting, H. R. 9556 from Pennsylvania Democrat Rep. Summer Lee, hasn’t moved since June 30. 
According to the bill:  “When section 412 of the Black Lung Benefits Act was enacted in 1969, a miner received about $144.50 per month to help support their cost of living, equating to about $1,252.53 annually in today’s currency, adjusting for inflation.” 
“The benefit rate, as established in 1969, has not kept up with the cost of living,” Lee’s bill states. “Today, miners receive nearly 40 percent less than the value of the original amount adjusting for inflation.” 
Kentucky Public Media and NPR reported in August that Appalachia is seeing the highest number of cases in 50 years. 
Appalachia’s black lung rates highest in nearly 50 years as miners’ protections stall

“Kentucky miners powered homes, communities and our economy for generations, and it’s important we show up for them in return by making sure they have the care and support needed to treat black lung disease,” Beshear said in a statement. “Unfortunately, the current system is inadequate, and the value of their benefits continues to shrink as inflation grows and costs continue to rise. Government is meant to help hardworking people like these miners, and Congress has a chance to make a difference by supporting this legislation.”
Although the Support Our Miners Act is supported by many local officials, including many Republicans, most off Kentucky’s federal delegation has stayed silent. A Kentucky Lantern story in July asked each member to respond; only Rep. Hal Rogers did so, saying Democrats “aren’t being transparent about their movement to destroy the trust fund through their targeted War on Coal, and sticking taxpayers with the bill.”

title: Millions of dollars of waste found in Trump administration push for immigration detention
text: WASHINGTON — Government investigators Thursday released a report that found the Department of Homeland Security wasted more than $20 million in federal funding in its rapid expansion of immigration detention, including warehouse purchases strongly opposed in numerous U.S. communities.The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office found that millions were wasted because DHS began expanding detention operations without putting a plan in place to meet U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's goal of detaining up to 100,000 immigrants. As the second Trump administration aims to deport 1 million immigrants a year, DHS has rapidly increased the numbers of people in immigration detention after congressional Republicans last year approved roughly $175 billion for immigration enforcement.“As ICE spends the unprecedented multi-year detention funding provided by (the One Big Beautiful Act) and the Secure America Act, it is critical that the agency uses these taxpayer dollars efficiently and effectively,” according to the report by the watchdog agency. “In the absence of a comprehensive strategic plan to guide detention expansion, ICE has wasted funds on unsuccessful detention initiatives and lacks important information about the long-term affordability of its investments.” Tents assembled, never usedIn the report, GAO found those detention expansion efforts wasted millions by using facilities that were high in cost or impractical, such as Naval Station Guantanamo Bay, which is so remote that water needs to be imported to the base, making it a costly operation. Inspectors with the Department of Defense and Department of State estimated that DOD spent $2.85 million to assemble tents that were never used and that ICE obligated $43 million from the start of fiscal year 2025 to June 30, 2026 for a small population at the base. GAO found that 16 noncitizens were held on average daily at Guantanamo in fiscal year 2026. Other efforts that lacked proper planning also included domestic military operations, such as the soft-sided facility, Camp East Montana, built on a military base in El Paso, Texas.GAO previously reported that ICE wasted more than $11 million in taxpayer funds in operating Camp East Montana, such as paying for meals when detainees had not yet arrived at the facility. Investigators noted that ICE had awarded another contract in March for Camp East Montana and “as of August 2026 had not yet incorporated these cost saving measures into the contract and continued to pay for services that it did not need.”Warehouses cost more than $1BInvestigators also examined the purchase of 11 warehouses at $1.07 billion for the purpose of immigration detention. The initiative was initially undertaken by former Homeland Secretary Kristi Noem, but she stepped down following the deaths of two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis who were shot by immigration officials. Her replacement, former Oklahoma Sen. Markwayne Mullin, paused the warehouse effort. DHS now plans to sell seven of the sites that were purchased. Investigators said the department’s change of course has led to nonrecoverable costs, such as $7.7 million spent in zoning assessments and title insurance. Additionally, ICE is still paying for utilities, security and other services at the warehouses it intends to sell, costing approximately $12.8 million as of last month.Investigators also warned that ICE’s separate move to purchase $1.5 billion in existing detention facilities has the potential to waste money because the agency has not assessed any long-term costs of operating the facilities. And GAO notes that while ICE did not have an agreement with the state of Florida to reimburse funds for its soft-sided facility, the now shuttered “Alligator Alcatraz,” DHS used funds from the Federal Emergency Management Agency to award $608.4 million to the state. No idea of long-term costInvestigators also raised concerns that ICE has not made an assessment for the long-term cost of operating the expanded detention facilities. “ICE has not projected the costs of these facilities beyond the first 3 years of operation, after which ICE will no longer have OBBBA and Secure America Act funds available for obligation because these funds are only available through fiscal year 2029,” according to the report. Investigators made a recommendation that the Director of ICE “should develop a comprehensive strategic plan to guide its detention expansion efforts that includes goals, activities, and resource needs.”GAO reported that the department agreed and that ICE would develop a strategic plan for its detention expansion, but that plan will not be completed until Aug. 31, 2027. “Given ICE’s unprecedented multi-year detention funding and the potential for continued waste of taxpayer dollars, more timely completion may be warranted,” according to the report. Congressional Democrats requested that GAO do the study. Those lawmakers include Rhode Island Sen. Jack Reed, ranking member of the Senate Committee on Armed Services, Michigan Sen. Gary Peters, ranking member on the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, Dick Durbin of Illinois, ranking member on the Senate Committee on the Judiciary and Mississippi Rep. Bennie G. Thompson, ranking member on the House Committee on Homeland Security.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Circuit court allows Ohio BMV to require proof of citizenship for voter registration
description: Ohio officials can continue using a new proof of citizenship requirement for people who register to vote at the Bureau of Motor Vehicles. In a divided ruling, The Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals lifted a lower court order on Wednesday. It comes less than two weeks before Ohio’s voter registration deadline. Under 2025’s Ohio House […]
text:
(Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Ohio officials can continue using a new proof of citizenship requirement for people who register to vote at the Bureau of Motor Vehicles. In a divided ruling, The Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals lifted a lower court order on Wednesday.
It comes less than two weeks before Ohio’s voter registration deadline.
The case
Under 2025’s Ohio House Bill 54, BMV clerks offer clients the opportunity register to vote, but only after completing a driver’s license application which requires documentary proof of citizenship.
Two civic organizations, The Ohio Alliance for Retired Americans and Red Wine & Blue, challenged those provisions.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The National Voter Registration Act, commonly known as the motor voter law, requires vehicle registration agencies to offer the opportunity to register when someone submits a driver’s license application. It also directs states to require the “only the minimum amount of information necessary.”
Voter registration forms — including those available at many other public agencies around Ohio — have no proof of citizenship requirement. Instead, applicants declare under penalty of perjury that they are eligible to vote.
Red Wine & Blue and the Ohio Alliance for Retired Americans argued the BMV conditioning access to voter registration services on proof of citizenship violates the minimum information standard.
The groups presented two members who were initially barred from registering, both women, whose documents didn’t reflect their name change after marriage.
In one case, Margaret Dutcher showed up with a valid U.S. Passport — documentary proof of her citizenship — but was still unable to register because she did not have all the documents necessary to get a license.
Research from the University of Maryland indicates 21 million Americans don’t have readily available, up-to-date citizenship documents.
The district judge attempted to cut a middle path. He ordered state officials to stop requiring BMV visitors produce proof of citizenship to register. He added that his order applied to those whose license applications are “ultimately unsuccessful” over lack of documents, but not those who affirmatively indicate they are not a citizen.
The Circuit Court majority opinion
Circuit Judges John Nalbandian and Whitney Hermandorfer, both Trump appointees, downplayed Ohio’s policy and the alleged injury the plaintiffs suffered.
Federal court blocks Ohio’s proof of citizenship requirements for voter registration

The BMV’s electronic system walks applicants through their license application and once it’s accepted, moves forward to a prompt asking the applicant if they’d like to use their information to register to vote. That’s a reasonable arrangement, the majority opinion concludes, because the universe of eligible license holders is includes minors and non-citizens — neither of whom can vote.
The majority also noted the BMV has paper forms available, and clerks are required to process applications. The state argued a more proactive effort to offer registration would require “wholesale retraining and restructuring of the BMV application process.” The majority bought that argument.
But the majority’s central problem with the case was the underlying harm.
The majority didn’t buy the idea that the individuals identified in the case had suffered an injury, and without injury, there’s no standing to sue.
“Neither Dutcher nor Fazio ever encountered anything having to do with the Associations’ H.B. 54 voter-registration challenge,” the majority wrote, “Instead, BMV officials rejected their driver’s-license applications based on independent paperwork defects.”
The majority contends the challengers aren’t so much finding fault with Ohio’s new law as its administration of drivers licenses, and so enjoining the law wouldn’t address their concerns.
The majority also determined the case is moot because the women in the case have since gotten their licenses and registered to vote.
The dissent
Circuit Judge Kevin Ritz, a Biden appointee, sees the case differently. He brushed aside the majority’s questions of standing and mootness. Two people who wanted to register weren’t afforded that opportunity when they applied for a license. “That is enough,” he said.
The plaintiffs later getting registered, doesn’t mean the case is moot, he added, because that injury could happen again to others.
“A contrary ruling as to rnootness would mean that potential voters who challenge an unlawful state law governing voter registration would have to forgo their registration and right to vote for as long as it took to litigate their challenge to the law,” he wrote. “I am reluctant to construct a Catch-22 that would require a litigant to renounce a ‘fundamental’ right in order to bring suit.”
Like the district court judge, Ritz focused on the importance of “submission.” Under the motor voter law, BMV clerks have to offer registration to people who “submit” a driver’s license application.
To Ritz and the district court, that happens when a person seeks a license, not when the BMV agrees to accept their application. So even people who don’t have all the documents necessary for a license should still be afforded an opportunity to register.
Ritz also said “there’s nothing in the record” to support the state’s argument that a more proactive approach to registration could create voter confusion.
“There is no proof, for instance,” he wrote, “that voters will be confused by a deputy registrar offering them a paper form that is already available elsewhere at the BMV.”

name: VTDigger
title: Don’t let scare tactics sink Proposal 4
description:
Warnings that an equal protection amendment will raise taxes and invite lawsuits don't hold up to scrutiny.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Don’t let scare tactics sink Proposal 4.
text:
Dear Editor,
Renee McGuinness’ recent attack on Proposal 4 implies that the purpose of the state constitutional amendment on the November ballot is to raise taxes, expand government bureaucracy, cancel rights and generate lawsuits.
Actually, passage of Proposal 4 would add Article 23 to the Vermont Constitution, prohibiting the denial of rights based on race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or national origin. The third and final sentence of the very brief article reads, “Nothing in this Article shall be interpreted or applied to prevent the adoption or implementation of measures intended to provide equality of treatment and opportunity for members of groups that have historically been subject to discrimination.” This is widely understood to mean that diversity, equity and inclusion programs may not be banned on the grounds that they discriminate against a traditionally privileged group. As of May, 30 states had civil rights provisions in their original or amended constitutions.
As is required of Vermont constitutional amendments, Proposal 4 passed both legislative houses in two successive sessions. In spring 2026, the proposed amendment passed the House by 128-14 and the Senate by 29-0. The overwhelming approval of the measure by members of all parties may explain why there has been almost no discussion or debate about it ahead of the coming elections. Organizations including the Vermont Human Rights Commission, the Vermont Racial Justice Alliance, the League of Women Voters of Vermont and the American Civil Liberties Union of Vermont endorse Proposal 4.

READ MORE

Unfortunately, there are those who do not want guaranteed rights for certain individuals and groups enshrined in the constitution and will fabricate some far-fetched scenarios to frighten and prejudice voters against Proposal 4. I am confident that Vermonters will see through this nonsense and resoundingly affirm Proposal 4’s important assurance of equality. 
Judy OlinickMiddlebury, Vt.

title: 4 candidates seek to fill Arkansas state Senate seat vacancy
description: Four Arkansans filed by Thursday’s deadline to run in the Jan. 5 special election to fill the Senate District 18 vacancy, according to the secretary of state’s office.  Independent candidates Steven McClelland and Trevor McGarragh, Democrat Camille Feyen and Republican Will Moore are seeking to replace Republican Jonathan Dismang, who resigned from the Senat[...]
text:
The Arkansas State Capitol and grounds seen from the southeast on Nov. 11, 2025. (Photo by Sonny Albarado/Arkansas Advocate)Four Arkansans filed by Thursday’s deadline to run in the Jan. 5 special election to fill the Senate District 18 vacancy, according to the secretary of state’s office. 
Independent candidates Steven McClelland and Trevor McGarragh, Democrat Camille Feyen and Republican Will Moore are seeking to replace Republican Jonathan Dismang, who resigned from the Senate earlier this month to take a job at Arkansas Electric Cooperatives. 
Sen. Jonathan Dismang, an architect of Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion, stepping down

Moore, Searcy’s city attorney, has been endorsed by Dismang and several other top Republicans, including Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders.
Dismang’s successor will serve the remainder of his term as the representative of Senate District 18, which includes White County and parts of Faulkner and Cleburne counties. Dismang, the former co-chairman of the Joint Budget Committee, was last elected in 2024 to a four-year term that ends in January 2029. 
The vacancy leaves Republicans with a 27-6 majority in the Senate.
Dismang’s seat will be the sixth legislative vacancy to be filled over the last year. Republican Sen. Brad Simon and Democratic Rep. Alex Holladay won special elections in March to represent Senate District 26 and House District 70, respectively. 
Republican Bill Teeter won the House District 44 special election in August to replace the late Republican Rep. Stan Berry.  
Eudora Mayor Tomeka Butler, a Democrat, and Rison Republican Harrell Wilson are vying for the Senate District 1 seat in a special election that coincides with November’s general election. The winner will replace former Republican Sen. Ben Gilmore who resigned in June to work for Attorney General Tim Griffin.  
Republican Kara Armas of Pea Ridge and Democrat Parker Stohlton of Bella Vista are facing each other to represent House District 8 in a separate special election that’s also scheduled during November’s midterms. 
The seat became vacant when former Republican Rep. Austin McCollum resigned in August following domestic violence charges. His resignation left Republicans with a 79-20 majority in the House.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont does not need proposed constitutional amendments
description:
Two ballot measures — one on equal protection, one on collective bargaining — are already covered by existing constitutional guarantees.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont does not need proposed constitutional amendments.
text:
Dear Editor,
In our statewide election this November, Vermont voters will see two amendments to the Vermont Constitution on the ballot: Proposal 3 and Proposal 4.
The proposed constitutional amendments were crafted and passed by the majority in the Vermont Legislature with legal end goals in mind. Gov. Phil Scott has zero control over constitutional amendments and cannot veto them. Scott said, “I encourage voters to do their homework before making their voices heard” regarding the amendments.
Interestingly, neither amendment is necessary, as the Vermont Constitution and the U.S. Constitution already guarantee equal rights to everyone under the law (Prop 4) and the right to form a labor union (Prop 3).
Here’s the bottom line on Prop 4. First, its title — “equality of rights” — is very deceptive. In truth, Prop 4 will give special rights to certain groups. It will also make Vermont less affordable because it effectively establishes a constitutional foundation for reparations — financial compensation to certain groups of people for harms done in the past. 

READ MORE

A constitutional expert and professor of law at Vermont Law and Graduate School, Peter Teachout, who is not a conservative, testified to the Legislature that although he supported the principle of an equal rights proposal, he would not vote for Prop 4 as it stands.
Please inform yourselves, your friends and your neighbors about the constitutional amendments before us.
Wendy WiltonMilton, Vt.
