name: Nevada Current
title: Ford and Lombardo aren’t leading Nevada’s data center debate. They’re just trying to navigate it.
description: Both Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo and the Democrat hoping to unseat him, Attorney General Aaron Ford, have been playing catch-up on data centers. Their positions have been reactive and unimaginative. It’s as if their hearts aren’t in it. Most of the Nevada press, and some national outlets as well, generously gave Lombardo ad-ready headlines last […]
text:
On data center tax breaks, as on economic policy in general, there isn't much daylight between Lombardo and Ford. (Photos: Ford's campaign; Lombardo's office)Both Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo and the Democrat hoping to unseat him, Attorney General Aaron Ford, have been playing catch-up on data centers. Their positions have been reactive and unimaginative. It’s as if their hearts aren’t in it.
Most of the Nevada press, and some national outlets as well, generously gave Lombardo ad-ready headlines last week about the governor announcing “guardrails” on data center development. 
Under an executive order accompanying Lombardo’s announcement, existing data centers would continue to get all the tax breaks they’ve always received, but new data centers would only get most of them.
Why remove just one slice of data center tax breaks. Why not toss out the whole tax break pie?
The order also creates a “community support commitment” under which new data centers wouldn’t be eligible for all those remaining tax breaks unless the facilities minimize water use and don’t stick the public with higher electricity bills.
Why tie those conditions to tax breaks? Why not just require data centers to meet those conditions or they can’t build in Nevada, period?
If we take Lombardo at his word, the answer to the aforementioned questions is in the second “WHEREAS” of his executive order:
 “…data centers are the means by which Nevada will meet an unprecedented challenge and realize an unprecedented opportunity, one of the most significant for economic growth and fiscal diversification this State has seen in a generation…”
He seems genuinely all in.
But over the summer, Lombardo also seemed genuinely all in on the proposition that Nevada already had excellent guardrails to protect the state’s resources and citizenry from any ill-effects caused by data centers.
“You’ve probably seen stories in the news about local residents in other states reporting low water pressure or huge spikes in their energy bills after a data center gets built,” Lombardo wrote in a guest column for the Reno Gazette-Journal in June. 
“But the truth is, it isn’t happening in Nevada – because we’ve made it clear that companies investing in Nevada must do so in a way that protects our resources, our communities and our quality of life,” Lombardo wrote, referencing requirements companies must meet to get tax breaks.
Two months later, in correspondence with Democratic U.S. Rep. Dina Titus over concerns about the state’s regulatory role regarding potential data centers on federal lands, Lombardo again gushed over the state’s wonderful process for permitting and awarding tax breaks to data centers.
“Abatements are an effective tool for attracting job creating projects that strengthen and diversify Nevada’s economy,” Lombardo wrote to Titus while failing to address her specific questions. “As you are aware,” Lombardo continued, “processes at the state and local levels have a high degree of transparency and offer significant opportunities for public participation and feedback.”
But Nevada must not have really “made it clear” to companies that they must do no harm. 
And Nevada regulatory processes, let alone those dealing with tax breaks, must not have had such “a high degree of transparency” after all. 
Or at least not enough to crow about while trying to neutralize a hot-button campaign issue.
Hence the governor’s executive order last week.
Ford, as you’ve no doubt heard and seen in countless attack ads by now, sponsored the original data center tax break bill enacted in 2015. (What you might not have heard, because it isn’t included in the attack ads against Ford, is that Republicans controlled both houses of the state Legislature in 2015 and the bill passed the state Senate unanimously; to reiterate, in 2015, Anthropic, OpenAI, and hyperscaling weren’t household terms.)
Ford had to be dragged kicking and screaming back to the data center issue over the summer, declining to answer a question about tax breaks in June, and saying “I will continue to look at this” in July.
But by August, scrambling just like Lombardo (and politicians coast to coast) to gain a toehold on the issue, Ford called for a pause on approving data center tax breaks until the effectiveness of the tax breaks could be reviewed. 
At the same time, Ford released a “Data Centers Accountability Plan” outlining conditions data centers would have to meet to qualify for tax breaks. It could have served as a template for Lombardo’s executive order last week, except without the Lombardo campaign’s laughably gimmicky inclusion of eliminating one portion of the tax breaks.
And so once again we find that all the rhetoric and the breathless ads notwithstanding, on data center tax breaks, as on economic policy in general, there isn’t much daylight between Lombardo and Ford. Both say they want to use tax breaks to make data centers behave.
It can’t be said that either candidate is shaping the state’s data center discussion. They’re merely navigating it
Perhaps the discussion could be opened up a bit.
For starters, let’s never forget that data centers are being built to meet the demands of a tiny band of oligarchs. The fabulousness of their wealth is exceeded only by the creepiness of their personality disorders and the arrogance of their disregard for mere mortals who work for a living.
Instead of counting on tax breaks to coax good behavior out of data center owners, operators, and the oligarchs driving the data center infestation, demand good behavior. Stop giving them tax breaks, and penalize bad behavior with heavy penalties and fines. The AI-driven data center industry can afford it.
Instead of giving data centers tax breaks, tax them more. Gaming, mining, insurance … Nevada has a long history of imposing industry-specific taxes. Create and impose one on data centers. Again, they can afford it.
And it wouldn’t be a bad idea to make data centers owners post substantial reclamation bonds up front, just in case somebody cracks the cold fusion nut or otherwise renders them obsolete.
Ford and Lombardo may feel they’ve charted courses that will safely traverse data centers as a campaign problem. Maybe they have. But neither candidate is anywhere close to adequately confronting the issue, let alone the deplorable tech lords who are recklessly inflicting it upon us.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Sun brace for ’emotional’ farewell as the WNBA franchise plays its final game
description: The Connecticut Sun plays its final game before moving to Houston after an impressive run for first independently owned team in the league.
text:
The Connecticut WNBA franchise will play its final game in the state before it moves to Houston next year after an impressive run for the first independently owned team in the league.
Texas will be the third stop for the franchise. The team moved to Connecticut in 2003 from Orlando. The Sun made three trips to the WNBA Finals, hosted a record four All-Star Games and Connecticut was the first team to turn a profit in the league’s history. The team, which was purchased for $10 million, was sold for $300 million.
“It’s been an emotional week,” team president Jen Rizzotti told The Associated Press. “The silver lining of the chapter closing is it forces you to look at what this franchise has meant for over two decades and make sure the story is told and the legacy lasts forever.”
The franchise is moving to the home of the former Comets, who won the first four WNBA titles. Its time in Connecticut will end Thursday when the Sun face Toronto in the regular-season finale.
[RELATED: The CT Sun is leaving. The sale has raised deeper questions.]
Rizzotti will move to Houston with the team as the president of basketball operations. She said that 75-80% of the front office staff will also make the move.
“It’s exciting to celebrate the past while also being emotional that it’s ending,” she said. “Thursday is a celebration of our fans with fan appreciation night. One game isn’t enough to show the appreciation of how much they poured into the franchise for 24 years.”
Why are the Sun moving?
The WNBA seems to have outgrown the Sun with the new collective bargaining agreement demanding standard amenities for all teams that include state-of-the-art practice facilities.
The Mohegan Tribe, which owns the franchise, sold the team to Houston Rockets owner Tilman Fertitta for $300 million.
The Sun had an offer for $325 million from a group led by Celtics minority owner Steve Pagliuca that would have moved the franchise to Boston. The WNBA basically blocked that deal from happening by saying that “relocation decisions are made by the WNBA Board of Governors and not by individual teams.”
Now the franchise is becoming the first to relocate since San Antonio moved to Las Vegas in 2017.
“It’s sad,” said former Connecticut Sun CEO Mitchell Etess in a phone interview. “I put a lot into it and to see it go is sad. It did confirm that it was a good business decision to bring it there in the first place. If I was still CEO I’d recommend we sell it for that much profit.”
Being in the smallest market in the WNBA led to difficulties for the franchise to attract top free agents. Over the past two years the team has gone from being a WNBA Finals contender to rebuilding mode.
Still, despite a 10-33 record, the Sun were drawing nearly 8,700 fans a game in the 10,000-seat arena.
Sun honored their past this season
Throughout the season Connecticut honored some of the franchise’s iconic players, including Jonquel Jones, Jasmine Thomas, Alyssa Thomas, Tina Charles along with coaches Curt Miller and Mike Thibault. The group joined other Connecticut standouts — Margo Dydek, Katie Douglas, Nykesha Sales, Taj McWilliams-Franklin, Lindsay Whalen and Asjha Jones — in the rafters at the arena.
Thibault was the last of the group to be honored as Connecticut hosted the event after last Sunday’s game against Minnesota. Whalen, Charles and McWilliams-Franklin were in attendance for that contest as well as dozens of other former employees and front office staffers.
They told stories and stayed well after the game reminiscing about the franchise. Rizzotti expects a similar celebration after Thursday’s finale.
“I know we’re going really blow the game out,” she said of celebration plans. “Lot of things we’re giving away, postgame mingles and autograph opportunities. When everybody leaves we’ll just pop Champagne on the court for the last time. I’m proud of what we built.”
Connecticut was ‘icebreaker’ with gambling partnership
Etess remembers trying to sell NBA Commissioner David Stern on moving a franchise to the Mohegan Sun. The late commissioner was concerned about putting a team in a casino, but as it turns out, he was ahead of his time.
“There was a lot of excitement at the beginning, still a casino and a professional sports team being together wasn’t well received everywhere,” Etess recalled in a phone conversation. “David Stern took a lot of the hard questions when that was happening. In retrospect, it was an icebreaker for a lot of the gambling stuff that happened since. The tribe was proud of having the team as it was great to bring national attention to the state and casino.”
The Mohegan Tribe bought the team for $10 million and with the WNBA in CBA negotiations the franchise had a few months to get everything ready to start in 2003. Thibault remembers when he was hired as the coach in January, the franchise had literally nothing.
Thibault said he had to order basketballs, uniforms and even sports bras for his players. The franchise quickly turned into contenders, reaching the WNBA Finals in 2004 and 2005.
Building a faithful fan base
Thibault joked that when the team first started fans came to games to cheer on former UConn players when they came to town, but soon they became fans of the franchise.
“The first year, we didn’t have as good attendance as we had hoped, but that changed quickly,” Etess said. “We didn’t give tickets away. After the second year we were always up there in total attendance for many, many years.”
The Sun became the first team in WNBA history to make a profit when they made it happen in 2010.
“It meant a lot to us,” Etess said. “We really focused on doing everything right, trying to run the team professionally.”
Etess is sad to see the state lose its last professional team in an area that has been a women’s basketball hotbed for so long.
“It’s odd that the league didn’t want the team to stay in Connecticut,” he said. “Connecticut is such a crucial part of women’s basketball. The state that loves women’s basketball isn’t going to have a pro team, doesn’t feel right to me.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: The number of food recalls are down, but individual outbreaks can be severe
description: The number of food recalls reported by the federal government have decreased in recent years. Last year, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration reported 1,500 food recalls, according to federal data. That was one of the lowest totals over the past decade, and this year is on track to be even lower — through mid-September, […]
text:
Vegetables and lettuces at a grocery store in Michigan. Lettuces and salad greens were a likely source in the nationwide cyclosporiasis outbreak, which sickened thousands of people. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)The number of food recalls reported by the federal government have decreased in recent years.

Last year, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration reported 1,500 food recalls, according to federal data. That was one of the lowest totals over the past decade, and this year is on track to be even lower — through mid-September, the FDA has reported about 950 recalls.
While the figures are down, individual outbreaks can be severe, and the Trump administration’s staffing and oversight cuts may worsen the situation.



This year, thousands of people fell sick after eating lettuce tainted with cyclospora, a parasite that causes violent spasms of watery diarrhea. The lettuce came from Taylor Farms, a Mexican operation that supplies Taco Bell, Wal-Mart and Costco, among others. More than 20 states were affected, and Kroger reported that so many people avoided buying lettuce the grocery chain’s bottomline was hit.
The FDA inspects foreign sites that grow food for U.S. consumption, but it had not inspected Taylor Farms since 2019, according to the Associated Press. Since that year, the outlet reported, the overall number of foreign food site inspections has fallen by about 35%.



While the Trump administration has cut staffing levels, it has not cut food safety inspectors at the FDA. However, it did fire staffers who handled travel arrangements for inspectors, according to the AP.
Once Taylor Farms was identified as the source of the outbreak, it took four weeks to get inspectors into Mexico — “too long to get boots on the ground,” a former top food safety official at the FDA told the AP.
Last year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — which, like the FDA, is under the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services — announced changes to how it monitors foodborne pathogens. The CDC said its early warning system named FoodNet, a collaboration with other federal agencies and states, would no longer track six pathogens, including cyclospora. The CDC has said other systems exist to perform the same function.
The federal government has struggled to contain some food outbreaks in recent years.
In 2024, Boar’s Head deli meat, a supermarket staple, was linked to a Listeria outbreak. At least 10 people died, making it the deadliest Listeria outbreak in recent memory. Prior to the outbreak, inspectors with the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which oversees the safety of meat in the U.S. food supply, documented black mold and flies at a Boar’s Head processing plant.
ProPublica revealed in 2021 an ongoing salmonella outbreak in chicken that food safety officials allowed to continue to make people sick. A few years earlier, officials detected the outbreak, which was sending people to seek medical attention. But, according to ProPublica’s reporting, officials closed the investigation into the outbreak without alerting consumers.
Investigate Midwest is an independent, nonprofit newsroom. Our mission is to serve the public interest by exposing dangerous and costly practices of influential agricultural corporations and institutions through in-depth and data-driven investigative journalism. Visit us online at www.investigatemidwest.org

name: Daily Montanan
title: Public Service Commission votes to take up merger decision with new member
description: A newly seated member of the Montana Public Service Commission is free to participate in the NorthWestern Energy and Black Hills Corp merger decision despite not being present at the hearing about it. That’s according to a unanimous vote this week by the PSC. But the question about whether Commissioner Kirk Bushman can vote on […]
text:
A power line is pictured crossing Beck Hill Road in Powell County, Montana on Thursday, June 11, 2026 (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)A newly seated member of the Montana Public Service Commission is free to participate in the NorthWestern Energy and Black Hills Corp merger decision despite not being present at the hearing about it.
That’s according to a unanimous vote this week by the PSC.
But the question about whether Commissioner Kirk Bushman can vote on the $15.4 billion merger is still pending in Lewis and Clark County District Court.
The issue arose because Bushman recently stepped into office at the PSC after Commissioner Brad Molnar was suspended. Molnar participated in the hearing in May on the proposed merger, but Bushman did not.
The decision will have implications for Montana ratepayers, and lawyer Monica Tranel argues the people making decisions on the merger should be the same ones who hear direct evidence about it.
In a filing with the PSC, Tranel argued that either Molnar needed to participate in the merger decision — since he attended all four days of the hearing — or the parties involved in the case needed a chance to present evidence to Bushman.
In a unanimous decision Tuesday, the PSC disagreed with Tranel’s argument and said Bushman won’t be excluded from the merger vote.
In an interview Wednesday, Tranel said the merger vote is the PSC’s only chance to exert influence on a new parent company before it absorbs NorthWestern — should the commission approve the merger.
After a merger, the PSC would continue to regulate the Montana utility, but Tranel said Montana regulators lose influence over the larger parent entity.
“We no longer have any authority or control over the parent company,” Tranel said.
Tranel represents the Montana Farmers Union and 350 Montana, which has a mission to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide and end fossil fuel burning. The parties argue the merger will hurt Montanans.
The PSC is made up of five commissioners, all Republican, from different districts in Montana.
In July, Molnar was suspended for one year for professional misconduct, and Bushman is serving in his place until next July.
Tranel wanted Bushman to hear evidence directly before voting on the merger, but the PSC said that would happen only if a majority of decisionmakers hadn’t heard the case.
In this case, four out of the five commissioners attended the hearing and can decide the matter, the PSC said in its decision.
The PSC also said the temporarily appointed commissioner takes on “all duties of a suspended commissioner,” and commissioners regularly make decisions in cases that started before their terms.
But Tranel said she disagrees with the PSC’s interpretation of the legal procedure and argues parties have the right to present evidence when a new commissioner steps into office.
Tranel had put the question to both the PSC and the district court, and the case is still pending in court.
Tranel shared one reason she believes it’s important for the new commissioner to hear from parties about the case directly.
She said at a recent PSC meeting, Bushman asked to confirm that the PSC continues to regulate NorthWestern if it merges with Black Hills, so “nothing changes.”
Tranel said staff and other commissioners agreed, and she said she too agrees the PSC continues to regulate the Montana utility.
But she said the context around the Montana utility changes.
“The question is what is that utility and where does it rest within the larger corporate structure?” Tranel said. “And that’s the problem.”
Currently, she said, NorthWestern Energy is 90% of the regulated portion of the overall organization, NorthWestern Energy Group, Inc.
If a merger takes place, she said, the Montana PSC will not regulate the new parent organization; it will oversee only the Montana utility, which will represent just 30% of the regulated portion of the new company. In other words, Tranel said, if NorthWestern needs money to cut down trees to help with fire mitigation, it will be vying for capital with other utilities in other states.
Regulators in other states have in similar cases imposed significant conditions from a parent company, Tranel said.
She said the merger vote is the only opportunity the PSC has to set those conditions, such as ensuring capital from Montana not be used to shore up problems in another state if, for example, a data center goes belly up elsewhere.
“This is the only time this commission will touch the parent entity, and it’s imperative conditions be imposed now,” Tranel said.
At a meeting this week, PSC chief legal counsel Amanda Webster said staff recommended against delaying the merger decision, which is due by Oct. 12 but could be extended to Nov. 10.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Ex-legislator Eichorn gets 16 months in prison in underage solicitation case
description: Republished from KAXE.  ST. PAUL — Ex-Minnesota state Sen. Justin Eichorn was sentenced to 16 months in prison Wednesday, Sept. 23, for planning to meet who he thought was a 17-year-old girl for paid sex last year. Eichorn’s sentencing comes 18 months after his arrest as part of an undercover law enforcement sting operation during […]
text:
Sen. Justin Eichorn (R-Grand Rapids), left, consults with former Sen. Scott Newman (R-Hutchinson), right, during a vote in a file photo. (Photo by Catherine J. Davis/Senate Media Services)

Republished from KAXE. 
ST. PAUL — Ex-Minnesota state Sen. Justin Eichorn was sentenced to 16 months in prison Wednesday, Sept. 23, for planning to meet who he thought was a 17-year-old girl for paid sex last year.
Eichorn’s sentencing comes 18 months after his arrest as part of an undercover law enforcement sting operation during the 2025 legislative session. Originally charged with soliciting a minor, Eichorn, 42, pleaded guilty to a lesser child pornography charge as part of plea deal.
The former lawmaker planned to meet with a police officer, who he believed was a 17-year-old girl, for paid sex and was arrested outside a Bloomington hotel in March 2025. During text conversations, Eichorn asked the officer for photos on multiple occasions after she told him her purported age.
The sentence from federal Judge Eric C. Tostrud is less than the five years requested by prosecutors and more than the request for no additional prison time beyond what he has served by Eichorn’s defense team.
The sentence is within what guidelines call for when taking into account the Grand Rapids Republican’s criminal history and timely acceptance of responsibility. The pornography charge carries a maximum prison sentence of 10 years, but the sentencing guidelines in Eichorn’s case range from 15-21 months. The original charge of soliciting a minor carried a mandatory minimum prison sentence of 10 years.
Eichorn was remanded back into the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service on Wednesday.
In an emailed statement after the sentencing, Eichorn’s defense attorney Brent A. Hannafan said his client accepted full responsibility for what he did when he pleaded guilty in May.
“Today he told the judge, ‘What I did was both morally wrong and a serious crime, and I have no one to blame but myself,’” the statement read. “ … He will serve his sentence and follow every condition of his supervision. He greatly appreciates all the love and support he has received from his family and friends.”
Eichorn must also spend five years on supervised release after serving his prison term.
Earlier this month, U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen and Assistant U.S. Attorney David Classen argued the nature and circumstances of the offense justified the longer prison term of five years.
“The defendant’s conduct demonstrates a wanton willingness to pursue sexual gratification at the expense of the safety and well-being of children, and a specific desire and plan to exploit and victimize a child,” the court filing states. “When perpetrators are successful, these crimes shatter childhoods and ruin lives.”
In response, defense attorneys Hannafan and Ryan Pacyga argued the government’s position “would create a massive sentencing disparity between Mr. Eichorn and similarly situated defendants.”
The Republican was first elected in 2016 and most recently represented Senate District 6, which includes Grand Rapids and Brainerd. The married father of four has often described himself as a “Christian family man” and touted family values. Eichorn resigned from his Senate seat three days after his arrest, triggering a special election that resulted in now-Sen. Keri Heintzeman winning the seat.
In February, Tostrud issued an order and opinion upholding a magistrate judge’s previous findings, rejecting motions for case dismissal and evidence suppression. Eichorn’s defense argued he was the target of vindictive and selective prosecution because of his status as an elected official, and that he was subject to warrantless search and seizure at the time of his arrest.


KAXE / KBXE (Northern Community Radio) is a nonprofit public radio station broadcasting in Grand Rapids, Bemidji, Brainerd and online. It is community licensed and supported by grants and donors as a 501(c)(3) organization. Questions? Email news@kaxe.org.

name: Mississippi Today
title: MS LIFT rolls out resources for rural families
description:
Children participate in a Touch-a-Truck event at the MS LIFT building in Pascagoula on Sept. 17, 2026.
The event featured one of MS LIFT’s Resource and Referral mobile units, which bring educational
materials and activities to families across Mississippi.
text:
LEAKESVILLE — Mississippi LIFT is taking educational resources on the road as part of an effort to reach families in rural communities, including a recent stop in Greene County. 
More than half of Mississippi children under age 5 live in rural areas, according to MS LIFT’s 2025 Needs Assessment and Strategic Plan. The organization is working to expand access to resources in rural and low-resourced areas through its Resource and Referral Network, including mobile units. 
Jayden Duplessis, a program associate with MS LIFT’s mobile team, recently brought Unit 4 to the Leakesville Public Library, where families could access toys, books and learning materials. 
Jayden Duplessis, a program associate with MS LIFT’s mobile team, interacts with children duringa Touch-a-Truck event Sept. 17, 2026, at the MS LIFT building in Pascagoula. Duplessis operates one of the organization’s mobile Resource and Referral units.  Credit: Justin Glowacki/RHCJC
“My goal is to reach out to those rural areas and set up more community events so they can know about the resources as well,” Duplessis said. 
Duplessis said families can use MS LIFT’s lending library to check out toys, books and learning materials for children up to age 12 at no cost. Items can be borrowed for up to 14 days. 
The Resource and Referral Network also provides families and child care professionals with access to services including printing, laminating and computers.
Duplessis joined MS LIFT in February and estimated that she has taken the mobile unit to more than 20 events. She said many families she meets are learning about the program for the first time. 
An MS LIFT Resource and Referral mobile unit is parked outside the organization’s building inPascagoula during a Touch-a-Truck event Sept. 17, 2026. The mobile units travel to communities across Mississippi to connect families and child care providers with educational resources.  Credit: Justin Glowacki/RHCJC
“Some people know, most people don’t,” Duplessis said.
She said families are often surprised to learn what is available through the program. 
“I love seeing … kids’ eyes brighten up to see all the toys and fun activities that we have,” Duplessis said. “I love to see the family members smile because they get very happy, like, ‘We never knew we had this resource available.’” 
MS LIFT’s Resource and Referral Network also helps families find child care and other services and provides support and professional development for child care providers. 
Duplessis said bringing the mobile units into communities can introduce families to resources they may otherwise not know about. 
“I hope that they can take away the fun experience and hopefully just the warmth and love from actually knowing that you do have these resources available in your community,” she said. 
Families can find upcoming MS LIFT activities and locations through the event calendar on the organization’s website.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: DCF to release internal report to Waterbury captivity victim’s lawyers
description: CT has agreed to share an internal Department of Children and Families report with a Waterbury man allegedly held captive by his stepmother.
text:
The state of Connecticut has agreed to share an internal Department of Children and Families report with the lawyers representing a Waterbury man allegedly held captive by his stepmother as the victim seeks permission to sue the agency.
Attorney Joel Faxon, who is representing the alleged victim — known as S — said he will get access to the document under an agreement to keep the material confidential.
“‘S’ appreciates that the Attorney General’s office recognized the fairness in providing ‘S’ confidential access to the internal DCF review of its many failures to intervene and protect him from a life of captivity,” Faxon said in a written statement. “Hopefully, DCF learns from its failures in this case and ensures that no other children will suffer a similar trauma.”
The alleged victim is pursuing a claim filed with the state Claims Commission requesting authority to sue DCF for failing to protect him as a child.
The state’s lawyers previously objected to Faxon’s request to obtain the report and other DCF records, claiming they were protected under a broad confidentiality law. Assistant Attorney General John Tucker also petitioned for the claim to be dismissed entirely because it was filed outside the state’s three-year time limit.
Tucker asserted that DCF last contacted S’s family in 2005. More than two decades went by before S filed his claim in 2026.
Faxon argued that DCF could have had an ongoing duty to protect S, but he couldn’t adequately determine that without access to records that document what the agency saw and did during visits to the home.
The most critical document for exploring that argument is an internal report into how the child welfare agency handled S’s case, Faxon said. His team accused the state of “actively hiding” that document from them in a motion filed in July.
The existence of the report was discovered through a public records request by Connecticut Public. However, the document has not been released to the public.
The Connecticut Freedom of Information Commission determined last month that the material is exempt from disclosure under a state law that prohibits the release of information created or obtained in connection with DCF’s child protection activities.
In testimony provided during the public records case, a DCF bureau director said the report includes an overview of the underlying case demographic history, findings of a critical incident evaluation tool used by DCF and an outline of areas of strength and system opportunities.
Claims Commissioner Robert Shea, Jr. recently determined access to the internal DCF report is necessary for S’s lawyers to argue their case. He granted a protective order this week putting the agreement into effect.
The commission must still determine whether it has jurisdiction and the claim can move forward.
Police allege the victim was confined in a small room that was locked from the outside for more than two decades by his stepmother, Kimberly Sullivan. Sullivan has pleaded not guilty to charges including kidnapping and assault.
Sullivan’s attorney, Ioannis Kaloidis, declined to comment on her stepson’s pending claim against the state.
“We are laser-focused on preparing for trial and the criminal defense of Kimberly Sullivan. We will not inject ourselves into the back and forth between the accuser and the state,” read a statement provided to Connecticut Public. “However, the characterization that Ms. Sullivan held the accuser hostage is patently false. The facts and evidence prove this and we look forward to presenting them to a jury.”
DCF investigated six reports about the victim’s well-being between 1996 and 2005, but didn’t remove him from his family’s home. The agency previously said there was not enough evidence to justify intervention.
This story was first published Sept. 23, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Nevada Current
title: Attorneys lambast DA’s decision to retry Rickie Slaughter, question conflict of interest
description: More than six months after Rickie Slaughter’s conviction was vacated by a district court judge after finding prosecutors withheld evidence in his case, he is still incarcerated at High Desert State Prison. Attorneys and local organizers are fighting for Slaughter to be released from prison as he awaits for a newly set trial date in […]
text:
Mark Geragos, a high profile criminal defense attorney representing Rickie Slaughter, speaks at a rally.(Photo: Michael Lyle/Nevada Current)More than six months after Rickie Slaughter’s conviction was vacated by a district court judge after finding prosecutors withheld evidence in his case, he is still incarcerated at High Desert State Prison.
Attorneys and local organizers are fighting for Slaughter to be released from prison as he awaits for a newly set trial date in early 2027, and they’re raising questions about whether it’s a conflict of interest for the Clark County District Attorney’s office to retry the case instead of releasing Slaughter, who has been incarcerated for more than 20 years.
Mark Geragos, a high profile criminal defense attorney now representing Slaughter, said Slaughter tried to dismiss the case in 2009 over the handling of evidence.
Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson’s office is choosing to retry Slaughter now. But when Wolfson was a criminal defense attorney in 2009, it was his law firm that represented Slaughter. Wolfson’s name appears on the 2009 motion seeking to dismiss the case. 
Now Clark County’s district attorney, then a defense attorney, Steve Wolfson’s name appears on the 2009 motion seeking to dismiss the case against Ricke Slaughter
“He represented Rickie on the very issue that the judge vacated the conviction,” Geragos said. “That is the most astonishing conflict of interest I’ve ever encountered in 43 years, especially when a federal district court judge adopted the motion that he filed under his name 17 years ago, and then ordered him to either retry (Slaughter) or dismiss it. Now he’s going to make that decision.”
The district attorney’s office declined an interview request and didn’t answer a list of questions Nevada Current sent. Among the questions were whether there was a conflict of interest and why seek to retry the case. 
“The DA’s Office will address its position on this matter in court,” Andryanna Sheppard, a spokesperson said in an email. 
Geragos, whose high profile clients have included Hunter Biden and Michael Jackson, joined speakers from the ACLU of Nevada, the National Action Network Las Vegas Chapter, the Mass Liberation Project, and Progressive Leadership Alliance of Nevada on Sept. 14 to discuss Slaughter’s case.  
For many, the case underscores long standing frustration with the criminal legal system, how it is overly punitive toward Black and brown people, and failures of the state, like the nation, to bring comprehensive justice reforms.
“The issues that we’re seeing today are products of bad policies that were put in place and a lack of accountability within every layer of government that’s existed,” said Athar Haseebullah, the executive director of the ACLU of Nevada. 
Slaughter, in a phone interview, said that at the core of this case is the question about “who has the right to be free.” Slaughter, who maintains his innocence, has been incarcerated since he was 19 and the conviction “stripped away my entire life,” he said.
Even after a judge vacated his conviction, he said he is still struggling to find justice. 
“They can just dismiss the charges,” Slaughter said of the DA’s office. “They want to follow one part of the order that says they can retry me but not the part of the order where the court says my conviction is vacated, which would release me from prison. Whether they retry me or not, I could be released from prison in the meantime.”
Slaughter’s retrial is scheduled for Feb. 8, 2027. 
He was arrested in 2005 and charged with conspiracy to commit kidnapping and robbery, attempted murder with the use of a deadly weapon, battery, and robbery with the use of a deadly weapon. 
He was convicted in 2012. After years of appeals, the court reopened his case May 11, 2022. 
Federal District Court Judge Anne Traum, who vacated Slaughter’s conviction in a March 3 ruling, wrote “suppressed evidence would have affected various parts of this evidence and strengthened” Slaughter’s defense.
During a second pretrial photographic lineup, none of the witnesses identified Slaughter. That information was never presented to the jury, according to the ruling.
The ruling noted that “the prosecution presented no forensic evidence, such as DNA, hair, or fingerprints, from the scene that linked back to Slaughter, no incriminating evidence from the search of Slaughter’s apartment, and no confession. Thus, the prosecution’s evidence of guilt would have been markedly weaker had the second lineup not been suppressed.”
Geragos and the ACLU have since argued in court that Slaughter should be released since the conviction was vacated.
Christopher Peterson, the legal director of the ACLU of Nevada, argued in May that since the order vacated Slaughter’s conviction, he should “be treated as a pretrial detainee,” which would mean “he cannot be held at the Nevada Department of Corrections under state law.”
The motion was denied. 
“The fact that a federal court has stated that his conviction has been vacated, and we are still in a state court that refuses to recognize that, and says that conviction only goes away the moment a retrial commences, flies in the face of the Constitution,” Haseebullah said at the rally.
In media interviews, including on Vegas PBS on Sept 18, Clark County Chief Deputy District Attorney Marc DiGiacomo has maintained that Slaughter is guilty. 
“I wasn’t in court to understand how Judge Traum reached what she reached,” he said during the interview. “There was no evidence ever suppressed. (The defense) had the line up and the ability to ask the witnesses about that lineup.” 
Sheppard, the spokesperson for the DA’s office, posted a video to the District Attorney’s social media page on May 5 saying Traum’s findings don’t equate to innocence.  
“The only thing the court found was there were some errors at trial that warranted giving him a new trial,” Sheppard said.
Haseebullah, who admonished the social media post, said it was not just case errors but Brady violations, referencing a U.S. Supreme Court case Brady v. Maryland that found suppressing “exculpatory evidence” that can prove innocence violates a person’s due process rights. 
“One of the key tenets of our Constitution is to protect against (Brady violations) to not allow for exculpatory evidence to lead to people’s wrongful convictions,” Haseebullah said. “The DA’s office has unilateral discretion as to whether to move forward on this case. Every single step of the way, they have rebuked the offer to engage in what’s just, and instead chosen the side of oppression.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Medicaid enrollee challenges Trump rule on work requirement exemptions
description: Emily Byrd has lost Medicaid coverage twice due to paperwork problems.  Both times, Byrd, of Kansas City, submitted documents requested by the Missouri Department of Social Services. But duplicate letters, late notices and “confusing, inconsistent information” made it difficult for Byrd to regain coverage — the second time forcing them to reapply. The 25-yea[...]
text:
Five Medicaid enrollees, six medical organizations and the City of Columbus, Ohio are plaintiffs in a federal lawsuit arguing the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid overstepped its authority in requiring "medically frail" adults to demonstrate their conditions hinder their ability to fulfill Medicaid work requirements in order to be exempted (Getty Images).Emily Byrd has lost Medicaid coverage twice due to paperwork problems. 
Both times, Byrd, of Kansas City, submitted documents requested by the Missouri Department of Social Services. But duplicate letters, late notices and “confusing, inconsistent information” made it difficult for Byrd to regain coverage — the second time forcing them to reapply.
The 25-year-old, who relies on Medicaid for services and medications to manage symptoms of autism spectrum disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder and other conditions, is one of five Medicaid enrollees from five states who filed a lawsuit last week challenging a Trump administration rule they argue unlawfully narrows exemptions from new Medicaid work requirements for people considered “medically frail” under federal law.
The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, asserts the rule violates the One Big Beautiful Bill Act by requiring people to prove that their medical condition “significantly impairs (their) ability to comply” with work requirements to be exempt. It asks the court to vacate that provision and another that excludes people “in stable recovery” from a substance use disorder from the exemption.
Starting Jan. 1, 2027, the federal law will require states to verify that adults ages 19 to 64 covered through Medicaid expansion — the Affordable Care Act provision that allowed states to offer coverage to more low-income adults — work, volunteer or attend school at least 80 hours a month to get or keep coverage. 
The law also directs states to exempt people in five “medically frail” categories from work requirements: those who are blind or disabled, have a substance use disorder, a “disabling mental disorder,” a “serious or complex medical condition” or “a physical, intellectual or developmental disability that significantly impairs their ability to perform one or more activities of daily living.”
Medicaid paperwork problems continue to cost thousands of Missourians coverage

The rule allows states to accept self-attestation of medical frailty throughout 2027 when there is no other reliable data source. Starting Jan. 1, 2028, states can only accept one self-attestation during an individual’s enrollment period. 
A federal judge in July denied a request from 25 Democratic-led states’ to temporarily block parts of the rule while their legal challenge proceeds.The states argued that the rule came months after they began consulting with the federal government about how to implement work requirements.
Amber Christ, executive director of Legal Aid of Western Missouri, which is co-representing Byrd, told The Independent that by requiring people to prove that their medical condition prevents them from meeting work requirements, the rule “adds a test that Congress didn’t write.”
“When the administration wrote the rule, it really stripped away the protection Congress gave to people with serious medical conditions,” Christ said.
Jane Perkins, litigation director at the National Health Law Program, which is working with state organizations to represent Medicaid enrollees in the lawsuit, told The Independent the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid exceeded its authority with the rule, imposing a “backdoor work requirement” on people Congress meant to exempt.
“Our argument is that this additional new requirement goes beyond the statute, and the (U.S.) Supreme Court has been very clear that federal agencies can only implement the statutes they have responsibility for,” Perkins said.
 ‘A backdoor work requirement’

Christ said the rule’s limitations on the “medically frail” exemption are likely to worsen a familiar problem in Missouri: eligible people losing coverage because of missed or unprocessed forms.
Of the more than 333,000 Missourians who lost Medicaid coverage from January 2025 through February 2026, nearly 92% were dropped due to paperwork issues, according to data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid — not because the state found that they no longer qualified.
The second time Byrd experienced a lapse in Medicaid coverage due to paperwork issues, they had to reapply to regain coverage, according to the lawsuit.
“The new rule will require even more paperwork, even more proof,” Christ said, “and if this is already happening to people, it’s just going to be compounded by this new rule.”
It’s unclear how states will ask applicants to demonstrate that they meet the “medically frail” exemption requirements. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid released non-binding guidance Sept. 8 suggesting states use a three-tier structure to determine medical frailty exemptions, including diagnoses that would automatically qualify someone, conditions that could qualify with additional information and cases with insufficient information that require an individualized review process.
The lawsuit says that for plaintiff Lauren Bush of North Carolina, uncertainty about how she would meet Medicaid work requirements — and how she would manage her type 1 diabetes without Medicaid — “causes her great stress and anxiety.”
In an email to The Independent, Baylee Watts, the department’s media director, said “Missouri is continuing to finalize its implementation approach for the federal Medicaid community engagement requirements, including the process for identifying and verifying individuals who may qualify for the medically frail exclusion.”
Watts said the department “has not yet finalized whether Missouri will use self-attestation during 2027 or what specific screening methodology it will adopt.”
During a meeting of the MO HealthNet Oversight Committee on Aug. 12, Social Services Director Jess Bax said the department would work with patient and healthcare advocates throughout 2027 to determine how to assess medical frailty when self-attestation is no longer allowed.
“We’ll utilize the period of having the ability to do self-attestation and develop a plan together with stakeholders to implement what…the technology side of that (looks) like as we go into that year two of community engagement requirements,” Bax said.
Watts said that while the department does not comment on individual cases like Byrd’s, it “remains committed to accurate and timely eligibility determinations and minimizing avoidable gaps in coverage for eligible participants.”
The federal lawsuit argues that the rule will require medical providers to assess whether patients’ medical conditions impair their ability to fulfill work requirements without clear criteria.
“The imposition of this responsibility on clinicians will cause patients to schedule appointments solely to obtain Medicaid eligibility documentation, reducing the overall capacity of clinicians to provide services,” the lawsuit says.
Besides asking doctors to make judgments outside of their medical expertise, the lawsuit contends that as people in need of ongoing medical treatment lose Medicaid coverage, medical providers and local governments will bear the cost of providing more uncompensated care.
Along with the five Medicaid enrollees, the lawsuit’s plaintiffs include six medical provider groups, among them the American College of Physicians and the American Academy of Pediatrics, and the City of Columbus, Ohio.
Perkins said that as people with serious chronic medical conditions lose Medicaid, community clinics and emergency medical services funded through local governments will see increased demand and less compensation.
“People who lose Medicaid because of this added requirement are going to with certainty continue to need healthcare,” Perkins said. “That’s going to be true because they’re medically frail, and they’re going to go to these payers of last resort….”
Cities like Columbus, the lawsuit says, provide medical services regardless of residents’ insurance coverage, and when patients are uninsured, they “must make up for this budget shortfall.”
Christ said most of her organization’s clients want to work. Uninterrupted Medicaid coverage, she said, “keeps them stable enough to do that, to even try.”
That includes Byrd, Christ said.
After graduating from high school, Byrd studied to become a certified nurse assistant but was unable to complete their training because of their mental health conditions, according to the lawsuit. They have also worked as an assistant manager, cashier and stocker at three retail stores, but they are not currently working.
Byrd “does not know how (they) will comply with the work requirements,” the lawsuit says.
The rule, Christ said, will make it harder for people to maintain Medicaid coverage that they are entitled to by law. 
“Our clients aren’t going to lose coverage because they don’t qualify,” Christ said. “They’re going to lose it because a form got missed, a deadline passed by them or a doctor couldn’t produce the letter that this rule now demands.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: All-party primaries would bring more competition and a more vigorous democracy
description: Open up the primaries to every voter, every qualified candidate, and we get more competition, higher turnout, and better results.
text:
If you voted in the primary earlier this month, did you notice anything striking on your ballot? Any races with just one name listed? Any incumbent candidates that nobody ran against? 
Most of you did, because most of our primary races are uncompetitive. This year, for instance, all 200 seats in the Massachusetts Legislature are on the ballot, but just 25 incumbents, 14 percent of those running for reelection, faced primary challengers. That number only increases to about a quarter when looking at the share of lawmakers who face challengers in the upcoming general election in November. 
That’s just the most recent data point in a long, disappointing trend. Since 2014, 52 percent of Massachusetts elections have had no real contest at all. No primary opponent, no general election opponent, nothing. In 2024, that number climbed to 62 percent. All told, 99 percent of our incumbents ultimately keep their seats, not because they’ve necessarily earned every vote, but because most have never actually had to ask for one. They are able to easily win reelection by default in uncompetitive, low-turnout races. 
I’ve spent my career fighting for a political system that actually listens to the people it’s supposed to serve, so that’s a tough pill to swallow. Our political system, the way it is structured and designed today, tells people that their vote is merely a formality. It tells them that the real decision was made somewhere else, by someone else, before they ever opened their ballot envelope or walked into the voting booth. And it lands the hardest on communities that the NAACP exists to serve: working people, communities of color, and neighborhoods that have learned, election after election, that showing up doesn’t change who shows up for them. We can, and must, do better than this. 
That’s why the New England Area Conference of the NAACP supports Question 3 on the November ballot: All-party primaries in Massachusetts. If the ballot question is approved, every candidate for a given office, Democrat, Republican, independent, Working Families and other political designations, would appear together on one primary ballot, where any voter can vote for any candidate, regardless of party. The top two vote-getters, regardless of party, move on to November. That’s it. 
With inherently more competition, elected officials are better incentivized to listen and deliver. This isn’t the “jungle primary” you may have heard a few opponents incorrectly invoke, in my view just to purposely scare and mislead voters. That term refers specifically to Louisiana’s primary model, where a candidate can win a seat outright in the primary, totally bypassing the general election.  
All-party primaries are a top-two system that always sends two candidates to the general election, so voters get the final say. And it isn’t untested or radical: It’s how cities and towns across Massachusetts, including Boston, elect their mayors and other municipal officials. We’re extending what already works at the local level to the state level offices that also shape policy surrounding education, infrastructure, health care and affordability.  
The Massachusetts reform also includes two safeguards you won’t find in other states: Political parties can place their endorsements right on the ballot, providing a high-information ballot for voters, and a write-in option is preserved for the general election. 
The reform also changes how candidates for statewide and federal office reach the ballot. 
Today, qualified candidates may be blocked from the ballot by party conventions that require support from a minimum share of those attending, meaning that party delegates can decide which candidates voters end up seeing on their ballot. Under all-party primaries, that step no longer determines ballot access. Conventions instead would be used for important organizing and, crucially, endorsements that could then be listed on the resulting high-information ballots of this reform.  
Under all-party primaries, every qualified candidate goes straight to the ballot, where voters get to choose who they want to advance to the general election. Voters get a fuller field of choices, and candidates have to compete for support. 
That, along with restricted, low-turnout primaries are how small, motivated factions keep control. Here’s the mechanism, plainly: In a low-turnout primary, incumbents or their challengers don’t need to win over most voters. They just need to turn out a small slice who will show up for them, vote their way and let everyone else stay home.  
Massachusetts already has the fewest contested elections in the country. That’s not an accident of civic apathy, but a strategy, and it works the same way, whether it’s an old-guard party structure protecting an incumbent or a special interest group trying to exert influence. Keep the electorate small and predictable, and you can control the outcomes without ever building broad support.  
We’ve seen how that works nationally. Regular people don’t see the positive effects of government or politics in their lives. It’s how Trump was elected nationally. And it’s how Massachusetts got the least productive, least transparent legislature in the country, with the fewest challengers of any state. 
Open up the primaries to every voter, every qualified candidate, and we get more competition, higher turnout, and better results. We get strong coalitions with the resiliency required to overcome the many challenges we’re facing. A more participatory and representative system is what helps us build the power required to truly meet the moment. 
The NAACP built its power by organizing, showing up, communicating to everyone and making the case, generation after generation. This includes communicating with people who might not already agree with us, or who are unaware of our work. That’s how you build political power. That’s how you build real coalitions that last through the good, the bad and the ugly. You build a tradition of persuading people, and not being afraid of doing so. 
All-party primaries ask the same thing of every candidate and every party: Earn the votes. Don’t count on a low-turnout primary to do the work for you. Go to every neighborhood, make the case and win support from people who might not have already been on your list. If our ideas are as strong as we say they are, that’s not a threat, but an opportunity to build actual political will and gain the very real policy results that come from it. 
Voters deserve straight answers, real choices and clear vision from their candidates. We need elected officials who listen and deliver. Competitive elections help ensure they do. Competitive elections strengthen our democracy.  
In November, voters have the chance to stop settling for one-name races and no results to show for it by voting yes on Question 3. 
Tanisha Sullivan is president of the NAACP New England Area Conference.

title: Federal judge orders White House must restore press passes to 3 banned news outlets
text: WASHINGTON — U.S. District Court Judge Timothy Kelly early Thursday issued an order that temporarily blocks President Donald Trump’s ban of three news organizations from the White House.Kelly, in the eight-page order, said that the White House must “immediately return, reinstate, and restore the White House ‘hard pass’ press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO that were revoked” Friday and over the weekend.His order will continue for 14 days while the case continues to be fought in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. Trump is scheduled to welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House Thursday.Although Trump has indicated he will appeal any court ruling on the matter, Kelly noted that temporary restraining orders are “generally unappealable.” He said he would schedule a hearing for motions for a preliminary injunction, which would last until the final outcome of the suit and could be appealed.The case began Monday when the three news outlets sued the Trump administration for barring their reporters from entering the White House grounds. The news organizations asked the district court to grant them either a temporary restraining order or a preliminary injunction that would require the White House to return the press passes, allowing the journalists to work from the complex once again. Kelly, who was appointed by Trump during his first term, had heard arguments in the case on Wednesday and appeared skeptical at the time of Department of Justice arguments. In his ruling, he said it appeared likely that the news outlets would succeed with their claim that journalists were denied their due process rights before their passes were confiscated.While the Department of Justice argued that earlier cases dealing with press access to the White House were wrongly decided in journalists’ favor, Kelly said that he was “bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop,” referring to earlier rulings by the appeals court.Kelly in his order also expressed doubt about Department of Justice arguments that the ban was in response to concerns about articles that dealt with national security or classified information, saying DOJ “offered little” to back up that contention. Some news articles cited by the administration as endangering national security were written by reporters who didn’t even have White House passes, he noted.Trump did not mention national security in announcing the ban and “instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly said. “For another—and simply put—the record lacks factual support for Defendants’ contention that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the Court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds,” Kelly said. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from States Newsroom.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: O’Leary says he didn’t defame opponents of his plan for a large Utah data center
description: The celebrity investor and Fox News Network want a judge to dismiss the case for good.
text:
Protesters demonstrate against a proposed Box Elder County data center at the Utah Capitol on Saturday, May 23, 2026. (Georgia Metcalf for Utah News Dispatch)Celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary and Fox News Network are asking a judge to throw out a defamation lawsuit from two Utahns O’Leary had labeled Chinese agents while defending his Stratos data center proposal earlier this year. 
Attorneys for the businessman of “Shark Tank” fame filed a motion to dismiss the case Monday in U.S. District Court in Utah, writing, “while O’Leary’s statements may have been critical of Plaintiffs, they do not rise to the level of defamation.”
Fox News Media agreed in its own filing Monday, joining O’Leary in asking for the case to be dismissed with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled at a later time. 
Utahns sue O’Leary, Fox News over ‘smear campaign’

In July, Joshua Kanter, founder of the left-leaning Alliance for a Better Utah, and Gabrielle Finlayson, of the Democratic and progressive political firm Elevate Strategies, sued O’Leary and Fox for a “weekslong smear campaign” against them. The Utahns are seeking damages to be determined at trial. 
It came in a season of intense public outcry against the proposed data center that had already spilled over into the courts. A Box Elder County citizens’ group filed its own lawsuit to pursue a referendum allowing voters to decide the fate of the project in the remote Hansel Valley, near the northern tip of the Great Salt Lake. 
In June, O’Leary acknowledged in a social media post he had “no evidence” Kanter, Finlayson or their organizations were funded by China. 
Kanter and Finlayson allege they suffered damage to their reputations despite the change in O’Leary’s message after he accused them of being “two cells inside of Utah” seeking to undermine American development of artificial intelligence on behalf of the Chinese Communist Party. 
Utah lawmakers get a primer on data centers after a summer of protests and political fallout 

They contend O’Leary had sought to discredit local opposition to the data center project in Box Elder County, approved first by Utah’s Military Installation Development Authority and then by the county’s three-member commission.  
The authority has said the project is paused as the still-pending referendum court case plays out. O’Leary has moved to dismiss that case, too, and so has the county. He has said the 20,000-acre data center project — down from 40,000 acres — is still moving forward. 
In this week’s court filings, attorneys for O’Leary argue the Utahns republished the alleged defamatory statements on their own social media platforms and used them as a fundraising tool. 
They contend in the motion that O’Leary, at the time of his comments, had “reasoned his way to the China connection from observed facts rather than publishing a statement he knew to be false.”    
For its part, Fox News Network said the plaintiffs didn’t get in touch with Fox or O’Leary to challenge the assertions or ask for a correction until weeks after O’Leary’s most recent appearance on the matter. 
“Once they finally did so, O’Leary posted a statement explaining that he had no evidence that the plaintiffs are funded by China or the Chinese Communist Party,” the motion states. “Fox then aired corrections on each of its programs at issue.”
