title: WA voters of color more likely to have ballots challenged, per report
description: Younger voters and voters of color in Washington state see their ballots challenged for signature issues more often than their older and white counterparts. That’s according to an analysis of state election data by University of Washington researchers presented to state lawmakers Wednesday. Meanwhile, thousands more votes than usual went uncounted in last mo[...]
text:
An election worker in Thurston County processes ballots on Thursday, Oct. 30, 2025, in Tumwater, Washington. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)Younger voters and voters of color in Washington state see their ballots challenged for signature issues more often than their older and white counterparts.
That’s according to an analysis of state election data by University of Washington researchers presented to state lawmakers Wednesday. Meanwhile, thousands more votes than usual went uncounted in last month’s primary due to delivery lags from the U.S. Postal Service.
Ballot signature challenges have declined in recent years, based on data from the general elections between 2020 and 2025.
“We hope that that will be a continued trend,” said Scott Allard, co-director of the UW Elections Database Project. “And it certainly was in the primary election in 2026.”
But while white voters have seen 1.5% of their votes scrutinized for signature discrepancies, it’s 1.9% for Black voters, 2% for Asian voters and 2.2% for Hispanic voters, according to the UW research.
Washington doesn’t collect race and ethnicity data from voters upon their registration, so researchers used an algorithm to identify their most likely race.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The disparity is more stark among age groups. Signature challenges decrease with age, from 5.3% among voters 18 to 25, to 0.7% for those 66 and older. 
There isn’t much of a difference in ballot challenges between urban and rural voters, Allard noted.
Voters returning their ballots in Washington’s vote-by-mail system must sign the return envelope they place in a mailbox or dropbox. 
But their votes won’t be accepted if their signature doesn’t match what the local election office has on file, or if it’s missing altogether. Those whose signatures are challenged can fix the issue, known as curing, to ensure their vote is counted. This can be done by filling out a form and returning it to the county election office.
If not cured, election officials won’t count the ballot. In the 2025 general election, 58.5% of challenged voters cured their ballots, according to the researchers.
“We actually do a really good job of curing our ballots in the state,” Allard said, while noting the percentage has slightly decreased in the past couple years. “Any efforts we can do to help improve those rates, I think, matter.”
The same disparities remain for those who cure their ballot. 
White voters reportedly fixed the issues on more than 59% of their challenged ballots, while Black, Hispanic and Asian voters corrected less than half. 
And the youngest voters also cure their ballots less than half of the time, compared to 72% for elderly voters. This means that white and older voters are less likely to have their votes rejected, according to the research.
Addressing this “is work that remains for us as a state,” Allard told lawmakers. 
Part of the issue, Allard said, is that letters to voters telling them they need to fix their ballot might not be translated into the language they speak.
The researchers also suggested adding more electronic forms of communication to reach younger voters telling them they need to cure their ballots.
“It’s really important that we meet voters where they’re at, and when we’re talking about 18 to 34-year-olds, that’s going to be on your cell phone,” said Julie Wise, director of King County Elections.
Between 2020 and 2025, about 1% of ballots cast have been rejected in general elections in Washington. Half are due to mismatched signatures; one-third because they arrived late; and a small percentage from being unsigned.
This has a downstream effect. Voters who see their ballots rejected are less likely to cast votes in the future, said Jake Grumbach, a colleague of Allard’s who is now an associate professor at the University of California, Berkeley.
“They feel a bit excluded from the process, but efforts at curing can signal that the state cares about the ballot and about the individual, and really can make up for some of that,” Grumbach said.
Another problem has cropped up this election cycle that led to more ballots rejected for last month’s primary. More than 20,000 ballots weren’t counted because they came in too late, thousands more than in 2024, amid alarm over U.S. Postal Service delays. Officials have been encouraging Washington voters to return ballots via dropbox or mail them back long before Election Day. 
Ballots are set to be mailed out to voters for the November election in less than a month.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi colleges open food pantries to help students meet basic needs
description: Volunteer coordinator Jennifer Ennis sorts clothing at Okra Threads, an on-campus thrift store at Delta State University on Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, in Cleveland.
text:
When University of Mississippi Medical Center administrators heard that some students were struggling to afford food and other necessities, they stepped up to help.
They held a food drive in August to collect items for a pantry to benefit medical and nursing students. Then UMMC opened a food pantry on Sept. 1, offering groceries and personal care products such as shampoo, laundry detergent pods and toothpaste. 
“Every student’s financial situation is different,” said Jonathan Nutt, director of student services at UMMC. “The hope is to serve any student who needs it.” 
Some students have little family financial support, and the demands of their academic programs can make it difficult to work enough hours to cover living expenses, Nutt said. 
Director of Student Services Jonathan Nutt and senior administrative assistant Anna Vancor unload boxes into the University of Mississippi Medical Center’s student food pantry. An Amazon wishlist was made available to employees or students who wish to donate. Credit: Melanie Thortis/UMMC Photography
Students across the state — and the nation — are facing similar challenges as costs for housing, groceries, transportation and other living expenses increase. A 2023 Hope Center for Basic Needs survey found that 59% of college students lack access to at least one basic need such as housing and transportation. Of students surveyed, 41% reported experiencing food insecurity. 
Such struggles are prevalent among students from low income backgrounds, the report notes. 
College students’ costs pile up
At the University of Southern Mississippi, staff and volunteers distributed more than 890 pounds of food, hygiene products and other items to 94 people who visited the Eagle’s Nest Food Pantry during the first week of classes in August. 
Last school year, the Eagle’s Nest recorded 2,785 visits, 81% of which were by students. Sirena Cantrell, dean of students and associate vice president of student affairs, expects another busy semester. 
“We’re beginning to see more students than ever,” Cantrell said. “Students are telling their friends that this is a campus resource. Faculty and staff are also sharing it with students they see are in need.” 
At Mississippi State University, some students rely on Bully’s Pantry while learning to budget and manage their cost of living, said Hali Hollman, who volunteered at the food pantry from 2023 to 2025 before graduating with the class of 2026.
Volunteer coordinator Jennifer Ennis hangs clothing at Okra Threads, an on-campus thrift store at Delta State University, Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, in Cleveland. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“We are juggling all kinds of expenses and also having to balance our classwork, extracurriculars, work and thinking about our future,” Hollman said.
Tuition and fees have increased at several Mississippi universities over the past two years. 

In-state tuition at the University of Mississippi rose 3.8%, from $9,412 in 2023-24 to $9,772 in 2024-25. Out-of-state tuition and fees rose 6% from $26,980 in 2023-24 to $28,600 in 2024-25. 
In-state tuition at the University of Southern Mississippi rose 4% from $9,618 in 2023-24 to $9,998 in 2024-25. Out-of-state tuition and fees rose by 3.3% from $11,618 in 2023-24 to $11,998 in 2024-25. 
In-state tuition at Jackson State University fell by 1.4% from $9,090 in 2023-24 to $8,965 in 2024-25. But out-of-state tuition and fees increased 18.3%, from $10,110 in 2023-24 to $11,965 the next year. 

At MSU, in-state tuition and fees have increased from $9,815 in 2023-24 to $11,095 this year. in 2024-25. Out-of-state tuition and fees increased from $26,580 in 2023-24 to $30,086 this year. The university estimates a total in-state cost of $26,295 for a full academic year. For out-of-state students, costs run up to $45,000 a year.
The costs of college textbooks and supplies have remained steady while food and student housing have increased in recent years, according to federal data. 
A growing need on Mississippi college campuses 
Amid rising costs and living expenses, visits to Delta State University’s food pantry, the Statesman’s Shelf, doubled in recent years from 672 visits in 2023-24 to 1,672 in 2025-26. 
Tuition at Delta State has remained flat in recent years, but the costs of food and on-campus housing increased 3.6% between 2023-24 and 2024-25. Those expenses have increased 2.4% for off-campus students, according to federal data.
Lacking transportation can also make it difficult for Delta State students to reach off-campus grocery stores, said Brandi Lovin, a Statesman’s Shelf volunteer coordinator. For example, when damage from Winter Storm Fern forced the campus to remain closed in January, the food pantry remained open. The icy roads and downed trees and power lines made it difficult to leave campus during the first few days. 
Brandi Lovin, volunteer coordinator for the Statesman’s Shelf Food Pantry at Delta State University, straightens cans of vegetables at the on-campus facility, Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, in Cleveland. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
The Statesman’s Shelf staff served 416 people in January, about half of them during the winter storm. The demand also helped relaunch Okra Threads, a campus clothes and resources closet that opened this semester, Lovin said.
The closet, originally called Okra Suits, provided business attire to students for career fairs, presentations, job interviews and special events. The resource expanded this semester to include everyday clothing items, shoes and accessories.  
Helping students secure food and other necessities supports their efforts to earn a degree and enter Mississippi’s healthcare workforce. 
“Food insecurity and basic needs access is an issue everywhere,” Nutt said. “We just want to ensure we are preparing our students for their careers and that they can eventually serve the health needs of Mississippians.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Trump gives China’s Xi a warm welcome. But criticism is loud on Capitol Hill
description: President Donald Trump salutes during a military flyover during an arrival ceremony with China's President Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews, Md., Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026.
text:
WASHINGTON — Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington is getting a much chillier reception on Capitol Hill than at the White House as lawmakers from both parties use the visit to denounce China’s actions on the world stage.
Lawmakers have long found little downside to taking a hawkish tone on China, but the U.S.’s war with Iran has inflamed tensions as U.S. officials accuse China of propping up Iran’s economy and supplying its military with components and intelligence, endangering U.S. service members in the Middle East.
In speeches, letters, press conferences and hearings, lawmakers from both parties aired criticism of Xi’s visit. Their actions and events stand in stark contrast to the warm welcome that Trump gave Xi on Wednesday as he arrived in Washington for a lavish state visit.
Republicans air their dissenting views
Sen. Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, took to the Senate floor Tuesday night, offering a list of issues for Trump to raise with Xi, but not before suggesting that Xi shouldn’t have been asked to visit Washington at all.
Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman Roger Wicker, R-Miss., questions witnesses during a hearing on Capitol Hill, June 10, 2025, in Washington.  Credit: AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta
“Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party,” Wicker said.
Wicker seemed particularly taken aback by the honor of a state dinner. Over the salad course, Wicker said the president could ask Xi about the Chinese Navy’s harassment of Filipino fishermen and sailors. Then, while the servers are “switching from chardonnay to cabernet at the fancy state dinner,” perhaps the president could turn to the issue of Taiwan, he said.
He went on to say he hopes some progress will be made when the president discussed trade and artificial intelligence with Xi. But concluded with this: “During every minute of dialogue, our commander in chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”
House committee weighs in with a critical video
Ahead of Xi’s visit, the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party released a highly critical video that had been viewed more than 245,000 times on X. In the video, the committee details Xi’s rise to power starting in 1974 and ends by labeling him “the biggest opponent of freedom and liberty in the world.”
The House created the panel in 2023. It’s held several hearings on human rights issues in China and advocates for legislation on an array of economic and military issues. For example, the committee’s chairman, Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., recently introduced a bill that would prohibit the manufacture or sale of Chinese cars in the U.S.
Republican senators press for Taiwan aid
Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and three other Republican senators used the Xi visit to press the Trump administration to move ahead with aid and arms sales to Taiwan.
In a letter, they reminded Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he had previously stated that “deterring an invasion of Taiwan must be our top priority.” And they noted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had once declared that the U.S. ”will not let our allies and partners be subordinated and intimidated.”
China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China.
“It is difficult to imagine how the United States might credibly project influence deterrence in the Indo-Pacific,” the senators wrote, “if the price of keeping up diplomatic appearances is denying our partners key deterrent capabilities.”
Democrats pile on the criticism
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and three other Democratic senators held a press conference to warn against the U.S. weakening export controls for advanced semiconductor chips and equipment. They’re concerned that such exports could erase the U.S.’s lead in artificial intelligence over China.
They touched on voter concerns about the safety of artificial intelligence and contrasted Democrats’ call for greater regulation with the president’s call to “encourage it, not rein it in.”
“We must reject the false choice Trump keeps making,” Schumer told reporters. “We can and must both maintain our lead on AI by restricting China’s access to our technology and put up guardrails to mitigate AI’s risk.”
Meanwhile, on the Senate floor, Democratic senators urged Trump to confront Xi directly about the support his country is providing Iran.
“If we want to bring this war to an end, we need to cut off the outside support that allows Iran to keep fighting, and that starts with China,” said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democratic lawmaker on the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Supreme Court considers whether towns must refund tax sale windfalls
description: A former East Orange property owner wants the city to pay money it kept when it sold her property for more than she owed.
text:
The New Jersey Supreme Court heard the case of a former East Orange property owner who wants the city to pay money it kept when it sold her property for more than she owed. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey’s Supreme Court is poised to decide whether municipalities are on the hook for millions of dollars in excess takings from tax sales made years ago, with several justices appearing skeptical of arguments that would allow governments to retain the money.
The case before the high court asks whether East Orange owes Lynette Johnson thousands of dollars in excess equity the city retained when it sold her home for more than Johnson owed in back taxes, utilities, and fees. The court’s decision is likely to have major implications for municipal finances across New Jersey.
Johnson’s excess equity dispute is the latest to measure the effects of the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in Tyler v. Hennepin County. In that case, a Minnesota woman named Geraldine Tyler owed the county $15,000 in unpaid taxes and fees, so the county sold her condo for $40,000 and kept the excess. The court ruled that by keeping the excess, the county violated the Fifth Amendment’s takings clause.
During oral arguments in the New Jersey case Wednesday, the justices questioned whether, for the purposes of a balancing test, it would be fair for governments to retain money unlawfully taken from residents.
“The polestar, as this court has said, is fairness,” Chief Justice Stuart Rabner said. “How is it fair to take and keep surplus equity that rightly belongs to the former property owner?”
In 2015, East Orange placed a lien for unpaid taxes on a burned-out commercial property Johnson had purchased the year earlier, and the city moved to foreclose it in 2017. A final judgment was issued the following year, and East Orange sold the property for $101,000.
The size of Johnson’s debt is disputed. Her attorneys in court filings said it totaled about $25,000, while the city claims it added up to $55,735 once overdue water bills and unpaid property registration fees were included. Johnson sued in late 2021.
Lawyers representing East Orange and the Office of the Attorney General argued Wednesday that Johnson’s lawsuit against East Orange is barred by the entire controversy doctrine, a New Jersey court rule that typically requires all related disputes be brought in a single case.
Because Johnson had not raised an unlawful takings claim during the foreclosure proceedings that, per New Jersey statute, ended her rights to the property, she could not raise them later in a separate forum, the attorneys argued.
“If an individual that is facing a tax foreclosure declines to assert a takings defense that was available and could have been asserted in the foreclosure action but many years later pops up and brings an independent takings suit, then you have to try to unwind that transaction many years after the property was sold, after the municipality gained any surplus equity, after those funds were long since spent,” said Assistant Attorney General Benjamin Shultz.
The justices questioned that timeline, noting it would require Johnson to seek recompense for a taking that had not occurred.
“I’m trying to imagine the scenario you’ve eloquently described: We go into the Superior Court, and the property owner says, ‘I insist that we tackle the question of surplus equity,’ and the judge says, ‘The property hasn’t been foreclosed. Thank you, counsel, let’s move on,’” Rabner said.
Justice John Hoffman noted that statute cannot overwrite a constitutional right, and Justice Wainer Apter said the timeline of events in Johnson’s case closely resembled the arc in Tyler.
Tyler filed her suit about four years after Hennepin County claimed her condo and three years before it sold it. Johnson sued roughly three years after a state Superior Court judge issued a final judgment barring her ability to pay the debt to reclaim her property.
“Why is this case not decided by the facts of Tyler itself?” said Justice Rachel Wainer Apter.
The governments argued that requiring the city to pay back the money earned from the property’s sale would be unfair. They said East Orange followed the law when it made that sale and could not foresee it would later be required to repay it.
“It offends principles of fair notice to hold the city liable. The city used the only mechanism to it to enforce tax delinquencies — a duly enacted law — and for conforming its conduct to the law, the city is now being held to account,” said Elliot Almanza, an attorney representing East Orange.
David Deerson, an attorney for the Pacific Legal Foundation who represented Johnson, said that was no different from any other excess takings case. The city would be equally on the hook six years later if it took trees from a private property and sold them, he said. The Pacific Legal Foundation represented Tyler before the U.S. Supreme Court.
Government attorneys predicted allowing Johnson to reclaim her lost equity would expose municipalities around the state to similar suits, risking legal fees and judgments in the millions of dollars. They said it could also impact private debt buyers whose purchases help municipalities keep budgets whole when property owners don’t pay their taxes.
“You are inviting a war between the municipalities and the lienholders who fund massive amounts of delinquencies every year — about $200 million every year in New Jersey are remedied by private lienholders who come in and make up for the deficiencies of the taxpayers,” Almanza said. “It’s going to be drawn out, and it’s going to be expensive, and it’s not going to be pretty.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Local taxpayers kept their promise. Missouri must keep its, too.
description: For years, I watched young families chase a familiar version of the American dream: land the right job, save enough money for a down payment, and find a home in a community where they could raise their children safely. One with a reasonable commute, maybe a park nearby and enough room in the backyard to […]
text:
Good schools are not only a local asset. They prepare the workforce, create jobs, support the economy, and give families confidence that their children can build successful fulfilling futures in our great state (Kevin Hardy/Stateline).For years, I watched young families chase a familiar version of the American dream: land the right job, save enough money for a down payment, and find a home in a community where they could raise their children safely. One with a reasonable commute, maybe a park nearby and enough room in the backyard to throw a ball. But almost always, near the top of the list, was a simple question: What are the schools like?
In Missouri, the connection between home values, local taxes, and strong public schools is not an accident. It is built into the state’s foundation formula: communities with higher property values and stronger local tax bases are expected to shoulder a larger share of the cost of educating their children.
For decades, most communities have done exactly what the system asked of them. Families planted roots, housing markets grew, local businesses opened, voters passed levies and bonds to support their schools, and, over time, communities in our state have built much of their identity around the quality of their public schools.
Missouri’s foundation formula has always assumed that districts with stronger property tax bases will carry more of the cost themselves. But that bargain only works if the state remains a reliable partner.
Today, debates over property tax reform, income tax cut proposals, expanded voucher-like programs, and reliance on less stable funding streams, like gaming, lottery, and tobacco revenue, all raise the same concern: the state is stepping back while local taxpayers are being asked to carry an increased share of the day-to-day cost of public education.
Today, Missouri asks local taxpayers to shoulder one of the heaviest local burdens in the country. In Missouri, local sources provide 57.5% of public-school funding, while the state provides just 28.6%. Nationally, the balance is nearly reversed: states provide about 45.1%, while local sources provide 42%. Property taxes alone account for 45% of Missouri’s public-school funding.
For some communities, this is not just limited to supporting their own schools through local levies or property taxes. In economically advantaged, fast-growing communities, families and businesses also help generate income and sales tax revenue that flows to Missouri’s general revenue fund that supports statewide priorities, like public education in other communities. The same families and businesses that have invested in their own public schools and help generate resources for the entire state are now being asked to watch Jefferson City step back from its responsibility.
The result is not a stronger public education system. It is a less stable one, with more pressure pushed down to the local level and fewer resources flowing back to the schools most Missouri children still attend. Every part of a child’s education depends on stability: stability at home, stability in the classroom, stability among teachers and staff, and yes, stability in funding.
Local control only matters if local communities have real choices.
When the state shifts costs downward and pulls resources away, local control becomes something much smaller. While school boards will still hold meetings, communities can still vote, and superintendents may still present budgets, their range of choices narrows significantly. And those choices are not theoretical.
As a superintendent, I have sat through those budget meetings. I have watched school leaders weigh class sizes against staff salaries, student programs against reserves, facility needs against safety improvements, and long-term planning against immediate classroom needs. Behind every line item is a child, a teacher, or a family. It is additional offerings for college credit, test prep workshops, cost-share career and vocational programs, or offering additional extracurricular or sports programs.
The challenges this creates look different from district to district, but they are all part of the same broken equation.
Missouri cannot keep asking local taxpayers to carry more while pretending the state has done enough. For too long, we have ignored the local sacrifice required to sustain the system we have. Now it is at a breaking point at the same time the state is stepping back from its responsibility to the public schools most Missouri children attend while calling the result “choice.”
If public schools begin to weaken, parents will not have more choices. They will have fewer.
Public schools are where children learn with their neighbors. It’s where teachers know the siblings coming next. It brings communities together to raise their children together and, eventually, watch and celebrate as their future walks across the graduation stage.
What is concerning now is not just a difficult budget year, but a political climate in Jefferson City that is slowly unraveling the public commitment families have built their lives around.
Families did what Missouri’s system asked them to do. The question now is whether Missouri will keep its end of the bargain.
Good schools are not only a local asset. They prepare the workforce, create jobs, support the economy, and give families confidence that their children can build successful fulfilling futures in our great state.
Local taxpayers have kept their promise.
Now Missouri must keep its too.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma’s next state auditor plans to tackle backlog by modernizing tech, rebuilding workforce
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Though the work might not be glamorous, the next state auditor says she finds fulfillment in holding government entities accountable for how they use Oklahomans’ money. Melissa Capps said she’s looking forward to having her chance to make the State Auditor and Inspector’s Office more efficient and responsive to Oklahomans by hiring […]
text:
Oklahoma's next State Auditor and Inspector Melissa Capps smiles in the State Auditor and Inspector's office in the state Capitol on July 17, 2026 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Though the work might not be glamorous, the next state auditor says she finds fulfillment in holding government entities accountable for how they use Oklahomans’ money.
Melissa Capps said she’s looking forward to having her chance to make the State Auditor and Inspector’s Office more efficient and responsive to Oklahomans by hiring young talent, utilizing artificial intelligence to work through the office’s audit backlog and bringing her staff’s findings to the public’s attention.
Capps, 52, of McLoud, won her bid to become the state’s next auditor and inspector after running unopposed, which is uncommon in a statewide election. She has 26 years of experience in the auditor’s office, where she now leads the division tasked with investigating the effectiveness and spending of about 85 state agencies.
When the Republican assumes the role on Jan. 11, she will have to manage a 115-person office that has struggled with retention and faced scrutiny over the time it takes to complete audits. 
“I’m very happy to do this job,” Capps said. “It’s a very challenging job because as the auditor, obviously you’re not always making people happy … But it’s also exciting because we’re holding government accountable, which is what the taxpayers expect us to do.”
Capps earned a bachelor’s degree in finance at the University of Central Oklahoma and is a certified fraud examiner, a specialty focused on prevention, detection and investigation. From leading the Performance Audit Division to her early experience investigating the state’s financial statements, Capps says she has been involved in almost every kind of audit the office is responsible for.
She worked on an investigation into the Oklahoma Department of Health that found the state paid $5.4 million for medical gear and services it did not receive during the COVID-19 pandemic. She was also part of the team that found the state was not properly verifying income eligibility for certain residents enrolled in Medicaid from July 2018 to June 2019.
Her goals
The auditor’s office has been criticized by at least one state leader for how long it has taken to complete investigations. The office works on about 350 audits a year, including 10 to 15 requested audits. Officials were not able to say how many special audits were currently pending.
Capps said this was fair criticism, though she noted that each audit requires a lot of information be gathered and reviewed. Auditors must be prepared to testify on findings. She wants to work through the office’s backlog of audits and improve the wait times for results.
She plans to modernize the auditing process by using AI to automate repetitive tasks and identify anomalies in financial reports. Capps said the office is still weighing costs, security and implementation strategies for the technology. She is watching how other states are using AI in their auditing process.
AI will not replace professional judgment, Capps said, but it would hopefully minimize the wait times for audits by reducing manual efforts.
“It’s going to take a little bit of time, but I know it will provide efficiency in our work,” she said.
Capps said the auditor’s office has also struggled with high staff turnover and replacing auditors has been challenging. 
Since 2018, the office’s turnover rate has decreased by about 14%, partly because current State Auditor and Inspector Cindy Byrd raised salaries by about $13,000. Most auditors now make between $60,000 to $65,000, Capps said. Oklahoma’s Statewide Official Compensation Commission raised the state auditor’s salary to $150,000 in November.
Capps hopes to retain staff by continuing to be more competitive with salaries, offering flexible work schedules and diversifying the assignments auditors work on.
She is also hopeful she can recruit new talent by showing up to career fairs and offering internships, with the goal of rebuilding the office’s staff.
This marked Capps’ first time running for public office, but she said running unopposed did not stop her from traveling around the state to meet with certified public accounting groups, Republican organizations and towns to explain what her office does and why she wants to lead it. 
She plans to continue these outings once she takes over the office, using the public appearances to explain audit findings to residents.
“Auditing can be very hard to understand,” Capps said. “…It’s a lot easier when you can go out and speak about it.”
‘Impartial judge’
Keeping politics out of the office is something former State Auditor and Inspector Gary Jones said Capps will have to do to be successful. 
Jones, who ran unopposed when he sought reelection in 2014, was the chair of the state’s Republican Party before resigning to run for state auditor. He said auditors before him often replaced the staff with members of their political party when they took office.
Losing this institutional knowledge, Jones said, was detrimental. It also introduced politics into the work, which Jones said made people question findings. 
“Your job is to be an impartial judge or report impartially, and let the facts fall as they may,” he said.
Jones worked with Capps while he was auditor and supported her candidacy. He says Capps succeeded in each role she held at the office and was “always able to step up to the task.”
Byrd, the current state auditor, said she worked closely with Capps and supported her candidacy because of her strong work ethic, professionalism and her commitment to the taxpayers of Oklahoma. 
“I think she’s a very smart, kind individual who has the best interest in place for Oklahoma, and I know that she will do a fabulous job,” ” Byrd said.
Earlier in Capps’ tenure with the office, she took off four years to raise her three sons. Now that her kids have grown up, Capps and her husband enjoy traveling whenever possible.
She said traveling helps her regenerate so she returns to the auditor’s office refreshed and ready to get to work.
“The work is so important,” Capps said. “The work is so important for state government, and however I can help everyone understand that or continue to understand that, is what I want to do.”

title: What will ‘super’ El Nino bring to landlocked, parched Wyoming?
description:
While poised to wreak havoc across the globe, El Nino might mean a closer-to-normal Wyoming winter after a wild, snowless one last season.
The post What will ‘super’ El Nino bring to landlocked, parched Wyoming? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
What does the “super” El Nino weather pattern gathering strength near the equator in the Pacific mean for landlocked Wyoming thousands of miles away?
For starters, less-than-average wind this winter. Additionally, between now and late spring, the southern half of the state can expect higher-than-average precipitation, while the northern part — especially the northwest corner — can expect less than average.
Despite El Nino’s global weather influence, however — and its roll-of-the-dice supercharged status — you can probably count on Wyoming to retain the core of its weather personality. The wind will still blow, and there will be events that buck the seasonal forecast, explained Cheyenne National Weather Service meteorologist Mike Natoli.
As for perhaps the top question on minds in Wyoming: Will it bring some relief after a winter of historically sparse snowpack? 





Click to enlarge: High winds toppled a train in December 2025 near Cheyenne. (Lacey Beck)

“It’s hard to do worse,” Natoli said. 
Wyoming has already encountered its share of unusual weather this year. Hurricane-level winds downed trees and knocked a train off its tracks. The notoriously chilly state experienced record winter high temperatures and brutally sparse snowpack — wounds to the state’s agricultural and outdoor recreational economy that were only exacerbated by this summer’s record-high temperatures.
Even northern portions of the state that are likely to experience below-average snowfall — a signature effect of El Nino’s influence here — might still do better than last winter, Natoli said.
Super El Nino
The El Nino phenomenon, which occurs about once every two to seven years, is shaping up to be the most intense in recent history, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. It’s borne and fueled by the cyclical convergence of warm ocean waters in the equatorial Pacific. It sends heat and moisture into the atmosphere and draws the global jet stream further south — about a nine-month-cycle that usually divides seasonal climate expectations in Wyoming on a latitude that might strike through Casper, or a bit further south.
Seasonal drought predictions — valid from Sept. 17 through Dec. 31, 2026 — forecast persistent drought conditions across much of northern and western Wyoming, with improvement in the south and eastern areas of the state. (Richard Tinker/NOAA/NWS/NCEP Climate Prediction Center)
Though NOAA avoids the term, climate watchers warn that human-caused climate warming is propelling this El Nino to “super” status, making it likely to “shift rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide and fuel extreme weather” far beyond a typical El Nino, the World Meteorological Organization says.
The oceanic center of the developing El Nino is unusually hot, already 5.4 degrees Fahrenheit above the average ocean temperature for the region, whereas a temperature anomaly of plus 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit would portend a “very strong” El Nino, according to data from the Columbia Climate School’s International Research Institute for Climate and Society. 
And it’s still gathering power, fed by a huge reservoir of warmer-than-usual ocean waters far below the surface. “The strength of this El Nino may be surpassing any one we have observed in the past, which could cause some unexpected things,” Natoli said. 
Even in Wyoming.
From Pacific waters to Wyoming skies
It’s tempting to say that the stronger the El Nino, the more that its typical-for-Wyoming outcomes — above average precipitation in the south, less-than-average elsewhere — are more certain and easier to predict in weekly forecasting, Natoli said. But, the intensity of this El Nino is a bit of a wildcard. “We may learn a thing or two this year from this event.”
But based on past El Nino events, the jet stream moves further south, and that means many of the storms it spins off will come up from Colorado. Those storms generally swirl up against the eastern slopes of mountain ranges, resulting in more snowfall on the eastern sides of mountains than the western slopes, Natoli said.
Still, “The northern part of the state generally tends to see below-average snowpack, which is partially due to the warmer temperatures and partially due to that southward shift of the jet stream and the storm track, sending more storms to the southern part of the state.”
Snowfall during moderate-to-strong El Niño winters (January-March) compared to the 1991-2020 average (after the long-term trend has been removed). Blue colors show more snow than average; brown shows less snow than average. (NOAA Climate.gov map, based on ERA5 data from 1959-2023 analyzed by Michelle L’Heureux)
That could mean some level of relief for drought-stricken regions like the North Platte River Basin spanning from southern Carbon County and bending toward the Nebraska state line, as well as the Laramie River Basin in the far southeast.
“Those two basins had some of the worst conditions last year,” Natoli said. “So we’re a little optimistic that the basins that did the worst last year will probably do a little bit better this year.”
That’s the big-picture snow forecast for Wyoming’s core winter months — December through February — the second-most predictable El Nino influence in Wyoming. Meanwhile, the biggest snow events are most likely reserved for the “shoulder seasons” — fall and spring, according to Natoli. 
If you’re a skier chasing powder, Natoli added, you might find your kicks in the central and southern portions of the state — like Hogadon on Casper Mountain, Snowy Range west of Laramie or Pine Creek outside Cokeville. Beyond Wyoming borders, El Nino typically tempts skiers to sojourn to slopes in southern Colorado and California.
The most predictable El Nino effect in Wyoming — and his favorite, Natoli said — is less-than-average winter wind.
“El Nino winters are associated with lower average wind speeds and a reduced frequency of high-wind events, for pretty much the entire state of Wyoming,” Natoli said. “Of course, we live in Wyoming, so it’s going to be windy. But there is decent confidence that you may notice a little bit less wind — particularly compared to last year.”

title: Who is the Christian legal group representing the Wind River church embroiled in sermon controversy?
description:
Amid tribe’s call for banishment, Florida-based Liberty Council says Foundations for Nations church “will not be leaving its property.”
The post Who is the Christian legal group representing the Wind River church embroiled in sermon controversy? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A church facing demands to leave the Wind River Indian Reservation after its pastor delivered a sermon urging Native congregants to renounce Northern Arapaho traditions has a formidable ally in its corner as tensions continue to simmer. 
Last month, the Foundations for Nations church lodged a complaint with state and federal agencies against the Food Bank of Wyoming, alleging the organization unlawfully cut off its support on the basis of religious, political and racial discrimination. According to Foundations For Nations Pastor Sarah Lucas, Food Bank of Wyoming ended the partnership after her controversial sermon, telling her that it was in response to a call claiming her message was discriminatory, the Ranger reported. 
Foundations for Nations church had the help of a legal group that has litigated cases across the nation involving religious belief. Liberty Counsel, a Florida-based Christian legal nonprofit, filed the complaint on the church’s behalf. The group was founded by conservative activist Mathew Staver, an attorney and former dean at Liberty University School of Law, and his wife, Anita. Before going to law school, Staver pastored several churches, according to his website bio. 
“We focus on three primary areas of life, religious freedom and the family,” said Richard Mast, senior litigation counsel with Liberty Counsel.  
Rowan County Clerk Kim Davis, center, with Republican presidential candidate Mike Huckabee, left, and attorney Mat Staver, right, founder of the Liberty Counsel, the Christian law firm representing Davis, at her side, greets the crowd after being released from the Carter County Detention Center, Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2015, in Grayson, Ky. Davis, the Kentucky county clerk who was jailed for refusing to issue marriage licenses to gay couples, was released Tuesday after five days behind bars.  (AP Photo/Timothy D. Easley)
A network of Christians, attorneys and churches alerted the organization to Foundations for Nations’ situation, Mast told WyoFile. Liberty Counsel is providing legal services to the church for free. “I’m hopeful that this is close to being amicably resolved, and everyone will continue living their lives,” Mast said. 
Liberty Counsel has taken on cases across the country in the name of religious freedom, including some that have landed before the U.S. Supreme Court. Many of these cases have dealt with abortion and LGBTQ matters. 
In the 1994 case Madsen v. Women’s Health Center, Inc., for example, the organization successfully challenged parts of a city of Melbourne, Florida ordinance imposing 300-foot buffer zones around abortion clinics and requiring that demonstrators get permission to talk to people connected with such clinics. The U.S. Supreme Court struck down the buffer zones and a ban against images that could be seen from inside the clinic.
Liberty Counsel also successfully defended a Kentucky clerk from lawsuits filed against her after she refused to sign her name to marriage certificates following the U.S. Supreme Court’s legalization of same-sex marriage nationwide. Across the country, the group has also pushed back on “conversion therapy” bans, arguing that such bans violate free speech and religious freedom rights. 
For Liberty Counsel, the Foundations for Nations’ conflict also ties to free speech and religious freedom concerns, Mast said. “Even though it might be offensive speech to some, we still have the right to say it, and people should not try to cancel others because of their faith,” he said of Lucas’ sermon and the resulting fallout from her message. 
Sarah Lucas, pastor of the Foundations for Nations church, is interviewed in Arapahoe on Monday, Aug. 17, 2026. (Thomas Peipert/AP Photo)
The organization has the help of “affiliated attorneys” who are on the ground in Wyoming. “When a matter arises in their local area, we reach out to them, offer them an opportunity to participate, and we are frequently taken up on that,” Mast said. “We appreciate our local counsel in Wyoming.” 
Liberty Counsel has previously taken on other Wyoming cases, Mast said. “People have reached out to us from Wyoming. We’ve come to their assistance, and at least one of those cases I recall was successful,” he said. The Wyoming cases he has been involved with were “privately resolved without public fanfare.” 
“I’m not at liberty to share what those cases are because of client privacy rights,” Mast said. 
The group has also dealt with Native American law matters before, though this will be the first time the group has undertaken a matter involving the Northern Arapaho tribe, Mast said. 
In addition to filing the discrimination complaint, Liberty Counsel sent a letter to Northern Arapaho Business Council Chairman Keenan Groesbeck in July after the council had adopted a resolution stating that outside organizations should consult with the council before initiating or expanding recurring organized activities on lands governed by the Northern Arapaho Tribe. While stating that the church believes it’s in compliance with the resolution, the letter asserted that the church “requires no authorization” from the Northern Arapaho Business Council “to conduct religious activities on its own private fee simple property,” and that the church “will not be leaving its property.” 
Following Lucas’ sermon, the Northern Arapaho Business Council told church officials to leave the reservation, and some called on the Northern Arapaho and Eastern Shoshone tribes to use the “bad men” clause in their treaties with the U.S. government to oust the church from the reservation. But in an Aug. 31 resolution, the Northern Arapaho Business Council stated that it doesn’t regulate activities on the church’s private property, and that it hadn’t designated the church or any person as “bad men.”

title: What, a bribe?
description:
President Trump pitched $5,000 to each American adult citizen as a "dividend" if Republicans win, but let’s not pretend to be fooled, writes columnist David Romtvedt.
The post What, a bribe? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

When I was a kid, I never thought much about an allowance. I knew my parents had a hard time getting by, so they didn’t have any spare change for me. I also knew my father, under the thumb of his bosses at work, was in charge at home. If I needed money, I had to ask. Usually he said no, and that was that.
As parents, we gave our daughter an allowance, believing it was a way to help her learn to make decisions and live with them. The money wasn’t tied to specific chores — if you clean your room, you can have a cookie; if you help with the yard work, you’ll get 50 cents; if you’re polite to your cranky auntie, we’ll slip a dollar your way. We wanted to avoid teaching bribery as the way of the world.
The Merriam-Webster Dictionary’s first definition of bribe is, “money or favor given or promised in order to influence the judgment or conduct of a person in a position of trust.” Stopped by the highway patrol, the driver attempted to bribe the officer to avoid getting a speeding ticket. The father bribed his daughter with candy to finish her homework.
At the recent Republican National Committee’s midterm convention, President Trump pledged to give $5,000 to each of the nation’s 270 million adult citizens if Republicans keep control of both the House and Senate in the upcoming elections. The president called his pledge a “Trump dividend” to be given as a result of the administration’s “tremendous economic success.” He compared it to the cash dividends corporations pay to shareholders. As if being a citizen is being a shareholder and as if the nation is a corporation. He also noted that the $5,000 could only be spent within the country. How you gonna police that one?
It’s estimated that the total of the $5,000 payments would add up to about $1.2 trillion. Where would that money come from? The president has said there’d be no need to use tax funds, that some of the money could come from the $100,000 fee he’s demanding of visa applicants and some from the profits from tariffs. He claimed the country has taken in “trillions of dollars in tariffs and other things.”
Treasury Department data cited by the Bipartisan Policy Center shows that tariffs have provided about $341 billion in net revenue, $166 billion of which the Supreme Court has ordered to be refunded. The remaining $175 billion is 14.6% of the $1.2 trillion needed to pay us each $5,000.
George Washington University law professor Paul Berman has commented that even if there were enough tariff revenue to cover the cost, “that’s money that goes back to the public fisc,” that is, back to the total pool of money the government holds and manages. Brennan emphasized that the president can’t unilaterally make such payments, as Congress holds the power to appropriate funds. The executive branch can’t spend public money without approval from Congress. 
While many commentators have weighed in on the president’s proposal, few have said out loud what the proposal is — a bribe. In offering each adult citizen $5,000 if Republicans maintain control of Congress in the upcoming elections, the president has made what is typically understood as the classic form of bribery — the payment of money or anything of value or the offer of such payment in exchange for casting or withholding a vote. By federal law, such a promise or payment is illegal.
State law also prohibits bribery. Title 6, Chapter 5, Article 1, Section 6-5-102 of the Wyoming statutes states that a person commits bribery if, “He offers, confers or agrees to confer any pecuniary benefit, testimonial, privilege or personal advantage upon a public servant as consideration for the public servant’s vote, exercise of discretion or other action in his official capacity; or, while a public servant, he solicits, accepts or agrees to accept any pecuniary benefit, testimonial, privilege or personal advantage upon an agreement or understanding that his vote, exercise of discretion or other action as a public servant will thereby be influenced.”
We commonly think of an individual bribing an elected official — a public servant. But President Trump’s proposal turns things upside down. He is the individual offering the bribe, and we are all public servants sworn in our official capacity to uphold democracy. As such, we must not sell our votes.
In Wyoming, the punishment for a bribery conviction is imprisonment for not more than 10 years, a fine of not more than $5,000, or both. If convicted, I can use the president’s $5,000 check to pay my $5,000 fine. The prison time’s another matter.

title: Nonprofit takes up work to overturn wrongful convictions after closure of Idaho Innocence Project
description: Charles Fain says his three favorite letters in the alphabet are D-N-A.  In 2001, Fain was exonerated and released from an Idaho prison after nearly 20 years on death row for a rape and murder he did not commit, using DNA analysis spearheaded by the Idaho Innocence Project.   That project has been shuttered for more […]
text:
Charles Fain, who in 2001 was exonerated and freed from prison after 16 years, speaks at a Sept. 17, 2026, event in Boise to announce a new nonprofit taking up the work of trying to overturn wrongful convictions in the state. To his right are retired founder of the Idaho Innocence Project Greg Hampikian and The Innocence Center Executive Director Mike Semanchik. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Charles Fain says his three favorite letters in the alphabet are D-N-A. 
In 2001, Fain was exonerated and released from an Idaho prison after nearly 20 years on death row for a rape and murder he did not commit, using DNA analysis spearheaded by the Idaho Innocence Project.  
That project has been shuttered for more than two years because of a lack of funding. However, on Sept. 17, Fain joined Innocence Project founder Greg Hampikian and fellow exoneree Amanda Knox to usher in a new group continuing the work of overturning wrongful convictions. 
The Innocence Center board member and exoneree Amanda Knox and retired founder of the Idaho Innocence Project Greg Hampikian. Hampikian lent his DNA expertise to Knox’s defense team to help free her from an Italian prison. (Photo by G Kenny3 Photography)
Knox sits on the board of The Innocence Center, a nonprofit, free law firm based in San Diego that will take on cases in Idaho to try and free wrongfully convicted inmates. 
Hampikian, a forensic DNA expert, also lent his expertise to Knox’s defense team in the highly publicized case and helped free her from an Italian prison after she was wrongfully sentenced for the murder of her roommate while studying abroad. 
“It would be a desperate situation if these projects didn’t exist,” Knox said in an interview last week in Boise. “And when I heard that the Idaho Innocence Project was shutting down, I was really, really worried for the state of Idaho, because who else is going to do it?” 
The Innocence Center Executive Director Mike Semanchik was admitted to the Idaho bar on Sept. 18 so that he may work as an attorney for these cases in Idaho. 
“We’re committed to making this happen and making sure that wherever there are innocent people in prison, there’s an organization to support them,” Semanchik told a small gathering last week to kickoff the new work. 
Hampikian said he personally selected The Innocence Center to take up the work. 
“My last great act, after 20 years of the Innocence Project, was to choose a successor,” Hampikian said. “… (Semanchik) said, ‘I’ll get barred in Idaho, and I’ll take the cases until we raise the money.’ And I was like, ‘Oh, this guy’s got skin in the game.’” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Edward Stevens, who was sent back to prison after being released, will be first case

Semanchik announced that the center’s first Idaho case to review would be for Edward Stevens — a man convicted of the 1996 killing of an 11-month-old in Ada County, who was released in 2018 and sent back to prison in 2019, the Idaho Statesman reported. 
Hampikian, who was not involved in Stevens’ case but knew his mother, walked Stevens back into prison. 
“We drive to the prison on a Sunday afternoon, and nobody could face walking back in except me,” Hampikian told the Idaho Capital Sun. “It was just a horrific experience.”
Idaho’s prisons are full. Corrections agency will request $45.3 million to open 3 new facilities.

Stevens was caring for his girlfriend’s 11-month-old son in late December of 1996 when the child sustained a serious head injury and died the next day in the hospital, the Associated Press reported. 
Prosecutors said Stevens shook the child and hit the child’s head on the bathtub. Stevens has said the child was injured in an accidental fall down the stairs. 
Stevens previously appealed his murder conviction and lost, and appealed again to Idaho’s U.S. District Court in 2014. A U.S. magistrate judge later ruled that Stevens had to be released or re-tried because prosecutors failed to disclose some favorable evidence to Stevens’ attorney.
A panel of Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals judges overturned the release in 2019, ordering him back to prison. Stevens is serving a life sentence at a prison in Orofino, according to Idaho Department of Correction records. 
Wrongfully convicted individuals can apply for assistance from the Innocence Center by filling out its application form. To qualify, they must have received a conviction and are currently incarcerated, are factually innocent, and have new, strong evidence of innocence. 
After review, the firm will decide whether to take on the case. 
 Semanchik: It ‘takes a village’ to free a wrongfully imprisoned person 

Semanchik told the gathering last week that community support would be crucial to continuing where the Idaho Innocence Project left off. 
“This work takes a village,” he said. 
The Innocence Center has freed 43 people. The average time the center’s clients spend in prison before being released is about 16.5 years, he said. Some are released after more than 30 years, he said.
Hampikian said he ran into problems with funding because a full-time lawyer needs to be on staff. Over the two decades he ran the Idaho organization, he had to pause work a couple times because of funding gaps. In 2024, he had to cease work completely. 
The project operated with about $100,000 a year, he said. 
“Those were very, very, very difficult times,” Hampikian said. “I am hopeful that I will never run a nonprofit again in my life. I much prefer doing science.” 
Knox said that, despite spending four years in prison for a murder she didn’t commit, she had an easier time being released than many of her counterparts in the U.S. She noted that appeals of Italian criminal convictions are easier to obtain, and juries there must provide a “motivation” for the sentence. 
That motivation document gave her defense team something to work against. 
“You have to get out to make your life back, and it is so hard to get out once you’ve been convicted,” Knox said. “I have to say one thing for the Italian justice system: It’s actually a lot easier to get out once you’ve been convicted.”
Knox noted that the work to free people in the U.S. can take decades, and it’s not easy. 
“It is heartbreaking work,” she said. “It will take and take and take from you, but in the end, there is another human being and another life that is saved on the other side.”

title: New lawsuit alleges sexual misconduct, retaliation against 14-year-old at Interlochen arts school
description: A new lawsuit against the Interlochen Center for the Arts, filed in federal district court in the Western District of Michigan on Sept. 16, alleges that a 14-year-old student at Interlochen’s boarding school was subject to sexual assault and harassment by fellow students as well as a teacher, and claims that after she reported that […]
text:
Getty ImagesA new lawsuit against the Interlochen Center for the Arts, filed in federal district court in the Western District of Michigan on Sept. 16, alleges that a 14-year-old student at Interlochen’s boarding school was subject to sexual assault and harassment by fellow students as well as a teacher, and claims that after she reported that conduct, school administrators retaliated against her by preventing her from re-enrolling.
The complaint alleges that the student, who is not named in the lawsuit but identified by her initials A.C., faced “severe, pervasive, and offensive sexual assault(s) and harassment” by her roommate and suitemate, as well as by staff at the Interlochen school, while she was a first-year student at the boarding school in the 2024-25 academic year.
An Interlochen spokesperson said that the events laid out in the complaint “simply did not occur as alleged,” and that the lawsuit is “filled with false allegations.”
The complaint also alleges that, when A.C. and her mother, Emily Cohen, who is named in the lawsuit on her daughter’s behalf, reported the alleged assault and harassment, Interlochen “did not investigate, repeatedly denied or delayed requests for a room/roommate reassignment, and refused to discipline A.C.’s assailants,” and that those perpetrators “grew bolder as Defendant ICA’s culture permitted it,” referring to the Interlochen Center for the Arts.
Todd Flood, who is representing the student in the lawsuit, said that the school’s lack of response is a central point in the lawsuit. 
“It’s a 14-year-old young girl away from home for the first time, and she cries for help,” he said in an interview with Michigan Advance. “When she cries for help, they don’t help, and then they retaliate against her. It really boils down to that.”
Scathing report shows decades of sexual abuse at Interlochen arts school, Epstein among those named

An astronomy teacher at the school is also a named defendant in the lawsuit, with the student A.C. having taken his class, which was generally reserved for older students, during her first year due to prerequisites for a summer program.
The claims against the teacher center around a series of “alternative assignments” to make up lost points on classwork, which included having the student “record herself using a protractor in the bathroom mirror,” and the complaint alleges that he “refused to accept the video unless A.C. emailed it to him directly, rather than submit it through the schools approved curriculum program,” after which point he informed the student that she was “required to attend his private office hours alone so that he could review her hand position and stance as depicted in the video.”
According to the complaint, a second alternative assignment required the student to write a poem entitled, “Gravity Does Not Ask for Consent,” and a third alternative assignment required students to examine and draw a telescope. The student in the lawsuit, after turning in her assignment, was allegedly granted a grade of zero and told by the teacher “that she would need to examine ’his telescope’ during a private meeting to earn the points back.”
Cohen filed a Title IX complaint in February against the teacher on behalf of her daughter, according to the complaint. That report was closed, the suit claims, even though the school “had not conducted any formal or meaningful investigation into A.C.’s complaints.”
A second Title IX complaint was filed in April, which was closed three days later, “without conducting any meaningful investigation,” according to the lawsuit, which continues on to say that “Through this sham investigation, Defendants effectively concluded that A.C., a fourteen-year-old minor, had consented” to the teacher’s alleged sexual harassment.
Flood said that the incident in which the teacher requested the video be sent to his private email represented an escalation of previous concerns, saying, “I don’t know what the teacher is doing with a 14-year-old girl sending a video to his private email, but normally, as I understand it, when you’re doing official school work, class work, you send it through proper channels.”
The complaint also alleges that Interlochen Center of the Arts leadership retaliated against the student for filing complaints against the teacher and against other students by preventing her from re-enrolling in Interlochen courses for the following school year.
Her enrollment for the 2025-26 academic year was formally rescinded on April 9, 2025, though “one week after A.C.’s enrollment was rescinded, A.C. participated in a course planning meeting with an advisor to discuss her academic plans for future years in preparation for college, reflecting that the rescission was not the product of any ordinary or anticipated academic process,” the lawsuit states. 
The claims of retaliation also include the grading practices that the teacher began after the initial Title IX complaint was filed, at which point he began giving the student no credit on her academic assignments. 
“The retaliation claim is clear. In April of 2025, the school offered to fix her grades if she left for good, right? So there was a faux pas in the grading system, but it sounded to me like a quid pro quo. We’ll take care of your grades; you just leave,” Flood explained. “And that’s in the complaint. About six weeks after the Title IX report, it took back her acceptance and re-enrollment. So, I think the retaliation is clear on its face.”

The Interlochen Center for the Arts, a prestigious arts school in northern Michigan with a history of successful alumni in the arts, also has a long history of sexual abuse — as detailed in a scathing investigative report that was released earlier this year showing that more than 70 alumni reported experiencing sexual abuse and misconduct from adults in Interlochen’s leadership.
The report showed that the majority of the alleged abuse began between the 1970s and 1990s, and four instances of abuse were reported as starting after 2000, implicating 47 adults in sexual abuse — including two reports tied to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. 
It detailed an overwhelmingly permissive culture for this type of conduct to have occurred at Interlochen — made possible by a number of factors, including limited contact with family members by students and the power dynamic between students and teachers. But the report concluded that the lack of response from Interlochen made the overall environment one where adults were able to get away with this type of behavior. 
The report, however, seeks to place the school’s issues with sexual abuse in its past, with President Trey Devey and Chair of the Board Barrett Rollins saying that “Interlochen will not tolerate predators or those who enable them. Our campus exists to protect, educate, and empower every student.”
This lawsuit, however, alleges that the problems of sexual abuse — and the school’s lack of response to that abuse — continues through the present, with the allegations taking place in 2024 and 2025. 
“Whether or not human nature has changed, I don’t think it has until there’s real reform,” Flood said. “Unfortunately, if we don’t work on studying history and studying human behavior, we unfortunately end up repeating it, and you know that that seems to be something that the school should be on uber lookout to make sure and protect students from harassment, from Title making sure that your Title IX protocols are, you know, every T crossed and every I dotted, and that there are guardrails put in place so we don’t end up repeating history.”
Matthew Curtis, a Southfield-based lawyer who represents four former Interlochen students abused by faculty in the 1970s, said that the new lawsuit shows that “Interlochen’s history of abuse is not a relic of the past.”
“Interlochen has spent the past several months telling the public it has reformed the systems that allowed decades of abuse to occur on its campus. A new lawsuit, filed within weeks of that public messaging campaign, describes the same pattern the school claims to have fixed,” he said in a statement. “Survivors of institutional abuse deserve more than a statute of limitations that expires before most of them are ready to come forward.”
This is the second lawsuit filed relating to these allegations — the first, which was filed in April 2024 by Emily Cohen, the mother of the 14-year-old student, was dismissed without prejudice due to the mother lacking standing to claim harms against herself for the abuse that she alleged her daughter experienced. 
Flood Law was not involved in that litigation, which alleged violations of the Americans with Disabilities Act, whereas the current lawsuit centers on Title IX concerns.
“The prior lawsuit, which raised related issues, was dismissed. Like the first lawsuit, this one is baseless,” the Interlochen spokesperson’s statement said. “Interlochen will vigorously defend this matter in court and is evaluating its own legal rights concerning the false allegations that this parent has made.”
Flood, however, noted that the cases are entirely separate, and he currently represents the minor student in this litigation specifically.
We don’t file frivolous cases,” Flood said. “All they’re trying to do is distract the shooter and have him take his eye off the ball. So I would make their defense akin to the distraction of those fans behind the basketball net.”

title: Democrat-leaning PAC goes after Republican congressional candidate over data centers
description: A Democrat-backing political action committee is getting into the 9th Congressional District race with an ad accusing Republican Sen. Brent Taylor of taking campaign cash from artificial intelligence companies and passing data center legislation. Three Star PAC released the independent ad Wednesday citing Taylor’s passage of Senate Bill 2128 and criticizing[...]
text:
A dark money Democratic-aligned PAC has released an ad accusing Sen. Brent Taylor, left, of taking money from AI companies and pushing data centers. Taylor is the GOP nominee for the 9th Congressional District, facing off against Democratic nominee, Rep. Justin J. Pearson. (Photos: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A Democrat-backing political action committee is getting into the 9th Congressional District race with an ad accusing Republican Sen. Brent Taylor of taking campaign cash from artificial intelligence companies and passing data center legislation.
Three Star PAC released the independent ad Wednesday citing Taylor’s passage of Senate Bill 2128 and criticizing him for “embracing Tennessee’s data center building boom.” It says a September poll of District 9 voters shows 68% of respondents oppose data centers and only 32% support them. Local governments across the state are starting to put a moratorium on data centers.
Taylor, an Eads Republican in the state Senate, is running against Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson of Memphis, an outspoken critic of data centers, including facilities in Mississippi and south Memphis that Pearson says are polluting the environment and harming residents.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
The ad is to run in the Nashville TV market and streaming services in the 9th District, which stretches from Shelby County to Williamson County. In a May special session, the legislature split a majority Black district in urban Memphis into three seats in an effort to help President Donald Trump maintain a Republican majority in the U.S. House in the midterm election.
Three Star PAC’s mission is to elect Democrats “who deliver for Tennessee,” it says on its website, which also describes the PAC as an independent expenditure-only committee registered with the Federal Election Commission.
Its latest FEC report shows receipts of $105,000 during the first half of 2026 and expenditures of $675, as of June 30. The funds come from four individuals, all with Massachusetts addresses.
The ad marks a new twist in the race with an environmental message from a dark money group going after a Republican candidate. An environmental group’s entrance into the 5th Congressional District primary helped vault Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher to victory over embattled U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles.
“They’re coming for our rivers, our neighborhoods, our farmland, because Brent Taylor wrote the law allowing massive data centers to take over Tennessee,” the ad says.
It also accuses Taylor of accepting more than $100,000 from corporate data center companies.
Taylor’s legislation allows data centers to produce power using gas-powered turbines or buy power from independent power producers that operate outside of utilities. If the data center buys power from a utility, data center owners must cover the cost of any infrastructure upgrades needed to support it. Improvements can’t lead to higher ratepayers costs unless the infrastructure benefits other ratepayers.
Tennessee bill gives data centers ability to self-power with limited regulation

Critics of the legislation say it gives companies such as Elon Musk’s XAI a loophole to use gas-powered turbines at facilities in northern Mississippi to run its Memphis data center.
Asked about the new ad Wednesday, Taylor said in a text response he passed the only data center regulation in the legislature this year, a measure that keeps companies from causing higher utility rates.
“My opponent, Democratic Socialist Justin Pearson, voted against this common-sense protection. That’s the problem with a chaotic activist: he prefers creating a problem rather than finding a solution,” Taylor said.
Even though Three Star PAC paid for a message criticizing Taylor, Pearson received an endorsement Wednesday from End Citizens United, a national group running an “Unrig Washington” program joined by 300 Democratic candidates. It said Pearson rejects corporate PAC money, backs a ban on congressional stock trading and is committed to removing dark money from elections.
A recent poll commissioned by Three Star PAC and TN Rise PAC also showed Pearson trailing Taylor 48% to 44%, before he started running campaign ads. TN Rise PAC is supported by officials with the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Resources Center, Equity Alliance and Planned Parenthood.
Pearson, who was to speak this week at Climate Forward in New York with environmental activist Erin Brockovich, said the bill Taylor and Republicans “wrote” with the data center industry “fails to adequately address the harms people in Tennessee are feeling or dangers from hyper scale data centers.” In a text statement, he said the bill allows “so many carve outs” for the industry that it doesn’t protect people from Memphis to Lawrenceburg who are coping with the prospect of more “illegal” gas turbines, “corrupt” non-disclosure agreements and millions of gallons of drinking water being used by computers, as well as negative implications for the workforce.
Pearson added, “I prefer to prevent problems from ever happening, that’s why I fought against Space xAI’s data center being powered illegally while (Taylor) celebrated and championed it.”
