title: Alabama State Employees’ Insurance Board approves first premium increase in 11 years
description: The State Employees Insurance Board Wednesday voted to increase premiums for state employees and dependents, citing rising healthcare costs and concerns over the stability of the program.  Premium rates will go up by $15 effective Jan. 1, the first across the board increase in 11 years. “I think it’s very important to note that the […]
text:
Stephanie Azar, CEO of the State Employees Insurance Board, speaks to SEIB members at its meeting on Sept. 23, 2026, in Montgomery, Alabama. The board Wednesday approved a $15 across-the-board premium increase, the first in 11 years, as officials cited strains from rising healthcare costs. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)The State Employees Insurance Board Wednesday voted to increase premiums for state employees and dependents, citing rising healthcare costs and concerns over the stability of the program. 
Premium rates will go up by $15 effective Jan. 1, the first across the board increase in 11 years.
“I think it’s very important to note that the reason for the recommended premium increases today is not because it’s been 11 years, but rather because the financials of the plan demonstrate necessity,” said Stephanie Azar, the Chief Executive Officer of SEIB, during the meeting.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The board oversees insurance for approximately 102,000 state employees and family members. Without the increased premiums, SEIB was projected to end fiscal year 2028 with a $81.4 million deficit. 
The increase passed with board member Bob Childree being the sole no vote. During the meeting, Childree said he wanted to exempt retirees from the increase because they have not received cost-of-living adjustments.
“We are in a crisis. We are in a serious crisis, and I’m going to tell you that retirees are suffering more in this crisis than any other constituency group,” Childree said.
Currently, there are over 20,000 retirees who use state insurance. Azar said after the meeting that the board’s expenditures have “been exceeding revenue for several years,” which is why retirees had to be included in the increase.
Earlier this month, the SEIB executive board recommended increasing the premiums by $20 across the board. Board member Connie Grier wanted to drop the cost to help alleviate financial strain on employees.
“To some people, $5 is $5, and those that are paying both those rates, that’s $10 less out of their household,” Grier said.
With the $15 increase, the estimated financial impact will be around $9 million instead of the $12 million financial impact the original $20 would have provided.
Along with the premium increase, SEIB also approved other changes to benefits, including:

$5 increase on single Standalone Coverage for Dental, Cancer and Vision ($15 to $20)
$6 increase on single Standalone Coverage for Dental, Cancer and Vision ($24 to $30)
Tier 2 60- and 90-day prescription drug costs: from 30, 60 and 90-day prescriptions having 20% copay with minimum $45, maximum $85; to only 60 and 90-day prescriptions having 20% copay with minimum $90, maximum $170
GLP-1 prescriptions: from having a 90-day supply to 30-day supply
Medicare Part D prescription cost share increases

Tier 1: 30-day copay $3 to $6; 90-day copay $12
Tier 2: 30-day copay $23 to $40; 90-day copay $80
Tier 3: 30-day copay $53 to $60; 90-day copay $120
Tier 4: 30-day copay $53 to $60; limited to 30-day supply



SEIB plans to sk the Legislature for a $75 per member per month increase for FY28, bringing the state rate to $1,250 per member per month. That is an estimated $480 million impact to the General Fund budget for SEIB’s roughly 32,000 active members.
Azar told the board there’s a possibility that with a tight budget, SEIB could remain level funded for FY28.
“Me being somewhat familiar with the headwinds that that general fund is facing, I would say there could be a possibility we will be level funded in 2028. I can’t speak to that, but it is something we have to assume could be a real possibility,” she said.
Faye Nelson, chair of the board, said the board should consider putting “skin in the game” in order to get funding from the Legislature.
“You are going to be dealing with a very tight budget and new legislators, new governor, and we need to find a way to empower her to have some level of negotiating when she’s talking,” Nelson said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: OpenAI, Anthropic and other artificial intelligence companies hire Tennessee lobbyists
description: ​America’s leading artificial intelligence companies started lobbying in Tennessee this year amid growing backlash to data centers and cameras using the technology. ​At least 11 companies tied to artificial intelligence and data centers have hired lobbyists in Tennessee, newly filed records with the state ethics board show. ​Anthropic, OpenAI, the Data Cente[...]
text:
A Meta data center in Gallatin, Tennessee, was opened in 2024. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)​America’s leading artificial intelligence companies started lobbying in Tennessee this year amid growing backlash to data centers and cameras using the technology.
​At least 11 companies tied to artificial intelligence and data centers have hired lobbyists in Tennessee, newly filed records with the state ethics board show.
​Anthropic, OpenAI, the Data Center Coalition, and the AI venture capital firm Andressean Horowitz are contracting with lobbyists in 2026 for the first time, joining companies such as Amazon, Axon Enterprises, Google, Flock Safety, Meta, Oracle, and Salesforce, which already have significant AI ties and were lobbying state lawmakers.
​The disclosures don’t show how much money companies like OpenAI, which owns ChatGPT, and Anthropic, which owns Claude, are paying yet, but they indicate the companies plan to start lobbying lawmakers ahead of the January legislative session.



Quotation







AI interests need to be active at the state level to counter the rising anti-data center movement.


– Brandon Glavin, OpenSecrets


​Brendan Glavin, director of insights with OpenSecrets, said some of the lobbying could relate to AI regulation but that it’s more likely to focus on data centers. OpenSecrets is a nonprofit that tracks political spending at the state and federal level.
​The companies enter Tennessee’s legislative landscape as the debate over data center expansion has led some local communities to impose moratoriums on construction because of concerns that they’re driving electricity price increases and environmental impacts.
“AI interests need to be active at the state level to counter the rising anti-data center movement,” Glavin said. “This was likely barely on their radar not that long ago.”
​In recent years, Tennessee has become a hub for technology company investments, including AI and non-AI projects.
​Google opened a data center in Clarksville in 2019, and Meta opened a Gallatin facility in 2024, the same year SpaceXAI opened in Memphis. Amazon opened a second headquarters in Nashville in 2023, and Oracle plans to join them with a campus in the coming years.
​SpaceXAI has not hired any lobbyists, according to the ethics commission’s database.
​Along with the data center backlash, state Rep. Aftyn Behn, a Nashville Democrat, has called on Tennessee officials to pause its tax breaks for data centers.
​Tennessee offers several incentives for data center construction and exempts data processing services from its sales tax. The state Department of Finance and Administration estimates the processing exemption resulted in nearly $110 million in tax savings for those companies in 2026-27.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Former House leader Amy Summers writes children’s book with goal of helping harmed kids
description: Amy Summers, a former member of West Virginia House leadership, released a children’s book that draws on her personal life on the farm along with her time as a lawmaker trying to reform the state’s troubled foster care system.
text:
Former Del. Amy Summers speaks on the final day of the West Virginia legislative session on March 9, 2024 in the House of Delegates Chamber in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)Amy Summers, a former member of West Virginia House leadership, released a children’s book that draws on her personal life on the farm along with her time as a lawmaker trying to reform the state’s troubled foster care system. 
Amy Summer’s debut children’s book, “Courageous Kitty.” (Photo courtesy of Amy Summers)
“Courageous Kitty,” her debut book,” was released this week.
The book began as Summers writing for her children and grandchildren. As the story developed, she focused it on children who have experienced abuse, neglect and other hardships. 
“It might be a bigger message for some children that have been through this, that have had to go to a new home and have not been cared for,” said Summers, who left the Legislature in 2024 after not seeking reelection. “It could help other children be empathetic to children that have gone through that.”
The book is described as “a heartfelt story about finding courage, learning to trust and discovering the power of hope and belonging.”
Summers said the kitten character is based on a cat that appeared at her family’s farm years ago in Mason County.

“We don’t know how this cat got here, but he was so scared, and he was so scared of humans, and it took him like a year to develop trust,” she said. 
Summers started thinking years ago about the idea for a children’s book based on the farm cat, but she developed a plot for the story after being in the Legislature.
A Republican, Summers served in the House of Delegates from 2014 to 2024 representing District 73. While in the Legislature, she served as House Majority Leader. 
Summers also chaired the Health Committee, where members often heard about the worst parts of the state’s overwhelmed foster care system and the children caught in it. The committee is tasked with oversight of the child welfare system. 
“After being in the Legislature and dealing so much with the opioid epidemic and all the children that were being abused and neglected … I decided to make him a kitten that was suffering,” she said. 
The book hopes to remind children that courage doesn’t mean never being scared and focuses on the importance of kindness and empathy.
“Courageous Kitty” is available for purchase on Amazon.
In celebration of the book’s release, Summers partnered with the West Virginia CASA Association to give readers an opportunity to donate copies of “Courageous Kitty” to children in need.
As a former CASA volunteer and longtime supporter of the organization’s mission, Summers saw the partnership as a natural extension of the book’s message.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: 1 in 7 Idahoans experiences food insecurity. SNAP, food charities must work together to help.
description: September is Hunger Action Month and a time to learn more about the challenges facing some of our neighbors. We know that hunger is a growing issue in Idaho, especially as the cost of groceries continues to take up a significant share of many households’ monthly budgets. Feeding America’s Map the Meal Gap report estimates […]
text:
An employee helps move food in the Idaho Foodbank's Lewiston warehouse. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Foodbank)September is Hunger Action Month and a time to learn more about the challenges facing some of our neighbors.
We know that hunger is a growing issue in Idaho, especially as the cost of groceries continues to take up a significant share of many households’ monthly budgets. Feeding America’s Map the Meal Gap report estimates that over 283,000 Idahoans, or about one in seven people, experience food insecurity. That includes over 84,700 Idaho children, or about one in six kids.
Idaho has second-lowest error rate in nation for SNAP payments

Those numbers represent people in every part of our state. They are families trying to stretch their grocery budget until the next paycheck, older adults living on fixed incomes, neighbors with a disability, and working households trying to balance food with rent, utilities, transportation, child care and other basic needs.
At the Idaho Foodbank, we know that addressing hunger takes more than one program or organization. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and charitable food assistance play different, but connected, roles in helping Idaho families put food on the table. Both are essential parts of the safety net that addresses food insecurity across our state.
SNAP, previously known as food stamps, helps eligible households buy groceries. For many families, that support can make a significant difference. It helps people keep food on the table and frees up their budget to pay for gas and other household costs.
SNAP dollars can be spent on food at participating retailers, allowing SNAP beneficiaries to spend that money at their local store. For every one meal provided by the nationwide network of food banks, SNAP provides nine meals.
But SNAP does not reach everyone who is food insecure. We know there are families who are struggling to make ends meet, but they make too much money to qualify for SNAP.
To be eligible for SNAP, the household income has to be at or below 130% of the federal poverty level. That is an income of $36,336 per year for a family of three. Income limits do not always reflect what a family has left after paying rent, utilities, transportation and other necessary expenses. When families fall into that gap, they often turn to food banks for support.
SNAP provides ongoing grocery assistance to eligible households. Food banks provide another layer of support for people who need help, including those who may not qualify for federal nutrition programs at all. Together, they are an important part of the network that helps Idaho families get through hard times.
Hunger does not have one simple solution. We cannot end hunger alone and our partnerships with organizations all over Idaho are a vital part of the work to interrupt the cycle of food insecurity and improve the lives of all of our neighbors. It takes SNAP, food banks, community organizations, and neighbors working together to make sure Idaho families can put food on the table.
To apply for SNAP or learn more about program qualifications, contact the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare.
During Hunger Action Month, we all have an opportunity to play our part and take action to help ensure their neighbors have access to the food they need to thrive. Contact your local food pantry or visit idahofoodbank.org to find food assistance, volunteer to help, or learn more about hunger in Idaho.
Workers with the Idaho Foodbank help distribute food in North Idaho’s Lapwai. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Foodbank)

text:
Greg Lange of Bismarck drops off absentee ballots for himself and his wife at the Bismarck Burleigh County Office Building on June 8, 2026. Absentee ballots for the November election are now available. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota voters can start receiving and casting absentee ballots for the general election beginning Thursday.
Voters can fill out an absentee ballot application via websites for the secretary of state or their county, or in person at their county auditor’s office. County election officials send voters a ballot after reviewing and verifying their application information, Secretary of State Michael Howe said.
Voters need to return their ballot before polls close on Election Day, Nov. 3. They can return their absentee ballot in person, by mail or county dropbox. Absentee ballots won’t be accepted at the polls on Election Day. Absentee voters should fill out and return their ballots as soon as they can, Howe said.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Voters also can stop by their county office, complete an absentee application, receive, fill out and return the ballot on the spot, Howe said.
“It is kind of a form of in-person early voting if you so choose,” he said. 
State law allows two weeks of in-person early voting. Seven counties offer it.
Burleigh begins Oct. 22. Stutsman and Ward start Oct 26. Cass, Grand Forks and Morton counties begin Oct. 27. Stark opens Oct. 29. In addition, Sioux County offers some absentee voting days starting Oct. 26.
North Dakota’s general election includes two ballot measures: Measure 1, to require at least 60% voter approval of constitutional amendments, and Measure 2, to fund free school meals.
Statewide races include North Dakota’s sole U.S. House seat, attorney general, secretary of state, agriculture commissioner, tax commissioner, superintendent of public instruction, two seats on the Public Service Commission and two seats on the state Supreme Court.
Additionally, 75 of 141 seats in the Legislature are on the ballot.
North Dakota – the only state without voter registration – had nearly 43% turnout in the 2022 midterm election. North Dakota has about 600,000 eligible voters.
Howe encouraged every eligible voter to participate and to take a look at a ballot measure guide his office sent out, as well as websites and for and against the measures.
“Don’t just take our word for it, too. We encourage everyone who is going to participate in this process to seek out more information,” Howe said. 
The League of Women Voters of North Dakota has an online voter guide at vote411.org/north-dakota, which also includes information on local races. 
North Dakota has no presidential, gubernatorial or U.S. Senate races on the ballot this fall, an oddity that last occurred in 2014.
Overseas and military voters have been able to request absentee ballots since Sept. 18.
Republicans hold all of North Dakota’s partisan statewide offices and congressional seats and have supermajorities in the Legislature. Heidi Heitkamp’s 2012 U.S. Senate victory was the last time a Democrat won a statewide election.

 Catching Our Eye

• Militarizing American elections? NPR reports, “There’s growing concern that Trump may deploy the National Guard ahead of elections.”
With Election Day less than 50 days away, a growing number of Democratic lawmakers, retired military leaders and civil society organizations are seeking assurance from members of the Trump administration that the U.S. military will not be deployed to or around polling places — while also preparing for such a move to occur.
Having armed federal agents — like the FBI or Immigration and Customs Enforcement — or military troops near the polls is clearly barred by federal law, but President Trump and several other key officials have recently sidestepped direct lines of questioning around the issue.
Some have even suggested that such a presence might be necessary to ensure trust in the vote, a claim that voting officials across the United States deny. Those voting officials say they plan on administering the midterm elections as usual and have been working hard to assure voters that plans are in place if armed federal officials do show up.
• Medicaid. The Columbus Dispatch’s Samantha Hendrickson reports, “Auditor finds Ohio doled out Medicaid money for dead, ineligible Ohioans.”
Millions in Medicaid benefits were paid out for Ohioans who were ineligible for them, or even dead, according to a new interim report from the Ohio Auditor of State’s Office.
In total, the auditor’s office found over $2 million in fixed monthly payments made to medical providers for those who shouldn’t have had or didn’t need Medicaid benefits.
• Medicaid work requirements. Signal Cleveland’s Celia Hack reports, “Bracing for new Medicaid work requirements? Here’s the latest updates.”
Health advocates, hospital systems and Ohio residents on Medicaid are all bracing for one thing in coming months: new work requirements for people getting government-sponsored health insurance.
• Police drones. The Dayton Daily News’ Avery Kreemer reports, “New Ohio law limiting police drone use in effect next month.”
Starting Oct. 6, Ohio will have a new law in place regulating law enforcement’s use of drones, including blocking lethal weapons and requiring warrants for drone surveillance.
“This law is the next logical step in ensuring public trust when our law enforcement and public safety agencies are using the technology provided through their tax dollars,” said state Rep. Bernie Willis, R-Springfield, in a press release announcing the forthcoming law.

title: Alabama’s attorney general can intervene in power rate hearings. Will AG candidates do so?
description: With Alabamians paying some of the highest residential power prices in the South, the question of intervention is weighing on the Alabama attorney general’s race. Under Alabama law, the attorney general can intervene in rate cases before the Alabama Public Service Commission on behalf of the public. However, with the PSC using a process that […]
text:
An electric meter. Democratic nominee for Attorney General, Jeff McLaughlin, said he wants to exercise more oversight over investor-owned utilities with the Public Service Commission, the agency that regulates utilities in the state. (Dave Cummings/New Hampshire Bulletin)With Alabamians paying some of the highest residential power prices in the South, the question of intervention is weighing on the Alabama attorney general’s race.
Under Alabama law, the attorney general can intervene in rate cases before the Alabama Public Service Commission on behalf of the public. However, with the PSC using a process that effectively guarantees a profit for utilities since 1982, the power was rarely used before this summer, when the AG’s office stepped into a case involving a natural gas company.
Alabama pays some of the highest rates for power in the region. According to the Energy Information Commission, residents paid 16.04 cents per kilowatt-hour for electricity in June, higher than the 14.89 cents on average that customers paid in the region.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jeff McLaughlin, the Democratic nominee for Alabama attorney general, said in an interview Monday that he would take the obligation to represent power customers “very seriously.” He said he would work to ensure they pay fair prices for electricity and other services and reduce the impact of data centers as residents become increasingly concerned about their footprint within the community.
“The AG’s Office needs to be the champion of rate payers in our state where energy bills are at least as high or higher than in the rest of the country,” he said.
Messages were sent to the campaign of Katherine Robertson, the Republican nominee for Attorney General, on Tuesday and Wednesday seeking comment. Robertson’s campaign website, which emphasizes support for President Donald Trump and law enforcement, does not include a section on utilities. Robertson currently serves as chief counsel for Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall.
McLaughlin said he will use the office to be an advocate for rate payers as they pertain to the cost of electricity with the PSC to ensure they are paying the appropriate price.
“I think it has been some 40 years since there was a rate case pertaining to some of the rates of Alabama Power,” McLaughlin said. “That has been a long time. My view is the AG’s Office ought to be more proactive in representing the rate payers and whatever falls in line with that.”
McLaughlin also said he wants to slow the proliferation of data centers, which consume large amounts of energy and could put pressure on electric bills.
“To the extent that the AG’s Office can put its weight behind a moratorium or the establishment of some kind of regulation, particularly procedural regulation, on how communities can protect themselves if a data center is not wanted, I would put the weight of the office behind slowing down these data centers and making sure of what we are getting ourselves into,” McLaughlin said.
Power issues have also surfaced in the governor’s race. The Republican nominee for Governor, Tommy Tuberville, said he wants to extend a existing rate freeze that Alabama Power voluntarily proposed past a 2029 expiration date.
The Democratic nominee for governor, Doug Jones, said he would push instead for the PSC to hold formal hearings on any rate increases proposed by Alabama Power, saying the existing, frozen rates are too high.
Jones has also called for a one-year moratorium on the construction of new data centers. Tuberville, who was initially dismissive of criticisms of data centers, opposes a moratorium but said he would work to ensure data centers pay for impacts on communities.
In the last few months, the AG’s office has used its oversight powers.  Earlier this year, the AG’s Office challenged the rate of return that Spire Energy, based in St. Louis, requested with the PSC. The PSC Board ultimately sided with the AG’s recommendation that the company be allowed to earn a 9.4% return on equity instead of the 10.5% return that the company had requested.
The AG’s Office also submitted a comment to the PSC in August that said board members must vote on whether to approve contracts made between energy companies and data centers instead of allowing staff to decide.
Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, an organization that advocates for more renewable energy in the state, said that the AG’s Office plays an important role in advocating rate payers with the PSC on their behalf considering the profit motive of utility companies. The AG’s Office has the same authority as the public to weigh in on requests from utility companies about the rates they want to charge customers.
“The Attorney General’s Office gets access to a lot more information that is not made public,” Tait said.
He added that, “if anyone knows what should be happening beyond the power company, it would be the AG because the office gets unredacted filings and a lot more data than the rest of us do.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginians don’t need to be taught the value of work
description: West Virginians know what it means to get up early, drive a long way to a job, work a second shift, care for a child or aging parent, go to school, volunteer in their community or keep working when they don't feel their best because the bills still have to be paid.
text:
Across the country, women make up about 61% of family caregivers.
(Photo by Halfpoint Images/Getty Stock photo)West Virginians know what it means to get up early, drive a long way to a job, work a second shift, care for a child or aging parent, go to school, volunteer in their community or keep working when they don’t feel their best because the bills still have to be paid. 
For many West Virginians, work isn’t an abstract political talking point. It is how they survive. That is why the new Medicaid work reporting requirements coming Jan. 1, 2027, deserve more than a debate about whether people should work. 
Under the new federal requirements, certain adults ages 19 to 64 enrolled in Medicaid expansion will generally need to complete 80 hours a month of work, education, job training or community service. 
Perhaps the U.S. House of Representatives needs work requirements. But I digress. 
On paper, 80 hours may sound straightforward. Real life isn’t. The people affected by these requirements are not numbers on a spreadsheet. They are people whose lives are already complicated. 
That’s something we’ve heard repeatedly through our work at West Virginians for Affordable Health Care and through our Echoes of Resilience storytelling project. When people talk about getting health care, they don’t talk about policy in isolation. They talk about the drive to the doctor’s office, missed hours at work, the cost of gas, who will watch the kids, whether they can afford to miss a shift and what happens when their health makes all those decisions harder. 
We learned during the Medicaid unwinding that paperwork matters. People can lose coverage not because they are ineligible, but because they don’t receive a notice, don’t understand what is being requested or simply can’t get the paperwork completed in time. We should not pretend that won’t happen again. 
If you or someone you love has Medicaid through the Adult Expansion Group, now is the time to understand what is coming. 
First, make sure your contact and household information are current with the state. Report changes in income, employment, household members, education, pregnancy or other circumstances through WV PATH. 
Second, know whether you qualify for an exclusion or exception. The rules are not one-size-fits-all. Certain pregnant people, parents and caregivers, people with significant health conditions or disabilities, some people in treatment or recovery, certain veterans, former foster youth and others may be excluded or exempt. 
If the requirement does apply to you, understand what can count. Paid work is not the only option. Education, job training, volunteer or community service, and certain unpaid or in-kind work can count. You may also meet the requirement through a combination of activities. For some people an income of at least $580 a month can satisfy the requirement, and seasonal workers may qualify based on their six-month average income. 
Keep records when appropriate, particularly if you are relying on unpaid or in-kind work or community service. Pay attention to your mail and WV PATH account. If the Department of Human Services asks for information, don’t ignore it. You generally have 30 days to respond. 
Most importantly, ask questions if you’re unsure. The West Virginia Medicaid Help website and Medicaid helpline at 1-877-716-1212 are available to help. 
The stories we’ve heard through Echoes of Resilience have reinforced something policymakers too often forget: people experience health policy in the context of their entire lives, not in the neat categories of a statute. 
Those stories don’t tell us that West Virginians don’t want to work. They tell us that work is only one part of a much bigger picture. A person can be working and still struggling. They can be working fewer hours because there simply aren’t more hours available. They can be providing unpaid care that never appears on a paycheck. 
And all of them can need health care. 
A mother working 60 hours one month and 90 the next is still working. A seasonal worker whose income fluctuates is still working. A caregiver whose labor doesn’t come with a paycheck is still contributing. A person dealing with a serious health condition may be fighting every day just to remain stable. 
And a person who misses a notice or cannot complete a form on time should not suddenly become less deserving of health care. Medicaid is not a reward for working. It is health coverage 
Health care should be a foundation people can stand on — not another obstacle they have to overcome.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: With Christie by his side, Bobby Charles distances himself from Trump
description: At a town hall in Lewiston joined by Chris Christie, Bobby Charles hopscotched across the Republican Party line. Campaigning with the former New Jersey governor 41 days before the Nov. 3 midterms, the GOP gubernatorial nominee broke with the Trump administration on several key issues affecting Maine, including tariffs and environmental policy, while echoing[...]
text:
Republican gubernatorial nominee Bobby Charles with former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie during a Sept. 23 town hall in Lewiston. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)At a town hall in Lewiston joined by Chris Christie, Bobby Charles hopscotched across the Republican Party line.
Campaigning with the former New Jersey governor 41 days before the Nov. 3 midterms, the GOP gubernatorial nominee broke with the Trump administration on several key issues affecting Maine, including tariffs and environmental policy, while echoing the president on others. 
He told the cheering crowd of 75 supporters that he wanted to dismantle Maine’s largest state agency, the Department of Health and Human Services. He blamed overdose deaths on syringe exchange programs and said he would get “socialism out of schools.” The latter stance is part of Charles’ pitch to rebuild the fraught relationship between Maine and White House, which has targeted the state since Gov. Janet Mills’ told President Donald Trump she’d see him in court over the state’s inclusive policies. 
“A governor can disagree with the president, but can repair the relationship with the federal government at large,” he said. “When we turn this state red, one of the things we get out of that is a rebuilding of the relationship together with an independent voice to confront the president.”
Republicans running for office across the country are distancing themselves from the president as his approval ratings have plummeted. In Maine, only 31% of voters approve and 63% disapprove of the way he is handling his job, according to Civiqs’ rolling tracker.  
Immigration
Charles struck a different tone on immigration on Wednesday. Having previously called state Rep. Deqa Dhalac (D-South Portland) a “radical Somalia-first” representative and saying he’d ask the Trump administration to send federal immigration agents to the polls, Charles was asked by a Bates student from New Jersey about the fear immigration enforcement has caused in Maine. 
In an apparent reference to the July killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford,
Charles said he was “mystified by why … we didn’t have body cameras on people.”
He also called himself pro-immigrant while advocating for balance, saying “this country was built on immigrants, but it was also built on respect for the Constitution and on respect for law.”
But Charles also blamed a recently enacted Maine law that restricts how local law enforcement agencies can cooperate with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, saying the limits on communication have led to bad outcomes.
“I think Bobby’s approach is absolutely right, he’s got to take both sides,” Christie said.  
“We cannot allow any leaders in this country to be telling us that immigrants are the problem,” Charles added. “Let’s make sure we protect people’s belief that if you come to this country and you work hard and you follow the law, that you can become anything. If we lose that, then we lose our identities as Americans.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Christie, who ran unsuccessfully for the Republican presidential nomination in 2016 and 2024 and later became an outspoken Trump critic, seemed to back Charles in that approach. Introducing Charles, he highlighted the nominee’s stance on Canadian tariffs as evidence that Charles would diverge from the party when he believes it benefits Maine.
“When he sees that something is happening that’s hurting Mainers, he stands up and he’s told the president … stop fighting with Canada,” Christie said.
“That’s the kind of governor you want. It’s not someone who’s going to pick on every little thing that happens in Washington, D.C. just to get themselves on TV, you want people who are going to focus their fire on the real problem.”
But while Charles and Christie emphasized places where the Republican nominee would break with Trump, their shared focus at the town hall was criticizing Mills and Democratic nominee 
Hannah Pingree. Several of Charles’ campaign promises involve rolling back policies and programs enacted during Mills’ two terms as governor.
“We are living in a state in which Governor Mills and Hannah Pingree together have driven every single major positive indicator down, and many of the negative indicators up,” he said.
Pingree, Charles and independent gubernatorial candidate Rick Bennett have all emphasized lowering costs, but Charles has focused on reducing property and income taxes as the solution.
Earlier this month, Charles’ sister, Anita Charles, endorsed Pingree. During a Sept. 9 press conference, the educator from Lewiston said her brother’s campaign was built on “denigrating others and targeting Mainers with mean-spirited rhetoric that aims to incite fear and hatred towards vulnerable groups.”
Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles with supporter Mary Leonas from Greene during a Sept. 23 town hall in Lewiston. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)
A focus on crime and drug use
Several supporters at the event said Charles’ positions on taxes and crime were among the reasons they backed him.
Mary Leonas, a Greene resident and former academic advisor at the University of Southern Maine, said she switched her party affiliation from Democrat to Republican a year ago. Leonas sat in the front row at Charles’ event and lined up to take a picture with him after. She appreciated Charles diverging from Trump on issues that impact Maine. 
“Nobody agrees totally with President Trump, there are some things that he does that are really questionable,” she said. “I appreciate that (Charles) thinks for himself.” 
In particular, his promise to reduce crime was one of the primary draws for her. 
While Maine continues to have one of the lowest rates of violent crime in the country, several Charles supporters said they are concerned about what they said was increasingly visible homelessness, crime and syringe waste on the streets of Lewiston, Portland and Bangor. 
Cracking down on drug use was also a major theme of Wednesday’s town hall. Charles praised Christie’s record of addressing opioid addiction while critiquing the expansion of syringe exchange programs in Maine. During Mills’ tenure, Maine shifted from a one-for-one syringe exchange model to one that allows syringe service programs to distribute up to 100 sterile syringes per participant per visit.
“How Orwellian is it that every single death in this state that occurs by injection drugs is probably occurring on a state-provided needle?” Charles asked while advocating for increased addiction services.
Research has found that syringe service programs reduce the spread of HIV and hepatitis C and do not increase illegal drug use or crime. But syringe litter has prompted some Maine communities to impose local restrictions. Sanford, for example, adopted a one-for-one exchange requirement in 2025 after city officials cited concerns about discarded syringes.
But Leonas said she believes Charles’ approach will limit syringe litter, which she said is a major concern in Lewiston.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: After Medicaid ban, Kentucky Planned Parenthood says it’s ‘not going anywhere’
description: “We're in Kentucky to stay. Planned Parenthood is not going anywhere.”
text:
Outside Planned Parenthood's Louisville Health Center on Sept. 18, 2025. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)LOUISVILLE — On the heels of a year-long Medicaid ban, Planned Parenthood officials say they are eyeing the midterms in November, which they believe could be a deciding factor in future funding stability. 
Jennifer Allen, the CEO of Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates and a policy expert with the organization, told the Kentucky Lantern Wednesday during a sit-down interview at the Louisville Health Center that keeping services available during the ban “stretched us.”  
During the year it was in effect, Rebecca Gibron, the CEO of Planned Parenthood’s largest geographic affiliate of health centers that includes Kentucky, said centers saw an increase in self pay as well as a “small decrease in our patients.” 
Jennifer M. Allen (left), the CEO of Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates, and Rebecca Gibron (right),the CEO of Planned Parenthood’s largest geographic affiliate of health centers that includes Kentucky, pose in the Louisville Health Center. Sept. 18, 2025. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)
The ban expired in July, meaning Kentuckians can once again use Medicaid at Planned Parenthood locations, which offer birth control services, HIV tests, pregnancy testing, prenatal and postpartum care, STD treatment and more. But Allen and Gibron said this isn’t the end of potential threats to funding. 
“Politically, we think it’s very calculated that that ban on Medicaid was allowed to expire and hasn’t been re-instituted yet, and that some other pieces of the ‘big bad bill’ that was passed at the federal level are still to come after the midterms,” Allen said. “We think it’s very calculated. Politicians know that it is not popular to attack Planned Parenthood and to attack reproductive health care, and so they’re waiting. They’re waiting until after this election cycle, and then …. we absolutely think that attack and others could be coming on people’s access to reproductive health.” 
Because of that, the organization is “working really hard,” said Allen, to “make sure that champions for reproductive health care get elected.” 
“It’s not going to change who’s sitting in the president’s chair,” she said, “but it can help with … stemming the tide of these kinds of attacks.” 
In Kentucky, the organization has its longest list of candidate endorsements yet, according to Tamarra Weider, Kentucky’s state director of Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates. 
“We are out on the doors. We are talking to people,” she said. “We’ve already hit almost 1,000 doors.” 
If future funding bans come down, Gibron said, “it will be a significant blow to the organization; It will be a significant blow to our patients.”  
Still, she said: “We’re in Kentucky to stay. Planned Parenthood is not going anywhere.” 
Looking to 2027 
Tamarra Weider,of Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates, speaks after Kentuckians defeated an anti-abortion constitutional amendment, Nov. 8, 2022. (Kentucky phot9 by Arden Barnes)
Planned Parenthood is planning to push for legislation in the 2027 General Assembly that would make Medicaid pay for sexually transmitted infections testing. 
“You can come in, and if you have symptoms or believe you’ve been exposed, they will charge you for the tests,” Weider said. “So we’re trying to get rid of the Medicaid test expense for that, and so we have a bill to make it more accessible for treatment and the testing. We’re really excited because it feels like common sense legislation that if you are showing symptoms, that you shouldn’t have to fight with insurance to get those tests.” 
She’s also planning to promote a bill to make it easier for Kentuckians to access hormone replacement therapy treatments for perimenopause and menopause symptoms.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Bring transparency back to Colorado courtrooms
description: Colorado law says state criminal courts must offer livestreams of their proceedings, but the state’s top judge has little use for that mandate. Citing abuse of the livestream feature, Monica Márquez, the chief justice of the Colorado Supreme Court, last week ordered a 90-day pause on the requirement that courts livestream their proceedings. It was […]
text:
Former Colorado Supreme Court Chief Justice Brian Boatright swears in Chief Justice Monica Márquez in a private ceremony July 26, 2024. (Colorado Judicial Branch)Colorado law says state criminal courts must offer livestreams of their proceedings, but the state’s top judge has little use for that mandate.
Citing abuse of the livestream feature, Monica Márquez, the chief justice of the Colorado Supreme Court, last week ordered a 90-day pause on the requirement that courts livestream their proceedings. It was a sweeping, unilateral elimination of transparency, which was especially alarming given that the activities at issue involve the awesome power of the state to deprive residents of their liberty.
Márquez’s very authority to take the action is uncertain. The law describes various circumstances under which a court might be exempted from the livestreaming mandate, but those circumstances are supposed to be evaluated on a case-by-case basis, not as part of a blanket directive to every court. The law explicitly says its livestream requirements “supersede any … judicial guidance, or chief justice directive limiting remote public observation of criminal courts.”
Márquez appears to acknowledge her own act of pulling rank in brushing aside the Legislature when in her directive she protests that the state constitution gives her “superintending” control of Colorado courts. In other words, “You think state laws will stop me? Go ahead and try.” Her directive could be legally challenged, but the case likely would end up before Márquez’s court, and the outcome’s not hard to foresee.
So what about the problem that prompted the pause?
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
It’s real. Viewers are strictly forbidden to record livestream audio or visuals. But unscrupulous users have repeatedly violated that rule, and they regularly post recordings to social media.
“The livestreaming technology that was intended to promote access to the courts has been subverted as a tool of disruption, disparagement, harassment, and private economic gain that is rapidly eroding the proper functioning of our system of justice,” Márquez wrote.  
Participants in legal proceedings are due fairness and safety. Illegally recorded hearings have included derogatory comments about participants, threats and other conduct that would never be permitted in person. 
“I cannot overstate the negative effects of this activity on our courts over the past two years,” Márquez wrote. “Hearings and trials have been thrown into disarray, delaying routine processes and preventing the efficient administration of our system of justice.”
That’s unacceptable, and a solution is necessary.
Jeff Roberts, executive director of the nonprofit Colorado Freedom of Information Coalition, has some ideas. He notes that Colorado district courts already offer permission-granted access to case filings in civil and other matters through the judicial branch’s Remote Public Access Terminal. Members of the public can request access by signing a user agreement and providing basic biographical information, such as name, email and phone number. 
“What about having something similar for this?” Roberts asked.
Such a system to grant access to court livestreams likely wouldn’t eliminate misuse, but it could significantly deter it. 
In her directive, Márquez said the judicial department needs time to consider better ways to manage online access, and she invited input from other “stakeholders.” Roberts wants in.
“We would like to be part of the conversation over the next 90 days to try to work out a solution,” he said, adding, “We’re not discounting the fact that there’s a problem, and that we want to find a solution to that problem.”
He wouldn’t be surprised to see legislators revisit state law around livestreamed court proceedings when they reconvene in January.
Open courts are among the features that characterize a free society. 
“It is the public policy of the state of Colorado to maximize transparency and accessibility of criminal court proceedings,” says the bill that established the livestream requirement. “All Coloradans benefit from consistent, predictable access to observe criminal court proceedings remotely.”
This is all the more important as the number of Colorado reporters, who often serve as the public’s eyes and ears in the courtroom, dwindles. Remote access helps ensure shrinking newsrooms can inform communities about cases they care about.
“This is a really important tool for making sure there are more eyes on the judicial system, and to make sure that the courts get adequately covered by journalists, because it’s so difficult these days for overloaded journalists to cover everything they need to cover,” Roberts said.
Márquez says she’s committed to providing public access to Colorado courts. The next several months will be a test of that commitment.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Republican veteran Tony Sabio is on a ‘mission’ to win Va.’s most Democratic US House seat
description: Tony Sabio — a security expert who served in the U.S. military, Secret Service and CIA — has an uphill objective this November: the Republican nominee is working to unseat a six-term Democratic incumbent and represent Virginia’s reliably blue 8th Congressional District. Sabio is drawing on his extensive background in national security and geopolitics to […]
text:
Republican Tony Sabio is  vying to replace Democratic incumbent U.S. Rep. Don Beyer in Virginia's 8th Congressional District race. (Photo courtesy of campaign)Tony Sabio — a security expert who served in the U.S. military, Secret Service and CIA — has an uphill objective this November: the Republican nominee is working to unseat a six-term Democratic incumbent and represent Virginia’s reliably blue 8th Congressional District.
Sabio is drawing on his extensive background in national security and geopolitics to challenge longtime U.S. Rep. Don Beyer, D-Alexandria, in a region home to the Pentagon and the country’s largest defense contractors.
The pragmatic Lorton resident, who also just wrapped up a short tenure budgeting capital projects as Purcellville’s interim Town Manager, is attempting to appeal to “all Americans” with “common sense” stances.
Beyer criticizes ‘Republican price tag’ ahead of November midterm elections

“Everything I’ve done has been focused on solving issues,” Sabio said in a wide-ranging interview with  The Mercury. “It was never about myself. It was always about ‘what can we do to solve these issues to accomplish the mission. That’s the same thing I’d bring to Congress. I am mission focused.”
Sabio is attempting to beat Beyer, who has not won an election by less than 70% since 2014, with a constituency that deeply disapproves of President Donald Trump, whom the GOP nominee aligns with on most issues. 
 A long resume in security 

As a counterintelligence and counterterrorism officer in the United States Central Intelligence Agency, Sabio’s job was to “locate and dismantle terrorist organizations” everywhere from Afghanistan and Iraq to South America. 
Now, Sabio continues that work by operating his own security consultancy in the Rockfinn Group. He collaborates with corporations and other clients to develop security plans and enact overseas safety missions. 
He named ABC News as a prominent partner, for whom he develops plans to rescue news correspondents when they are stuck overseas. He developed gear to help their camera crew be more mobile while documenting war in Ukraine. 
“It’s not politics. It’s not right side, left side. They’re all Americans,” Sabio said. “Taking care of people is something I have a passion for,” he continued. 
Tony Sabio, who is running as Republican to represent Virginia’s 8th Congressional District, is a security expert who served in the U.S. military, Secret Service and CIA. (Photo courtesy campaign)
Sometimes Sabio is the man with the plan, and other times he embarks on extraction missions himself. 
He drew attention in 2022 for rescuing a 15-year-old boy from Ukraine at the start of the country’s ongoing war with Russia. Sabio told People Magazine at the time that declining the mission “just wasn’t an option,” despite the dangers. 
After the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks on Israel, Sabio conducted a ground operation in Gaza to identify the locations of Israeli hostages taken by the Palestinian militant group and political party Hamas. He would not say which client sponsored the mission. 
“We were going in the streets and just identifying possible areas, we were talking with people, getting intel where these hostages were being kept at and gathering a ground network of intelligence,” Sabio recalled. 
Sabio hopes the voters of Arlington, Alexandria and parts of Fairfax County will recognize his foreign relations experience at the ballot box this November. 
 Sabio’s ‘Promise for America’ entails nuclear energy, private sector expansion

Sabio’s list of “ready-to-go” policy proposals revolve around his vision to transform the economy of Northern Virginia to be less reliant on the federal government and more centered around private sector manufacturing. 
“So when the federal government plays its games and shuts down, it doesn’t affect Northern Virginia as hard,” Sabio said.
Sabio hopes to alleviate rising energy costs by integrating nuclear energy within the regional economy, particularly by producing small modular reactors to power data centers. Northern Virginia is home to the densest cluster of data centers in the world.
Beyer, who is asking voters to elect him to a seventh term in Congress, has also advocated for nuclear energy production, and previously called himself a top “champion” on the Hill for bringing fusion energy to Virginia.
Sabio said his plan is “more robust” than Beyer’s, in that he would make Virginia one of a handful of designated “nuclear grid nodes” that would export to the rest of the country. 
Other pillars of Sabio’s policy framework include creating tax incentives for small business owners, increasing funding to law enforcement agencies — including immigration enforcement — and reforming healthcare to retain the “good parts of Medicare for All” while maintaining free market competition. 
Sabio said safety nets for people with preexisting conditions should be preserved. But he does not want to force American families into a “one-size-fits-all” Medicare plan. 
 To win, Sabio must overcome rising costs, DOGE grief 

Voters focused the district’s Democratic primary in August on the rising cost of living and sweeping federal layoffs initiated by Trump and tech billionaire Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency — both issues Beyer’s campaign has addressed head on.  
Sabio said he is “80-90% in agreement” with the Trump Administration’s policies. 
Asked of how he would win over voters frustrated with Trump, some of whom are former federal workers experiencing months-long waits for their pensions to process, Sabio reiterated his idea of creating a larger, “more sustainable” private sector job ecosystem. 
“Like right now, as a federal worker, you’re gonna get your money back,” Sabio said. “You may be sitting at home for 60 days. It’s gonna be stressful. You’re gonna tighten up the belt, because you’re gonna pay for your essentials, your mortgage, your electric bill, and so on. But you’re not gonna go out. You’re not gonna do all the small things that you normally would do. Not until you’re done being furloughed, and the checks are coming back in.”
Sabio is concerned about the small businesses that rely on revenue coming in from federal workers that have to shut down when the job market takes a hit. 
Beyer “says a lot of things,” but has failed to deliver on promises to constituents, according to Sabio.
“Its all playing upon politics. It depends upon what his party wants. Nothing he does is for Northern Virginia,” he added. “We have a Congress that has lost the ability to understand that they work for the people, not the other way around.” 
A spokesperson for Beyer declined to comment. 
Early voting is underway and Election Day is Nov. 3. Read The Mercury’s voter guide to learn more about the congressional candidates and stakes of the races. Take our reader survey to share the issues that will motivate you to vote this fall and inform our elections reporting.

title: Federal judge strikes down SNAP deadline that put Virginia at risk of added costs
description: Virginia and other states cannot be penalized under a Trump administration deadline that gave them too little time to put new federal food assistance rules into effect, a federal judge in Oregon has ruled.  The decision also rejects federal guidance that would have denied benefits to some lawful permanent residents, including people who previously entered […[...]
text:
Canned foods line grocery store shelves. A federal judge has struck down Trump administration SNAP guidance that threatened penalties for Virginia and other states. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Virginia and other states cannot be penalized under a Trump administration deadline that gave them too little time to put new federal food assistance rules into effect, a federal judge in Oregon has ruled. 
The decision also rejects federal guidance that would have denied benefits to some lawful permanent residents, including people who previously entered the country as refugees or were granted asylum. 
The Sept. 17 ruling resolves a lawsuit brought by a coalition of 22 states, co-led by Oregon and New York. Virginia joined the case in January, after the court had issued a preliminary injunction in December. 
For Virginia, the decision removes a potential source of added costs as state and local agencies work through changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. 
It does not undo the changes Congress made to the program in its 2025 tax and spending law H.R. 1, including a provision requiring states with higher payment error rates to cover part of the cost of benefits beginning in fiscal 2028. 
Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones welcomed the decision in a statement Wednesday, describing access to food assistance as a priority for his office. 
“Virginians are already stretching paychecks as far as they can,” Jones said. “We will not stop fighting for the programs and agencies created to support our most vulnerable Virginians.”
Jones’ office announced Virginia’s joining the lawsuit in February, following a review of existing litigation after he took office in January. 
At the center of the case was a 120-day grace period intended to give states time to put new SNAP rules in place without mistakes counting against their payment error rates. 
The U.S. Department of Agriculture treated that period as beginning July 4, 2025, the day the law was enacted. But according to the court ruling, the agency did not issue its first implementation guidance until Aug. 29 that year and waited until Oct. 31 to tell states how to handle changes to noncitizen eligibility. 
That left states just one day under USDA’s timeline to make those eligibility changes. A later memo, issued Nov. 14, told them the grace period had already expired. 
U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai rejected that approach, finding that states could not reasonably be expected to implement federal changes before USDA told them how to do it. 
The agency’s position “unfairly exposes Plaintiffs to financially ruinous penalties,” Kasubhai wrote. 
He vacated the deadline in USDA’s guidance and ordered the agency to give states 120 days after issuing an implementation memo, along with adequate notice of when changes must be made. 
For most states, those deadlines carry potentially significant financial consequences. 
Payment errors can include benefits issued to ineligible households as well as overpayments or underpayments to people who qualify. Under the 2025 law, a state’s error rate can determine how much it must contribute toward SNAP benefits in future years. 
Virginia’s SNAP error rate was around 11% as of January of this year, and the state’s SNAP Forward initiative is designed to reduce it to 6% or less to comply with the new federal standards.  
States argued that counting mistakes made while they were still waiting for federal instructions could drive up those costs. Kasubhai found USDA’s approach particularly difficult to square with the agency’s own timing, noting that it took months to issue some of the guidance states needed.  
The ruling also settles a dispute over which noncitizens remain eligible for SNAP. 
The 2025 law includes lawful permanent residents among those who may qualify, but USDA’s guidance excluded some people who had gained that status after entering the country as refugees or seeking asylum. 
Kasubhai found that their previous immigration status does not disqualify them. He also ruled that those lawful permanent residents are exempt from the usual five-year waiting period for SNAP benefits.
USDA later issued an explanation consistent with the states’ interpretation, but continued defending its earlier guidance in court. Kasubhai found the dispute was therefore not moot and formally declared that lawful permanent residents are eligible regardless of their prior status. 
The court fight unfolded as states prepared for a much larger shift in how SNAP is funded and administered. 
The 2025 reconciliation bill changed eligibility requirements and shifted more of the program’s costs to the states. Earlier this year, Virginia lawmakers set aside $135 million in the state budget to prepare for a possible SNAP cost share if the state cannot lower its payment error rate to the required level. 
About 740,000 Virginians received SNAP benefits in July, the latest month for which the state has published a participation report.
Gov. Abigail Spanberger directed state agencies in August to help eligible Virginians retain food and health benefits as the federal changes take effect. The work includes explaining new requirements to recipients and trying to prevent eligible people from losing assistance because of missed paperwork or confusion over the new rules.
The Oregon case is not Virginia’s only legal fight with the USDA.
The commonwealth is part of a separate challenge to federal conditions on funding SNAP and other programs. In June, a judge temporarily blocked conditions concerning diversity programs, gender identity and benefits for undocumented immigrants while that case proceeds.

title: Southern faculty voice fears over political interference, academic freedom erosion in annual survey
description: Most faculty members from Virginia and Southern states say they would not recommend their state as a desirable place to work, citing concerns about political interference and academic freedom, according to a recent survey by state conferences of the American Association of University Professors. The responses come from AAUP’s annual Faculty in the South surv[...]
text:
Tim Gibson, vice president of the George Mason University chapter of the American Association of University Professors, said Southern university faculty want "affordable public universities where the money goes to the classroom, not the administrative suite" after the recent release of AAUP's annual Faculty in the South survey. Gibson is seen here addressing a crowd outside the GMU Board of Visitors meeting on Aug. 1, 2025. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Most faculty members from Virginia and Southern states say they would not recommend their state as a desirable place to work, citing concerns about political interference and academic freedom, according to a recent survey by state conferences of the American Association of University Professors.
The responses come from AAUP’s annual Faculty in the South survey, which asks professors in selected states about their jobs. In the survey, 59.4% of faculty members said they would not recommend their state as a desirable place to work for graduate students or other colleagues, up 5% from last year’s results. 
Here are key takeaways from the survey’s results. 
 Advocates say university workers deserve to unionize

Virginia faculty leaders, including Bethany Letiecq, president of the Virginia Conference of the AAUP, say one way to improve faculty recruitment and retention is for Virginia lawmakers to allow collective bargaining for public workers, which lets employees negotiate with their employer over issues such as wages, benefits and working conditions.
“The only thing that professors and other university workers want is the right to choose to collectively bargain,” said Letiecq. “This is a freedom enjoyed by every single private sector worker in Virginia. We just want the same rights as everybody else.”
Efforts to repeal the 1946 Jim Crow-era law that denies state workers the right to unionize were vetoed by Gov. Abigail Spanberger in May.
‘This is about equity’: In Richmond, Va. workers, lawmakers push for inclusive labor rights for all

In Virginia, faculty organizations are also concerned about rising costs, which they say stem from leadership hiring “high-paid” administrators. That concern leads them to argue for unionization as a way to address wasteful spending.  
“If professors and other campus workers were allowed to organize into unions, you can bet your life that we will try to put an end to this wasteful bloat and overspending,” said Tim Gibson, president of the George Mason University AAUP chapter. “We want what Virginia families want: affordable public universities where the money goes to the classroom, not the administrative suite.”
Jim Finkelstein, a retired professor of political science, said advisory groups like faculty senates lack legal weight. He said collective bargaining is essential to give workers a formal, legally protected voice in their institutions.
“If Virginia wants to recruit and retain outstanding faculty and staff, it cannot focus only on what it pays them,” Finkelstein said. “It also has to pay attention to whether they have a meaningful voice in the institutions where they work. Collective bargaining provides that voice.”
 Faculty name concerns about government intrusion, with many uncertain if they will remain in the field

New to the survey this year was a question about artificial intelligence, which has raised questions about privacy and security.
A total of 85% of respondents said yes, they believed their academic discipline would survive in an AI era. AAUP did not ask faculty to identify their academic discipline.
Faculty also fear government intrusion into the curriculum and the future of college faculty in the South. The AAUP survey found a 6% increase in administrators questioning faculty’s curriculum and a 10.6% increase in faculty saying the Trump administration ended their federal contract.
Those concerns come alongside broader signs of uncertainty in the field. A total of 19.1% of faculty surveyed said they did not plan to remain in academia long-term, and 30% plan to apply to other higher-education jobs in the coming year, a 25% increase from last year.
Virginia was not among the states receiving the most faculty applications, according to the survey. States that received the most applications included California, Colorado, Illinois, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, and Pennsylvania.
 Feedback on proposed accreditation shift 

The survey also asked about accreditation, which holds institutions accountable to standards for academic resources, student support, and financial and administrative practices.
Faculty surveyed were asked about a new accreditor that closely resembles the Commission for Public Higher Education, and nearly three-quarters opposed their institution using it.
CPHE is a new accrediting organization established in 2025 by six public university systems to create an accreditation model for public universities, emphasizing student outcomes, academic quality, and more efficient accreditation. 
The proposal is uncommon because accreditation in the United States is typically conducted by independent organizations that serve institutions in particular regions or nationally. CPHE is proposing an accreditor whose founding institutions are public university systems.
The survey did not name CPHE when it described the new, unnamed accreditation group seeking federal approval, noting that both were created by public university systems in several Southern states and that the board included top employees from those systems.
Some faculty organizations say they are concerned about the CPHE proposal because it originated with state university systems and emerged amid political conflicts over higher education. 
Critics also say the new accreditor could give government-controlled university systems greater influence over the accreditation process.
