name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia Democrats are bullish on chances of flipping state House this year, but it won’t be easy
description: Georgia House Democrats say 2026 is the year they’re going to take control of the state House, ending more than two decades of Republican rule. “We are 10 winnable seats away from a majority for the first time since 2004.” said House Minority Leader Carolyn Hugley of Columbus during a press conference Wednesday. “The state […]
text:
Georgia House Minority Leader Carolyn Hugley says her party will win control of the state House after November's election. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderGeorgia House Democrats say 2026 is the year they’re going to take control of the state House, ending more than two decades of Republican rule.
“We are 10 winnable seats away from a majority for the first time since 2004.” said House Minority Leader Carolyn Hugley of Columbus during a press conference Wednesday. “The state House decides what happens to Georgia families on the issues that matter most: property taxes, how schools are funded, whether their votes are protected.”
Republicans say they’re not worried.
“I’m pretty sure they said the same thing in 2024, 2022 and 2020,” said Carmen Bergman, director of the Georgia House Republican Caucus. “We’ve heard this line before. We feel very confident about our ability to not just keep the majority, but grow the majority.”
Democrats picked up 11 seats in 2018, when frustration with the first Trump administration led to higher Democratic turnout and organization. Party leaders say the nation is in a similar mood and that population growth has made Georgia younger and more diverse.
Hugley’s confidence also comes from a new report from Democratic pollster Z to A Research.
Pollsters talked to Georgians in 13 highly competitive legislative districts and found that, after respondents were given a description of each candidate and “heard the case against” the Republican candidate, the Democratic candidate finished ahead in 12 of the 13 races.
Before hearing the information, Democrats only won one of the districts.
Rep. Farooq Mughal. 2023 file photo. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Democrats control 81 seats in the 180-member chamber, which means a gain of ten members would put them in the majority, allowing them to elect leaders like speaker and committee chairs and set the agenda for the upcoming legislative session.
The party in charge also leads the usually once-a-decade effort to revise legislative maps, which means many districts are drawn to be safe for either party. That’s why even if statewide Democratic candidates like U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff win more than 50% of the vote in Georgia, Republicans – who drew the current political maps – could continue to dominate the Legislature.
Nonpartisan political observers aren’t convinced that Georgia’s House chamber is in play, though. The University of Virginia’s Center for Politics, for example, acknowledged Georgia Democrats’ optimism after winning a pair of seats on a state regulatory board last year. But the center still classified both chambers of Georgia’s Legislature as “likely Republican” earlier this year.
The national party may also still need convincing. Will Rusche, vice president of marketing and communications at the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, which seeks to elect Democrats to state legislatures, said his organization is targeting 500 seats in 27 states, including Georgia, but he declined to say how much the committee is spending in Georgia.
“Right now we’re kind of in the phase in the last few weeks before the election of tracking this polling information, figuring out where resources in the final week are going to be spent, and I think it is a fluid situation,” he said. “We’re going to keep an eye on things.”
Democrats see their best shot at flipping seats in the north Atlanta suburbs 
The first step on what Democrats call their path to taking the House includes four Republican districts in northern metro Atlanta won by Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

Buford Republican state Rep. Sandy Donatucci, who narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Farooq Mughal by just 80 votes in 2024 and is now facing a rematch with Mughal.
Republican state Rep. Matt Reeves of Duluth, who was first elected in 2022 and narrowly won re-election in 2024, defeating Democrat Michelle Kang, who leads a nonprofit, by 621 votes out of more than 29,000. Kang is running for the seat again.
Sandy Springs Republican state Rep. Deborah Silcox, who won by more than 1,300 votes in 2024, but Harris took 53% of the vote in that election. Democrat Beth Fuller, a former contractor with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, is hoping to take her down this year.
Peachtree Corners Republican state Rep. Scott Hilton, who outperformed President Donald Trump in 2024, taking nearly 55% of the vote in a district where Harris won 50.6%. He’s facing Democrat Adam Cleveland, an attorney.

Longer shot opportunities
State Rep. Don Parsons. 2025 file photo. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
The other six seats Democrats say will bring them to the majority are likely to be significantly tougher. Each of the Republican incumbents won by around 15% in 2024, but Democrats say their new polling predicts they are flippable.

District 44 in Cobb County where Republican state Rep. Don Parsons of Marietta faces Democrat Danielle Bell, a healthcare advocate.
District 34 in Cobb County where Republican state Rep. Devan Seabaugh of Marietta faces Democrat Titus Nichols, an attorney and Army Reserve officer.
District 19 in Cobb and Paulding counties where state Rep. Joseph Gullett of Dallas faces Democrat and educator Cynthia Starke-Jones.
District 147 in Houston and Peach counties where Republican state Rep. Bethany Ballard of Warner Robbins faces Democrat Renita Duncan, a retired U.S. Army command sergeant major and federal worker.
District 81 in Henry County where Republican state Rep. Noelle Kahaian of Locust Grove faces Democrat Mishael White, a commercial truck driver.
District 45 in Cobb County where Republican state Rep. Sharon Cooper of Marietta faces Democrat Michelle Schreiner, a psychologist.

Lauren Groh-Wargo, CEO of left-leaning voting rights organization Fair Fight Action, said Democrats have some wiggle room if some of these races don’t go their way. She said at least 10 other districts appeared promising in Democratic polls or saw a strong performance by Harris in 2024.
“These six, were we to win them, would bring us a majority, but we have room to miss,” she said. “We have additional seats that are competitive.”
Republicans planning their own flips
Rep. Eric Gisler. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Bergman with the House Republican caucus said the Georgia GOP will not rest on its laurels this November.
Even if voters are frustrated with Republicans at the federal level, Georgians largely report satisfaction with the party at the state level, she said.
“Voters are smarter than I think some politicos give them credit for,” she said. “They can separate out different levels of government, different levels of responsibility and will take action in the voting booth to support the good common sense governance they’re seeing at the state level.”
Bergman said several Democratic seats are ripe to be flipped, starting with Democratic state Rep. Eric Gisler of Watkinsville, who won his seat in a special election last year in a conservative district after the previous representative stepped down. Gisler defeated Republican Mack “Dutch” Guest, who works for his family trucking business, by around 200 votes.
Republicans blamed the loss on an off-year election during a time when Democrats were more motivated to vote, and Guest is set to face off against Gisler once more this year. Democrats’ new polling shows the race tied.
Bergman said Republicans are eying other Democrat-held seats including:


Rep. Mack Jackson. 2023 file photo. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
District 128, represented by Democratic state Rep. Mack Jackson of Sandersville, who is not running for re-election. Jackson won by just 48 votes in 2024. Democrat Tyrone Evans, a certified public accountant, will face Republican Trey Sheppard, co-owner of a family-owned shipping business.
District 145 in Bibb and Houston counties, where Democratic state Rep. Tangie Herring won by just 273 votes in 2024. Former Forsyth Mayor Eric Wilson, a Republican, is challenging Herring.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio’s 2026 governor race: Where the candidates stand on fracking
description: Ohio’s candidates for governor differ greatly when it comes to fracking in the state.  Ohio Democratic candidate Dr. Amy Acton recently announced she would impose a “three-year moratorium on issuing additional permits for the drilling of wastewater injection wells and on the further injection of fracking wastewater in Washington County while the state conduc[...]
text:
Ohio Democratic governor candidate Amy Acton, left. (Campaign photo). Ohio Republican governor candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, right. (Getty Images.)Ohio’s candidates for governor differ greatly when it comes to fracking in the state. 
Ohio Democratic candidate Dr. Amy Acton recently announced she would impose a “three-year moratorium on issuing additional permits for the drilling of wastewater injection wells and on the further injection of fracking wastewater in Washington County while the state conducts a thorough investigation on the impacts of wastewater migration.”
Ohio Libertarian candidate Don Kissick also supports a temporary pause on more wastewater injection activity in Washington County while the state conducts an investigation. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“That should include aggressive groundwater and drinking-water monitoring, transparency around migration data, and accountability when an operator causes contamination or damage,” Kissick’s running mate James Mills said in an email. 
“Washington County residents should not have to choose between supporting an important local industry and confidence in the safety of their drinking water.” 
Washington County residents have been raising concerns that injection wells leaking brine waste could contaminate Marietta’s drinking water. Fracking is the process of injecting liquid into the ground at a high pressure to extract oil or gas.
“To take a break and have a study done is in the interest of everybody in this county, not Democrats, not Republicans, everyone alike, and so it’s a bipartisan issue down here, and it’s a reasonable ask,” said Marietta City Council President Susan Vessels. 
“We’re asking for the simple rule: don’t allow oil field waste injection near public drinking water aquifers. So that should be simple.”
Bob Wilson, an oil producer in Washington County stands in front of one of his production wells. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).
Vessels, who is a Republican, endorsed Acton. 
“It’s very encouraging that her campaign heard about this problem, and studied it, and then thought that it was something that they could help with,” she said. 
In making her announcement, Acton said that in Washington County, injection wells are leaking fracking wastewater, flooding conventional oil and gas wells, leaving folks without heat, destroying local businesses, and potentially contaminating Marietta’s drinking water.
“This poses a serious threat to the safety and quality of life of Washington County residents,” Acton said. “That is why I support imposing a three-year moratorium on issuing additional permits for the drilling of wastewater injection wells and on the further injection of fracking wastewater in Washington County while the state conducts a thorough investigation on the impacts of wastewater migration.”
She said Ohioans deserve reliable heat, clean water, and to feel safe and secure in their community.
“I will always put the health and safety of Ohio families and communities above corporations and special interests,” she said.
Ohio Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign did not respond to questions sent by the Ohio Capital Journal. He has consistently expressed his support for oil and gas extraction in the past.
“Yeah, this isn’t that complicated, guys. Unlock American energy, drill, frack, burn coal, embrace nuclear,” he said during a 2024 Presidential debate.
While Ramaswamy has declined to respond to the Capital Journal and other local Ohio media about the issues of fracking and fracking waste injection, his campaign did provide comment to the New York Times on Acton’s proposal.
“A campaign spokesman for Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy said Dr. Acton’s position is ‘hollow and can’t withstand scrutiny,'” the Times reported.
Washington County has 17 injection wells with permits to inject, but only six are active, Vessels said. 
‘The precipice of an emergency.’ Marietta residents worry drinking water could become contaminated.

Ohio Oil and Gas Association President Rob Brundrett said a moratorium is not a solution. 
“Science, facts, and sound regulation, not politics and campaign rhetoric, are what will ensure both safe operations and a strong future for Ohio’s oil and natural gas industry,” he said in a statement. 
“The path forward is to allow Ohio’s regulatory process to work as designed while protecting the conventional production and supporting infrastructure that provide significant benefits to communities across our state.”
Acton wants to end fracking under Ohio’s state parks and wildlife areas according to her campaign, while Ramaswamy said it was “good news” when the state approved to frack more than 15,000 acres of Ohio’s public land over the summer. 
“Energy abundance is the foundation of a manufacturing boom in Ohio,” he said in a June 30 post on X. “We have unparalleled natural resources & now it’s time to get the red tape out of the way.”
Ohio law allows the Ohio Department of Natural Resources to lease Ohio state parks and public lands for fracking. 
Since this law took effect in 2023, fracking has been approved in Salt Fork State Park in Guernsey County, Egypt Valley Wildlife Area in Belmont and Guernsey counties, Jockey Hollow Wildlife Area in Harrison County, Leesville Wildlife Area in Carroll County, and Keen Wildlife Area in Harrison County. 
Ohio law requires at least 30% of the money goes towards improvements at the state parks where drilling is happening. 
“It’s great for nature. It’s great for our ability to enjoy our natural gifts, enjoy our state parks, while also enjoying the fruits of the natural resources that are underneath them,” Ramaswamy said in a June 7 video posted to Facebook.  
Kissick opposes fracking in state parks. 
“They belong to the people of Ohio, and the short-term revenue from extraction does not fully account for the value of preserving an irreplaceable public asset for future generations,” Mills said in an email.
Kissick is in favor of fracking on private property “where property rights are respected and strong environmental and safety standards are met,” Mills said in an email.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wolf delisting in Wisconsin: Why Tom Tiffany has been a hindrance and not helpful.
description: While gray wolves in Wisconsin and the Great Lakes region have been considered recovered by the federal government since the early 2000s, wolves currently continue to be listed as endangered in Wisconsin and Michigan, and threatened in Minnesota.  Delisting was intended to give states and tribes flexibility to manage wolf populations when wolves are no […]
text:
A gray wolf (Getty Images).While gray wolves in Wisconsin and the Great Lakes region have been considered recovered by the federal government since the early 2000s, wolves currently continue to be listed as endangered in Wisconsin and Michigan, and threatened in Minnesota.  Delisting was intended to give states and tribes flexibility to manage wolf populations when wolves are no longer at risk of extinction. There has been a complicated history of delisting and relisting in the Great Lakes region, between 2007 –2022.  Each time the federal government attempted to delist wolves in the region, some group opposing delisting has filed lawsuits and managed to get wolves relisted as endangered (or threatened in Minnesota).
Tom Tiffany, as a member of the Wisconsin Assembly, the state Senate, , and as a member of Congress, has been an especially vocal supporter of  intense management of the state wolf population, and has attempted to delist wolves through congressional action. But Tiffany’s own rhetoric, exaggerations and misleading comments have not been useful at attaining delisting, and may have emboldened efforts to challenge such delistings through the courts.
As an Assembly member, Tiffany helped co-author a wolf hunting bill in 2012 that forced DNR to hold a wolf hunting and trapping season whenever wolves were not listed as threatened or endangered.  Unlike most hunting seasons that allowed DNR broad authority to regulate the harvest, the legislated wolf hunting season represented a major political overreach, which may have been a factor that resulted in wolves being relisted at the end of 2014.
In 2018, as a state senator, Tiffany attempted to defund wolf conservation in Wisconsin until federal delisting occurred.  Such defunding would have made it difficult to determine wolf abundance and the sound scientific management of the wolf population to allow delisting to occur. Luckily the bill to defund wolf conservation did not pass.
Tiffany has frequently made false claims about wolf attacks on people, exploding wolf population, and exploding rates of depredations on pets and livestock.  No wolf attack on humans has been documented in Wisconsin, and Tiffany’s references to attacks are cases of wolves losing fear of people and displaying bold behavior, but none have resulted in physical attacks on people. Depredations on pets and livestock peaked in Wisconsin in 2010, and have declined since then.  Most years less than 10% of state wolf packs attack pets or livestock, and wolf depredation represents much less than 1% of all the things that kill cattle in Wisconsin.  The wolf population in Wisconsin has mostly stabilized at 1,000-1,200 wolves since 2018, and is not increasing exponentially as often suggested by Tiffany
In the U.S. Congress, Tiffany has tried in two bills to attempt nationwide gray wolf delisting.  The bills included “Trust the Science Act” and “Pet and Livestock Protection Act.” Neither bill has succeeded thus far.  In support of these bills, Tiffany has insisted the Wisconsin DNR is very capable of managing the state wolf population.  But at an open house event in Wisconsin, after running for governor, he called the state wolf plan passed by the Wisconsin DNR “not a wolf management plan” and an “impediment to management of the wolf.”  Tiffany totally rejects the carefully crafted and science-informed wolf plan developed by the Wisconsin DNR over a three-year period and approved in 2023.  Tiffany has implied that major reductions are needed to reduce wolves to 350 or 500 wolves.  This would require very intense controls and eliminating wolves from 60-70 % of their range in Wisconsin.  Such intense controls would look more like the extermination programs that caused wolves to become endangered, and not like the proper management of a recovered wolf population. While Tiffany adds his name to the “Trust the Science Act”, he certainly shows no trust for scientific estimates of the state wolf population, or the science-based state wolf management plan.  
Wolves in the Great Lakes states should be delisted, and state and tribal wildlife agencies should be authorized to manage local wolf populations. Some farmers have had extensive problems with wolves and more flexible management including removal of problem wolves by government agents and landowners will help reduce conflicts.  The Wisconsin DNR has a well-designed wolf management plan, which allows some level of hunting and trapping as is required by law, but the plan also focuses on ecological and cultural benefits of wolves, while still helping reduce conflicts. 
Yes, Wisconsin DNR can manage wolves, and delisting and sound management can best be achieved if politicians such as Tom Tiffany stay out of the way.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Wealthy interests in Ohio and America entrench power in the name of philanthropy, report says
description: Wealthy interests are socking a growing amount of money into tax-subsidized philanthropic accounts. Meanwhile, many of the wealthiest foundations are barely paying out the minimum required amount to charities whose needs are exploding, a new report says. At the same time, many billionaire contributors are doing little to oppose laws that shred the social saf[...]
text:
People shop the shelves at the Ritenour Co-Care Food Pantry just outside of St. Louis last week. The nonprofit has seen rising need as grocery prices soar and thousands of Missourians lose federal food assistance. (Photo courtesy of Ritenour Co-Care Food Pantry)Wealthy interests are socking a growing amount of money into tax-subsidized philanthropic accounts. Meanwhile, many of the wealthiest foundations are barely paying out the minimum required amount to charities whose needs are exploding, a new report says.
At the same time, many billionaire contributors are doing little to oppose laws that shred the social safety net, it said. Nor are many speaking out against attacks on democracy, it added.
But some charitable foundations are showing solidarity with groups that have found themselves under attack — including an Ohio voting-rights group that was subject to a statewide FBI search earlier this year, it said. 
Overall, the report says, much of modern American philanthropy isn’t helping the poor, it’s really helping the rich entrench their wealth, the report, Gilded Giving 2026, by the Institute for Policy Studies says.
“For many extremely wealthy Americans, philanthropy — ostensibly a form of generosity — has become part of that defense of extreme wealth,” it said. 
“Philanthropy is definitionally a phenomenon of wealth inequality: Someone with resources to spare chooses how and where to deploy them,” it said. “But whatever good charity, voluntarism, or institutional giving can do is undercut by our tax code, which turns philanthropy into a vehicle for defending wealth and status.”
More billions
Assets of the 144 charitable foundations with $1 billion or more grew from $420 billion in 2020 to $597 billion in 2024 — a 42% increase, the report’s analysis of IRS data said. 
Meanwhile, charitable grants grew from $25 billion to $34 billion over the same period — a comparable, 36% increase, it said.
However, the report said, the median annual payout by the foundations was 5.1% — barely above the IRS requirement that the foundations’ annual payouts and administrative costs total more than 5% of their assets.
Also, the Institute for Policy Studies analysis said, the rules allow foundations that pay more than 5% in a given year to pay less than others. Some foundations connected with booming corporations seem focused on giving just the bare minimum, it said.
“The nation’s now-largest foundation, the Lilly Endowment, reached a 5% payout in 2025 for the first time since 2009,” the report said. “Their payout was just 3% in 2024 and 3.4% in 2023. Their assets have more than doubled in value since 2022 due to the popularity and proliferation of GLP-1 drugs.” 
It’s important to note that the GLP-1 maker, Indianapolis-based Eli Lilly and Co., and the Lilly Endowment are separate legal entities, but they are connected.
“The Lilly Endowment was created in 1937 by J.K. Lilly Sr. and his two sons, J.K. Lilly Jr. and Eli Lilly, who also headed the pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly and Company,” Influence Watch reports. “Although the endowment and the company are legally separate, the endowment remains a substantial shareholder in the company.”
The Lilly Endowment said it didn’t agree with the Institute for Policy Studies’ characterization of its giving.
“A private foundation such as Lilly Endowment is required under federal tax law to make eligible charitable expenditures that equal or exceed 5% of the average fair market value of the foundation’s investment assets during a given year, subject to adjustments as provided in that law,” Judith Cebula, the endowment’s communications director, said in an email. 
“This amount, which is determined by a complex calculation, must be paid over a two-year period including the year of the calculation and the following 12 months. The amount varies each year based on the value of Lilly Endowment’s investment assets. Lilly Endowment has always exceeded its required payout.”
 Strong tax incentives, mild courage

Others note that as the extremely wealthy sock money into foundations, they get big tax breaks for doing so — a de-facto tax subsidy.
“Higher-income individuals generally save more taxes by giving to charity than those with lower incomes for two reasons: they have higher marginal tax rates, and they are more likely to itemize deductions and take advantage of the tax savings,” the Tax Policy Center reports.
A 2019 academic paper by two tax experts said those subsidies can be big — as high as 74%.
As tax-exempt contributions accumulated in billion-dollar foundations, a critical mass of rich-and-powerful givers did little to stop President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the report said. 
That law gave $1 trillion in tax breaks to the wealthiest 1% of Americans while slashing a similar amount from Medicaid and federal food assistance. In other words, it gave additional cuts to billionaires giving tax-free donations to charitable organizations while slashing resources to a group that would seem the most likely object of their charity.
Not only does it accuse many billionaire philanthropists of failing to protect struggling Americans, the Institute for Policy Studies report said they capitulated to authoritarian attacks on charitable organizations that fight hate and promote democracy.
For example, charitable organizations affiliated with financial services giants Fidelity, Vanguard, and Charles Schwab earlier this year blocked contributions to the Southern Poverty Law Center after the Trump Justice Department indicted the anti-hate watchdog on charges of committing financial crimes.
 Criticized by independent organizations as politically motivated, the poverty law center has asked that the charges be dropped on grounds of vindictive prosecution.
“The administration has continued to ramp up pressure on funders and nonprofits to curtail activities it now defines as ‘illegal’, even absent any new statutes,” the report said. 
“This has the effect of instilling fear among funders, and caution in supporting groups and programs targeted by the executive branch and fiery Congressional hearings.”
Some foundations fight back
The Institute for Policy Studies report said that some foundations have come to the defense of groups it sees saw as victims of Trump’s anti-democratic attacks.
FBI agents in June conducted a statewide sweep targeting the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a group that promotes voting rights — particularly those of historically disenfranchised groups. 
When it did, the head of one foundation, Democracy Fund President Joe Goldman, put it in the context of the administration’s other actions.
“They are a coordinated effort to raise the cost of every part of the democratic process, from running a nonprofit to registering a neighbor to showing up on Election Day,” the report quoted him as saying. 
“President Trump (has) raised the specter of widespread election fraud and manipulation, while his administration dismantles the institutions responsible for identifying and preventing threats. The only reasonable conclusion is that manufactured fears of fraud are being used to expand political control over elections.”

title: ICE deportation flights surge at Ohio’s Akron-Canton Airport as unpaid landing fees mount
description: AKRON, Ohio — Unpaid landing fees are mounting for the three air charter companies providing deportation flights out of the Akron-Canton Regional Airport for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Invoices released recently show that Eastern Airlines, Global X and Air Wisconsin owe a combined $46,513 for 148 landings since the end of April, $33,927 of […]
text:
Detainees board a plane chartered by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by David Ryder/Getty Images)AKRON, Ohio — Unpaid landing fees are mounting for the three air charter companies providing deportation flights out of the Akron-Canton Regional Airport for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Invoices released recently show that Eastern Airlines, Global X and Air Wisconsin owe a combined $46,513 for 148 landings since the end of April, $33,927 of which is past due for landings in May, June and July. Airport vice president Lisa Dalpiaz said the charter companies have not communicated with the airport about the late fees.
Not included in the billing is the long week from Friday of Labor Day weekend to the following Friday, which may have been the busiest period so far. 
Through Sept. 17, the total landings had risen to 167 since ICE moved deportation flights to Akron-Canton from Youngstown-Warren Regional Airport, which partially closed its longest runway for repairs. 
The flights
Akron-Canton has become a Great Lakes hub, with planes landing here in the evening, often from a major ICE prison and deportation center in Alexandria, Louisiana, and on occasion directly from Tapachula, Mexico, the end point for many of the deportees. 
The flights can be tracked on the website FlightAware.com which maintains a robust database of commercial and private plane fights.
The plane rests on the tarmac of a private contractor, Avflight, at the northwest corner of the airport on West Airport Drive. Avflight is a Michigan-based company that provides flight services to aircraft owners — a service known as Fixed Base Operator.
On the morning of Wednesday, Sept. 9 alone, three prison buses, transport vans from the Corrections Center of Northwest Ohio west of Toledo and Butler County Jail near Dayton, federally licensed vehicles and privately licensed black SUVs arrived to load an Eastern Air Express Boeing 737. 
The jet would make a short stop in Indianapolis before heading to Alexandria, Louisiana, according to FlightAware.com. 
Three hours earlier, a Global X jet departed for Alexandria from the same Avflight facility.
The Boeing 737s operated by Eastern Air Express and Airbus A320 and A319 range in capacity from 125 to about 180 passengers. 
Sept. 9 was one of the most active days in at least the last six weeks and was watched by a small group of protesters near the site. 
Erin Bracken-Sanchez of Canton said that as one of the buses turned onto West Airport Drive she could see the silhouettes of the prisoners looking  through the smoked glass.
“It was ominous. We may be the last people they see on this side who support them,” she said. 
Bracken-Sanchez said she is a member of the Buckeye Veterans Coalition and former member of the Army and Ohio Air National Guard. She said she’s in disbelief as she watches deportation activities across the street from the Air National Guard station where she previously was assigned.
States fight to inspect federal immigrant detention facilities

The Labor Day week’s heavy activity began with a Global X Airbus A320 arriving early Sept. 5 from Alexandria. Within two hours of landing, the plane was back in the air to Alexandria. 
This was unusual because to date almost every flight by Global X, Eastern Air Express and Air Wisconsin arrived in the evening, sat on the tarmac overnight and then left the next morning.
Since Labor Day week, traffic has lightened. A Global X Airbus that arrived Sunday directly from Tapachula, Mexico, remained idle on the tarmac through Wednesday and Eastern Air skipped two days.
Most of the information for this story was obtained by observations by a reporter, sometimes several times a day at the airport, and the use of the FlightAware. 
Only the Akron-Canton Regional Airport Authority has been forthcoming with prompt answers to questions and records requests — and the airport has no direct involvement in the deportation operations.
Observations suggest a routine for departures, which most frequently occur between 8 and 11 a.m. A flight plan is filed several hours before planned takeoff, workers arrive at Avflight and begin preparations, then prison vehicles, ICE cars and black SUVs with tinted glass arrive about 90 minutes before departure.
Vehicles line up outside the gate until all have arrived, then the gate is opened to move all vehicles onto the tarmac. Every detainee’s wrist and ankle binders are checked before boarding. Buses then move outside and stay until the plane rolls away — too late for a lawyer to extract a client from the plane.
A variety of vehicles have been observed, among them transport vehicles operated by the private prison company CoreCivic, a white unmarked turtle top bus from Butler County, and black Ford transit vans from Mahoning County.
Though the turtle top and transit vans are unmarked, ownership of the county vehicles was confirmed by license plate checks through the Ohio Department of Public Safety. Ohio agency plates are public record.
U.S. government vehicles, including a transport van, also have been observed in the past two weeks.
Weeks of records requests and questions directed to government agencies and private contractors have been largely unanswered except with a common refrain: Talk to ICE. 
Butler County
On Aug. 12, the Butler County sheriff acknowledged receipt of a reporter’s questions about the logistics of transporting ICE prisoners to Akron-Canton, a nearly four-hour trip. 
The Butler County Sheriff has been a major collaborator with ICE and the county jail is used to temporarily house Haitian immigrants captured in the Springfield, Ohio, area.
Ohio ICE detentions of Haitians have more than doubled after Trump ended protected status

The sheriff was asked to explain how deputies on a Butler County prison bus received instructions for an Aug. 6 trip to the airport. The sheriff was asked where prisoners were picked up and how many were eventually delivered to the airport. There also was a request for financial information on payments from the federal government.
After no response for two weeks, the sheriff’s office was asked about the status of the records request.
Jonathan Davidson, a lawyer for the sheriff, responded: “The only information that I would be able to provide in response to your request is the financials that were submitted to ICE for transportation. All of your other requests would need to be directed to ICE.”  
Arrests
Emails to ICE media relations have been unanswered for more than two weeks. However, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin traveled to Ohio Labor Day weekend for a meeting with police, ICE and other federal authorities and announced the arrest of 50,925 people across the country in August.
The Springfield Sun-News reported that Mullin also disclosed that 380 were arrested in Springfield, but there was no timeframe for the arrests. Cleveland.com reported a one-day sweep of 51 people in Lorain County. Transporting the arrestees from just those two cities could require three jets.
The Ohio Immigrant Alliance recently released a report showing that 448 people were booked into four publicly owned county jails on behalf of ICE between July 27 and Aug. 31. The numbers came from the jails and other federal booking data. 
The jails are in Butler County, which the report shows accounts for more than two-thirds of all immigrant detentions, Mahoning County, the Corrections Center of Northwest Ohio and the Seneca County Jail. The Geauga County jail doesn’t publish data online and a privately run prison in Youngstown, a major immigrant detention facility operated by CoreCivic, does not disclose numbers. 
Landing fees
The Akron-Canton Airport is still waiting to get paid its landing fees for the ICE transports in recent months.
Vice President James Krum provided copies of invoices showing that Eastern Airlines owed $41,900 for 136 landings of three versions of the Boeing 737 during the first four months of operations. 
Global X owed $2,657 for 13 landings in July and August by two versions of an Airbus. 
Air Wisconsin, which was added to the flights in July, owed $921 for 18 landings by a much smaller jet, a CRJ200.  
The total for three months of landings is $46,513 – an amount that’s equal to roughly 4% of the airport’s total land-fee revenues of $1.1 million in 2025. 
The airport is a public agency bound by public records laws. While ICE is obliged to disclose contracts and provide arrest and deportation data – and is dragging its feet at that – the federal agency  has turned over the daily business of deportations to private contractors who are not required to discuss details of their work.  
None of the airlines — Eastern Airlines, Global X and Air Wisconsin — responded to emails to their media portals submitted on Sept. 1.

Avflight, the private contractor that services the deportation planes and provides access to the West Airport Drive tarmac for ground transportation, was twice asked a series of questions, beginning in July,  about how it coordinates with the charter companies and prison buses. 
On Sept. 4 the company emailed this response from company senior vice president Joe Meszaros:
“Avflight does not publicly disclose non-public commercial, billing, contractual or operational information regarding the aircraft and operators it services. This includes information regarding invoices and payment arrangements, service coordination, passenger activity and specific flight-handling details.
“As a fixed-base operator at Akron-Canton Airport, Avflight provides aviation services on a non-discriminatory basis in accordance with applicable FAA and airport requirements. Questions regarding flight operations or government activities are best directed to the appropriate aircraft operator.”
Return to Youngstown?
When the deportation flights were relocated to Akron-Canton from Youngstown there was an understanding at the airport authorities that the traffic would return to Youngstown. The construction was completed in the last week of August. 
Neither airport has heard whether ICE will return to Youngstown Warren, which is in a more remote location and only about 15 minutes from the CoreCivic private prison in Youngstown, which is a major ICE contractor. Youngstown Warren also is in a far more remote location than Akron-Canton, which is on a major interstate between two large cities.
Youngstown-Warren airport director of engineering and construction Randy Partika said on Sept. 1, “The runway re-opened last week. Any Homeland security flights would be handled thru JETS FBO and though we know their intent is to maybe return, you should reach out to them for any details.” 
An email to JETS has not yet been answered.
Doug Oplinger is a Pulitzer-Prize winning journalist and former reporter and editor at the Akron Beacon Journal. He can be emailed at oplingerdoug@gmail.com

title: Politicians continue campaign of dehumanizing trans people as affordability crisis crushes families
description: When you are pumping gas into your car at $4.50 per gallon and watching the metered price zoom into the stratosphere, I’m guessing the last thing on your mind, as the grand total clicks into place, is how midterm election candidates stack up on transgender issues. Chances are you’re thinking about how much more you’re […]
text:
Getty PhotosWhen you are pumping gas into your car at $4.50 per gallon and watching the metered price zoom into the stratosphere, I’m guessing the last thing on your mind, as the grand total clicks into place, is how midterm election candidates stack up on transgender issues. 
Chances are you’re thinking about how much more you’re paying this week than last. I’ve got bad news for you. Energy experts and prediction markets are forecasting an even bigger jump in gas prices soon — maybe breaching the $5.00 threshold nationwide as Donald Trump’s war of choice with Iran drags on and on. 
Diesel, which powers trucks, farm machinery, construction equipment and other parts of the economy responsible for producing and moving goods, hit a record national average of $6.51 per gallon Monday — the highest level ever recorded in the United States.
The prospect of paying higher fuel costs for longer — on households that can’t break even now with ballooning expenses — is what keeps folks up at night. 
What doesn’t is whether literally a handful of transgender athletes (out of hundreds of thousands of athletes) can participate in women’s sports, or whether the government should decide what’s best for a transgender minor (not a doctor with parents and child), or whether the tiny fraction of transgender Americans in the U.S. should be subject to bathroom bans, etc. 
None of those manufactured political crises has any connection to the real-life financial crises affecting millions of households in the country. But Republicans are still recycling their ugly anti-trans ads from the 2024 election in the final stretch of the 2026 midterm campaigns. 
Forget about the disastrous war nobody wanted, or your wallet drained by crippling expenses. Instead, be afraid of a small, defenseless community the GOP has scapegoated as the “Other” and reject as extremist any candidate who dares acknowledge its humanity. 
Fear is powerful motivator and the party used it effectively two years ago in a deluge of hateful attacks on transgender people to motivate voters to the polls on hostility and dread. 
The same strategy is being replicated to hammer Democratic candidates in the lead up to the Nov. 3 election. 
A ton of Republican aligned money has been poured into smarmy TV ads to remind voters how scared they should be about transgender issues and how radical Democrats are about transgender rights. 
It is a desperate attempt to divert the electorate’s attention from the dismal state of the union under a government controlled by Republicans. 
But the old playbook, to dehumanize a marginalized group of human beings, may not work as well this time. T
rans bashing and wild claims about Democrats supporting sex-change surgeries for children seems irrelevant to the struggle at hand of millions of Americans. 
Why would transgender policy be top of list for voters who are seething every time they fill up their tank, who are maxing out credit cards, cutting back on groceries, forgoing healthcare that could bankrupt them? 
When you’re anxious about another rent hike, or monthly bills that overwhelm take-home pay, or medical premiums going through the roof, or $5.00 gas because of a never-ending war, do you care about trans issues that affect less than 1% of the populace and have no  bearing on your life? 
Most folks are focused on their paychecks vanishing in a blink. 
But instead of recognizing their pain, those running the American ship of state into the ground dismiss it. 
They brush off the compounding hardships of the people who elected them as “temporary” or no big deal. 
Trump said the financial distress of Americans did not concern him. His Republican rubber-stamps in Congress insist their Dear Leader has made America great — in an alternate universe — and argue voters should give them “another chance” to keep making it so great. 
But the reality-based world is suffering. The country is mired in a Middle East war actively spreading to new fronts. The costly military entanglement, with no exit strategy, continues to wreak severe economic havoc at home and globally. 
Yet Republicans have settled on the anti-trans card as their ace in the hole distraction to win the midterms. 
To blunt the insidious attacks, several Democratic candidates in tight races have recalibrated their approach to transgender issues and pointedly distanced themselves from their party’s unflinching support for the transgender community. 
There is a definite shift on this divisive culture war by battleground Democrats in key races. They’ve moved to moderate or conservative anti-trans messaging to appeal to swing voters. 
Some, like Ohio’s Democratic nominee for governor Amy Acton, have come out in support of policies — aligned with a clear majority or Americans — that would bar transgender female athletes from competing in women’s and girls’ sports. 
Others, like Ohio’s 9th District congresswoman, incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur, actually co-opted right wing propaganda: “I voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools” and “boys should not play in girls’ sports.”  
While many in the Democratic base are dismayed by their party’s candidates embracing anti-trans rhetoric to win difficult seats, some rank-and-file Democrats view the tack to center-right on trans issues as politically smart. 
But what about the transgender community exploited by Republicans and betrayed by Democrats to make voters forget about the cost-of-living? 
What about the lasting harm to people cruelly portrayed as something to be feared and/or erased? 
“Transgender constituents are stuck between a rock and a hard place,” wrote one transgender activist, “and left wondering what the point of their vote is if both candidates view them as disposable and subhuman.”

title: Ohio is the nation’s No. 1 for business. Our challenge is to become No. 1 for students.
description: With the new school year underway, Ohio students have returned to their classrooms, settled into new routines, and started thinking about what they hope to accomplish during the school year ahead. Teachers and families are helping them set goals, measure progress, and understand that academic improvement rarely happens by accident. Ohio should approach its f[...]
text:
Students walk down the hall at a public elementary school. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel, States Newsroom.)With the new school year underway, Ohio students have returned to their classrooms, settled into new routines, and started thinking about what they hope to accomplish during the school year ahead. Teachers and families are helping them set goals, measure progress, and understand that academic improvement rarely happens by accident.
Ohio should approach its future with the same sense of purpose.
CNBC recently named Ohio the nation’s top state for business in its annual and widely followed assessment. That’s an achievement worth celebrating but one that also creates responsibility.
If Ohio wants to remain the best place for starting and growing a business, it also needs to become the best place for every student to learn, prepare for a career, and build a successful life.
Accomplishing this must be the education goal placed before Ohio’s next governor, regardless of which party wins the November election. By 2035, Ohio should strive to be the nation’s top-performing state in K-12 academic performance and postsecondary outcomes.
Business organizations that advocate for stronger education and workforce-development success in Ohio — including the non-partisan groups we represent — have long been committed to supporting this goal.
The need for that commitment is clear. Respected studies tell us that while Ohio ranks between 7th and 14th on national outcome measures, even that leaves many students woefully unprepared for the world ahead.
Consider these statistics: only 36% of Ohio children enter kindergarten ready to learn, while only 32% of fourth graders are proficient in reading and 43% are proficient in math on the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP). By eighth grade, on this same national measure, proficiency stands at 32% in both readingand math.
Ohio’s latest school report cards show encouraging gains in reading and math, and educators deserve credit for that progress. But nearly 4 in 10 students remain below proficiency in reading and more than 4 in 10 in math on state tests.
Our next governor must build on these gains, close persistent achievement gaps, and hold the state accountable for better results.
The next governor’s administration should commit to the goal and to the strategies that have propelled students in states across the country toward higher achievement. Ohio Excels has studied the best practices across the country and identified models in each area for emulation.
A student’s readiness to succeed begins by making high-quality early education more accessible and affordable, particularly for low-income families, while fully funding all-day kindergarten so that more students are prepared to succeed in the following years. Colorado provides an excellent example of achieving this.
As students enter elementary school, Ohio must lead the nation in reading and math by maintaining high expectations, using evidence-based strategies such as the Science of Reading, supporting educators, and insisting that major reforms are implemented in good faith rather than replaced before they have a chance to work. The “Southern surge” (Mississippi miracle) demonstrates significant performance gains. Ohio has begun the work, but success requires sustained commitment.
Every family should have transparent and understandable information about school performance, along with access to a high-quality district, charter, or private school. When schools consistently fail to improve, the state must provide stronger leadership, targeted support, appropriate incentives, and real accountability. Texas’s reporting and accountability system is a strong example.
Ohio must also expose every student to career paths by expanding awareness, advising and real-world learning. Higher education, technical training, and apprenticeships should all be more affordable, more accessible, and more clearly connected to careers that offer economic mobility and a return on a student’s investment. Mississippi and Indiana offer models to emulate in career coaching and alignment.
Finally, business groups cannot simply ask schools to do it alone. Companies should open their doors through internships, co-ops, job shadowing, apprenticeships, and other work-based experiences that help inform and inspire students and educators and then provide them with an understanding of the preparation needed to pursue them.
Accomplishing all this by 2035 is ambitious but intentional, spanning two terms and providing enough time to achieve meaningful change without becoming an excuse for delay. Ohio should establish annual benchmarks, report progress publicly, and tie funding to outcomes.
Our students are already setting goals for the year ahead. Ohio’s next governor should be prepared to set one for the state that is every bit as ambitious. Ohio Excels, and our business groups, are ready to partner in this effort.
Being No. 1 for business is an extraordinary achievement, and now Ohio must become No. 1 for students.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Rezoning Florida scout camp land for development has deep ramifications
description: Back when my kids were in Boy Scouts, our troop spent a lot of time at the Sand Hill Scout Reservation in Brooksville. We always brought home a lot of that sand — in our tents, in our uniforms, and in our shoes and socks. Still, I found that place amazing. Just an hour north […]
text:
The vast DIePolder caves, one of them the deepest cave in the Florida aquifer, lie directly beneath the Sand Hill Scout Reservation in Brooksville. This photo of it by Wes Skiles appeared in 1999 in National Geographic. (Photo courtesy of Tessa Skiles)Back when my kids were in Boy Scouts, our troop spent a lot of time at the Sand Hill Scout Reservation in Brooksville. We always brought home a lot of that sand — in our tents, in our uniforms, and in our shoes and socks.
Still, I found that place amazing. Just an hour north of where we lived in Florida’s most densely populated county were 1,300 acres where the boys could camp, hike, and swim amid Florida’s natural splendor. They could work on merit badges while seeing sand hill cranes, raccoons, and gopher tortoises.
The camp prayer, the “Sand Hill Grace,” was a way of saying thanks for this gift. It begins, “For the hills, for the sand, for the bounty of the land, for water bright and the pristine sunlight.” (I always mumbled over the mention of “sand.”)
But now it’s Sand Hill itself that’s standing in the need of prayer.
Tessa Skiles via subject
Turns out the owners of the place full of camp sites named things like “Possum Hollow” are trying to put about half of it into a new category: “Developer’s Delight.”
Scouts usually come across as a bunch of Dudley Do-rights, but this seems more like something from villainous Snidely Whiplash. A lot of people are unhappy about it, too.
“Dozens of residents and Eagle Scouts protested the potential sale of a portion of the Sand Hill Scout Reservation in Brooksville,” WTVT-TV reported last week.
They were incensed by a notice from the Hernando County Commission that the county was considering a requested change to the zoning from “recreation” to “planned development district.”
Possible uses of the rezoned land, the notice says, “would include commercial on the State Road 50 frontage and mixed use (office, professional, multifamily, etc.) south of that.”
That would go against the wishes of the landowner who first donated the property to the Boy Scouts.
There’s another group that’s alarmed about possible Sand Hill development, people whose concerns have been out of sight and out of mind for a long time: cave divers.
They’re up in arms because the Sand Hill property includes the entrance to the deepest cave in the Floridan aquifer, the source of our drinking water.
“Everybody’s livid about it,” said Tessa Skiles, a cave diver who runs an underwater cinematography company called Karst Productions. “I mean, it’s a reservation!”
 Water’s journey
Most people in Florida have no idea of the vast subterranean world beneath their feet, even though it’s vital to their continued existence.
The fact is, some 90% of the water we use for drinking, bathing, and watering our lawns comes from the Floridan Aquifer. The aquifer is a pool of freshwater covering about 100,000 square miles from the Panhandle to north of Lake Okeechobee.
Too much pumping from that aquifer — to irrigate golf courses, boost crops, and provide lush suburban lawns — has lowered the pressure in a number of our taxpayer-owned springs, lessening their once-forceful flow.
That loss of flow is an indicator of what’s happening with our water supply. Most of the state is still dealing with drought conditions. We just went through the driest August since record-keeping began in 1895.
The safest way to experience our aquifer is by watching a movie called “Water’s Journey: The Hidden Rivers of Florida,” made by Skiles’ father, Wes, a legendary diver and photographer.
The film shows a pair of cave divers exploring the twisting, turning openings in the Swiss cheese of limestone formations beneath the earth. Meanwhile, above ground, Skiles and an electrical engineer follow radio signals showing their progress.
As they track the two divers, the aboveground pair pass through a barbecue joint, a bowling alley and a golf course. Along the way, they take note of how pollution from such mundane sources dribbles down through the ground and contaminates the source of the precious liquid we all need.
That’s why the divers are so concerned about any development replacing the natural bounty of the Sand Hill land.
Wes Skiles via Tessa Skiles
 The beauties and benefits
Larry DiePolder, the son of a lighthouse keeper, had been a World War I pilot and a boat builder and racer. He wound up a cattleman in Hernando County. He cared deeply about his Sandy Hills Ranch.
He died in 1978. In his will, DiePolder decreed that ranch should go to the Boy Scouts to protect it. He said that the property would allow the Boy Scouts to “enjoy the great outdoors and the beauties and benefits of nature.”
If the scouts were ever to decide they didn’t need his property, DiePolder’s will said they should sell it to the county to become a public park. That way it would remain preserved and pristine.
About a year after DiePolder donated the land, the first cave diver jumped in to explore the water-filled caverns beneath it. One is about 300 feet deep. The other is 365 feet, which according to the Cave Atlas website makes it the deepest cave in not just the aquifer but the entire continental U.S.
Other divers followed, astounded by the massive caves and the subterranean life of such creatures as the blind crayfish.
One was Wes Skiles, whose breathtaking photo from inside one DiePolder cave ran in National Geographic in 1999. He used that photo to lobby for state protection of all of Florida’s springs and aquifer.
“No place on earth better exemplifies the beauty, wonder and intrigue of cave diving inside of the Floridan Aquifer,” Wes Skiles wrote of the photo in “Advanced Diver” magazine.
“This image is his best for the sole purpose of illustrating the incomprehensible vastness of the Floridan Aquifer, and he used it for exactly that purpose,” Tessa Skiles said.
Ted McCoy via subject
Diving can be a dangerous sport. Wes Skiles died in 2010 during a dive. But in 30 years of exploration, only one diver — an Italian tourist — died inside the DiePolder caves, according to Ted McCoy, part of a team of 12 guides who took divers into them.
“We would charge a small fee for guiding people,” McCoy told me, “and we had our own Lloyd’s of London insurance policy in case anything went wrong.”
One day 10 years ago, McCoy was preparing to take someone on a dive at the DiePolder caves when he got an email with disquieting news: “The Boy Scouts said no more diving was allowed.”
“It was pretty clear they were concerned about liability,” said Charles Roberson, who was the DiePolder dive program coordinator at the time. The fact that divers had been exploring the caves for three decades meant nothing to the Scout executives.
The guides offered to buy the 5 acres around the entrance to the caves, Roberson said, “but they turned us down. They said that wasn’t going to work for them.”
No one has seen inside the DiePolder caves since. And no one from the council seems concerned about the impact of developing that property on the aquifer.
Protesters outside Sand Hill Scout Reservation. (Photo via Eric Cupps)
 Two digits down
The protest last week was led by a former scoutmaster named Eric Cupps. As a teen he earned Eagle, the top rank in Scouting. As an adult, he volunteered at Sand Hill as a camp manager.
His Save Sand Hill Scout Reservation group has been battling the Greater Tampa Bay Area Scout Council over the fate of Sand Hill for two years. The battle began when word first got out that the council planned to sell 50 acres of the camp to the Withlacoochee River Electrical Cooperative.
Eric Cupps at Sand Hill via subject
To Cupps, the council’s disregard for their donor’s desires feels disrespectful. It’s like they’ve taken the famous three-finger salute and lowered two digits, leaving just the middle finger upraised.
“I don’t think they really understand the impact of what they’re doing,” Cupps told me.
I asked him if this was part of Scouting America’s nationwide effort to raise $2 billion to pay a legal judgment against the organization. He said no, the Greater Tampa Bay Council had already sold off land in Hillsborough County to pay its portion of the debt.
This appears to be nothing but a fundraising alternative to selling Trail’s End popcorn outside Publix.
 Rubbing their hands
When Sand Hill first opened to the scouts, it was way out in the country. State Road 50 was a two-lane blacktop where you could drive for miles without seeing a house or business.
Now, urban sprawl lines both sides of the six-lane highway, bumping up on the camp’s boundaries and clogging the road. The scout camp is the one piece of “Old Florida” that’s still hanging on.
“You just know the developers have been rubbing their hands waiting for access to that place,” McCoy told me.
I looked over the proposed comprehensive plan amendment that the council filed with Hernando County. I think it must have been written by some near-sighted Mr. Magoo, because it misses a lot of obvious stuff.
For instance, it says it covers 604 acres of the 1,300, which it contends “consists almost entirely of sand hills and has minimal environmental features.”
To me, that’s wrong. I think any place in Florida that’s still full of sand hills, oaks, pines, cranes and other wildlife has nothing BUT environmental features worth preserving. That’s especially true as the rest of Brooksville has become wall to wall sprawl.
Also, I noticed that the application contains absolutely no mention of the DiePolder caves. It’s as if they don’t exist and thus merit no consideration from elected officials — even though they probably drink water themselves.
The scout council has said little in public about the controversy. The one exception happened in 2024, when the council posted a statement on its website that says it’s not bound by DiePolder’s will.
“Following the passing of Larry DiePolder in 1978, there was a family dispute regarding his will,” the council wrote. Ultimately, his oldest stepson, Main Henderson, took charge of the estate. Henderson handed over the deed to the scouts, “free and clear of any use restrictions.”
To be certain they could ignore DiePolder’s will, the council took their deed to court. “In January 2024, the court confirmed the council’s full rights over the Sand Hill property,” the council wrote.
I’m no marketing expert. But it seems to me that if your only public comment is, “We know people think this looks bad, but it’s perfectly legal!” then you’ve lost the PR war.
There was also a Q&A video posted in 2024. In it, a scouting executive said they were just exploring how much money the camp might be worth. It appears that they’ve progressed beyond that now.
I tried repeatedly this week to get some more current comment from the adults who run scouting here. Unfortunately, the council continued keeping its own counsel.
I also tried reaching Hernando County Commissioner Ryan Amsler, a mortgage broker who lives near the camp and may care about the aquifer beneath it. He didn’t respond to my calls and emails, either.
I think if the scout council is serious about pursuing this development idea, members need to open up about their plans and their reasoning. They need to talk to the community and explain what their goal is. And they need to show everyone how they’re going to protect the drinking water in the DiePolder caves beneath the camp.
Otherwise, they should make some changes to the Scout Oath that every Tenderfoot has to memorize and recite.
The current version says, “On my honor I will do my best to do my duty to God and my country and to obey the Scout Law, to help other people at all times, to keep myself physically strong, mentally awake and morally straight.”
The updated version could be, “On my dishonor, I will do my best to avoid responsibility for environmental degradation, dodge what the donors want, and uphold the hypocritical legality of what makes the most money for the organization.”
You’ll have to forgive me for hoping any attempt to bulldoze this property runs into a major obstacle. Maybe it’ll wind up with a lot of sand in its gears.
Sand Hill Scout Reservation entrance sign on State Road 50 in Brooksville. (Photo via Sand Hill Scout Reservation)

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Food insecurity is growing in Greenwich
description: Neighbor to Neighbor has served Greenwich for more than 50 years, and we have never seen demand grow as fast as it is now.
text:
Every week, Patty, 78, walks through the doors of Neighbor to Neighbor for groceries. She isn’t there because of an emergency. She comes to the pantry because the math no longer adds up. “Money got a little bit tighter as the years went on,” Patty says.
Patty is a senior living alone in Greenwich, one of the wealthiest communities in the United States. She spent her working years here, built her life here, and planned to retire here. What she did not plan for was Social Security that would fail to keep pace with rising rents, utility bills that climb year after year, and a water supply in her building so unreliable that she and her neighbors haul in their own. By the time the bills are paid, there is little left for food. Patty says, “Seniors get forgotten — and the added costs, they just throw them through without realizing we’re living on Social Security.”
Patty’s story may surprise you. Not because it is unusual — but because it is happening here, in one of the most prosperous communities in the country. Across the country, 48 million Americans face food insecurity, including one in five children. And hunger does not discriminate by Zip code. It exists in rural towns, urban neighborhoods, and in our own backyard.
Here in Greenwich, 27% of residents can’t afford the basics, including food, housing, child care, and transportation, according to United for ALICE. And that number is climbing. Over the past year alone, Neighbor to Neighbor has seen a 14% increase in clients, driven by rising food and gas costs and federal cuts to SNAP benefits that have left thousands of families across Fairfield County with a widening gap in their monthly budgets. As Greenwich’s only food pantry, Neighbor to Neighbor is on the front lines of meeting this need.
Greenwich United Way’s Needs Assessment shows that Connecticut now ranks as the most food-insecure state in New England and second in the entire Northeast, with 14.3% of residents facing food insecurity. Statewide, food price inflation has risen 3.6%, while the number of Connecticut residents receiving SNAP has declined by 11%. That’s 41,845 fewer recipients in December than in January alone. Fifty-seven percent of food-insecure individuals in Connecticut are estimated to live in households below the SNAP eligibility threshold, with one in six Connecticut children experiencing food insecurity.

The Neighbor to Neighbor food pantry Credit: Neighbor to Neighbor

Neighbor to Neighbor has served Greenwich for more than 50 years, and we have never seen demand grow as fast as it is now. To meet the moment, we are redoubling our efforts to serve our neighbors. Over the past year, we have expanded our community garden program, grown our volunteer corps, partnered with the PTA to support the Care Closet at Greenwich High School, and distributed 33,750 meals to families with children who lose access to school meals during the summer. This holiday season, we will distribute 600 complete Thanksgiving meals to families across Greenwich.
We have always believed we are stronger together, which is why we are deepening our commitment to working with our partners across town to meet this moment, as rising prices and SNAP cuts will ripple through all of our organizations and the communities we serve.
This September, during Hunger Action Month, we are asking you to stand with us and donate to Neighbor to Neighbor’s virtual food drive. Every dollar donated goes directly toward feeding the 900+ households that rely on Neighbor — including clients like Patty, who are one unexpected bill away from going without. 
The need is real, it is local, it is growing — and this is the moment to act. Donate now, spread the word, and learn more about how to get involved: ntngreenwich.org/hungeractionmonth
Sonya Keshwani is Public Affairs Manager at Neighbor to Neighbor

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: What CT needs to hear about jobs
description: We need immediate, state-level action to balance the increased cost of living with the harsh realities of the middle and working classes.
text:
A recent CT Mirror article highlighted that Connecticut is tied for the highest unemployment rate in the nation at 5.2%. This statistic confirms what the working class has already started to perceive: severe job scarcity and an impossible cost of living.
In metropolitan areas like New Haven, it is becoming nearly impossible to find a job that covers basic bills, let alone one that provides for a family, secures future savings, or allows the lower working class to progress.
The article points out a contradictory trend: while total jobs are slowly increasing, the vast majority of working people find it drastically more difficult to acquire and retain employment at any level. 
This shift directly affects minorities, women, and young adults. Because average retail and minimum wage positions are now increasingly held by older adults, finding work has become a literal “Hunger Games” for teenagers and young adults. 
With the direction in which we are heading, our economic development is regressing. State claims and general economic statistics do not favor the working class, but rather mask the deep financial struggles of the population of Connecticut as a whole.
We as a people need more jobs, a higher state minimum wage, as well as a clear explanation from state leaders as to how we are supposed to continue to live off of and survive with the current minimum wage of $16.94 per hour. 
Compounding this issue is the sudden increase in work stipulations required for SNAP and other vital state benefits. Forcing the working class to prove an average total of 80 hours of employment per month shows that the government is actively putting immense emotional stress and unrealistic expectations on hardworking citizens. 
If we look closely at the numbers behind our state safety net, they show that a staggering 28% of the unemployed are actually receiving unemployment benefits. This leaves nearly three out of four jobless residents completely stranded without a baseline safety net while they search for work.
I strongly agree with the article’s stance that we need immediate, state-level action to balance the increased cost of living with the harsh realities of the middle and lower working classes. As a representative of these groups, I believe our state should actively create more entry- and mid-level job opportunities catered specifically to youth and young adults who are trying to get a foothold in the economy.
If we continue at this current rate, how is the next generation of the working class supposed to succeed in building a future? The current economy is teaching the youth that finding a job is a luxury rather than a basic necessity. We must invest heavily in our workforce infrastructure. Right now, our state is in a severe crisis of structural inequality that heavily favors the wealthy and the financially comfortable at the expense of everyone else.
Trenitee Soares lives in New Haven.
