name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC service members need more affordable housing, military leaders say
description: Military leaders praised the state's education efforts while worrying about having enough housing for service members.
text:
Veterans' Affairs Secretary Todd McCaffrey, Gov. Henry McMaster and House Speaker Murrell Smith, R-Sumter, oversee a conference of South Carolina military leaders at the University of South Carolina alumni center in Columbia, S.C., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — South Carolina’s military forces are growing, but they need more places to live, military leaders told top lawmakers Wednesday.
Affordable housing, education and support for military spouses are among the biggest concerns service members face when relocating, leaders of South Carolina’s military installations said during a round-table meeting with the governor and legislators as part of an annual conference.


SC military installations
The military bases represented at Wednesday’s meeting were:

Beaufort Naval Hospital in Port Royal
Coast Guard Charleston in North Charleston
Fort Gordon in Augusta, Georgia
Fort Jackson in Columbia
Joint Base Lindsey Graham in North Charleston
Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort in Beaufort
Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island in Port Royal
National Guard
Shaw Air Force Base in Sumter County

Source: Veterans’ Affairs office


The conference is meant to identify military bases’ biggest successes and challenges in South Carolina, with the goal of giving lawmakers ideas on how they can help out.
Participants come from military installations across South Carolina, as well as Fort Gordon located just across the border in Augusta, Georgia. A law passed in 2024 officially added it to South Carolina’s list of installations qualifying for state grants.
This year, most of their needs centered not around service members themselves but around their families. Making sure communities have resources for families is key for encouraging people to enlist and to work at South Carolina’s bases, leaders said.
“You recruit a service member, but you retain a family,” said retired Army Maj. Gen. Todd McCaffrey, who leads the state Department of Veterans’ Affairs.
That’s especially true as South Carolina’s population continues to boom, McCaffrey said.
The Palmetto State has seen a surge in population in recent years, with one of the highest growth rates in the country. That squeezes an already tight market, making buying a home even harder in already pricey parts of the state. Those areas include Beaufort County, which has Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island and the state’s Marine Corps Air Station, and Charleston, with Joint Base Lindsey Graham, which was renamed last month to honor South Carolina’s late senator.
Along with the strains of a growing population, more service members are being assigned to South Carolina, installation leaders said.
Beaufort, especially, has seen a surge in Marines assigned to the air station there. It’s expected to grow from about 4,700 Marines to as many as 6,000 in the next four years, said Col. Trevor Feltor, the station’s commander.
Even more service members might come to South Carolina as the war in Iran continues, military leaders said.
“That causes compression, and compression could be a challenge if you don’t have the infrastructure, you don’t have the housing, the schools,” McCaffrey said. “You hear that from these military members.”
When the number of service members grows quickly, bases run out of space to house them all.
That often leaves people scrambling to find leases or mortgages they can afford nearby for themselves and their families, said House Speaker Murrell Smith, whose district includes Shaw Air Force Base.
“We’re going to have to take on the issue of how we’re going to house people in military communities, especially when we’re in a time of war and we have been transitioning on and off the bases,” the Sumter Republican said.
He floated the idea of expanding the state’s Palmetto Heroes homebuyers’ program, which helps active-duty military, teachers, nurses, law enforcement and other public sector employees buy homes.
SC approves $72M in low-interest loans to help its ‘heroes’ buy homes in the state

The program offers $10,000 in forgivable down payment loans and low, fixed-rate mortgages until funding is depleted. This year, the $74 million SC Housing had to spend ran out after less than a month, the quickest in the program’s history, according to the agency.
Smith didn’t give details on how legislators might look to expand the program to further help service members, and McCaffrey didn’t offer specific ideas. But both agreed affordable housing was a major challenge for military members.
“You’ve got to be able to take care of families, you’ve got to be able to take care of service programmers, and you’ve got to be able to generate readiness,” McCaffrey said.
Concerns about housing for service members often center around those with families, but fresh recruits often need somewhere to live, too, several base leaders said.
Many service members don’t have driver’s licenses or cars, having gone straight from high school to basic training, said Capt. Jason Anderson, deputy commander of Joint Base Lindsey Graham. If they can’t stay on the base, which sometimes happens when they run out of space, that makes it even more essential to have housing nearby, he said.
Beaufort Naval Hospital is dealing with that pressure during renovations of its onsite barracks, said Capt. Juan Rosario, the military hospital’s commander. Around 20 sailors had to move off base during the improvements, and the hospital struggled to help them find places to live that they could afford, he said.
“Parents expect me as a leader to help their children, to keep them safe, so that they can do what they were called to do, and that is to serve our nation,” Rosario said. “In order to do that, I need to find an affordable, safe house where I can put them.”
For service members with families, making sure their spouses have job opportunities and their children have access to high-quality education is essential to keeping South Carolina a military-friendly state, leaders said.
“The reality is, when these young people decide to join the military and have families, they have an expectation — and, frankly, they’re right, I think — to have the kind of housing, the schools and the job opportunities that all Americans want to have,” McCaffrey said. “South Carolina’s working really hard to provide that.”
In July, the federal government relaunched the SpouseWorks program to help spouses of active-duty military members get jobs when they relocate. The program offers career coaches, job boards and scholarships for career-advancing degrees.
Statewide, K-12 public schools that go above and beyond to help military families can receive a Purple Star designation. Criteria for becoming a Purple Star school include designating a liaison to help with military-specific challenges, providing extra training for school staff and making sure policies are in place that allow transfer students to join sports and clubs throughout the year.
A state law passed last year also gives children from military families enrollment preference in charter schools that use a lottery system.
Programs like those “give Marines a valuable peace of mind,” said Col. Clark Mitchell, of Parris Island. “It allows them to focus on the mission, knowing their family is supported by a grateful community.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: MAP: Arkansas’ most populous county passes data center regulations
description: Pulaski County’s top elected official has seven days to decide whether to veto new regulations on data centers approved by the county’s quorum court. The majority-Democrat panel in Arkansas’ most populous county voted 11-4 Tuesday night in favor of the new rules. County Judge Barry Hyde, a Democrat, has seven days to veto it. The […]
text:
An audience member attending a Pulaski County Quorum Court agenda-setting meeting holds a sign opposing data centers on June 9, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Pulaski County’s top elected official has seven days to decide whether to veto new regulations on data centers approved by the county’s quorum court.
The majority-Democrat panel in Arkansas’ most populous county voted 11-4 Tuesday night in favor of the new rules. County Judge Barry Hyde, a Democrat, has seven days to veto it. The measure was written by Wendell Griffen, a former circuit and appeals court judge and current Democratic nominee for county judge, and sponsored by Justice of the Peace Julie Blackwood, a Democrat. 
According to the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, Hyde did not say whether he planned to sign the measure and appeared skeptical of it during Tuesday’s meeting. The regulations can also become law without Hyde’s signature if he does not sign or veto them after seven days. 
The regulations touch on noise, and water and power use, requiring prospective data center projects to submit to the county electrical load analyses, water and wastewater plans, land-use suitability studies and a decommissioning plan, among other requirements. Prospective data center projects are required to demonstrate that the development won’t “materially impair” utilities and other public infrastructure that serve surrounding properties under the new regulations, but do not limit the amount of water or power a project can use.
Since the quorum court first considered data center regulations for Arkansas’ most populous county in May, the opposition to the power-hungry computing hubs has grown, with polling showing increasingly broad unpopularity among Americans. 
That unpopularity has pit pro-data center interests such as the Little Rock Regional Chamber of Commerce against Pulaski County residents opposed to the AVAIO data center project in the unincorporated part of the county. 
AVAIO is one of six planned data center projects in the state. Two of those projects, in West Memphis and Clarksville, are already under construction.
The effort to regulate data centers in Pulaski County has seen fits and starts, even as Little Rock passed its own requirements over the summer. Data center opponents rejoiced in June after a temporary moratorium appeared to pass, only for the county clerk to announce days later that there had been a vote miscount. 
Debate has also raged over whether to exempt the AVAIO project from the regulations. Blackwood told the Arkansas Times that AVAIO would be required to comply with the new regulations.
The fight over data centers has cut across party lines, with elected officials in other states losing their seats amid the backlash.
The push to build more and more data centers comes as internet giants like Google, Open AI and Meta seek to capitalize on the rapid growth of artificial intelligence models. While data centers have existed for decades, powering everything from email to social media, the AI models created by tech companies require massive amounts of computing power.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Van Buren County deputy accused of excessive force
description: An Iowa man is suing the Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office, alleging excessive force was used against him by one of its officers. John Michael Orndoff, 25, of Milton, is suing Van Buren County and Deputy Adam McIntyre, who has been employed by the county since 2018. According to the lawsuit, McIntyre was working on […]
text:
(Photo by David Talukdar/Getty Images)An Iowa man is suing the Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office, alleging excessive force was used against him by one of its officers.
John Michael Orndoff, 25, of Milton, is suing Van Buren County and Deputy Adam McIntyre, who has been employed by the county since 2018.
According to the lawsuit, McIntyre was working on Oct. 15, 2024, when he observed Orndoff driving a vehicle without license plates. Before McIntyre could initiate a traffic stop, Orndoff parked the car and began walking away. After speaking to the county dispatch staff, McIntyre learned that Orndoff’s driving privileges had been revoked, and informed Orndoff that he was being cited for driving with a revoked license.
Orndoff objected and asked to speak to the county’s chief deputy, according to the lawsuit. McIntyre denied the request, then took hold of one of Orndoff’s arms and directed him to place his hands behind his back. “Orndoff did not immediately comply, but did not strike, threaten or in any way assault McIntyre, and did not attempt to flee,” the lawsuit asserts. “Within seconds of first taking hold of Orndoff, and after a single warning, McIntyre threw Orndoff head-first to the ground …  Because McIntyre was controlling Orndoff’s arms, Orndoff was unable to break his fall or to protect his head as he was driven to the ground.”
According to the lawsuit, Orndoff’s head struck the concrete and he was immediately rendered unconscious before convulsing.
“Orndoff sustained a severe head injury, including a skull fracture and brain bleed, as a result of the takedown,” the lawsuit asserts. “Orndoff posed no immediate threat to McIntyre or to anyone else; Orndoff was unarmed, and Orndoff was not actively resisting arrest or attempting to flee but was, at most, passively resisting.”
Orndoff was taken to Van Buren County Hospital and then transferred by air to the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics in Iowa City, according to the lawsuit.
Court records show Orndoff was later charged with, and convicted of, driving with a revoked license and interference with official acts.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages for alleged violation of Orndoff’s constitutional rights and for alleged assault and battery. The county has yet to respond to the lawsuit, and Van Buren County Attorney H. Craig Miller declined to comment on the allegations.
Court records indicate that in July, Orndoff was charged with livestock neglect. Police alleged that along with a veterinarian, they investigated several complaints of animal neglect on Orndoff’s property and found a young cow in an emaciated condition that was suffering from a lack of feed and potable water. The veterinarian noted the cow’s visible spine, ribs, and pelvic bones, as well as signs of muscle wasting. “This animal is in need of immediate sustenance and veterinary care,” Dr. Emma Fryauf Fallis wrote in her report on the cow’s condition.
Four weeks after the charge of livestock neglect was imposed, it was dismissed by the court at the request of county prosecutors, although Miller said he could not comment on the reasons for the request.
Orndoff is currently facing a charge of failure to properly dispose of dead animals. A county deputy alleges a dead pig was found in a feed bag on Orndoff’s property and a “skinned animal” of some kind was found hanging from a tree in his yard. According to the deputy, Orndoff said he was using the dead animals to feed to his dogs.
Orndoff has pleaded not guilty to the charge. A trial date has yet to be scheduled.

title: Demuth-affiliated political action committee receives $10 million infusion
description: A super PAC backing Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth’s campaign for Minnesota governor received a $10 million cash infusion in recent weeks, cutting into Sen. Amy Klobuchar’s longtime financial advantage in the race. Restore Sanity — a political action committee that has provided the most significant outside money in support of a statewide Republican can[...]
text:
House Speaker Lisa Demuth, R-Cold Spring, announced she is running in the August GOP primary election during a press conference in front of the Minnesota Capitol. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)A super PAC backing Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth’s campaign for Minnesota governor received a $10 million cash infusion in recent weeks, cutting into Sen. Amy Klobuchar’s longtime financial advantage in the race.
Restore Sanity — a political action committee that has provided the most significant outside money in support of a statewide Republican candidate in years — received $10 million in the past four weeks from the Restoration of America PAC, which is primarily funded by Wisconsin billionaire duo Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein. The Uihleins own one of North America’s largest distributors of shipping and packaging supplies.
The Uihleins have donated $70 million this election cycle in favor of GOP candidates and causes, making them the fifth-largest donors in the midterm election so far, according to the Washington Post.
The Restore Sanity PAC has spent nearly $4.4 million on digital and TV ads in support of Demuth’s campaign for governor and nearly $1.8 million on ads against Klobuchar’s campaign, according to campaign finance reports released Wednesday that detail spending and fundraising up to Sept. 15. The independent expenditure committee has raised $14.1 million, of which over $13 million came from the Uihlein-funded PAC. Restore Sanity has nearly $7 million in cash in the final weeks leading up to the Nov. 3 election.
The cash infusion suggests at least some big-money Republicans see glimmers of hope here in Minnesota, where Democrats haven’t lost a statewide race since 2006 but have been weighed down since by embarrassing stories about the looting of the state’s safety net by fraudsters.
Klobuchar, who is ending a 20-year Senate career to run for governor, has raised over $12.5 million since launching her campaign at the end of January and has spent $9 million, mostly on consulting and ads. Her campaign has over $3.5 million in cash.
Demuth’s gubernatorial campaign has raised nearly $2.6 million this year, half of which came from a $1.3 million public subsidy payment last month. The state provides the subsidy to candidates who agree to spending and fundraising limits. Klobuchar opted out of the subsidy, which allowed Demuth to receive a larger payment. Klobuchar didn’t participate in the subsidy because she would have had to cap her fundraising.
Klobuchar’s cash advantage will likely be compounded by Democratic-Farmer-Labor-aligned allies like the Alliance for a Better Minnesota, which has historically been backed by wealthy benefactors like Rockefeller heiress Alida Messinger and public-sector unions.
The Alliance for a Better Minnesota PAC has raised $3.55 million this year and has spent over $1.3 million on digital ads against Demuth.
In addition to the governor’s race, all 201 seats in the Minnesota Legislature will be on the ballot in November, so the rival legislative caucuses and political parties are fundraising and will spend big to gain control of state government.
House Democrats have raised $5.6 million this year and have $3.2 million in cash in the final weeks before the midterms. House Republicans have raised over $2 million this year and have about $2 million in cash.
Senate Democrats have raised $5.7 million and have nearly $5.2 million in cash. Senate Republicans have raised nearly $3 million this year and have $3.8 million in cash.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana community colleges face faculty poaching from new industry
description: Major companies investing in Louisiana are looking to the state’s community and technical colleges to supply their workforce, and they are also poaching the instructors who teach there, the school system’s leader said this week.  A series of major industrial projects are coming to Louisiana, touting numerous high-paying jobs that require specialized training[...]
text:
Louisiana Community and Technical College System President Richard Nelson. (Greg LaRose | Louisiana Illuminator)Major companies investing in Louisiana are looking to the state’s community and technical colleges to supply their workforce, and they are also poaching the instructors who teach there, the school system’s leader said this week. 
A series of major industrial projects are coming to Louisiana, touting numerous high-paying jobs that require specialized training, most notably the Hyundai steel plant in Ascension Parish, the Meta Hyperion data center in Richland Parish and a Space X launch facility in Vermilion Parish. 
Their staffing demands are straining the state’s ability to train enough students to ensure the new jobs go to Louisianians, Louisiana Community and Technical College System President Richard Nelson told the Board of Regents at its monthly meeting Tuesday. 
Another challenge for the system as it tries to fill those jobs is the companies hiring highly-skilled tradespeople from community colleges who are training the next generation of workers, higher education leaders said at a budget hearing Tuesday. 
“We can’t produce 10 times, 100 times more welders or plumbers if everyone is poaching all of our faculty,” Commissioner of Higher Education Kim Hunter Reed said. “So that issue has to be resolved, and companies need to stand in partnership with us as we try to do this work.” 
In addition to luring away faculty, Nelson said some companies are hiring students before they complete their training to meet their need for workers with even basic technical skills. 
Entry-level positions at the Meta data center start at $44,200 a year, according to figures from Louisiana Economic Development. The annual pay for lowest-paid workers at the SpaceX facility will be $78,000, while Hyundai has not made entry-level compensation for its steel mill jobs public.
Nelson said the demand for workers is so high that the system would have to double its enrollment for Louisiana residents to fill the available jobs. The system enrolls more than 100,000 students annually and awards credentials and degrees to over 30,000 students a year. 
To meet the workforce demand, Nelson said the LCTCS budget would have to increase more than $100 million annually. Its budget for the current academic year is $340 million. 
“What (we) really have to do is build that infrastructure to provide a much greater level of workforce than what we’ve been used to,” Nelson said. 
Nelson said the additional money could be used to pay skilled faculty enough to remain in their jobs, to build new training facilities and provide students with wraparound services, such as childcare and transportation.  
Starting up new programs to meet the needs of the companies currently hiring is more expensive than maintaining existing programs, according to Nelson. The cost primarily falls on the state rather than on the businesses, he said. 
Providing the funding needed to train their workers should be part of the conversation when big employers are looking to come to Louisiana, Nelson added.
“Once they sign the paperwork, well, now you have to actually provide the people, and it’s going to be over a period of years after that,” he said. “If there’s no funding to do that, what position are we in?”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Federal judge tosses Nessel suit accusing fossil fuel industry of anti-trust violations
description: Earlier this year, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel joined a number of states across the country in taking legal action against the fossil fuel industry when she filed a suit against four of the world’s energy companies and a major oil lobbying group accusing them of violating state and federal anti-trust laws to discourage competition […]
text:
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel speaks at a press conference on her lawsuit, alongside 25 other state attorneys general and governors, for a restraining order on the pause for SNAP benefits on Nov. 1. Oct. 29. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Earlier this year, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel joined a number of states across the country in taking legal action against the fossil fuel industry when she filed a suit against four of the world’s energy companies and a major oil lobbying group accusing them of violating state and federal anti-trust laws to discourage competition from renewable energy. 
However, a U.S. District Court judge on Tuesday determined Nessel lacks the standing to pursue federal anti-trust claims, granting in-part a motion to dismiss the case.
In the suit filed on behalf of the state of Michigan, attorneys for the state alleged that BP, Chevron, Exxon Mobil, Shell and the American Petroleum Institute had violated the Sherman Antitrust Act, the Clayton Antitrust Act and the Michigan Antitrust Reform Act. 
The suit argues the defendants had conspired with each other for decades to preemptively limit competition from renewable energy in order to maintain dominance over the energy market, resulting in harm to Michigan residents through overpriced energy, a lack of energy options on the market and increased costs to implement measures to counter the negative effects of fossil fuel use.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In her order, Judge Jane M. Beckering of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan determined that even if Michigan had adequately pleaded a conspiracy, “the antitrust laws protect against none of the injuries for which Michigan seeks a remedy, except for overcharges for energy.”
Beckering wrote that the state had plausibly alleged that the fossil fuel companies stifled innovation in and adoption of renewable energies, but ultimately determined that the state failed to show proximate cause proving that this conspiracy led to higher costs for Michigan residents.
“This decision adds to the growing list of federal and state courts that have dismissed climate lawsuits,” Chevron’s attorney, Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., said in a statement. “These climate suits are baseless no matter plaintiffs’ attempts to concoct new litigation theories, like these meritless antitrust claims.”
In a statement to Michigan Advance, Nessel Press Secretary Danny Wimmer noted the attorney general’s disagreement with the decision.
“Our office is reviewing the opinion in full and considering our options.” Wimmer said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: GOP general treasurer candidate pledges greater scrutiny of RI pension system
description: In politics, having connections can sometimes be the easiest way to get something done. But the Republican nominee for general treasurer, Micholas Credle, says you shouldn’t have to “know a guy” to get answers about how Rhode Island manages its money. Credle, who ran unopposed in the GOP primary, stood in the State House rotunda […]
text:
Micholas Credle, the Republican nominee for Rhode Island general treasurer, speaks at a State House press conference attended by other GOP candidates and retirees on Sept. 23, 2026. At far left is Rhode Island GOP Chairman Allyn Meyers. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)In politics, having connections can sometimes be the easiest way to get something done. But the Republican nominee for general treasurer, Micholas Credle, says you shouldn’t have to “know a guy” to get answers about how Rhode Island manages its money.
Credle, who ran unopposed in the GOP primary, stood in the State House rotunda Wednesday, alongside other Republican candidates and a handful of retirees, and pledged to bring greater transparency to how the state oversees its pension investments and other financial initiatives.
“Answers should not depend on connections,” Credle said during a press conference that drew only two reporters. “Rhode Islanders should not have to guess what happened to their money, they shouldn’t have to chase documents or know somebody to know something.”
A retired U.S. Army officer who was born in North Carolina, Credle grew up in Illinois and Indiana, and moved to Rhode Island in 2019. But he said Wednesday that he considers himself a Rhode Islander nonetheless.
“I live here, I pay taxes, I serve here,” said Credle, who resides in Providence.
The first-time office-seeker then offered his own example of a “guy” whose record, he said, should prompt Rhode Islanders to ask questions.
“I know a guy who holds public office and has been entrusted with responsibility,” Credle said. “I know a guy whose public record has generated questions about transparency and the stewardship of public resources.”
When announcing his bid for a second term earlier in April, General Treasurer James Diossa said he had worked to “protect the financial future of all Rhode Islanders,” highlighting the growth of the state’s pension fund and other efforts to manage the state’s money. 
But Credle said Rhode Islanders deserve more than assurances about how their money is being managed.
“Open the books,” he demanded. “Release every record.”
Credle also challenged Diossa to debate him, saying the sitting office holder has declined to acknowledge his candidacy or answer his questions.
Diossa was seen outside the State House about 10 minutes after Credle left the building. Asked by Rhode Island Current whether he would debate his Republican opponent, Diossa replied only that his campaign strategy is “traveling the state interacting with the voters.” He declined to comment on Credle’s press conference.
Credle said greater scrutiny of the state’s pension system is needed because many retirees remain frustrated with the state overhaul more than a decade ago championed by then-General Treasurer Gina Raimondo and enacted by the General Assembly. The changes suspended the 3% annual cost-of-living increases retirees had received before 2011 and instead tied increases to the pension’s funding level, investment returns and inflation.
“This is a miscarriage of justice,” Sandra Marzilli Paquette, a retired special educator who helped found the Advocates for COLA Restoration and Pension Reform group, said in an interview after the press conference. “People cannot afford medications. People cannot afford heat. They cannot afford to fuel their cars.”
Pensioners received a one-time 2% COLA adjustment after a 2015 settlement. Subsequent changes to the COLA structure came in 2023 and 2024, with the latter providing a fully calculated annual COLA to retirees who retired on or before June 30, 2012.
Paquette said she and other members of her group are supporting Credle because she believes retirees need someone in the Treasurer’s Office who will listen to their concerns and examine the pension system’s finances.
“He is acknowledging the fact that what occurred in 2011 should not have occurred, and he is acknowledging the fact that when he is [in office], he is going to look into this,” Paquette said of Credle. “He is going to see what went wrong, what our assets are.”
Credle  has worked in executive compensation and described himself Wednesday as an educator and “financial student.” He has also served as chairman of the Ward 12 Republican City Committee in Providence.
Early voting begins Oct. 14 ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Conversation: ‘There was some justice.’ Hisham Awartani on enduring and speaking out for Palestinian lives.
description:
Awartani was gravely wounded in 2023 when he and two friends were shot by Jason Eaton. A Vermont jury delivered a measure of justice this week when it convicted Eaton of three counts of attempted second-degree murder.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: ‘There was some justice.’ Hisham Awartani on enduring and speaking out for Palestinia[...]
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Hisham Awartani testifies during Jason Eaton’s trial in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Monday, September 14, 2026. Eaton is accused of shooting a now-paralyzed Awartani and two other Palestinian students in November of 2023. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Hisham Awartani thought he was going to die. That’s what he told a police dispatcher in desperation as he lay on the ground after being shot by Jason Eaton in November 2023. Awartani and two friends, all of whom are of Palestinian descent, were walking down North Prospect Street in Burlington when Eaton, whom they did not know, stepped off his porch and began firing at them without saying anything. All three friends were wounded, but Awartani, who was 20, was the most seriously injured.
A Vermont jury delivered a measure of justice this week when it convicted Eaton of three counts of attempted second-degree murder for the unprovoked shooting of the three young men. The weeklong trial included searing testimony from the survivors and the replaying of Awartani’s call to 911.
“There was some justice dealt, but obviously it doesn’t change what happened,” Awartani told me about the verdict. 
Awartani, Kinnan Abdalhamid and Tahseen Aliahmad have been friends since childhood in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. They were classmates at a Quaker high school in Ramallah and were all attending universities in the U.S. They were on Thanksgiving break and were visiting Awartani’s grandmother, who lives in Burlington.

READ MORE

The jury delivered its verdict in under two hours and rejected Eaton’s insanity defense, holding him fully responsible for his actions.
The verdict offered some closure on a shocking act of violence that drew national and international attention, coming two months into the latest Israel-Hamas war.
Awartani was gravely wounded in the attack. A bullet lodged in his spine, and he is now paralyzed from the chest down.
Awartani told me he is grateful for the medical care he received at UVM Medical Center and Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital in Boston, as well as an outpouring of community support in Vermont. But he has had mixed feelings about the extensive attention to his case. “To have access to such great healthcare and then at the same time, just see the large-scale destruction and death that was happening in Palestine … that part was dissonant for me definitely.”
“In Palestine, every single person who died, their life is just as rich as mine.” 
The death toll from the war in Gaza has topped 73,000 since Hamas forces attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. More than 1,200 Israelis were killed that day. 
Awartani said there is a connection between what is happening in Palestine and what happened to him. “Palestinian identity has become vilified,” he told me. 
Tahseen Aliahmed and Hisham Awartani outside of the Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington during the trial of Jason Eaton in September 2026. Contributed photo
“Violence against Palestinians being excused on a mass scale in Palestine … carried over to here, where simply wearing Palestinian clothing and outwardly identifying yourself as Palestinian is enough to be considered a terrorist and therefore getting shot.”
The families of the three young men released a statement after the verdict. “After three years of sorrow, loss, and struggle, our families finally feel relief,” they wrote. Although Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George said the evidence did not support a hate crime charge, the families insist that the young men were targeted in an act of hate.
They wrote, “We continue to work toward a world where hateful violence against Palestinians is called out for what it is — and stopped.”
Awartani is now 23. He graduated with honors from Brown University in May with a degree in archaeology and math. He plans to return to the West Bank for a year and then pursue graduate studies, perhaps in archaeology. 
As a Palestinian survivor of violence, Awartani feels a special responsibility. “I’ve been given a voice, and I would like to use that voice to amplify other people’s voices that have been silent or silenced,” he said. 
What gives him hope?
“Being surrounded by friends and family, both in the United States and in Palestine … helps us endure and be together,” he replied.
He is also encouraged by the shift in public opinion toward Palestine and the campus protests in support of Palestinian rights. “It’s building political machinery that hopefully … can effect large-scale positive change both in the United States domestically and internationally.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: 1,500 miles in six days: A two-day guaranteed package’s journey on the Postal Service scenic route
description: On Tuesday, Sept. 15, I paid $36 to send a small box containing a Minnesota Vikings jersey from Watertown to Rapid City by two-day mail guaranteed to arrive Thursday. It arrived Monday.  By then, U.S. Postal Service tracking information indicated it had traveled some 1,500 miles: from Watertown to Huron, Fargo, West Fargo, possibly Clearwater, […]
text:
A Postal Service sign marks the location of a post office in Rapid City, South Dakota, on Sept. 22, 2026. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)On Tuesday, Sept. 15, I paid $36 to send a small box containing a Minnesota Vikings jersey from Watertown to Rapid City by two-day mail guaranteed to arrive Thursday. It arrived Monday. 
By then, U.S. Postal Service tracking information indicated it had traveled some 1,500 miles: from Watertown to Huron, Fargo, West Fargo, possibly Clearwater, Minnesota, Sioux Falls, then back to Huron, Fargo, West Fargo, Sioux Falls and finally Rapid City. 
The second trip from Sioux Falls to Huron is where the routing system evolved from absurdity to performance art.
My usual route from Watertown to Rapid City is 360 miles, but perhaps I am not curious enough about the world.  
After its first arrival in Fargo, the location data next placed it in Clearwater at 5:04 a.m. Thursday. Clearwater is southeast of St. Cloud — roughly 130 miles east of Fargo and decidedly not on the way to Rapid City. 
Postal Service’s plan to speed up delivery in South Dakota is a ‘good first step,’ US senator says

It then supposedly reached Sioux Falls at 6:45 a.m. Either the Clearwater entry was delayed, or my box covered a four-hour drive in 1 hour and 41 minutes. If the Postal Service can move that fast, missing the two-day guarantee becomes even harder to explain.
The box also was recorded passing through Summit on Interstate 29 — maybe stopping for gas and directions. 
The package likely passed through Watertown five times — plenty of time to see attractions including the Redlin Art Center and Bramble Park Zoo, and maybe a boat ride on Lake Kampeska.
Somewhere inside the Postal Service, there must be a Scenic Route Division — an office where someone says, “Sure, Rapid City is west, but have we considered that it might take two trips to see all the sights in eastern South Dakota and North Dakota before moving on to Wall Drug and Reptile Gardens?”
In 1860, the Pony Express could move a letter more than 180 miles a day by changing horses and riders. My box had trucks, scanners and a two-day guarantee. The horses have a better performance record.
A friend of mine who owns a ranch in Wyoming has a building full of original Pony Express equipment. Who thought 166 years later he might be on the cutting edge of a new delivery system?
Meanwhile, Amazon says U.S. Prime members received more than 8 billion items the same or next day in 2025. 
A colleague said I should have just ordered a new Vikings jersey from Amazon. But this one is a replica of the one former Vikings quarterback Brad Johnson once wore. 
U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, has been asking for explanations for two years. He mailed a test letter from Rapid City to Pierre. According to Rounds, it visited Colorado, Nebraska, Iowa and North Dakota before reaching Pierre 10 days later.  
That’s nothing compared to what a woman in line Monday in Watertown said. Her mail from June just reached its destination. “And it was all local,” she said.
Rounds asked the Postal Service inspector general to investigate, invited South Dakotans to document delays, proposed withholding bonuses from postal executives when service fails and put a hold on nominees to the Postal Service’s governing board.  
The rest of the delegation also raised concerns. In 2024, Rounds, Sen. John Thune and Rep. Dusty Johnson warned postal leadership that moving processing out of South Dakota could mean delays and higher costs for rural communities. Johnson pressed the postmaster general again in July. Rounds has been the most persistent public voice in this fight. Thune, as Senate majority leader, needs to put more weight behind the demand for answers.


Let us know what you think...


 

The independent Postal Regulatory Commission warned of harm to rural communities and found that pilot versions of one transportation change slowed mail without producing the hoped-for savings. Somebody ought to ask executives how a missed guarantee, 1,500 miles worth of fuel and a subsequent refund fits in the savings calculation.
A glimmer of hope arrived Tuesday when the Postal Service announced improvements to its Sioux Falls plant that will keep more South Dakota mail in South Dakota for processing, hopefully reducing delivery times for some packages.
Meanwhile, there is a second trip in this story: mine. I took the package to the post office anticipating only one trip. I was told if it didn’t arrive by the guaranteed time to return with the receipt for a refund. I returned Friday and was told a refund must wait until the box was delivered.  
I returned Monday after it was delivered. They gave me a $36 postal money order redeemable at the post office. “But we can’t cash this one for 24 hours,” the clerk said. Even the refund can’t be delivered on the day it was promised.
So, I must return again. Maybe they will give me a commemorative stamp.
The package’s tracking receipt also doubles as a recruitment tool: “Looking for a new opportunity? Join a team that delivers!”
I may apply. The travel benefits look excellent.

name: VTDigger
title: As pharmacies across Vermont close, North Star Health opens 3 new ones
description:
The pharmacies take advantage of the health center’s federal designation that allows them to pay less for drugs, charge patients lower costs and still meet their bottom line. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  As pharmacies across Vermont close, North Star Health opens 3 new ones.
text:
North Star Health’s chief medical officer, pediatrician Dr. Sarah Weidhaas, pharmacy manager, Samantha Tyrrell, and CEO, Josh Dufresne, (right to left) officially open the Springfield Health Center’s pharmacy on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. Photo by Olivia Gieger/VTDigger
SPRINGFIELD — In the era of independent pharmacy closures and ballooning drug costs, a new pharmacy that charges less for drugs seems counterintuitive, if not impossible. 
But that’s exactly what North Star Health, a Federally Qualified Health Center that operates medical clinics in Vermont and New Hampshire, did when it officially launched three new pharmacies in Springfield, Londonderry and Charlestown, New Hampshire, on Tuesday. 
In Springfield, pharmacists, patients and local leaders filled the bottom floor of the old mill building that North Star now occupies for the official ribbon cutting of the small pharmacy. The space itself is hardly bigger than a telephone booth. Over the counter drugs — Tums, Advil, eye drops — line one wall, while two consultation windows, which open onto a larger pharmacy workspace, occupy another. 
The Springfield center also includes primary care clinics, behavioral health specialists and vision care.
As a Federally Qualified Health Center, North Star is eligible for certain federal funding opportunities and different Medicaid and Medicare reimbursement rates than other clinics and hospitals. Health centers like North Star are designated as federally eligible if they’re nonprofits serving medically underserved areas. Their pharmacies are also eligible to buy pharmaceutical drugs at a steep discount through a federal pricing initiative called the 340b drug pricing program.  

The small pharmacy within the Federally Qualified Health Center aims to fill a gap left by a series of independent pharmacy closures in southern Vermont. Photo by Olivia Gieger/VTDigger

With it, North Star’s pharmacies are able to buy drugs for far less than the sticker price, mark them up enough to make a profit and still charge patients less than what a for-profit retail pharmacy needs to charge. That reduction is especially important for brand-name drugs that have no generic alternatives, Samantha Tyrrell, the pharmacy manager at the Springfield center, said.
Without the program, the pharmacy would make no financial sense for North Star, Josh Dufresne, the CEO of the Springfield Health Center, told VTDigger. 
“We just barely make it work all the time. This (pricing program) is one of those pieces that if it went away, there needs to be another reimbursement mechanism or something that helps us break even,” he said. “We’re able to take that margin and offset the cost of providing primary care, which isn’t reimbursed very well, or behavioral health or whatever else.” 
Local pharmacies have certainly felt the squeeze in recent years. In May, Smilin’ Steve’s Pharmacy abruptly closed its Springfield, Ludlow and Woodstock locations. A year earlier, Rite Aid announced its bankruptcy and closed stores across southern Vermont. 
Between 2019 and 2024, Vermont lost 28 pharmacies, nearly one in five at the time, the state’s Board of Pharmacy told VTDigger in 2024. That same 2024 article analyzed pharmacy deserts in Vermont and found that more than one-fifth of the state’s census tracts had low access to pharmacies — with some of the least access in Windsor and Rutland counties, where North Star serves patients.  
Many attribute the trend to the ever-shrinking margin pharmacies are able to make from drugs. It’s not unusual for drugstores to be reimbursed for less than it cost them to purchase a drug, the Vermont Pharmacists Association has said. People point to the pervasive intermediary operators, known as pharmacy benefit managers, as shrinking the profit for pharmacies while inflating it for insurers and pharmaceutical companies. In 2025, only three companies — CVS’s Caremark, Cigna’s Express Scripts and UnitedHealth Group’s Optum Rx — processed 80% of the country’s prescription claims. 

Springfield Health Center’s pharmacy is able to sell many over-the-counter drugs at a reduced price from what many commercial pharmacies charge. Photo by Olivia Gieger/VTDigger

North Star and its patients saw the gap these national trends created in southern Vermont. Dufresne said the organization began exploring opening pharmacies in response to patient requests. 
Though Tuesday marked the pharmacies’ official ribbon cutting, the Springfield location began operations in November for patients who were willing to pay out of pocket or those covered by some commercial insurers. Now, it’s established contracts with Medicare, Medicaid and most insurers. 
When Smilin’ Steve’s pharmacy closed in May, the pharmacy saw an influx of patients, seeking to transfer prescriptions from a patchwork of specialists and doctors.   
“They came down here with a ream of paper that was transfers this thick,” Tyrell said, holding her thumb and index finger more than three inches apart.
Another benefit she and Dufresne both see of having in-house pharmacists is more organized care. 
North Star’s pharmacists read patient’s health records and consult with primary care clinicians one floor up. Dufresne sees that coordination as particularly beneficial for recruiting young primary care providers fresh out of school, which he said is one of the biggest challenges the health center faces.
Dufresne’s hope is that the pharmacy can slot neatly into North Star’s suite of primary care, vision, dental and behavioral health services. A truly healthy patient, he said, is one whose clinicians prioritize preventive care and keep them less reliant on pharmaceuticals altogether.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Childcare workers struggle to afford care for their own kids. NC communities are testing solutions.
description: DURHAM — At Kate’s Korner, the day begins early – children arriving, classroom doors opening, small voices calling for teachers, parents saying quick goodbyes before heading to work.  For the childcare center’s staff, the morning comes with one less worry: they don’t have to figure out how to pay for care for their own children.  […]
text:
The staff of Kate's Korner Childcare Center stands in front of the entrance in Durham. (Photo: Courtesy Kate's Korner)DURHAM — At Kate’s Korner, the day begins early – children arriving, classroom doors opening, small voices calling for teachers, parents saying quick goodbyes before heading to work. 
For the childcare center’s staff, the morning comes with one less worry: they don’t have to figure out how to pay for care for their own children. 
Kate’s Korner in downtown Durham serves more than 60 children from newborns to toddlers. The center offers a subsidy for workers with children of their own. (Photo: Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)
The center provides employees with free childcare, a benefit owner Kate Goodwin says is an intentional investment in the workers who care for other people’s children. Some employees use vouchers, but for those who can’t, the center covers all but one week of care a month. 
“As a business owner, I made a decision that my margins will be slimmer than most because I felt like this was the commitment I needed to make,” she said. “What we hear often is that our childcare providers can’t pay for the type of care and education they’re providing to others for their own child,” she said. 
The approach comes as childcare providers across North Carolina continue to grapple with recruiting and retaining workers.
If childcare workers can’t afford care for their own children, it becomes harder for centers to maintain the workforce they need. Staffing shortages take the shape of smaller classrooms, shorter hours and reduced enrollment.
Kate’s Korner isn’t alone in offering childcare for its employees. In a survey of about 1,200 childcare providers across the state, 61% of directors said their programs already offered a childcare benefit to their employees. 
But the way those benefits are funded varies. At Kate’s Korner, Goodwin said the center absorbs most of the cost. Meanwhile, other communities are testing whether businesses, nonprofits and governments can help shoulder that expense. 
 A local experiment 

Watauga County offers an example of how communities can help offset those costs, while also supporting the broader workforce. 
North Carolina’s labor force participation rate, or the percentage of those working or actively looking for work, is hovering around 58%, which is lower than the national average of around 61%. Business leaders say a lack of affordable childcare is a big part of the problem.
NC budget offers rural childcare businesses financial help they’ve sought for years

Childcare is one of the state’s lowest-paid professions. A study from Appalachian State University found that childcare workers earned an average of $30,600 a year, while the median monthly cost of childcare was $900. For a worker earning that average salary, one child in care would consume about a third of their gross income. 
And for workers earning even less, including in rural counties, the cost of caring for their own children can push them out of the industry in search of higher-paying work. 
To help ease a shortage of childcare in Watauga, the Boone Area Chamber of Commerce Foundation launched a childcare assistance initiative last year to help childcare workers pay for the care of their own children with $40,000 in funding from local donors and businesses. 
The program provided assistance to 18 childcare employees with 22 children, averaging $684 per child. 
David Jackson, Boone Area Chamber of Commerce president, said childcare is not just a family issue, but a workforce issue that directly impacts Watauga County’s economy. (Photo: Boone Area Chamber of Commerce)
David Jackson, president of the chamber, said programs like the one in Watauga can also help strengthen local workforces by giving employees another reason to stay with a center. 
“Center directors do not want to see their staff members just essentially handing their paycheck back,” he said. 
The initiative is part of a larger effort to support the childcare workforce and help providers who are still recovering from the loss of federal funding that helped stabilize the industry.
 A statewide model

Kentucky has taken a different approach to supporting providers statewide by investing state dollars. 
The state launched its Free Child Care for Child Care Workers Program in 2022, which subsidizes care for workers who work at least 20 hours a week at a center, regardless of household income. 
Kate Shanks, senior vice president of public affairs for the Kentucky Chamber of Commerce, said more than 5,300 families working in childcare benefited from the program over the past year. 
She said lawmakers made the program permanent earlier this year. 
“Quality childcare is a critical part of Kentucky’s economic infrastructure,” she said. “Childcare professionals provide an essential service that allows thousands of parents to go to work every day.” 
At least nine other states have since enacted similar policies, according to the Kentucky Chamber of Commerce. 
Goodwin said she supports creating a similar program in North Carolina to subsidize childcare for workers at centers across the state, and maybe expanding it to teachers, too.
“I don’t care if you say all childcare workers and educators get free childcare,” she said. “That’s an investment in our education system, all the way around.”

title: Most Georgians struggle with cost of living, researchers say
description: As many as 70% of Georgia residents are struggling to afford basic necessities, such as food, housing, healthcare or childcare, according to new data from the Georgetown Center on Poverty and Inequality. The data was released as part of the center’s national family economic well-being index, which measures the economic pressures that families are facing […]
text:
In Georgia, 36% of respondents said they were burdened by the cost of food according to new data from the Georgetown Center on Poverty and Inequality. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderAs many as 70% of Georgia residents are struggling to afford basic necessities, such as food, housing, healthcare or childcare, according to new data from the Georgetown Center on Poverty and Inequality.
The data was released as part of the center’s national family economic well-being index, which measures the economic pressures that families are facing and how severely they are being squeezed by the cost of living. In Georgia, 36% of respondents said they were burdened by the cost of food, and 48% said they faced challenges related to healthcare costs. Forty percent of respondents said they struggled to afford multiple basic needs.
Affordability is more than a political buzzword for many Georgia voters 

The data, researchers said, helps illustrate how rising costs of living are affecting Americans, particularly as affordability continues to be a central issue in the midterm elections.
“We’re hearing stories from people at all income levels who feel squeezed by the costs of those everyday essentials,” said Lelaine Bigelow, the center’s executive director. She added that the goal of the index was “to bring a data frame to this and see how widespread those pressures have become.”
One of the most striking results, she added, was the extent to which concerns about the cost of living crossed socioeconomic classes. Ninety nine percent of respondents in the bottom 20% reported facing at least one economic burden, but nearly half the population in the upper-middle 20% did too.
Economic hardship, Bigelow said, “is not limited to families who are experiencing poverty. It reaches well into the middle class.”
Policies at the state level also impact residents’ ability to afford things like healthcare and childcare, said Danilo Trisi, one of the researchers behind the index. In many southern states that chose not to fully expand Medicaid, a higher share of residents reported concerns about healthcare costs.
“The states that didn’t [expand Medicaid] have higher insurance costs and therefore show up in our index as having a higher percentage of the population burdened by healthcare costs,” Trisi said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT farmers protested a tax hike. This working group is offering solutions
description: The group was tasked with reviewing decades-old state farmland preservation law known as Public Act 490.
text:
State officials on Tuesday unveiled the final recommendations of a working group convened by Gov. Ned Lamont earlier this year to stave off a expected tax hike on many Connecticut farmers and come up with a way to overhaul the state’s process for setting farmland values.
The working group was asked to review and recommend changes to a decades-old state law known as Public Act 490, which aims to preserve farmland and open spaces by taxing those parcels of land according to their current use — rather than the fair-market value they could attract from developers.
Under the law, state officials are supposed to survey farmers every five years to come up with a new schedule setting the value of different types of farmland. Local assessors then use those values to calculate the owner’s property taxes.
When officials set out last year to conduct the regular revaluation, however, their efforts were plagued by low response rates and incomplete data. That, in turn, led to calculations that increased the value of the most productive types of farmland by over $1,000 per acre.
The biggest increases, however, came on the least valuable land — classified as swamp, ledge or scrubland — which saw its value increase by 2,325%. After many farmers protested the increases, Lamont cancelled the revaluation in January and assembled the working group to look into the issue. 
“The the big issue was the lack of data,” said Ben Freund, the co-owner of Freund’s Farms in East Canaan and a member of the PA 490 working group. “They tried to construct the recommended… valuations based on a limited [set of] data that they had. In some of the categories, you’re talking about very, very few data points. So we ended up with some extreme perversions of the valuations based on that — because they had nothing better.”
In order improve data collection moving forward, the working group recommended requiring landowners who participate in the PA 490 program to report certain data on leases and land use to town officials annually, rather than on a five-year cycle. Farmers will also be able to report information about land that is rented out via barter or for free. That information had previously been left out of the state’s calculations for land values.
During revaluations, any increase of more than 20% for a particular type of land over the previous valuation will automatically be reviewed by a committee made up of farmers, municipal leaders and assessors. 
Several of the group’s recommendations, including the annual reporting requirement, will require legislative action from lawmakers to take effect. Legislators are expected to take up the issue when they convene for their next session in January.
It will take at least two years of data collection under the new criteria before new land values for farmland are established, members of the working group said. Until then, local assessors will continue to utilize the 2020 values for tax purposes.
In a statement on Tuesday announcing the release of the working group’s final report, Connecticut Agriculture Commissioner Bryan P. Hurlburt  thanked members of the group, including several farmers, for their months of input. The group met more than a dozen times before voting unanimously to approve final recommendations on Tuesday, according to the meeting minutes. 
The new recommendations, Hurlburt said, “honor the spirit and intent of the original PA 490 program.”
“Connecticut is committed to keeping land available for farming, and your contributions have helped shape a path toward that goal,” Hurlburt said. “These recommendations will serve as a strong foundation as the legislature and others consider how best to support the future of agriculture in our state.”  
Connecticut Farm Bureau President Paul Larson, who also served as a member of the working group, said the recommendations will ensure farmers have more predictability and stability in their annual tax bills.
“[Lamont] personally assured me that we’re not going rush this. We want to do this and do it right,” Larson said. “We’re not going to institute new values until we know that they accurately reflect the proper value for farmland and the various classifications.”
The group’s other recommendations included revising the existing system for classifying farmland — which dates back to soil surveys from the 1960s — with new categories that are based on common uses such as annual crops, orchards, woodlands and pasture. The final report also recommended continuing to use a calculation based on rental rates to determine the value of most agricultural land (with the exception of forest and woodlands, whose values have traditionally been determined by the state Department of Energy and Environmental Protection).
Another issue the working group identified with the prior land valuation process was that it took parcels containing several different types of land classifications — such as tillable land and swamps — and averaged out the rental payments across those classifications. But officials determined that renters were likely only paying for certain types of usable farmland, which skewed the results.
To address the issue, Hurlburt said the group recommended the reporting form be simplified to allow landowners to specify how their leased lands are being used.
Kim Grijalva, who operates a 100-acre cattle in North Stonington, was among the most vocal critics of last year’s revaluation effort before being appointed to the working group. After what she described as a slow start in several early meetings, Grijalva ultimately praised Hurlburt and Office of Policy and Management Undersecretary Martin L. Heft for facilitating the group’s discussions.
“Overall, I think the state had a bit of a come-to-Jesus [moment] and said, you know, ‘Farmers are watching, they’re listening, and we don’t want to go there again,’ right?’ Grijalva said. “They don’t want to be the bad guys.”
Norwich Assessor Bill Lee was one of two representatives of the Association of Assessing Officers to serve on the PA 490 working group. On Wednesday, Lee said he hoped the publicity surrounding the failed revaluation and subsequent working group would spark renewed interest in the PA 490 program and the need for accurate data.
“At the end of the day, we’re counting on the people that need to return those surveys — and do it accurately — to actually do so,” Lee said.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana Supreme Court allows Butte data center initiative onto ballot
description: The Montana Supreme Court ruled this week that a Butte-Silver Bow citizens’ initiative to require voter approval of data center construction will appear on the November ballot.  In an order filed Tuesday, the court overturned a decision by the county elections administrator to retroactively change the deadline for submitting signatures for the initiative, wh[...]
text:
Historic uptown Butte, Montana (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan).The Montana Supreme Court ruled this week that a Butte-Silver Bow citizens’ initiative to require voter approval of data center construction will appear on the November ballot. 
In an order filed Tuesday, the court overturned a decision by the county elections administrator to retroactively change the deadline for submitting signatures for the initiative, which would have left the measure off the ballot. 
The measure came from grassroots citizens group, 406 People First, one of two groups seeking oversight of data center construction through ballot measures in Montana, with another in Yellowstone County. 
According to court documents, the county informed the organization that it had until Aug. 14 to collect the 3,652 signatures needed to get on the ballot, but on Aug. 10, the elections administrator said the submission deadline was actually July 13.
The change was in response to a new part of Montana law that passed the 2025 Legislature, increasing the time between signature submission and when election administrators had to verify signatures and approve ballots. 
That law, enacted through Senate Bill 11, passed unanimously and added a requirement that signatures be submitted four weeks before ballot certification — 10 days earlier than prior years. 
District Court Judge Frank Joseph issued a temporary restraining order on Aug. 12 while the matter wound through the court system, but on Aug. 28 ultimately sided with the city-county, concluding that the citizens group had to follow statutory deadlines regardless of how they were conveyed by elections staff. 
Denise Kelly, who is behind 406 People First, filed an emergency motion requesting an injunction with the supreme court seeking to overturn the district court’s decision. 
In its order, the high court determined the issue was of great public interest, citing the initiative’s efforts to exceed the number of individual signatures required to get onto the ballot — more than 3,652 county residents signed onto the petition. 
“The public interest is served by allowing the voters to decide their initiative powers,” the court wrote. 
However, the primary focus for the court was whether greater harm would occur if the initiative was left off the ballot, wrongly, or if it was put on the ballot, approved and then invalidated in the future for statutory violations.
The latter option — an approved initiative ultimately being overturned — is “a result we are loathe to contemplate,” the court wrote. 
“However, if we deny proponents injunctive relief with the result that the initiative does not appear on the November ballot, and we ultimately determine the district court erred, the result would be that the electorate would be denied their right to vote on an initiative that met the threshold requirements to appear on the ballot,” the order states. “The latter is the greater evil.”
The ballot initiative prohibits “any necessary authorization to construct or expand any data center within the city-county” without approval from voters.  
A similar effort for a ballot initiative in Yellowstone County faced a nearly identical problem with retroactively changed submission deadlines, but efforts to appeal the decision have not been successful.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Facing a lawsuit, SC Ports ratifies former CEO’s severance deal a year later
description: The South Carolina State Ports Authority retroactively voted on the nearly $1 million payout to its former CEO but denied it did anything to violate state laws.
text:
Barbara Melvin resigned from the S.C. State Ports Authority on Aug 21 2025, receiving a severance package of nearly $1 million. The deal has drawn the scrutiny of a public records advocate. (File photo courtesy of the S.C. State Ports Authority)MOUNT PLEASANT — The South Carolina State Ports Authority, embroiled in a lawsuit over its former director’s severance package, this week retroactively voted on the nearly $1 million payout to Barbara Melvin but denied it did anything to violate state laws.
The maritime agency’s board of directors on Tuesday unanimously approved the severance deal Melvin received in August 2025 after she abruptly resigned as president and CEO.
The severance package had not been previously voted on in public, prompting a lawsuit by Frank Heindel, a retired Mount Pleasant businessman and long-time public records advocate.
Heindel, in the lawsuit filed last month in Charleston County, alleges the authority violated both the state’s Freedom of Information Act and a separate law governing the maritime agency when it failed to vote on the severance deal.
Lawsuit argues SC Ports’ payout to former CEO violated state law

State law requires the authority to publicly vote on compensation — including severance — for the authority’s executive director and division directors.
The authority, in its response to the lawsuit filed last week, denied any wrongdoing and said the separation agreement did not require a public vote.
However, following a closed-door session Tuesday, authority board member and treasurer James Burns called for a vote on the matter, saying the lawsuit “is a distraction from the port’s overall mission, and I think we need to move forward.”
Burns said the severance package was part of an employment agreement the board had previously voted on but asked that it be ratified separately after the fact. There was no further discussion following the unanimous board approval.
Heindel this week questioned the board’s reasoning.
“If no public vote was required, as the ports authority told the court last week, there was nothing to ratify,” Heindel said. “The board’s vote confirms what the law required all along. It just came a year late and after a lawsuit.”
Heindel’s lawsuit also alleges the authority repeatedly violated public records laws by failing to state the specific purpose of closed-door sessions. Historically, authority chairman Bill Stern has recited a boilerplate list of all allowable purposes for an executive session without specifying which ones will be discussed.
On Tuesday, Stern stated just the two issues that would be discussed behind closed doors: contractual matters and the receipt of legal advice regarding agency personnel.
Heindel said that still doesn’t comply with state law.
“Announcing a ‘proposed contractual matter’ doesn’t meet FOIA’s specific-purpose requirement,” Heindel said, adding Stern’s description isn’t specific enough.
The state’s Supreme Court ruled in 2015 that FOIA law “is not satisfied merely because citizens have some idea of what a public body might discuss in private,” he said.
Heindel said he doesn’t want to litigate the terms of the severance agreement, which gave Melvin $822,780 in pre-tax salary continuation payments and a $100,000 contribution to her state retirement account.
Instead, Heindel said he wants a judge to declare the authority violated state law. He also wants an injunction banning the authority from taking similar action in the future, and he wants the agency to pay his attorney’s fees.
In addition, Heindel wants the authority to be ordered to post any finding that it violated state law on the agency’s website for six months.
A court hearing is scheduled for Oct. 19 in Charleston.
Melvin, who held the authority’s top job for a little more than three years, resigned without prior public notice on Aug. 21, 2025. She did not give a reason for her departure, other than to say she planned “to pursue other opportunities.”
Heindel has taken legal action in the past to hold public entities accountable.
For example, he sued Dorchester County in 2024 over its refusal to publicize the amount of water a Google data center will use once it is completed at the county’s Pine Hill Business Campus. The county ultimately relented after fighting for nearly a year in court, reversing its previous stance that the information was a closely guarded trade secret.
Last fall, Heindel sued for information on how the University of South Carolina distributed money to student athletes, which resulted in the state Legislature passing a law this year to keep such payments secret. The exemption from the Freedom of Information Act became law after legislators overrode Gov. Henry McMaster’s veto.
