outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: US Senate Republicans spotlight trans athletes issue as midterms approach
text: WASHINGTON — Republicans on the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee used a hearing Wednesday to continue voicing opposition to transgender athletes competing in women’s sports, which the top Democrat on the panel called a distraction from cost-of-living issues voters are more concerned about.Republicans, vying to defend their majority in the House and Senate in the midterm elections less than six weeks away, have pursued a broad anti-trans agenda alongside President Donald Trump’s administration. Republicans on  Wednesday framed the issue as protecting women’s sports. “Biological women should not be asked to accommodate men who, for reasons of identity or otherwise, choose to compete in (the) women’s category instead of (the) men’s or co-ed category,” said Sen. Chuck Grassley, chair of the Judiciary panel. “Women were last to get the vote, to participate in professions, to serve on juries, get credit cards in their own names and so much more,” the Iowa Republican said. “Women should not again be asked to cede their opportunities just to make men comfortable.” The GOP-led panel brought in advocates, who spoke out against transgender athletes’ participation in sports that align with their gender identity. Dems absentDemocrats on the panel largely sat the hearing out, drawing the ire of GOP members.In the only statement by a Democrat during the hearing, the panel’s ranking member, Sen. Dick Durbin, used his opening remarks to question his GOP counterparts’ priorities amid Americans’ affordability concerns. “If you ask the American people, ‘What are the priority issues you hope Congress will address as soon as possible?’ the issue of this hearing would not be in the top 10, maybe not the top 20,” the Illinois Democrat said. “People are concerned about the cost of living, they’re concerned about the ability to pay for the college education of their kids, they’re concerned about their utility bills, they’re concerned about their grocery bills — they want to know what we’re doing about it,” he added. Republicans on the panel noted Democrats’ absence.“Not one member on the other side of the aisle has had the respect for women to come in here and ask questions, to figure out how we get this right, how we stand up for fairness, for safety, for an opportunity for young women across the country,” GOP Sen. Katie Britt of Alabama said at the hearing. “It’s absolutely absurd.”But Durbin pointed to a similar 2024 hearing that saw NCAA President Charlie Baker tell senators that of the more than half-million total athletes in NCAA schools, he knew of fewer than 10 who were transgender. “We can all agree that we want to be fair and safe in women’s athletics, but this vendetta against a small number of people in the trans community affects everyone, including cisgender girls who can be subject to inappropriate gender verification checks,” Durbin said. At a press conference after the hearing, GOP Sens. Ashley Moody of Florida, Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, Darline Graham of South Carolina and Britt, along with several athletes and advocates, continued to blast the inclusion of trans athletes on women’s sports teams. “It shouldn’t be complicated,” Moody said. “Men do not belong in women’s sports. Women’s sports exist for a reason, and if we’re going to have women's sports, we must protect women’s sports.”Hot topicThe issue has been the subject of intense debate in recent years.The House passed a bill in January 2025 that would bar trans students’ participation in women’s school sports teams consistent with their gender identity. But Senate Democrats blocked an effort in March of that year aimed at imposing such a ban and codifying Trump’s 2025 executive order on the issue. The U.S. Supreme Court in June upheld state laws banning transgender athletes from participating on women’s and girls’ sports teams.The court’s decision — which has no impact on states without such bans — marked a major setback for transgender rights across the nation. Meanwhile, a major bipartisan bill to regulate college athletes’ compensation and establish additional protections for women’s and Olympic sports continues to advance in the Senate.Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans have made clear that the bill would not preempt state laws regarding the participation of trans athletes in women’s sports.

name: Delaware
title: What Delaware Republicans say they’d do if voters give them the chance
description: This week, Republicans unveiled their ‘2026 Contract with Delaware Voters’ DOVER, Del. — State Sen. Bryant Richardson, R-Seaford, and Delaware Republicans are pitching voters on a 10-bill platform ahead of November’s general election. It promises no state tax on overtime or tips, help for first-time homebuyers, deferred property taxes for seniors, and new ru[...]
text:
This week, Republicans unveiled their ‘2026 Contract with Delaware Voters’
DOVER, Del. — State Sen. Bryant Richardson, R-Seaford, and Delaware Republicans are pitching voters on a 10-bill platform ahead of November’s general election. It promises no state tax on overtime or tips, help for first-time homebuyers, deferred property taxes for seniors, and new rules on school sports and civics education.
Richardson unveiled the “2026 Contract with Delaware Voters” Tuesday at an event at the Delaware State Police Museum in Dover. It is modeled on the 1994 “Republican Contract with America,” the national platform U.S. House Republicans released weeks before the 1994 midterm elections, when they won control of the U.S. House for the first time in 40 years.
Delaware Republican Party Chairman Gene Truono said the Contract is important for the people of the state. “Like the Contract with America in the 1990s, the Contract with Delaware will help drive bipartisan conservative policy for generations to come,” Truono told Delaware LIVE.
What’s in the ‘2026 Contract with Delaware Voters’
The 10 bills fall into three categories:  Affordability Acts, Good Governance and Our Youth. Below are summaries of each. Click here to read the full “2026 Contract with Delaware Voters.”
1.) Affordability Acts:  Creates a tax-advantaged savings account for a first-time home down payment; lets homeowners 65 and older defer property taxes until the home is sold; eliminates state income taxes on overtime pay and tips.
2.) Good Governance:  Ensures police presence to prioritize neighborhood safety and keep repeat offenders off the streets; adds “informed choice” requirements for abortion; returns local control over issues such as right-to-work ordinances and offshore wind siting.
3.) Our Youth:  Requires student athletes to compete in sports matching their biological sex; requires students to learn what it’s like to live under communism, totalitarianism, and other political ideologies, alongside the principles of freedom, democracy, and individual liberty; creates Education Empowerment Accounts for tutoring, special education services, and instruction at public or private schools.
Why Republicans say their bills get stuck
Richardson’s central argument is that many of these ideas never get a vote. In Delaware, a bill needs signatures from a majority of a committee’s members before the full Senate or House can vote on it. Democrats hold 15 of 21 Senate seats and 27 of 41 House seats, and they control every committee.
His Fairness in Girls’ Sports Act is one example. Richardson has introduced a version in each of the last three General Assemblies, most recently as Senate Bill 215 in January, and none has been released from committee. The bill would have schools label each team boys’, girls’ or coed based on students’ sex as recorded at or near birth, while letting girls play on a boys’ team when no girls’ team exists.
Richardson says it protects fairness and privacy for female athletes; opponents have argued such bills discriminate against transgender students. Richardson said keeping it in committee lets lawmakers avoid taking a public stand.
Richardson says the “deeper problem” is that “when one side holds the votes to pass anything it wants, it no longer has to listen to the voices of those who disagree.” That’s a line from his self-published booklet, “Citizen’s Guide to Delaware Public Policy,” which he had available on a table at the event and told attendees to take.
“Eleven Republican senators could make a huge difference,” Richardson told supporters. “We would be the heads of the committee. We would get things out of committee for a full vote on the Senate floor.”
What it would take for Republicans to win a majority
Richardson acknowledged the climb is steep. With supermajorities in both chambers, Democrats can pass certain measures, like tax increases, without a single Republican vote.
To take the majority, Republicans need five more Senate seats and seven more House seats. Only 11 Senate seats are on the Nov. 3 ballot. Republicans hold three of them and have candidates in six of the eight held by Democrats, according to the Delaware Department of Elections’ candidate list, so a Senate majority would mean winning most of those races outright.
Two of those Republican candidates were at the event: Brent Burdge, running in the 5th Senate District, and Chris Rowe, running in the 7th. Rowe said voter education should extend to candidates themselves: “We just started electing people to office that don’t know the Constitution.”
State Rep. Lyndon Yearick, R-Magnolia, thanked Richardson: “You’re the tip of the spear, but it’s gonna take everybody.”
Sen. Dave Lawson, R-Marydel, who is not seeking reelection, closed with a direct appeal to the room: “Delaware needs this. Every one of you has a Facebook, and has friends. If you’re not handing this out, you’re not helping your grandchildren.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: House GOP bill would require secretary of state to step aside from election duties if on the ballot
description: Democratic members serving on a state House election integrity panel said Tuesday that they had concerns about a Republican bill that would require Michigan’s secretary of state to recuse themselves from election-related duties if they are also on the ballot in a given election year. The legislation, House Bill 5968, aims to protect the state’s […]
text:
Michigan Capitol | Susan J. DemasDemocratic members serving on a state House election integrity panel said Tuesday that they had concerns about a Republican bill that would require Michigan’s secretary of state to recuse themselves from election-related duties if they are also on the ballot in a given election year.
The legislation, House Bill 5968, aims to protect the state’s elections from what Republican members of the House Election Integrity Committee have called potential biases from an incumbent secretary of state with a vested interest in winning or retaining their seat. 
Sponsored by state Rep. Jennifer Wortz (R-Quincy), the bill wouldn’t just affect a secretary of state who is seeking their respective office again, but also if that current secretary of state was seeking another high office, such as the governor, attorney general, the state Legislature or either chamber of Congress.
While Republican supporters have described the measure as an additional accountability safeguard established by the Legislature, Democrats see the bill as patently political, aimed squarely at Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who is the Michigan Democratic Party nominee for governor, running against Republican U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township.
Benson has rejected concerns about her being on the ballot this year and also being the head of Michigan’s Department of State — mainly by noting that the state has a decentralized election process that is run by county and local clerks, and with oversight from the Bureau of Elections rather than Benson personally.
Still, in her presentation of the bill to the House committee on Tuesday, Wortz specifically called out Benson’s presence on the ballot as a major concern, and said that it wasn’t just her being the head of the office. Wortz also detailed concerns that the department promulgates election-related rules and hands out process manuals with specific instructions to local clerks, and that those rules and instructions can sometimes change year to year.
“When Secretary Benson announced her run for governor last year, one of the first questions I began discussing with colleagues and constituents was, ‘Who carries out her election duties?’” Wortz said. “We dug into the law and found that there are actually no ethics provisions on this in Michigan statute currently. I see this as a clear problem.”
State Rep. Jennifer Wortz (R-Quincy) gives a presentation to the Michigan House Election Integrity Committee on House Bill 5968 on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. (Screenshot)
Wortz said she’s had conversations with constituents on both sides of the aisle about the ethical issues that might arise from a campaign that includes the state’s chief elections officer. 
“Everyone seems to agree that there is no downside to requiring more protections and common sense accountability measures,” Wortz added.
The bill states that recusal would be required, not voluntary, and that the deputy secretary of state would be appointed to oversee the state’s election if the secretary was on the ballot in any capacity.
State Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren) was among the first to raise questions about the process proposed by the legislation, and its legitimacy overall.
“Respectfully, you know, and everyone in the Legislature here knows, that our elections are run by local clerks, county, township, city,” Xiong said. “I’m just trying to understand your logic behind the secretary of state administering elections because elections are managed at the local level. Our elections are decentralized, and even in 2018, when state Sen. Ruth Johnson ran for secretary of state, she ran her own election.”
Johnson is a Republican.
Xiong asked Wortz if she would entertain an amendment that would require any local or county clerk seeking higher office to recuse themselves from running their individual elections. The amendment would impact Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini, who manages elections for one of the largest counties in the state, and is currently the Republican nominee for Secretary of State.
State Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren) reacts to a presentation to the Michigan House Election Integrity Committee on House Bill 5968 on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. (Screenshot)
Wortz did not acknowledge Xiong’s mention of Forlini’s race but did argue against her call for an amendment.
“I would say quite the opposite,” Wortz said. “What we actually see is where rules are being set, and guidance is being offered, decisions that are being made from the secretary of state’s office that local clerks are required to implement. Rules sets that change without any oversight by the Legislature. I’ve sat on the Joint Committee on Administrative Rules for two years. We’ve yet to meet at all this year. When that rule set change came in and was proposed, we didn’t have a quorum, so we couldn’t vote.”
Wortz said that the House, as elected leaders, should be the ones making the laws, and that they don’t even have the ability to weigh in on election rules because of the way the system is set up to allow the department to promulgate those rules or set new guidelines.
State Rep. Matt Koleszar (D-Plymouth Township) raised concerns about the proposed statute calling for the deputy secretary of state to be appointed in the secretary’s stead if they were up for an important office. Koleszar noted that the deputy secretary of state position is not detailed in state law, and that a future secretary might not see a need to appoint a deputy at all.
If that were the case then, Koleszar asked, then who would be appointed for the role instead?SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Of note, Deputy Secretary of State Aghogho Edevbie was at one time a secretary of state candidate in the 2026 primary, but dropped out after Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist entered the race.
Wortz didn’t have a clear answer for either situation, but said that she and the bill’s drafters could look into it.
State Rep. Pat Outman (R-Six Lakes) had concerns about a situation where the deputy secretary of state may have made donations to the incumbent secretary’s political campaign. He asked if there would be an ethics provision baked into the law.
Wortz said there was not, but admitted that was an interesting point that she hadn’t considered. She said that would also be something to think about as the bill moves along in the process.
Members of the committee adopted substitute language for the bill but did not vote to report the bill to the House floor.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: UL System schools share team-level revenue sharing budgets despite new state law
description: Louisiana Tech University will spend nearly $2 million in public money to pay its student-athletes this year, while the University of Louisiana at Lafayette will devote $1.5 million to its sports teams.   Team-level payout details for four UL System sports programs, money for which comes from revenue generated on each campus, were accidentally included in […[...]
text:
Louisiana Tech’s Trey Baldwin and Levi Bell play against Southeastern Louisiana University at Joe Aillet Stadium on Sept. 11, 2021. Tech won 45-42.  (Photo by Emerald McIntyre/Louisiana Tech University)Louisiana Tech University will spend nearly $2 million in public money to pay its student-athletes this year, while the University of Louisiana at Lafayette will devote $1.5 million to its sports teams.  
Team-level payout details for four UL System sports programs, money for which comes from revenue generated on each campus, were accidentally included in documents posted online for last month’s University of Louisiana Board of Supervisors meeting. 
Earlier this year, Louisiana lawmakers overwhelmingly passed Act 818 by Rep. Tehmi Chassion, D-Lafayette, which allows universities to shield how much they pay to individual athletes and each athletic team from public view. The law specifies that only the total spent on all teams must be disclosed. 
The law applies to athletic departments’ self-generated revenue, which Division I schools are allowed to use to directly pay players for their name, image and likeness. It is separate from private NIL deals athletes make with sponsors that are protected from public scrutiny.
Louisiana law treats all self-generated revenue from state college campuses and other agencies as public money that requires legislative approval for how it is spent. 
Despite the new law on revenue-sharing details, team-level information from the UL System schools was disclosed in documents posted online for the Aug. 27 UL Board of Supervisors meeting. At the time this report was published, the information was still available online. 
Brandon DeCuir, an attorney who represents the UL System, said the information was disclosed in error. He said the information should not be used without authorization and asked the Illuminator to delete the documents, which are still posted on the system’s website. 
Scott Sternberg, a First Amendment attorney who has represented the Illuminator, said journalists have a right to publish information they obtain legally. 
“Documents that are made publicly available by the government are fair game, even if the government made a mistake,” Sternberg said. “It’s a long-held principle in the law that as long as [journalists] obtained it legally, [they] can report on the documents.”   
Chassion’s law, which passed with the support of athletics officials from the UL System and LSU, nullified a lawsuit reporters from the Illuminator and other news outlets filed to find out how much public money LSU was paying to student athletes.
The UL board meeting documents show that of the schools participating in revenue sharing, only Grambling State University did not disclose team-level data. Grambling’s total amount budgeted for the current academic year is $460,000. 
McNeese State, Nicholls State and the University of Louisiana at Monroe will not use public money to pay players. ULM spokesman Adam McDonald said its athletic program’s private NIL budget was approximately $2 million, which meant it did not need to rely on public money for its athletes.   
Louisiana Tech reported budgeting $1.98 million to pay players, of which $1.2 million will be used for football, nearly $500,000 for men’s basketball, $200,000 for baseball and $86,000 for all women’s sports. 
Northwestern State’s $750,000 will be spread out, with $300,000 for football, $350,000 for men’s basketball and $100,000 for all women’s sports. 
The University of Louisiana at Lafayette budgeted $1.5 million for revenue sharing, of which $591,895 is for football, $647,500 for men’s basketball, $120,600 for baseball and $157,354 for all women’s sports. 
Southeastern’s revenue sharing was erroneously reported in the wrong budget category in the UL board meeting documents. School spokesman Mike Rivault clarified in a written statement that its budget for paying players is $454,000, with $404,500 for men’s basketball and the rest for all women’s sports.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: State to help fund Rapid City office building for defense contractor Northrop Grumman
description: RAPID CITY — Getting Ellsworth Air Force Base removed from a closure list 21 years ago was the beginning of the work needed to secure the base’s future in western South Dakota, Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said Wednesday. “Once we knew Ellsworth was safe, we also knew that building up the base’s infrastructure and […]
text:
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden speaks on Sept. 23, 2026, at the David Lust Accelerator Building in Rapid City during the announcement of a planned addition to the facility that will house an office for defense contractor Northrop Grumman. Seated around Rhoden, from left, are Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun, Northrop Grumman Vice President Nikki Kodama, Elevate Rapid City CEO Jack Valentine, Air Force Col. Erick Lord and Ellsworth Development Authority Executive Director Scott Landguth. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)RAPID CITY — Getting Ellsworth Air Force Base removed from a closure list 21 years ago was the beginning of the work needed to secure the base’s future in western South Dakota, Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said Wednesday.
“Once we knew Ellsworth was safe, we also knew that building up the base’s infrastructure and developing the region to attract others in the defense industry was the best way to prevent future threats,” Rounds said.
Over the past two decades, local and state officials have worked to expand the base’s training airspace, add a remotely piloted drone unit, clear potential crash zones of development, and make Ellsworth the first base to host new B-21 stealth bomber planes next year, among other initiatives. The goal is retaining the estimated 9,000 people the base brings to the area, including military members, their families and civilian employees, and the estimated $800 million annual economic impact they help generate.
The latest effort came to fruition Wednesday with the announcement that Virginia-based defense contractor Northrop Grumman — which is developing B-21s for the Air Force — will establish an office in an $18 million building to be constructed in Rapid City, less than 10 miles west of the base.
Elevate Rapid City, a local economic development partnership, will build the facility on undeveloped land next to its David Lust Accelerator Building, a business incubation complex in eastern downtown Rapid City’s Innovation District. The accelerator building hosted Wednesday’s announcement.

Conceptual drawings of a planned addition to the David Lust Accelerator Building are displayed in the Rapid City building on Sept. 23, 2026, during an announcement that defense contractor Northrop Grumman will anchor the addition. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)

The announcement did not include an estimate of the number of jobs Northrop Grumman will bring to the city, but an executive said the company has scheduled about 50 interviews for the “first wave” of future employees. The combined number of the company’s employees at Ellsworth and the Rapid City office could ultimately number in the “hundreds,” said Elevate CEO Jack Valentine in an interview with South Dakota Searchlight. Elevate will work to recruit additional tenants to the facility.
The state and the Ellsworth Development Authority will each contribute $1 million to help Elevate with the project.
State lawmakers created the authority in 2009 to help secure the base’s future, and Executive Director Scott Landguth told Searchlight the authority has been self-funded for about six years through land deals, federal grants and other sources.
Gov. Larry Rhoden announced that the state’s contribution will be a $1 million grant from the Future Fund, a pool of economic development money under his control. The money comes from a fee paid by employers when they submit taxes to support unemployment benefits.
“Northrop Grumman is sending a strong signal about their belief in the opportunities that are available right here in South Dakota,” Rhoden said.
Rhoden was among dozens of state, local and military leaders in attendance Wednesday. Rounds submitted his comments by video from Washington, D.C.
The state’s support of the project furthers Rhoden’s goal, which he announced nine months ago in his annual State of the State address, to make national security the next big industry in South Dakota.
In April, Rhoden awarded a $6 million Future Fund grant to create the South Dakota Defense Institute, which will work to attract more defense contractors to the state. The institute has since been organized as a nonprofit with a board that is searching for a CEO.
The institute will be housed in a building acquired by Elevate at 14 St. Joseph St. in Rapid City, about a block away from the accelerator building.


 A map shows the locations of Ellsworth Air Force Base, the David Lust Accelerator Building in Rapid City and the neighboring site of a planned $18 million addition, and the future site of the South Dakota Defense Institute.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Federal disaster aid unlikely for many more Indiana counties from August storms
description: Indiana officials don’t expect many more counties will be added to the 21 already approved for federal disaster aid from last month’s severe storms and flooding.
text:
Indiana Gov. Mike Braun speaks alongside state Department of Homeland Security Executive Director Jonathan Whitham during a news conference in the State Emergency Operations Center on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana officials don’t expect many more counties will be added to the 21 already approved for federal disaster aid from last month’s severe storms and flooding.
Gov. Mike Braun told reporters Wednesday that more than $100 million in disaster assistance had been distributed in Indiana by the Federal Emergency Management Agency related to the storms that crossed the state starting Aug. 11. 
Braun and other officials outlined the progress of the state’s debris-removal program, through which nearly 80,000 cubic yards of debris such as damaged home belongings and downed trees have been removed in 33 communities.
At least an estimated 190,000 cubic yards of debris is still awaiting clean up from riverbeds and elsewhere, the governor’s office said.
A federal major disaster declaration was approved last month for 21 Indiana counties after Braun had requested that designation for 54 counties.
With most damage reports already submitted, Braun said it was unlikely that more counties would qualify.
“I’d be surprised if that’s going to happen, but we do get a little bit coming in, even though it’s been some time,” Braun said.
Nevertheless, state Homeland Security Executive Director Jonathan Whitham said about 14 counties remained under FEMA review on whether they had enough storm-related damage to qualify for federal assistance.
“We’ve got a list of counties that have been requested that we’re still waiting to hear back on,” he said. “So outside of those, I don’t expect a significant surge. There may be one-offs. We have been continuing to gather data, even as recently as yesterday (Tuesday), from some of these counties.”

The Louisiana Office of Motor Vehicles has replaced its 50 year-old electronic driver's license system with new software, Gov. Jeff Landry announced Tuesday. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)Louisiana has upgraded its technology for issuing driver’s licenses, an improvement that Gov. “We came into office with a promise to fix it and we did,” Landry said in a video his communications office released Tuesday. 
The state Office of Motor Vehicles replaced its decades-old system with a platform from CHAMP Titles Inc., a Cleveland, Ohio-based company. OMV locations were closed statewide last week to give the agency time to switch to the new system. 

Landry said the new software is going to “cut hours off of getting your driver’s license.”
“We promised we were going to make getting a driver’s license kind of like going to Disney World and we are instituting it right here,” Landry said in a social media video.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana to study adding more wildlife crossings
description: The Montana Department of Transportation wants to improve wildlife crossings along U.S. Highway 89, near Dome Mountain in Park County. The state announced on Monday it was launching a feasibility study into wildlife fencing and two different wildlife overpasses along the highway. “This section of U.S. 89 serves as an important corridor for both travelers […]
text:
Rep. Ken Walsh speaks during a bill signing ceremony at the Jens exit of I-90 near Goldcreek, Montana on Monday, Aug. 26, 2025. That MDT fencing effort was part of an effort to direct elk off the interstate as Montana continues to look for ways to address animal strikes. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)The Montana Department of Transportation wants to improve wildlife crossings along U.S. Highway 89, near Dome Mountain in Park County.
The state announced on Monday it was launching a feasibility study into wildlife fencing and two different wildlife overpasses along the highway.
“This section of U.S. 89 serves as an important corridor for both travelers and wildlife. Animals, including elk, deer and other species, regularly move through the region, and high rates of animal vehicle collisions … occur,” a MDT project webpage states. “The purpose of the study is to explore whether wildlife mitigation improvements can reduce crashes while maintaining safe movement across the landscape.”
Wildlife overpasses have been used in Montana, with one example being on Highway 93 entering the Flathead Indian Reservation. The state of Washington has also built wildlife overpasses as a way to reduce conflicts between humans and animals.
The concept includes an 8-foot tall fencing along the highway, with the barrier naturally pushing animals to one of the wildlife overpasses. Wildlife overpasses are essentially large structures that have grass and plants on them, which animals can then follow over the roadway instead of moving onto the highway. 
Montana has recently been focused on the issue, and Gov. Greg Gianforte signed two bills at the site of a recently completed MDT project last summer that created a program for wildlife crossings and a mechanism to fund it.
The cost of the study is $601,000 according to Big Sky Public Relations, which is handling the communication work for the project.
Research from State Farm has indicated Montanans have the second-highest chance of striking an animal of any state in the country. 
“This study is an important first step in understanding what wildlife crossing improvements may be feasible along this section of U.S. 89,” Kelly Williams, an MDT consultant design engineer, said in a press release. “At this stage, we are evaluating options, not advancing a construction project. The study will provide information that can help inform future decisions about whether a project should move forward.”
The study is expected to be completed next year and an informational meeting is scheduled at Six Mile Creek Picnic Area on Bridger Hollow Road in Pray, Montana, from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m., Sept. 24.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CCSU president resigns following complaint of bullying, retaliation
description: Central CT State University President Zulma Toro announced she will resign. The move comes after allegations Toro bullied employees.
text:
This story has been updated.
Central Connecticut State University President Zulma Toro said she plans to resign in a letter circulated university-wide Wednesday morning. 
The announcement came in the wake of a complaint against Toro, in which school administrators alleged she had bullied and intimidated employees.
The president of CCSU’s administrative faculty union, Lisa Bigelow, filed the complaint following an incident at an off-site leadership retreat in August. CT Examiner reported that during the retreat, Toro allegedly screamed at an administrator who contradicted her, then screamed at the rest of the staff before canceling the remainder of the event.
The complaint also alleged Toro had verbally abused staff on other occasions and made staff members take care of her mother and dog.
In her letter Wednesday, Toro made only an oblique reference to the allegations against her, writing, “It is time now for new leadership to tackle the challenges ahead. The last few weeks have been unbelievably hard on me, my family, and so many across our Central community.”
She also praised the university’s accomplishments during her tenure of almost 10 years and painted its future in optimistic tones. “We have worked hard and accomplished extraordinary things together; because of that hard work, I truly believe that Central’s best days are still to come,” Toro wrote.
The Connecticut Mirror’s attempts to reach Toro and Bigelow Wednesday were unsuccessful.
Wednesday was Toro’s last working day. According to an agreement between Toro and the university, viewed by CT Mirror, she will remain an employee until Oct. 1, at which point she will formally retire.
Sam Norton, a spokesperson for the Connecticut State Colleges and Universities system, said in a statement that Toro’s resignation “follows discussions between Dr. Toro and CSCU leadership about the best path forward for Central.”
Norton also addressed the allegations. “Recent concerns regarding Central’s workplace environment are serious, and CSCU has an obligation to listen when members of our community raise concerns, respond appropriately, and ensure our campuses are places where people are treated with dignity and respect.”
But the investigation into Toro’s conduct will not continue following her resignation and retirement, Norton said. An announcement regarding interim leadership will be made in the coming days.
Toro’s is the latest in a string of recent high-level departures from the CSCU system. 
Earlier this year, Interim Chancellor John Maduko resigned in response to allegations of sexual misconduct. Not long after, the chair of the CSCU Board of Regents, Marty Guay, resigned amid allegations he had urged a victim of Maduko’s not to report the misconduct. CSCU General Counsel Karen Buffkin has also been placed on paid administrative leave amid questions over how she handled the complaint against Maduko.
State Sen. Derek Slap, D-West Hartford, who is co-chair of the legislature’s Higher Education and Employment Advancement Committee, called on CSCU to be more careful in selecting Central’s next leader.
“It is clear that the vetting process has not worked as intended and campus stakeholders know what kind of leadership is required to ensure success. I implore the Board to make listening a key piece of their next steps,” Slap said in a statement.
The ranking Republican on the committee, Sen. Henri Martin, R-Bristol, said in an emailed statement, “What students, faculty, lawmakers and overburdened taxpayers want and deserve boils down to one word: Accountability. But that accountability is unfortunately in very short supply.”

text:
The website of Connect for Health Colorado, the state's health insurance marketplace, is pictured on Aug. 27, 2025. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Coloradans who buy their health insurance on the individual market, rather than getting coverage through their employer, will see around a 10% increase in their premiums next year, the state’s Department of Insurance announced Tuesday.
The state’s average is less than the 15% national median, but it differs based on region. People in the Grand Junction area will experience a 15.5% increase, while those in the Eastern Plains are on the lower end with a 5.9% increase.
In the small group market, premiums are expected to increase by 14%. Rates increase every year to some extent.

“Despite the loss of the enhanced premium tax credits, we are doing everything we can to keep health insurance prices down so Coloradans can afford access to health care,” Michael Conway, the state’s insurance commissioner, said in a statement. “I want to thank our rate review team for all their hard work this filing season. Because of their diligence, we are saving Coloradans millions of dollars. But make no mistake: Congress still needs to restore the subsidies that millions of Americans relied on to afford their health insurance.”
Conway was referring to Congress’s failure to extend subsidies, known as enhanced premium tax credits, that helped people afford health insurance on the individual market set up by the Affordable Care Act.
Colorado’s individual health insurance marketplace is called Connect for Health.
Colorado lawmakers passed a bill this year to fund its own smaller insurance subsidy. Financially-assisted customers in Colorado will have a monthly premium increase of around $20, versus around $69 per month without the support, according to the state.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: ‘Let the little children come to me’: SC moms lack childcare options
description: I spent an afternoon calling more than 50 childcare centers in one Sumter ZIP code. I called every single one. A mother we were trying to help had an infant and a school-age child, whose father had been deployed. She needed care for both children on a schedule that didn’t align with 9 a.m. to […]
text:
According to a survey released in August 2025, childcare disruptions cost South Carolina an estimated $997 million annually in employer costs and lost tax revenue. (File photo by Vanessa Nunes/Getty Images)I spent an afternoon calling more than 50 childcare centers in one Sumter ZIP code. I called every single one.
A mother we were trying to help had an infant and a school-age child, whose father had been deployed. She needed care for both children on a schedule that didn’t align with 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Her job, like so many available to mothers here, needed her some evenings and weekends, not the typical daycare center’s hours.


To read more commentaries in this series, click here.


Fifty-plus calls. Not one center could take both children.
I hung up the phone feeling like a failure. One number at a time, I had personally confirmed that Sumter did not have a place for her children to be cared for while she went to work.
For mothers raising children alone, work is an economic necessity, and for many families receiving public assistance, it is also a condition of receiving help.
Parents receiving temporary cash assistance must work, seek employment or participate in job training. Food assistance has similar requirements if their children are older than 13.
Even childcare assistance is largely tied to employment.
The logic makes sense: help families while parents work toward greater stability. But it creates an impossible equation when the childcare required to go to work is unaffordable or simply doesn’t exist. We can require a mother to work. We cannot require a childcare slot to appear.
I am a working mother of four. I have not worked full-time since we had children. Even with a spouse, grandparents and neighbors who help, a church preschool program, in-home daycare,
a stretch of years as a stay-at-home mom, and for a while, a part-time nanny, it has never stopped being a juggling act.
Today it’s afterschool care, summer camps, and backup plans stacked on backup plans. And I am, by any honest accounting, one of the fortunate ones.
If it takes that much outside support for someone with every advantage stacked in her favor, what does it mean that the mother I was calling on behalf of had almost none of it?
I’ve since learned that some local mothers are selling plasma to pay for childcare. I heard that at a listening session from a provider watching families leave her program after eligibility changes cost them the childcare scholarships that made care affordable. Nearly every child in her care depends on financial assistance.
Parents are scraping together tuition from grandparents, friends, and their own blood.
Everyone loses. Without subsidized care to fall back on, the mother often loses her job and with it, any stability she’s built for her family. The provider loses enrollment and may have to close her doors.
Childcare disruptions cost South Carolina an estimated $997 million annually in employer costs and lost tax revenue, according to a survey released in August 2025.
Childcare workers lose, too, earning an average $13.34 an hour as of May 2023. That’s far less than a living wage. Center-based care for two children now costs more than average rent in every state, and help is disappearing.
South Carolina has paused new and renewal applications for its Working Families childcare scholarship, citing insufficient funding.
Children lose the most of all.
High-quality early care strengthens language, social skills, and school readiness, particularly for children from low-income families. Statewide, fewer than 4 in 10 South Carolina kindergartners arrived ready for school in 2024, with children who lack access to quality early education facing the greatest barriers.
According to an often cited (but outdated) statistic from 2018, 42% of South Carolinians live in childcare deserts, where there are more than three young children for every licensed childcare slot. Availability could be worse today.
I didn’t need that statistic. I’d already experienced it.
When the disciples tried to turn children away, Jesus stopped them.
“Let the little children come to me,” he said.
Children belong first to their families, but they also grow up within communities.
What happens to them matters to all of us.
That conviction runs through the rest of Scripture too. Widows and orphans are named again and again as a community’s responsibility, not a private misfortune for one family to bear.
A single mother raising children alone occupies much the same place today. Yet, we often leave her to figure it out by herself.
We say we value families, yet we have built a system that makes it nearly impossible for many mothers to care for their children and hold down a job. The mother I called on behalf of is still cobbling something together out of friends, luck, and an employer’s patience that could run out any day. I don’t know how her story ends. Neither does she.
What would it look like if we meant “let the little children come” — not only as something we say, but as something our systems made possible?

name: Mississippi Today
title: 2nd man denied bond in death of Tasia Fortune, as Jackson police search for more suspects
description: Christy Spivey poses with a portrait of her late daughter Tasia Fortune, Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, in Marion, Ky.
text:
A second man was denied bond Wednesday in connection with the killing of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four who was found last month hanging from a tree in west Jackson. 
Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney announced the arrest of Earnest Lloyd Jr., 25,  Tuesday at the Jackson City Council meeting. She said the Jackson Police Department is seeking help from the U.S. Marshals Service to arrest at least one other person. 
Last week, police charged Jarques Ratliff, 51, with Fortune’s killing. He pleaded not guilty and remains in custody after being denied bond. His attorney said a preliminary hearing is scheduled for Friday.
“I will guarantee you, there are actually more arrests to come in this incident,” Brackney said at the meeting.
Fortune’s death became national news, as the story of a Black woman found hanging harkened back to the Mississippi’s dark history of racist terror lynchings. Both Lloyd and Ratliff are also Black.
On Aug. 3, Fortune’s body was found hanging from a tree outside a vacant house on the 500 block of Road of Remembrance. She was 29 years old.
Christy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, was at the meeting when the police chief announced the latest arrest. She and her husband traveled from Kentucky to be in Jackson this week to attend the court dates of the two suspects and to visit Fortune’s children. 
She held a press conference with Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes before the Tuesday council meeting. Stokes is trying to schedule a meeting with the U.S. Attorney and the FBI.
“You know, she didn’t have a lot to give, she was struggling,” Spivey said at the press conference. “But she would do anything to help anybody.”
Spivey told Mississippi Today that the recent arrests, after a “brutal silence,” have given her hope that authorities are now more aggressively seeking justice for her daughter. She said the family is anxious about any additional arrests.
Spivey also visited the crime scene for the first time on Tuesday. 
“It was hard, but I felt like I owed it to Tasia,” she said.
Spivey described seeing cardinals flying, and she took pictures of her daughter’s memorial, a small mound of flowers, balloons, teddy bears and pinwheels surrounding a framed picture of her.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington nears final step in joining California-Quebec carbon market
description: Taking the stage at Climate Week in New York City Wednesday morning, California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced his authorization to move forward with linking Washington into its carbon market that’s shared with Quebec, Canada, the next-to-last step in California’s process to complete the merger.  On the same day, Washington state officials completed the rulemak[...]
text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom announces his authorization to link Washington state in its carbon market during Climate Week in New York City on Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Washington State Department of Ecology)Taking the stage at Climate Week in New York City Wednesday morning, California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced his authorization to move forward with linking Washington into its carbon market that’s shared with Quebec, Canada, the next-to-last step in California’s process to complete the merger. 
On the same day, Washington state officials completed the rulemaking process to allow the linkage. California and Quebec will still need to complete regulatory changes, the final step, before merging can occur.
In June, the three jurisdictions signed a linkage agreement to fully join operations in 2027. Washington hopes that joining the older and well-established carbon market will stabilize prices for businesses, which have swung wildly in recent years on the state’s 5-year-old market.
“By joining forces with our partner in Washington state, we will build a stronger, more durable carbon market that will drive investment, cut pollution and power the clean economy of the future,” Newsom said. 
For more than a decade, California’s carbon market has sought to cut climate pollution by setting a cap on greenhouse gas emissions and requiring major polluters to buy allowances to cover their share of emissions. In 2014, its market linked with Quebec. 
Former Gov. Jay Inslee signed Washington’s carbon market into law in 2021 under the Climate Commitment Act. Since the state’s first auction in 2023, it has raised just over $5 billion in revenue.
A Washington-California-Quebec carbon market will put the same price on greenhouse gas emissions across an economy that ranks as the third largest in the world, said Caroline Halter, communications manager at Washington’s Department of Ecology. 
“Linkage isn’t just good climate policy — it’s smart economics,” said Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson in a press release. “Linking will unlock greater emissions reductions, lower the cost of clean technologies, and create good‑paying jobs in high‑growth industries.”
Both supporters and critics of Washington’s carbon market say that linking would stabilize prices and cut costs for polluters who have navigated an uncertain market with widely fluctuating allowance prices.
Large polluters covered under Washington’s carbon market are required to obtain allowances for each metric ton of greenhouse gases they emit. 
In Washington’s first year of auctions, the highest allowance cost soared to $63 per metric ton of emissions, and the state raised nearly $2 billion in revenue. In 2024, amid the campaign for an initiative to eliminate the Climate Commitment Act, allowance prices dropped dramatically. When that measure failed, the market bounced back. 
In December of 2025 Washington’s allowance prices hit a peak of $70 per ton. During its most recent auction earlier this month, allowances were $39. 
Meanwhile, allowances in the California-Quebec market have been comparatively stable and hover around $30. Its most recent price was $32. 
Newsom added that the linkage would create “more reliable pollution reductions and local investments, no matter what happens in DC,” in a post on X.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Collins, King urge feds to release heating oil supply amid price surge
description: U.S. Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King of Maine are calling on the federal government to release reserve heating oil as fuel prices continue to surge while temperatures drop.  In a letter to President Donald Trump Tuesday, the senators urged him to release supply from the ​​Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to “protect Mainers from […]
text:
Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. (Photo by gmnicholas/ Getty Images)U.S. Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King of Maine are calling on the federal government to release reserve heating oil as fuel prices continue to surge while temperatures drop. 
In a letter to President Donald Trump Tuesday, the senators urged him to release supply from the ​​Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to “protect Mainers from the very high prices that are imposing a difficult financial burden.” 
The reserve holds 1 million barrels of ultra low sulfur diesel, designated for heating oil, to protect the Northeast if there is a disruption in the heating oil supply. 
The Maine Department of Energy Resources reported last week that the average statewide price of heating oil was $5.77 per gallon, a 74% increase from this time last year. The department estimated that it will now cost nearly $675 more this year to fill a standard 275-gallon oil tank. 
“As the most heating oil-reliant state in the country, Maine people are particularly exposed to oil market price spikes,” Celina Cunningham, department acting commissioner, said in a press release. “Rising global energy prices driven by conflicts abroad are putting added pressure on households as we head into the winter heating season.”
Everyday increases cost Maine households $4,300 since Trump returned to office

Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. That number is down from 70% of households in 2010, according to the department. 
The Natural Resources Council of Maine on Monday released an analysis of heating oil costs, estimating that this winter Maine households will pay an additional $319 million to heat their homes, compared to last year. 
On average, that would mean a household could pay $1,262 more for heating oil this winter. 
In their letter, Collins and King noted that earlier this year the president ordered a release from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and said the “same urgency now applies” to the heating oil reserve. 
They also said the wars in Iran and Ukraine have prevented additional supplies from reaching the global market. 
“Maine is particularly vulnerable to global supply shocks because our state imports much of our home heating oil,” Collins and King wrote. “With both domestic and international supplies running low, a release from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve would help ease these prices.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Warnock urges greater federal oversight of automatic license plate readers
description: U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock is calling for federal guardrails around the use of automatic license plate readers, citing multiple cases of law enforcement misusing the cameras to stalk and harass U.S. citizens. Warnock, a Democrat, is teaming up with U.S. Sen. Katie Britt, an Alabama Republican, to urge the U.S. Department of Justice to issue […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock called for greater federal guidance around the use of automatic license plate readers. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderU.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock is calling for federal guardrails around the use of automatic license plate readers, citing multiple cases of law enforcement misusing the cameras to stalk and harass U.S. citizens.
Warnock, a Democrat, is teaming up with U.S. Sen. Katie Britt, an Alabama Republican, to urge the U.S. Department of Justice to issue guidance on the subject. Earlier this week, the two sent a letter to U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche urging the department to issue guidelines for state and local law enforcement and disclose how much federal funding has gone toward purchasing license plate readers. The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
GOP lawmakers call for more oversight of license plate cameras after string of misuses in Georgia

“We are deeply concerned about the misuse of ALPR systems and believe that appropriate safeguards are necessary to protect against unauthorized access and abuse,” the letter states. “We also want to ensure that funding of these technologies is paired with appropriate oversight to ensure that the funding is not used to facilitate such abuse.”
Automatic license plate readers, such as the ones made by Atlanta-based Flock, work by capturing license plate data, along with other information like a car’s make and color, and storing that information in a searchable database. Law enforcement agencies that contract with Flock can use the database to track down stolen vehicles, locate missing people and solve other crimes.
But the cameras have also drawn controversy after a number of law enforcement officials across the country have been found searching the databases for personal uses. According to the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, at least 19 people who work in law enforcement or emergency services have been arrested and charged this year for misusing a state law that restricts use of the cameras to only official law enforcement purposes. 
Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“Right now, there are no federal policies to punish or even track when one of the 140,000 law enforcement officers across the country with access to license plate tracking data misuses that information,” Warnock said in a press conference Wednesday. “Unfortunately, we’ve seen dozens of cases of women being stalked by ex-boyfriends or husbands who have been given unrestrained access as law enforcement officers to this surveillance technology.”
Sen. John Albers. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Last month, two Republican members of the Georgia Senate called for greater oversight over the cameras, with Roswell Republican Sen. John Albers announcing plans to collaborate with law enforcement associations to address misuse of the technology. 
Warnock condemned the lack of national guidance, noting that many municipalities have purchased license plate readers with federal funds. In the absence of clear guidelines, he said, state and local governments are left with a “patchwork system” that undermines public trust in the technology.
“The technology can’t be trusted to manage itself,” he said. “And right now there are no guardrails at all.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Bipartisan bills would allow 17-year-olds in Michigan to receive EMT license with parent permission
description: As Michigan reckons with a shortage of emergency medical personnel, a pair of lawmakers are looking to help grow the number of emergency medical technicians by tweaking the age requirements for an EMT license. Members of the House Health Policy Committee met on Wednesday to consider House Bills 5488 and 5489, introduced by Reps. Angela […]
text:
Getty ImagesAs Michigan reckons with a shortage of emergency medical personnel, a pair of lawmakers are looking to help grow the number of emergency medical technicians by tweaking the age requirements for an EMT license.
Members of the House Health Policy Committee met on Wednesday to consider House Bills 5488 and 5489, introduced by Reps. Angela Witwer (D-Delta Township) and David Prestin (R-Cedar River). If signed into law, the policies would allow 17-year-olds to obtain their EMT or medical first responder license, if a parent signs off on the application. 
Prestin, himself a licensed paramedic, explained that these bills focus on the two entry level licenses for emergency medicine, noting that a first responder can be trained in 60 hours, while an EMT can be trained over the course of a semester.
EMT’s must have a minimum of 32 hours of clinical experience, including direct patient care in hospital emergency departments.
“By the time a student completes an approved EMT program and passes the national registry exam, they have already been exposed profoundly to real life emergencies,” Prestin said. “Community colleges have long provided these programs, and high schools across the state have increasingly embraced them through career and technical education.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Students are generally 17 or 18 when they graduate high school, Prestin noted, with the state’s current rules around licensure forcing some graduates to wait several months before they can begin working in their trained profession.
“For students who, like my younger self, don’t have their heart set on a certain career path and are seeking opportunity, whenever and wherever it appears, these artificial barriers can push them into a different career path and we lose them forever,” Prestin said. “These bills allow graduates to enter the workforce sooner, support both full-time and volunteer ambulance services, and give high school career technical programs a clear pathway to employment.”
For those with concerns about whether 17-year-olds are emotionally ready to work as an EMT, Prestin stressed that the real world experiences students gain through the training programs vet out those who are not ready. 
Additionally, these students will not be driving ambulances, Prestin noted, explaining that drivers must be 18 or 21 depending on the agency, and must undergo additional training in order to drive.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Johnston and Grimes join dozens of cities suing fire truck manufacturers
description: The cities of Johnston and Grimes are joining Des Moines and dozens of other municipalities in suing the some of the nation’s biggest providers of fire trucks over alleged parasitic pricing. Johnston and Grimes, as members of the Johnston-Grimes Metropolitan Fire District, are suing REV Group and more than a dozen of its affiliates in […]
text:
The cities of Johnston and Grimes are joining Des Moines and dozens of other municipalities in suing the some of the nation’s biggest providers of fire trucks. (Stock photo by Perry Gerenday via Getty Images)The cities of Johnston and Grimes are joining Des Moines and dozens of other municipalities in suing the some of the nation’s biggest providers of fire trucks over alleged parasitic pricing.
Johnston and Grimes, as members of the Johnston-Grimes Metropolitan Fire District, are suing REV Group and more than a dozen of its affiliates in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa. Other defendants include American Industrial Partners and its affiliates, Oshkosh Corporation, Pierce Manufacturing and Boise Mobile Equipment.
The lawsuit challenges what it calls “the defendants’ multi-year, anticompetitive schemes to consolidate and ‘roll up’ markets for critical lifesaving apparatuses — fire trucks and the chassis on which they are built — and exclusionary restraints in the markets for replacement parts for their apparatuses.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The lawsuit claims the defendants have methodically acquired industry competitors, as well as key companies in the apparatus supply chain, and that Oshkosh and Pierce have restricted fire departments’ ability to replace parts — all with the intent of lessening competition.
Through these “illegal schemes,” the lawsuit alleges, the defendants have “reaped extraordinary profits on the backs of fire departments, taxpayers, cities, and counties.” This has resulted in Johnston and Grimes paying “substantial overcharges” and reduced  equipment value, the lawsuit claims.
Specifically, that lawsuit claims that in November 2024, the Johnston-Grimes Metropolitan Fire District purchased a Pierce firefighting truck for $1.7 million. In October 2025, the district purchased a Pierce pumper truck for roughly $1 million. Those prices, the lawsuit alleges, include “hundreds of thousands of dollars in anticompetitive overcharges.”
In addition, the lawsuit claims, the defendants have drastically extended the delivery dates for purchased equipment, with Johnston-Grimes’ wait time to receive the pumper purchased in October 2025 now estimated to be more than three years.
The lawsuit claims that beginning in 2008, AIP embarked on a decade-long strategy to consolidate the markets for fire apparatus and chassis manufacturing with its acquisition of E ONE, then one of the largest fire apparatus manufacturers in the United States.
In 2015, AIP allegedly accelerated its consolidation strategy under the REV Group of companies, and acquired Kovatch Mobile Equipment Corp. In 2017, AIP and REV Group acquired Ferrara Fire Apparatus and three years later acquired Spartan Emergency Response.



Quotation







The markets for fire apparatuses, chassis, and Pierce replacement parts are no longer competitive. They are markets dominated by powerful behemoths.


– Lawsuit filed by the cities of Johnston and Grimes


Eventually, the lawsuit asserts, nearly a dozen once-independent companies were rolled into a single corporation, and the REV Group began shutting down manufacturing plants, causing significant price increases as well as product-order backlogs estimated at $4.2 billion in value.
“The markets for fire apparatuses, chassis, and Pierce replacement parts are no longer competitive,” the lawsuit claims. “They are markets dominated by powerful behemoths. These manufacturers bought their way to dominance, and they are now in full extraction mode, deliberately suppressing output, withholding supply, delaying deliveries, restricting competitive options, and charging supra-competitive prices without consequence … Our fire departments do not deserve this. Our firefighters do not deserve this. The taxpayers those firefighters swear an oath to protect do not deserve this. The extraction of excessive private rents from the public must stop, and it must stop now.”
In April, a federal court consolidated the claims of more than 60 cities into a trio of antitrust class action lawsuits to be tried in a Wisconsin court.
In June, the City of Des Moines sued the REV Group, 14 of its affiliates and 11 other companies that produce firefighting trucks, parts and equipment. The claims in that lawsuit are virtually identical to those in the newly filed Johnston-Grimes case.
As part of its lawsuit, Des Moines claims it has ordered firefighting apparatus with a delivery date 42 to 45 months away — although the equipment’s useful life is no more than 10 to 20 years.
The lawsuits filed in Iowa and elsewhere allege private equity has played a pivotal role in the alleged reduction of competition. In 2018, the lawsuits claim, REV Group’s then-CEO Tim Sullivan told investors, “We like backlog, we love backlog.”
The lawsuits seek not only unspecified financial damages to recover money lost to the allegedly illegal anticompetitive actions of the defendants, but also an injunction that would prohibit any such conduct in the future.
In various court filings, the REV Group and other defendants have denied any wrongdoing and asserted the COVID-19 pandemic “prompted skyrocketing demand and disrupted supply chains, causing price increases and longer wait times.”
By some estimates, three manufacturers now control 70-80% of the U.S. fire truck market, and according to the International Association of Fire Fighters, fire engine prices have nearly doubled since 2020, from about $589,000 to more than $1 million.
Last fall, at a U.S. Senate hearing on the consolidation of fire equipment providers, Dennis Rubin, the fire chief in Kansas City, Kansas, told federal lawmakers, “There must come a day of reckoning when the manufacturers of our most important tools are held accountable for runaway pricing and extended delivery times.”
In July, U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, and U.S. Sen. Jim Banks, an Indiana Republican, along with Democratic Rep. Becca Balint of Vermont and Republican Rep. Ben Cline of Virginia, filed a resolution directing the Federal Trade Commission to investigate the consolidation in the fire truck manufacturing industry.
