name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Nonprofit launches Eastern Kentucky birding ‘hotspots’ to encourage bird documentation
description: A land conservation nonprofit in Kentucky is using grant funding to add signs near birding “hotspots” in Eastern Kentucky that people can use to document birds through an app supported by an ornithology lab at Cornell University.  The Kentucky Natural Lands Trust is using part of a $10,000 grant from the Cornell Lab of Ornithonology […]
text:
Cardinals were recognized as the state bird of Kentucky in 1926. (Getty Images)A land conservation nonprofit in Kentucky is using grant funding to add signs near birding “hotspots” in Eastern Kentucky that people can use to document birds through an app supported by an ornithology lab at Cornell University. 
The Kentucky Natural Lands Trust is using part of a $10,000 grant from the Cornell Lab of Ornithonology to place six signs at various Eastern Kentucky trailheads and spots as a part of the “Pine Mountain Birding Trail” along the Pine Mountain mountain ridge that stretches about 125 miles from Tennessee through Kentucky. 
One of the signs placed along the Pine Mountain Birding Trail in Eastern Kentucky. (Courtesy Joe Manning, Kentucky Natural Lands Trust)
Visitors can use QR codes on the signs that direct people to the Cornell lab’s eBird app where users can document birds they see, create birding checklists and share the data as a part of a crowd-sourced effort.
The nonprofit describes the region as “one of the most biodiverse temperate regions” in the world and a “key link in an intercontinental migration route” for hundreds of millions of birds every year, according to a Tuesday press release.
In a provided statement, Sara Barker, the Land Trust Bird Conservation Initiative Program Leader at the Cornell lab, said the lab wanted to work with an organization like the Kentucky Natural Lands Trust that is “rooted in the land, trusted by local communities, and equipped to work across property lines to safeguard and elevate awareness of this region’s extraordinary biodiversity.” 
“Central Appalachia’s forested ridges are among the most critical — yet often overlooked — corridors for birds in the Mississippi Flyway,” Barker said. “The partnership between the Kentucky Natural Lands Trust and Cornell Lab is turning Pine Mountain into meaningful data for hemispheric bird conservation.”
The sign locations are at the Chained Rock trailhead in Bell County; the Blanton Forest State Nature Preserve in Harlan County; the Pine Mountain Settlement School in Harlan County; Kingdom Come State Park in Harlan County; Little Shepherd Trail in Letcher County; and the Bad Branch State Nature Preserve in Letcher County. 
The grant funding has also been used to offer guided birding hikes, free public workshops and other programming and research, according to a release from the Kentucky Natural Lands Trust. The nonprofit lists the Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet, Kentucky State Parks and the Pine Mountain Settlement School as partners involved in the birding trail.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: “Go and Do Likewise:” Beshear’s book touts Christian values (except when it comes to Bevin)
description: If there are one or two of you out there who still have doubts that Gov. Andy Beshear will run for president in 2028, doubt no more. This week, he officially released “Go and Do Likewise: How We Heal a Broken County,” joining the Presidential Hopeful section of your local bookstore already stocked with choices […]
text:
Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, flanked by Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and his family, takes in the celebration at his reelection party on Nov. 7, 2023, in Louisville. (Austin Anthony/Kentucky Lantern)If there are one or two of you out there who still have doubts that Gov. Andy Beshear will run for president in 2028, doubt no more. This week, he officially released “Go and Do Likewise: How We Heal a Broken County,” joining the Presidential Hopeful section of your local bookstore already stocked with choices such as “Young Man in a Hurry: A Journey of Discovery” by Gavin Newsom, “Where We Keep the Light: Stories From a Life of Service” by Josh Shapiro, “Crisis of the Common Good: The Fight for Meaning and Connection in a Broken America,” by Chris Murphy. You get the idea – first you set up a PAC, then write a book with a colon in the title and you’re halfway to New Hampshire.
“Go and Do Likewise: How We Heal a Broken Country,” was released this week by Gov. Andy Beshear. (Photo courtesy St. Martin’s Press)
Luckily for these busy men, 1) Donald Trump has provided an excellent opening to talk about such hopeful, healing topics, and 2) there are many talented ghost writers out there. Mark Tabb, who is thanked by Beshear in the acknowledgements, keeps a light touch and a fast pace with the greatest hits of the Kentucky governor. 
Luckily for Tabb, Beshear has a truly unusual number of high-drama moments from his years in office, which also provide him with excellent examples of his Biblical themes, the good Samaritan etc. From COVID to the West Kentucky tornadoes to the Eastern Kentucky floods, Kentuckians shine in crises – neighbors helping neighbors – in all the ways that are antithetical to the Trumpist individualism that has poisoned our public discourse.
Trump will not be on the ballot in 2028 (we hope) so it’s interesting the book is so focused on him, but it’s clear that Trumpism is what Democrats will have to continue to run against, and thus is how Beshear has structured the book. (He may not have imagined Trump’s polls being this low as he and Tabb wrote it.)
Luckily for us readers, Beshear is not so filled with the Holy Spirit that he leaves out any thoughts of payback. Kentucky’s favorite bad guy, former Gov. Matt Bevin, is referred to throughout as Trump Lite, and their political tussles are highlighted with more candor than previously encountered.
There is, for example, the time then-Attorney General Beshear was crossing the Capitol parking lot when he ran into then-Gov. Bevin, and chastised him for not doing his job after a Louisville child was hit by a stray bullet.

“Eyes wide, Bevin leaned toward me and snarled, ‘Spare me your talking points. If you want to get political, I’ll knock your f—— head off!’ 
I stared directly into his bugged-out eyes. ‘Are you threatening me, Governor?’ I said as calmly as I could but, raising my voice, added, ‘Cause I don’t take kindly to being threatened.’ 
He shot back, ‘I didn’t threaten you.’ 
‘You just said you’d knock my head off,’ I replied. I could see in his face Bevin knew he’d made a mistake, not that he’d admit it. Ever. Instead, he shook his head and scoffed, ‘Is this how you people act?’”
 


	It turns out “you people” are Democrats, and Beshear uses the moment to further explore the ongoing political divide expertly manipulated by Trump and the ever charming Trump Lite.
But Bevin is not the only politician who doesn’t like to admit he made a mistake. In the book, Beshear mentions only a few of his own, such as Tupac Shakur’s unemployment application during COVID. He does not write about the entire debacle over unemployment benefits, or the many problems in his Department of Juvenile Justice so aptly documented by the Lexington Herald-Leader, or the various travesties around the Kentucky Wired program.
But generally speaking, people writing books before they run for president aren’t going to explore those themes.
The most affecting chapters are about abortion rights advocate Hadley Duvall, who almost certainly made the difference in his second gubernatorial election, the mass shooting at Louisville’s Old National Bank that killed one of his closest friends, and America’s civil rights history, and the removal of the Jefferson Davis statue from the Capitol. 
I think it’s smart of Beshear to talk about his faith because so many people perceive the Democratic Party as one full of atheists; his willingness to talk about God is part of what has created a genuine rapport with Kentuckians. One of Beshear’s greatest strengths is his ability to do the right thing while seeing clearly how to reap political rewards from it. For example, his daily COVID briefings brought real comfort to thousands of people, and beamed his awkward dad jokes and Mr. Rogers persona into an indelible image that clearly helped him win a second term in a deep red state.
What’s still unclear is whether Beshear, despite the sharp political instincts and prodigious fundraising, has the charisma to appeal to people outside Kentucky, and whether this book will help him do so. He’ll sell plenty of copies; on Wednesday, Tom Loftus reported that in addition to the Kentucky Democratic Party spending $10,000 to buy books, Beshear’s PAC, In This Together, bought $9,000 worth of them. Will your average voter in Iowa or South Carolina join this group? In the runup to a presidential campaign, does it even matter?

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Gov. Landry’s order waives some limits on off-road diesel use to lower fuel costs
description: Farmers and timber harvesters can use off-road diesel fuel for all purposes for the next 30 days under an executive order Gov. Jeff Landry issued Wednesday.
text:
A farmer harvests corn beside Iowa Highway 163. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Farmers and timber harvesters can use off-road diesel fuel for all purposes for the next 30 days under an executive order Gov. Jeff Landry issued Wednesday. 
The governor cited soaring prices for diesel fuel as the reason behind his action. He’s also called on the Trump administration and Congress to halt all diesel exports for 90 days to address the high costs.  
“We’re not going to sit on the sidelines while Louisiana farmers are paying record prices to harvest the crops that feed our families and support our economy. We have an opportunity to provide immediate relief, and that’s exactly what we’re doing,” Landry said in a statement from his office.
The executive order applies to what’s known as dyed diesel, which is intended for off-road uses such as tractors, heavy equipment and irrigation systems. Louisiana does not apply its 20-cent-per-gallon motor fuel tax to off-road diesel, which is tinted red to distinguish it from regular diesel fuel
Landry’s executive order is in effect through Oct. 22 and applies to vehicles registered as Class 2 (forest products) and Class 5 (farm use). The governor has also directed the state revenue department to ask the Internal Revenue Service for relief from any penalties that might result from the state suspending its off-road diesel use limitations. The federal government tax on diesel is 24.4 cents per gallon, though it is not assessed on off-road fuel.
The average price per gallon for diesel fuel in the U.S. has exceeded $6 for the past two weeks, setting a new record. According to the governor’s office, this level is 112% higher than LSU AgCenter forecasters projected when they calculated their forecast for farmers’ crop budgets in 2026.
Higher demand for diesel in European markets is behind the higher prices, according to market analysts. The global supply has been disrupted by Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine as well as the ripple effects of the conflict between the U.S. and Iran.   
President Donald Trump said Tuesday his administration would make a decision soon about whether to embargo U.S. fuel exports in response to high prices. The refining industry has said it would most likely curb production of diesel if foreign shipments are stopped, which analysts say would not create the desired cost relief.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware wins SNAP deadline case while facing high payment error rate
description: Judge rejects USDA’s timetable and clarifies immigrant eligibility, but federal rules aimed at improving state payment accuracy remain in place DOVER, Del. — Delaware has won a court ruling that prevents the Trump administration from counting certain food assistance errors against states under a deadline a federal judge found unlawful. The victory protects t[...]
text:
Judge rejects USDA’s timetable and clarifies immigrant eligibility, but federal rules aimed at improving state payment accuracy remain in place
DOVER, Del. — Delaware has won a court ruling that prevents the Trump administration from counting certain food assistance errors against states under a deadline a federal judge found unlawful. The victory protects the state from potential future costs tied to that deadline, but it does not resolve a separate problem: Delaware’s SNAP payment error rate was 16% in fiscal 2025, well above the national average.
The Sept. 17 ruling also confirmed that certain lawful permanent residents, including people who were previously refugees or granted asylum, remain eligible for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program without waiting five years. It did not overturn the 2025 federal law requiring states with high payment error rates to pay a share of SNAP benefit costs.
The case for state accountability
Congress changed SNAP last year to give states a stronger financial reason to determine eligibility and benefit amounts accurately. Under the law, states with error rates of at least 6% can be required to cover 5%, 10% or 15% of benefit costs, depending on their rate. The requirement generally begins Oct. 1, 2027.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture reported a national payment error rate of 10.62% for fiscal 2025, representing $10.1 billion in improper payments. The measure includes benefits paid above and below the correct amount. It is not a fraud rate.
“These payment error rates are further proof that state accountability is severely lacking in SNAP,” Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said when USDA released the figures. She said the department wanted states to curb waste while serving needy families and protecting taxpayers.
Delaware’s error rate
Delaware’s fiscal 2025 rate was 16%, compared with the 10.62% national rate and the law’s 6% cost-sharing threshold. That makes payment accuracy a substantial issue for the state, independent of its dispute with USDA over the new law’s implementation. The figure does not mean 16% of Delaware recipients committed fraud; it includes overpayments and underpayments.
Delaware’s rate is high enough to qualify it for a delay in the new benefit cost-sharing requirement. That gives the state more time to improve accuracy before it must begin paying a share of benefits under that provision. The delay comes from the law itself, separate from the court ruling.
Why the judge rejected USDA’s deadline
The lawsuit focused on how USDA put the 2025 law into effect. SNAP rules provide a 120-day adjustment period during which certain errors arising from a policy change are excluded from a state’s payment error rate. USDA said the period began July 4, 2025, when the law was enacted, and ended Nov. 1.
But USDA did not issue its guidance on noncitizen eligibility until Oct. 31, leaving states one day under that timetable. Other instructions arrived weeks or months after USDA said the clock had started. U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai ruled that the department had not given states adequate notice. He set aside its deadline and required a full adjustment period following proper implementation instructions.
The judge also found that USDA’s October guidance wrongly indicated that some lawful permanent residents were ineligible for SNAP or subject to a five-year waiting period. USDA issued a clarification in December. The ruling confirms that lawful permanent residents who were previously in specified humanitarian categories retain their exemption from the waiting period, provided they meet other SNAP requirements.
What Jennings’ criticism means
“This entire ordeal was a blatant attempt by the Trump Administration to take food away from families in need, to destroy a plank of the social safety net, and to degrade our state’s financial standing,” Attorney General Kathy Jennings said in announcing the decision.
Jennings’ accusation goes beyond what the judge decided about the administration’s intent. USDA says it is seeking to reduce improper payments, save federal money and hold states accountable for administering SNAP accurately. The court nevertheless found that USDA’s initial guidance misstated eligibility for some lawful permanent residents and that its deadline unfairly exposed states to future costs.
The distinction does not erase the effects of the broader 2025 law. The Congressional Budget Office expects its tighter eligibility and work rules to reduce the number of people receiving SNAP. Its projected $187 billion in federal savings over 10 years includes those changes; it is not an estimate of fraud eliminated. The court ruling establishes that USDA went beyond a lawful implementation of the changes at issue, but it does not establish that denying food to needy families was the administration’s purpose.
For Delaware, the ruling means USDA cannot use the deadline the judge rejected to count implementation errors against the state. Delaware must still follow the new law and address its high payment error rate. Both facts matter to understanding what the state won — and the work that remains.
TO GO BOX | The SNAP ruling

Who: Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings joined other states in suing the Trump administration over USDA’s SNAP guidance and deadline.
What: A federal judge set aside USDA’s deadline for counting certain implementation errors and clarified eligibility for some lawful permanent residents.
When: The ruling was issued Sept. 17, 2026.
Where: The decision came from the U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon and addresses USDA guidance to states.
Why it matters: Delaware avoids errors being counted under the rejected deadline, but its 16% fiscal 2025 payment error rate remains high. The federal law requiring states with high error rates to share SNAP benefit costs remains in effect.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Mixed signals for housing costs in Alaska
description: Apartment rents in Alaska rose 2.1% over the past year, the most modest increase in five years, according to analysis by the state Department of Labor and Workforce Development. The statistics on rental costs are part of a package of articles about housing costs published in the September issue of Alaska Economic Trends, the monthly […]
text:
A sign seen on April 9, 2025, advertises rental availability at an apartment building in Anchorage's Turnagain neighborhood. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Apartment rents in Alaska rose 2.1% over the past year, the most modest increase in five years, according to analysis by the state Department of Labor and Workforce Development.
The statistics on rental costs are part of a package of articles about housing costs published in the September issue of Alaska Economic Trends, the monthly magazine of the department’s research section.
Rental statistics, based on prices recorded in March of this year, show some striking geographic differences.
The Wrangell-Petersburg area in Southeast Alaska had the cheapest rent of the 11 cities and areas analyzed, with a median monthly rate of $1,288 for a two-bedroom apartment. Bethel, a rural hub in Western Alaska, had the highest rents, with a median of $2,030 a month for a two-bedroom apartment.
Kodiak, Anchorage, the Fairbanks North Star Borough and Juneau were behind Bethel with monthly median rentals above $1,700.The Matanuska-Susitna Borough, just north of Anchorage, was on the low side for median rents, at $1,567 a month, but it had the biggest yearly increase, measured at 12.8%.
That reflects demographic characteristics in the bustling borough, where many residents are commuters who work in Anchorage, said Gunnar Schultz, a state labor economist and one of the authors of the housing-cost stories.
“Mat-Su obviously has been growing in contrast to most of the rest of the state,” he said. “So I think that that obviously puts upward pressure on price.” Proximity to Anchorage is another contributor because it means money is coming into the borough from the state’s largest city, he said.
The analysis is part of the department’s regular monitoring of housing costs. The rental comparisons covered much but not all of the state; the North Slope Borough and Bering Strait region, for example, were not included.
For homebuyers in Alaska, there are some economic headwinds, according to the economists’ analysis. Mortgage costs are much higher than they used to be, they said.
For a 30-year fixed rate mortgage on a $415,000 Alaska home — the median value — the monthly payment in 2025 was about $2,050. That is 84% higher than the estimated median monthly mortgage payment in 2019, the analysis said.
A big driver is the rise in home values, from an average of about $300,000 in 2019 to an average of $415,000 just six years later. Another factor is the increase in interest rates, from a median under 3% in 2020 to 6.5%in 2023, the analysis said.
But while home values and thus monthly mortgage costs increased, so did wages in Alaska.
The result of all those combined changes was that purchasing a home became marginally more affordable in 2025 than in the two years prior, according to the analysis.
Alaska’s Housing Affordability Index,  the number that represents how many people earning the average monthly are needed to make mortgage payments, dropped a bit in 2025 to 1.37. That is down from last year’s index of 1.39 and from the 2024 index of 1.4, which was the highest in recent years. But it is above the indexes measured in previous years; from 2019 to 2021, the index was below 1, indicating that a single person earning average Alaska wages had enough money to afford monthly mortgage payments.
Despite the slight improvement in the affordability index, buying a house remains a hefty burden in Alaska, Schultz said. “It’s still so much higher than it was during COVID and before,” he said.
A slight decline in interest rates last year was a contributing factor to the small improvement in housing affordability. However, interest rates are now heading up, the analysis pointed out.
Also affecting housing affordability is the availability of homes, and on that subject, there is positive news for would-be buyers, according to the economists’ analysis.
Housing construction in 2025 hit a 10-year high after years of increases that followed the big drop during the COVID-19 pandemic. A total of 2,261 single-family and multifamily housing units were built last year, the analysis said. That compares to 1,747 in 2020 and 1,726 in 2021. Home construction has been steadily rising since those years, according to the data.
The Alaska Economic Trends articles did not compare housing costs in the state to those nationwide, but the U.S. Census Bureau has some U.S. statistics that provide some contest.
Nationally, home ownership costs remained flat from 2020 to 2024, while rents increased by $100 more a month to a median $1,413 during the period, according to the Census Bureau. The analysis considers areas around the nation with populations over 5,000, so most of Alaska’s rural communities are not included.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico behavioral health committee closes in on goal of approving 13 regional health plans
description: The committee tasked with rebuilding New Mexico’s behavioral healthcare infrastructure has approved 11 of 13 regional plans, the committee chair told lawmakers on the interim Legislative Finance Committee during their Tuesday meeting.
text:
The Behavioral Health Reform and Investment Act’s executive committee, pictured on Aug. 5, 2025, has approved 11 of the 13 regional plans to rebuild behavioral health infrastructure, committee Chair Nick Boukas told state lawmakers on Sept. 22, 2026. (Source NM file photo)The committee tasked with rebuilding New Mexico’s behavioral healthcare infrastructure has approved all but two regional plans, the committee chair told a panel of state lawmakers Tuesday.
Nick Boukas, the committee chair and director of the state Health Care Authority’s Behavioral Health Services Division, told lawmakers on the interim Legislative Finance Committee that he and his colleagues have signed off on 11 of the state’s proposed 13 regional behavioral healthcare plans.
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed Senate Bill 3, known as the Behavioral Health Reform and Investment Act, into law in 2025. It created 13 behavioral health regions mirrored after the state’s 13 judicial districts. Local officials with counties, tribes and cities within each region have crafted unique plans to identify their communities’ biggest gaps in behavioral healthcare and to set goals for addressing them.
The law is aimed at bringing providers back to New Mexico, particularly rural areas, after former Republican Gov. Susana Martinez accused several providers of fraud, which led to a mass departure.
While needs vary from region to region, Boukas said that they have largely held four priorities in common: expanding access to behavioral health treatment and recovery services; strengthening youth, family, school and caregiver support; addressing housing and transportation; and building and retaining a behavioral health workforce.
New Mexico lawmakers express frustration with long process to rebuild behavioral health system

A Tuesday LFC brief says the state invested $565 million for behavioral health services in 2025, yet has “little data” to indicate whether outcomes are improving or whether “access is better today than it was when the state began making these investments.” So far, the 13 plans carry a price tag of $110 million, according to the brief.
Some lawmakers in attendance expressed frustration over the slowgoing process, which has become a common theme in this summer’s legislative hearings on the matter.
“We’ve spent a whole lot of money with zero results yet,” Rep. Mark Duncan (R-Kirtland) told Boukas.
Boukas told lawmakers that the seemingly slow nature of SB3’s implementation is to be expected.
“When I say that this is working, it’s that we’re getting folks to start talking to each other. None of the programs have rolled out yet to where we can start collecting data,” he said.
The Behavioral Health Reform and Investment Act Executive Committee is scheduled to meet in Santa Fe on Oct. 6. Boukas previously told Source NM he hopes to have all 13 regional plans approved by the end of the year.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska can cut property taxes. It can’t eliminate the bill.
description: Affordability is on nearly everyone’s mind. With homeowners and prospective homeowners looking for every way they can to save on the necessities of life, it is only natural to consider that expense that is itself a perennial topic in Nebraska: how to reduce the property tax burden. But lowering property taxes is not easy, and […]
text:
A tax statement with 'special messages' box regarding past due taxes. (Courtesy of Lancaster County Treasurer)Affordability is on nearly everyone’s mind. With homeowners and prospective homeowners looking for every way they can to save on the necessities of life, it is only natural to consider that expense that is itself a perennial topic in Nebraska: how to reduce the property tax burden. But lowering property taxes is not easy, and the simplest-sounding solutions come with hard compromises for our communities. When property tax revenue declines, so does the funding available for the local services and investments that shape our daily lives.
In Nebraska last year, $5.6 billion of property taxes was levied in Nebraska:

$3.3 billion was levied in support of local school districts, including bonded indebtedness. 
$975 million was levied for counties.
$653 million was levied for cities. 
The remainder was levied by townships, fire districts, natural resource districts, educational service units, community colleges and miscellaneous districts like libraries and ag societies. 

While the state of Nebraska partially offset those levies with over $1 billion of relief (through mechanisms like the property tax credits and the homestead exemption), that is still a lot of money for a state of just over 2 million people. Nearly every dollar raised through property taxes, however, stays in the local economy, funding the local workforce and purchasing local goods and services.
Strong schools. Safer neighborhoods. Reliable roads. Modern libraries. Parks and recreation. Emergency services. These are not abstract benefits. They are the foundations of thriving communities, and property taxes pay for them.
In Nebraska, the property tax debate affects more than homeowners. Farmers, ranchers and rural communities also feel the pressure of property taxes. Local property tax revenue helps support the critical infrastructure urban and rural Nebraska communities depend on. For homeowners, property taxes assess an illiquid household asset; for farmers and ranchers, they tax the productive land required to make a living. As Nebraskans consider additional property tax relief, the challenge is not simply how to lower the tax bill, but also how to ensure our communities can continue funding the services and infrastructure Nebraskans demand.
Eliminating or significantly reducing property taxes does not eliminate the cost of providing public services. It simply shifts that cost somewhere else and through a different revenue source. A common refrain is that local governments need to “tighten their belts,” as if local governments can simply disregard duties and services mandated by the state. Further, if things that impact our quality of life are reduced or eliminated in the name of property tax relief, we have seen those communities less and less likely to retain the next generation of citizens and property owners.
Alternatively, shifting funding to sales or income taxes introduces severe budget volatility, as these revenues generally fluctuate more with economic conditions, making long-term budgeting more difficult.
Property taxes offer something especially valuable: stable, locally controlled and locally invested funding. Residents elect the officials who set budgets and tax rates, giving taxpayers a far more direct role in how their community’s money is raised and spent, as opposed to asking the state legislature for money to fix a bridge or to hire a special education teacher. Locally elected officials want lower property taxes, too. They live in the communities they serve, own property and pay the exact same taxes they levy.
That local connection matters. It allows communities to set priorities based on their own needs rather than relying more heavily on decisions made at the state level. Replacing local tax authority with state funding or other revenue sources inevitably shifts decision-making to the state Capitol. As the old saying goes, “Whoever has the gold makes the rules.” 
Property taxes are more than a line on a tax bill. They are one of the primary tools communities use to invest in the places people call home. As we consider property tax reform for Nebraska, the most important question is not “How much should we cut?” but more accurately, “What do we need to pay for, and who should pay for it?”
A sustainable path forward requires two things:

Broadening our economic base: Growing local business, housing and agricultural development allows the cost of essential services to be shared across more people and more property, lowering the individual burden naturally.
Aligning state and local responsibilities: If the state asks local property owners to carry duties that are statewide in scope, the state should assume and fund them. Conversely, if certain local programs are deemed too expensive for local taxpayers to sustain, communities should have the choice to scale them back locally.

At the end of the day, basic infrastructure and public safety are expensive needs. Meaningful property tax relief begins with growing our communities and conducting an honest assessment of local government’s responsibilities – not an uncalculated shift of the bill.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: ‘A self-fulfilling cycle’: Why Gateway Cities consistently have lower voter turnout
description: Cities like Worcester — where the poverty rate is twice as high as the state’s — may have trouble getting people to the polls this November. The state’s most disadvantaged and diverse urban communities often have some of the lowest voter turnout rates. In the last midterm election year, nine of the 10 municipalities with the lowest voter turnout were Gateway[...]
text:
IT’S ELECTION SEASON in Massachusetts, and that means officials, experts, and strategists alike are keeping a watchful eye on voter turnout.
Statewide turnout in the September 1 primary election hit nearly 23 percent — the highest it’s been in a midterm election year since 2006. It’s a promising outcome, suggesting the Bay State could ultimately see higher voter turnout on November 3 than in previous election years. After all, this year’s ballot will feature an unusually high number of widely debated ballot questions, as well as other high-profile races.
But cities like Worcester — where the poverty rate is twice as high as the state’s — may still have trouble getting people to the polls this November. The city’s turnout in this month’s primary was just over 15 percent, though it was a notable increase from the city’s 11.5 percent turnout in the 2024 primary.
During the 2022 midterms, Worcester County’s voter turnout was 51 percent, which mirrored the state average. But, only 38 percent of voters turned out to vote in Worcester, even though it was a year in which the governor was on the ballot. That same year, Worcester had the lowest voter registration rate in the county at 66 percent, while the state’s voter registration rate was 86 percent.
Gateway Cities — some of the state’s most disadvantaged and diverse urban communities — consistently have some of the lowest voter turnout rates in Massachusetts. In 2022, nine of the 10 municipalities with the lowest voter turnout in the state were Gateway Cities, with rates ranging from just 23 percent in Lawrence to 35 percent in Lynn.
The phenomenon is hardly unique to Massachusetts’s low-income cities. A 2023 report published by the Pew Research Center found that those who are least likely to vote are younger, more racially and ethnically diverse, and have received less formal education than likely voters. Research consistently shows that those with higher incomes also vote at higher rates than those with lower incomes. That discrepancy translates to more affluent people and communities having more of a say in who gets elected.
Ahead of the state election this fall, civic organizations in Central Massachusetts and beyond are grappling with how to solve this persistent problem, and how to increase turnout among those who face countless barriers to civic participation.
“We often hear that these voters are disengaged or not particularly interested in politics. I think people need to be careful about saying those things,” said Shanique Rodriguez, executive director of the nonprofit Massachusetts Voter Table, which works to increase voter turnout in Boston and the Gateway Cities. “The people who are least likely to vote are often the people who are most affected by decisions made through policy.”
Rodriguez said those with more economic stability often have more time, flexibility, information, social connections, and transportation means, which makes civic participation much easier. The Voter Table and its partners target voters in Gateway Cities who make $40,000 a year or less, she added, giving them resources and information about registration and voting.
“People who are worried about rent and food are less worried about how they are going to get to the polls, especially when they’re just trying to pay their utility bills or get to their job,” Rodriguez said.
A survey of 800 registered voters conducted in 2026 by the MassINC Polling Group found that 69 percent of respondents in Gateway Cities said it would be easier to get out and vote if public transportation were free on election days. (The polling group is part of the same organization that publishes CommonWealth Beacon.)
Those in Gateway Cities were more likely to say they use public transportation every day than respondents outside of Gateway Cities. Other groups that rely on public transportation were also more likely to think it would make voting easier, including non-white voters (72 percent compared to 46 percent of white voters) and lower-income voters (62 percent compared to 46 percent of higher-income voters).
In Central Massachusetts, the communities with the highest poverty rates — including Worcester, Fitchburg, and Southbridge — have some of the lowest voter turnout rates in the county and the state. During the last midterm election year in 2022, Southbridge saw just 34 percent turnout even though 89 percent of eligible voters were registered. Worcester and Fitchburg saw 38 and 39 percent turnout, respectively.
Despite the uptick in turnout for the primary election this year, Rodriguez predicted that cities like Worcester and Fitchburg will see between 35 and 39 percent turnout again this November. She and Celia Johnston Blue, president of the Massachusetts Women of Color Coalition, say the civic participation problem lies less in registration and more in turnout, especially since the state passed the VOTES Act in 2022, which created automatic voter registration. Before that, Massachusetts passed a law that allowed young people to pre-register at the age of 16. Since then, voter registration across the state has increased.
“More and more people who are registered to vote are experiencing huge economic inequalities,” Rodriguez said. “We’ve done a really good job of removing the barriers to registration, but we haven’t removed some of the other barriers to actually keep people engaged.”
A 2020 report published by the Worcester Regional Research Bureau revealed stark racial disparities when looking at turnout in the 2019 municipal election. In census tracts where white residents represented less than 60 percent of the population, voter turnout was 10 percent. In tracts where white residents made up more than 80 percent of the population, voter turnout was 28 percent. (Municipal elections typically have lower turnout than midterm or presidential years.) In wealthier neighborhoods in Worcester, voter turnout in municipal elections can reach 40 percent, while in lower-income neighborhoods like Main South, it can drop to just 15 percent some years.
The report also noted that in 2019, occupants of single-family homes made up 63 percent of all voters in Worcester, while those living in multi-unit developments represented just 34 percent of voters. (This is despite the fact that 56 percent of Worcester residents live in multi-unit housing structures and 44 percent live in single-family homes.) Single-family homes tend to be owner-occupied while multi-unit buildings tend to be renter-occupied, and people with the means to purchase land and homes have higher incomes, on average, than renters.
Rodriguez explained that in cities like Worcester, poverty often creates residential instability, which affects voter registration and turnout.
“People who are moving constantly face barriers to voting and participation. Often, they’re not re-registering in time or can’t re-register in time for a primary, for example,” Rodriguez said.
Rodriguez pointed to rent stabilization as one potential solution to the problem, though a controversial ballot question proposed this year that, if passed, would have enacted one of the strictest rent control laws in the nation, was ultimately blocked by the Supreme Judicial Court in June.
In Worcester, municipal election turnout typically lands between 17 percent and 20 percent. Low participation means races can be decided by small margins — sometimes just a few hundred votes.
The consequences of low voter turnout can be dire, said Ann Lisi, vice president of the League of Women Voters Worcester, leading to unresponsive local and state governments.
“It’s a self-fulfilling cycle, because if you’re a voter who is feeling checked out and doesn’t really vote, a habit has been formed. We try to help people overcome that by promoting early voting,” she said.
To help boost already low voter turnout and engagement during municipal election years like 2025, Blue said the Women of Color Coalition has hosted candidate forums featuring local office holders and office seekers.
“That gives people an opportunity to really hear from their candidates, and we try to make sure our diverse communities are part of that audience,” Blue said.
Still, Rodriguez said Gateway Cities have a long way to go before the gaps in voter turnout are closed.
“Increasing voter participation isn’t just about getting more people to the polls,” Rodriguez said. “It’s about making sure that people who have historically had the least amount of power have a meaningful voice in our democracy, and that is just not what’s happening in Massachusetts.”

title: Minneapolis needs a stronger rental housing vacancy fee
description: The tragic and unconscionable situation at the Heritage Park complex of homes in North Minneapolis this summer, where renters have endured rats, mold and flagrant disrepair, shows yet again that residents have been failed by local housing policies and lack of attention from elected city leaders.  Due to lack of basic maintenance by the corporate property […]
text:
"A stronger vacancy fee," the authors argue, "would ensure that housing units under corporate property or landlord management receive timely repairs and upkeep, since the vacancy fee incentivizes them to keep their units occupied." (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)The tragic and unconscionable situation at the Heritage Park complex of homes in North Minneapolis this summer, where renters have endured rats, mold and flagrant disrepair, shows yet again that residents have been failed by local housing policies and lack of attention from elected city leaders. 
Due to lack of basic maintenance by the corporate property management, and a lack of oversight by city and Minneapolis Public Housing Authority officials, more than 200 residential units in Heritage Park — about half — are vacant. If these units have been empty for over six months, which seems likely due to longstanding maintenance issues, they are chronically vacant. 
Why is chronic vacancy important in the rental market? Because in a city with few options for genuinely affordable rent, and in a city with an ever-shrinking stock of naturally occurring affordable housing, every unit matters.
If a derelict landlord or out-of-state, corporate property manager allows dozens and dozens of units in a Minneapolis residential building to sit empty for more than six months — and sometimes over a year — that’s fewer units on the market. It’s holding desperately needed housing units away from the very Minneapolis residents this housing is supposed to serve.
This is why we support a vacancy fee on chronically vacant residential units. Any corporate property manager or absentee landlord that allows a residential unit to remain chronically vacant for six months or more should pay Minneapolis a robust fee. That money would be automatically earmarked for building or supporting affordable housing options across the city. The current vacant building registration fee is far too small for such a large sector of housing enforcement. It’s also based on self-reporting or tips from city residents, rather than proactive city enforcement. 
A stronger vacancy fee would ensure that housing units under corporate property or landlord management receive timely repairs and upkeep, since the vacancy fee incentivizes them to keep their units occupied. 
Some out-of-state property managers and developers of large-scale Minneapolis apartments would be incentivized to lower their skyrocketing rental costs to attract tenants, since sitting on empty units for six months or more would no longer just play into their investment and speculative portfolios.
Neighborhoods that have long dealt with vacant homes that attract crime and bring down nearby property values would see these homes converted into something else or filled with tenants, since a vacancy fee would continually charge the absentee owner of the vacant home. 
Recently, the Minneapolis Board of Estimation and Taxation endorsed exploring ways to implement a vacancy fee on chronically empty residential units as an alternative source of revenue. In a city facing a precarious fiscal future, a vacancy fee would offer valuable resources for affordable housing policies and construction. 
Finally, a vacancy fee can begin to repair a usurious housing system that punishes average renter families, saps homeowners of nearby property values, and keeps city government chronically three steps behind absentee and profit-driven housing interests.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Hundreds of CT affordable homes, apartments to be built using state tax credits
description: More than 450 affordable homes and apartments will be constructed with $10.4 million in state tax credits, distributed to 24 nonprofits.
text:
More than 450 affordable homes and apartments will be constructed using about $10.4 million in state tax credits. The funds, distributed by the quasi-public Connecticut Housing Finance Authority, CHFA, will go to 24 nonprofits across 15 municipalities.
Large and small communities will benefit from the funding, including Bridgeport, Norwalk, Sharon and Middletown, according to CHFA’s Senior Director of Research, Marketing, and Communications, Marcus Smith.
The timelines vary for each project given the different types of development, which range from rehabilitating historic sites and constructing new homes, Smith said.
“A lot of these are shovel-ready, and they could be ready to go in the next six months, and some of them might be just maybe a little bit longer to get going depending on what the use is for,” Smith said.
Connecticut needs 100,000 more affordable housing units, according to several studies, including one conducted by Connecticut’s Office of Policy and Management.
How the program came to be
The State Housing Tax Credit Contribution (HTCC) Program was established in 1987 and has helped create, preserve and rehabilitate more than 12,000 units of housing since 2010, according to Smith.
“It’s evolved over the years to become less of a gap filler for those big dozens of units or 100-unit multifamily projects that the state supports, and more towards funding the unique developments and the unique types of housing that, but for the HTCC program, just wouldn’t have access to the resources.”
Some unique types of housing supported by the project include owner-occupied multifamily buildings and supportive housing, designed to help formerly homeless residents transition to stable housing.
Additionally, three programs funded will provide downpayment assistance for homeowners. Six units of supportive housing will also be funded across Norwalk and Middletown.
CHFA allocates up to $10 million annually in state tax credits under the HTCC program to nonprofits developing very low-, low- and moderate- income housing. The funding is set by the state and, Smith said, over the years more money has been requested.
This year, there were far more applications than could be fulfilled with the allotted funding, Smith said. The 37 applications amounted to a request for $16 million. Ultimately, 24 were funded.
Last year, the program had to provide two application rounds to use up the funds.
“Consider last year as a blip, and this year demonstrating that there is a strong desire for this type of flexible support from the state,” Smith said.
Eversource is typically the main investor, he said, and as soon as nonprofits get the equity from Eversource the projects “should be up and running.”
Awardees must file quarterly reports to ensure the funding is being properly utilized, Smith said.
“Connecticut’s housing challenges are complex, and meeting them requires a broad and flexible set of tools,” Nandini Natarajan, CHFA’s CEO and Executive Director, said. “HTCC is an important part of that toolkit because it can support so many different housing needs, from creating new affordable rental homes and homeownership opportunities to preserving the housing we already have.”
This story was first published Sept. 23, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Maggie Hassan won a bipartisanship award. Please hold your applause.
description: In ways too numerous to count, the political events of the past two years have been tragic for this country. But because despair isn’t an option, my survival technique is to view much of it as comedy. Granted the violence, cruelty, and callousness of this moment make that difficult, but hopelessness is a trap that […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan speaks at a press conference on June 25, 2025, at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., is at right. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)In ways too numerous to count, the political events of the past two years have been tragic for this country. But because despair isn’t an option, my survival technique is to view much of it as comedy.
Granted the violence, cruelty, and callousness of this moment make that difficult, but hopelessness is a trap that I want no part of and which none of us can afford.
And so I watch the absurdity of this president fussing about the Kennedy Center, his ballroom, and reporters who hurt his feelings all while a new quagmire of his own making opens up in the Middle East, rising consumer prices put added pressures on American families, and one existential crisis (climate change) worsens while another (artificial intelligence) emerges.
Et cetera.
And then, amid so much calculated death and destruction, comes the dark hilarity of watching the 1980s teen movie villainy of Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and House Speaker Mike Johnson, among countless others. (Hegseth is perfect as Chet in “Weird Science,” of course, but how about Vance as Kent in “Real Genius”?)
There is no doubt in my mind that history will not be kind to these people, and you can bet that they’re going to dedicate a lot of time and resources into rehabilitating what’s left of their images once the “stable genius” is out of the picture. It’s already begun for some of them — Marjorie Taylor Greene is one and Tucker Carlson another. But then there are the quieter examples of attempted repentance and rebirth, like former Republican U.S. Sen. Rob Portman of Ohio.
I’m singling out Portman only because on Monday, New Hampshire’s junior U.S. senator, Maggie Hassan, gleefully sent out a press release celebrating a “Bipartisan Public Service Award” she was given by the University of Cincinnati’s Portman Center for Policy Solutions.
“Granite Staters have always prioritized solutions over partisanship,” Hassan said in the release. “That’s why I am dedicated to working with anyone to get things done for New Hampshire.”
Portman happily seconded the boast.
“I know firsthand that to get things done in Congress you need to work across the aisle,” he said. “Maggie Hassan and Todd Young (Republican of Indiana) are two of the best bipartisan legislators, and our new ranking system verifies that.”
Before New Hampshire Democrats crack open the champagne for their aisle-crossing U.S. senator, it’s important to understand a little more about the guy bestowing the award.
Portman endorsed President Donald Trump in 2016, withdrew the endorsement after the “Access Hollywood” tape, and then endorsed him again in 2020. (If this reminds you of Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s unprincipled flip-flop on Trump, well, it should.) 
“I’m going to vote for him, and I’m helping him, and I’m endorsing him,” Portman told CNBC in February 2020. “I cannot believe the change we have seen in terms of our economic growth, in terms of restoring our military strength. He’s done a lot of great things.”
When Trump was defeated in that election (sorry, Republicans, but he really did lose) and instigated the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection, Portman took a stand. Well, it was more of a pose.
“On the night it happened, I took to the Senate floor and gave an impassioned speech about democracy and the need to protect it. So that’s who I am,” he told The Atlantic’s Jeffrey Goldberg in 2022.
“But,” Goldberg wrote in his 2024 piece, “this is incorrect. This is not who he is. Portman showed the people of Ohio who he is five weeks later, on February 13, when he voted to acquit Trump, the man he knew to have fomented a violent, antidemocratic insurrection meant to overturn the results of a fair election.”
The title of Goldberg’s piece is “A study in Senate cowardice: Republicans like Rob Portman could have ended Donald Trump’s political career. They chose not to.”
And this — this! – is what Hassan and the rest of New Hampshire’s congressional delegation don’t seem to understand. While a lot of their constituents (myself included) are grateful they are not among the politicians throwing gasoline on the vast dumpster fire that is this American moment, now is not exactly the time to be taking a bipartisan victory lap. It’s great that they’re trying to douse the inferno with their chilled bottles of spring water and everything, but it would be a whole lot better, for everybody, if they tried a little harder to wrest the gas cans away from the arsonists.
How does a minority party accomplish that? I’m not sure, but I’ll let you know when I see it.
I do know, however, that it’s not enough for the state’s delegation to take occasional aim at the easy, neon-clad targets like Trump, Hegseth, and gravel-chewing Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The Portmans of the world — the “compassionate conservative” enablers of so much dark comedy, horror, and tragedy — bear much of the responsibility for lending the far right enough cover to take, hold, and exert power. The center-right, which apparently exists solely to reduce the complexity of the world to matters of deregulation and privatization, may not have fully joined the cult but they seem to enjoy wearing the uniform. I suspect that’s because it pays so well, and not just for them but also their benefactors at the top of the wealth ladder who move members of Congress around like chess pieces.
And you know, it occurs to me now that as much as I despised the bullies in those ’80s teen movies, it was always their pals just standing around smirking while it all went down who bothered me the most. Portman may not be bad guy Hardy Jenns (with two N’s) in “Some Kind of Wonderful,” but he absolutely appears as “Hardy’s friend” in the closing credits.
So forgive me for not joining the bipartisanship parade that New Hampshire’s Democratic congressional delegation takes so much pride in leading. I guess I’m still working through my ‘80s issues.

name: Maryland Matters
title: New data centers in Maryland to get additional scrutiny under governor’s order
description: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) is commissioning a new state task force to examine new data center proposals.
text:
Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore announces a new executive order on data center projects on Sept. 23, 2026. The order establishes a state task force to examine data center proposals. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore is commissioning a new state task force to examine new data center proposals, and advise local jurisdictions considering the projects.
The final decision on data center projects still rests with local governments, he said during a news conference Wednesday morning in Annapolis, during which he signed an executive order on the subject. Many county governments in Maryland have placed temporary pauses on new data center development, and one county has banned the projects.
“Our administration will always stand with the people, and the state will not go around a local community’s ‘no,’” Moore said.
Moore said he also plans to advocate for the repeal of a state tax exemption for data centers, established in 2020, during the next legislative session, which is set to begin in January.
Moore’s new task force, which will be staffed by seven state agencies, will evaluate proposals based on whether they protect electricity ratepayers from cost burdens, whether they include sufficient environmental protections and whether they have the support of the community, among other factors.
“They need to pay their own way, or they need to go away,” Moore said.
The task force will decide whether projects are “aligned, conditionally aligned, or not aligned” with the state’s principles.
The governor also established a public online dashboard, which will be updated monthly and list data center proposals and certain specifications about them.
“Any company seeking the state’s help will have to make commitments that are specific, that are measurable, and importantly, that are public,” Moore said.
This article will be updated.

title: Hallmark Actor Comes to Delaware for Special Film Celebration
description: Kristoffer Polaha, actor in 21 Hallmark movies, will be at UNITED Church’s Milford Campus on Friday, Oct. 23 By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist,  Delaware LIVE Hallmark fans will have a chance to see one of the network’s familiar leading men in Delaware this fall when actor Kristoffer Polaha visits Milford for a special evening celebrating an upcoming f[...]
text:
Kristoffer Polaha, actor in 21 Hallmark movies, will be at UNITED Church’s Milford Campus on Friday, Oct. 23
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist,  Delaware LIVE
Hallmark fans will have a chance to see one of the network’s familiar leading men in Delaware this fall when actor Kristoffer Polaha visits Milford for a special evening celebrating an upcoming film and the real-life mission that inspired it.
Polaha, who has appeared in 21 Hallmark movies along with numerous television, film and stage productions, will be at UNITED Church’s Milford Campus on Friday, Oct. 23, for the CUPS Comedy Cast Party.
The event celebrates the completion of the production phase of Rescued, the working title of a film starring Polaha and based on the story of comedian Mike Williams.
Williams moved with his wife and three children to the Dominican Republic in 2010. While there, he became involved in an effort to rescue a Haitian refugee from Russian human traffickers. That experience ultimately led to the establishment of CUPS Mission, which now works in three countries on two continents to fight poverty and provide children with education, training and opportunities that can help them avoid trafficking.
“When I heard Mike’s story, I knew I had to be a part of it,” said writer and director Trey Reynolds. “This film is for every person who has ever felt the pull to do something greater than themselves and wasn’t sure if they were brave enough to do it.”
The movie was filmed on location in the Dominican Republic during March and April and is currently in post-production, with a projected release in late 2027. Reynolds’ previous credits include Blue Miracle, The Forge and Family Camp.
For Polaha, making the film became about more than simply playing a role.
“To make a movie is a blessing. To make this kind of movie is life-changing,” Polaha said.
During production, Polaha described how the cast and crew worked to leave a lasting impact on the community where they were filming. Their efforts included cleaning a river, stuccoing and painting the village church and painting nearby homes. The word “HOPE” was also painted on the church wall.
“We’re leaving this community better than how we found it,” Polaha said.
Children from the community spent six days with the film crew, playing games, becoming comfortable around the cameras and eventually appearing in the movie.
The Bridge, a Christian radio network with stations in Delaware, Maryland, Virginia and New Jersey, is hosting the Milford event. The network has supported CUPS Mission for years, and its listeners sponsor La Union Abajo, a village near Puerto Plata. Bridge staff members and listeners
have contributed funding, equipment and volunteer labor to CUPS Mission projects for nearly a decade.
Williams, whose credits include Dry Bar Comedy and Dove Award Comedian of the Year, will also appear at the Delaware event. He and his family have helped thousands of children during the past 15 years.
Polaha and Williams will be joined by Reynolds, Executive Producer Jack Eason, Associate Producer Benjamin Weeks and others involved with the film. The evening will include a question-and-answer session, exclusive behind-the-scenes footage and a first look at a clip from the movie.
“This is exactly the kind of story that reminds us what is possible when ordinary people choose to live for something bigger than themselves,” said producer Darren Moorman. “Mike Williams stepped away from personal success to answer a deeper calling, and the ripple effect of that decision is still being felt today.”
Polaha is well known to Hallmark audiences, but his acting credits extend far beyond the network. He has appeared in North Shore, Life Unexpected, Wonder Woman 1984, Jurassic World Dominion, Mad Men and CSI: Miami. He also stars alongside Jon Hamm in the upcoming MGM+ psychological thriller American Hostage.
The CUPS Comedy Cast Party begins at 7 p.m. Friday, Oct. 23, at UNITED Church, Milford Campus, 985 N. Dupont Blvd. The event is open to the public. Early bird tickets are $20 through Aug. 31, with prices increasing Sept. 1. A limited number of $100 VIP Red Carpet Reception tickets are also available and include a private reception with Polaha, Reynolds and others involved with the film.

name: VTDigger
title: Celebrating National GEAR UP Week: five Vermont students who are lighting the way
description:
This week we spotlight Vermont students who are working with VSAC’s GEAR UP to grow, lead, and prepare for what's next. From leadership workshops to college fairs to career goals, these five students are just a few of the thousands turning opportunities into achievements.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Celebrating National GEAR UP Week: five Vermont stud[...]
text:
Since 1999, GEAR UP (Gaining Early Awareness and Readiness for Undergraduate Programs) has helped students from modest-income and first-generation families discover their path to postsecondary education and training. This week, VSAC celebrates National GEAR UP Week to share more about the program and its resources, and spotlight a handful of students who working with VSAC’s GEAR UP to grow, lead, and prepare for what’s next.
VSAC’s GEAR UP serves 2,000 middle and high school students in 33 schools across the state. In addition, the program serves approximately 300 students in their first year of postsecondary education or training. Students and families receive one-on-one college and career exploration, counseling, and family engagement opportunities. The program also supports school-based initiatives, educator training, and partnerships with colleges, training programs, and state agencies, all working to strengthen Vermont’s college and career-ready culture.
As we celebrate GEAR UP week this year, we’re highlighting a few extraordinary GEAR UP students from around Vermont—and how VSAC’s GEAR UP is helping them light the way. 
LILLY SCHLEGEL
An eleventh grader at Oxbow High School, Lilly Schlegel is eager to take on new opportunities and challenges that will help her grow as a student and as a person. She hopes to become a postpartum nurse, supporting parents and newborns as they transition from childbirth.
Through GEAR UP, Lilly traveled to Washington, D.C., for the Youth Leadership Summit, an experience she says helped her grow. “This was an amazing opportunity that created a welcoming environment for people who want to improve their leadership skills,” she shares. “People from around the country met in D.C. for this event. I really enjoyed meeting people from different places and backgrounds.”
Kassidy Moore, Lilly’s VSAC GEAR UP outreach counselor, says, “Lilly is an amazing member of our GEAR UP community. She is involved with GEAR UP not only to prepare for her own future but also to help other students. She is making GEAR UP better for everyone in her community!”
ROWAN DRESSEL
Rowan Dressel is a ninth grader at Springfield High School with a passion for writing and journalism. He plans to go to college and build a career in the field. His GEAR UP counselor, Jessi Krause-Heron, describes him as magnetic and thoughtful, “one of those students who pushes the group to get the most out of every lesson.”
Rowan says SEEDS leadership training, offered through VSAC’s GEAR UP, has been one of the highlights of his time in school so far. Held at Vermont State Randolph, the SEEDS overnight leadership camp helps Vermont middle and high school students build confidence and social-emotional skills.
“From the moment Rowan walked into his first meeting, I could tell he was going to lead the group to squeeze the value from every lesson,” Krause-Heron says. “The positive energy and enthusiasm he brings to every space he enters is palpable and appreciated by educators and students.”
GRAYSON STAPLES
Grayson Staples is a ninth grader at North Country Union High School. He’s in advanced rock band and says he is trying to put himself out there as much as possible this year. GEAR UP has helped him grow his confidence. 
Like Rowan, Grayson enjoyed the GEAR UP leadership training. “One cool thing I have been able to do with GEAR UP is their summer SEEDS program bringing together leaders from across the state to help teach us how to be leaders in our communities.”
His GEAR UP counselor, Amanda Frattaroli, describes Grayson as comfortably and authentically himself. “He is smart, kind, funny, and makes everyone around him feel comfortable,” she adds. “He is a joy to work with and watching him grow and learn has been a privilege. I know his determination and big heart will take him far!”
BROOKLYNN LETOURNEAU
As she’s entering her final year at Richford Junior Senior High School and Cold Hollow Career Center, Brooklynn Letourneau is excited to experience everything senior year has to offer, while preparing for a future as a nurse. 
“I want to be a kind, caring, and hard-working nurse who everyone enjoys working with,” she says. “I want to make my patients feel comfortable, supported, and cared for, while also educating them to better understand their health.” 
Through GEAR UP, Brooklynn has had opportunities like attending a college fair at St. Michael’s College, which helped her learn about different colleges and the application process. “It was a really helpful experience because it gave me a better idea of what I want to look for in a college and helped me feel more prepared for my future,” she says.
Brooklynn says her GEAR UP counselor, Matt Mitchell, has been a great resource, helping her organize her applications and manage all the pieces of applying for college and financial aid. “Brooklynn is a leader in her class and at the school,” Mitchell says, “including serving as captain of the varsity soccer team and treasurer of her class office.” Her leadership skills are sure to take her far.
AMELIA MUNGER
A junior at Vermont State Castleton, Amelia Munger is looking forward to gaining more clinical experience in a hospital setting as she works toward becoming a registered nurse. She plans to specialize in complex skin wounds, ostomy, and continence care at her local hospital.
VSAC outreach counselor Tia Stillman helped Amelia identify her next steps starting in middle school. “I’ve had GEAR UP by my side since junior high, helping me get to where I am now,” Amelia says. “They helped me start thinking about my goals early, and every time we met, they built my confidence to follow through. They helped me establish a path to get there; without GEAR UP, I wouldn’t be where I am today.”
VSAC’s GEAR UP is a powerful tool in closing opportunity gaps and building pathways to success for Vermont students, ensuring that thousands of students receive personalized support, guidance, and resources they need to pursue their goals beyond high school—whether that’s college or career training.
These five are just a handful of the incredible students in Vermont’s middle and high schools that benefit from GEAR UP support. We can’t wait to see what they do next!

The Vermont Student Assistance Corp. was created by the Vermont Legislature in 1965 as a public nonprofit agency. We advocate for Vermont students and their families to ensure that they have the tools they need to achieve their education and training goals. We create opportunities for all Vermont students, but particularly for those—of any age—who believe that the doors to education are closed to them. Growing families save for education with VT529, Vermont’s official 529 savings program. To help Vermonters plan and pay for college or job training, our counselors work with students in nearly every Vermont middle school and high school, and are also available to work with adults. Our grant, scholarship, and workforce development programs create opportunity, help students re-skill or learn new skills, and grow the economy. VSAC’s loan, loan refinance, and loan forgiveness programs provide competitive education financing to students and families. Find us at www.vsac.org or visit Facebook, Instagram, or LinkedIn.

description: The Maternal Mental Health and Family Wellness Award will recognize work that advances maternal health for women and families throughout Delaware. text:
Nominations are now being accepted for five awards that will be presented during a ceremony in December. Delaware residents have until Friday, Oct. 9, to recommend an individual, program or organization for recognition.
The Maternal Mental Health and Family Wellness Award will recognize work that advances maternal health for women and families throughout Delaware.
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE
Delawareans have an opportunity to recognize the people and organizations working to improve mental health, support recovery and strengthen the well-being of families and communities across the First State.
The Office of Lieutenant Governor Kyle Evans Gay has announced the return of the annual Lt. Governor’s Challenge, featuring a refreshed vision that focuses on contributions to behavioral health and mental health outcomes throughout Delaware.
Nominations are now being accepted for five awards that will be presented during a ceremony in December. Delaware residents have until Friday, Oct. 9, to recommend an individual, program or organization for recognition.
“I’m thrilled to bring back the Lt. Governor’s Challenge to celebrate individuals and organizations in our state who go above and beyond in prioritizing mental health and raising awareness,” Gay said.
“As Chair of the Behavioral Health Consortium, it is my honor to celebrate individuals and organizations across our state whose work has changed lives and reduced stigma in Delaware and beyond,” she added. “In honoring this year’s awardees, we are first and foremost saying ‘thank you’ and, as we continue to learn more about what is working in the First State, we hope that opportunities for connection and care continue to grow statewide.”
Nominees may include Delaware residents as well as programs and organizations that serve or operate in the state. Regional and national organizations may also be considered when a nomination specifically recognizes their work and impact in Delaware.
The five award categories reflect a range of efforts to improve behavioral health and well-being.
The Youth Mental Health Champion Award will recognize leadership, advocacy or service that advances the mental health and well-being of young people in a school or community.
The Community Mental Health Innovation Award will honor an individual, program or organization that has developed creative approaches to improving access to mental health services and support.
The Workplace Mental Health Leadership Award will recognize efforts to create a workplace culture that prioritizes employee mental health and well-being.
The Recovery Champion Award will honor someone who serves as an inspiration or advocate for others. This category highlights the importance of recovery support, and the role individuals can play in encouraging and guiding people facing behavioral health or substance use challenges.
The Maternal Mental Health and Family Wellness Award will recognize work that advances maternal mental health, perinatal well-being, reproductive justice or equitable access to care for women and families throughout Delaware.
Following the Oct. 9 nomination deadline, an extensive review process will begin to select this year’s award recipients. Reviewers may include people with experience in behavioral health, health care, education, public service, recovery, community engagement and related fields.
The winners will be announced during the Lt. Governor’s Challenge ceremony on Tuesday, Dec. 8, at Delaware State University’s Schwartz Center for the Arts in Dover.
By inviting the public to submit nominations, the initiative gives Delawareans a direct role in identifying people and programs whose work may not always receive widespread attention. It also provides an opportunity to share successful approaches, raise awareness of available support and encourage stronger connections among those working to improve behavioral health across the state. Nominations may be submitted online at de.gov/ltgovchallenge.
Anyone who requires language or disability access, technology assistance or another reasonable accommodation to complete the nomination process may contact Fiona Pando at fiona.c.pando@delaware.gov.
