name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas lawmaker cries foul over voter registration gift cards, asks Kobach to investigate
description: TOPEKA — A Kansas legislator is demanding an investigation into a League of Women Voters chapter that gave $5 gift cards to high school students who registered to vote, a move he said violates election laws.  Rep. Pat Proctor, who is running for secretary of state and is chairman of the House Elections Committee, asked […]
text:
Rep. Pat Proctor, shown here at a candidate forum on Aug. 27, 2026, made a complaint to the attorney general about a League of Women Voters group in Leavenworth that gave high school students $5 Starbucks gift cards if they would register to vote. Although Proctor said he wants the group investigated, he asked that students who were "unwitting" participants not be investigated. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A Kansas legislator is demanding an investigation into a League of Women Voters chapter that gave $5 gift cards to high school students who registered to vote, a move he said violates election laws. 
Rep. Pat Proctor, who is running for secretary of state and is chairman of the House Elections Committee, asked Attorney General Kris Kobach to investigate the group, which in May held voter registration drives at Lansing and Leavenworth high schools. 
In a Facebook post with photos, the League of Women Voters of Leavenworth County showed students registering to vote. The post included a photo with a sign on the table that read: “Register to vote get a $5 Starbucks gift card.”
Photos also showed students holding up the gift cards.
Federal law makes it illegal for anyone to pay, offer to pay or accept payment for registering to vote, and the crime is punishable by up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine, Proctor said in a news release. 
“I have, for many years, heard reports of this organization engaging in activities that call into question its supposed nonpartisan status and could well jeopardize its tax-exempt status,” Proctor said. “But this activity is not just rank partisanship; it’s illegal.”
While Proctor asked that the children who were “unwittingly involved” not be investigated or prosecuted, it is also illegal to accept payment for voting or registering to vote.  
Marlene Merrill, president of Kansas League of Women Voters, said she had no comment. The group has reached out to its national organization to discuss the situation. 
The Kansas attorney general’s office has not been in touch with the League of Women Voters yet about the issue, she said. Attorney General Kris Kobach’s spokeswoman did not reply when asked to comment on whether the situation would be investigated. 
Brendan Fischer, director of strategic investigations at the Campaign Legal Center, a nonpartisan legal organization focused on democracy, said federal law prohibits paying anyone to register to vote or for their vote. 
“Given the breadth of the law, well-intentioned groups seeking to encourage civic participation can accidentally cross a legal line,” he said.
In 2008, for example, Ben & Jerry’s planned to give free ice cream to anyone with an “I voted” sticker, Fischer said. Because doing so would have provided something of value in exchange for voting, the company made free ice cream available to everyone on election day, he said. 
“The details of the offer matter a lot,” Fischer said. “A business may give everyone free ice cream on Election Day, but it may not condition the free ice cream on someone registering or voting. The law also does not prohibit civic groups or others from offering assistance to prospective voters.”
That law, however, is “unlikely” to prohibit candidates from making promises to deliver economic benefits to voters if they win an election, Fischer said. 
President Donald Trump recently promised $5,000 to every voter if the Republicans win in the midterm elections. 
“As the Supreme Court noted in a 1982 case, ‘there are constitutional limits on the State’s power to prohibit candidates from making promises in the course of an election campaign,’ provided that the benefits are achieved through the normal processes of government rather than a private arrangement,” Fischer said.
Proctor posted his letter about the League of Women Voters on his Facebook campaign page and Rep. Kirk Haskins, D-Topeka, noted in a comment that Proctor could be violating campaign law. 
“FYI- Pat, ironically, it appears you may be violating Kansas campaign laws by posting your letter on state produced/designed letterhead on your campaign influencing FB page,” Haskins wrote. “K.S.A. 25-4169a. The statute specifically bars using state ‘machinery, equipment and supplies’ or public resources to influence an election.”
When reached for comment, Proctor said he had nothing to say before any questions could be asked.
Haskins called Proctor’s posting in violation of campaign law a “minor misstep,” in a message to Kansas Reflector. 
“However, it deserves more than a cursory glance,” he said. “Public officials do have a duty to address matters of public interest. However, this action of Rep. Proctor is indicative of a glaring political culture of selective attention and bias.”
Proctor highlighted the grassroots voter registration effort while ignoring Trump’s $5,000 proposal, which Haskins interpreted as a cash bribe for votes. 
Haskins called the double standard something that “damages public trust in our elected officials and ultimately our democracy.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Families of people killed by ICE say feds have slandered the victims
description: Family members of those killed by federal immigration agents told Democratic members of Congress Tuesday that they’ve been victimized twice over by the Trump administration’s pattern of obstruction and lies about the shootings — and about the victims themselves. The shadow hearing, which was held in Washington, D.C., sought to draw attention to the lack […]
text:
Sean Murphy, an attorney representing the family of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was killed in Biddeford, Maine, in July, told a Democratic congressional panel that "the dehumanization of the victims of these crimes is despicable.” (Screenshot via Oversight Dems YouTube)Family members of those killed by federal immigration agents told Democratic members of Congress Tuesday that they’ve been victimized twice over by the Trump administration’s pattern of obstruction and lies about the shootings — and about the victims themselves.
The shadow hearing, which was held in Washington, D.C., sought to draw attention to the lack of justice given the victims of the many questionable shootings by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, who serves as ranking member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, said that when Markwayne Mullin was tapped to replace Kristi Noem as Department of Homeland Security secretary, “There was hope that (ICE) would abandon the physical brutality and inhumanity of its tactics on the streets, there was hope that there would be accountability.”
That hope has been dashed, he said, most recently with the weekend shooting of a Venezuelan man in Austin, Texas.
California U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia, ranking member of the U.S. House Oversight Committee, said that as of September 2026, Democrats on the committee have documented over 1,000 “credible and verified instances (of) abuses” under President Donald Trump’s second administration, including 20 people shot by ICE, while 58 have died in ICE custody.
With a lack of subpoena power, Democrats do not have the ability to compel officials from the administration to testify. Instead, they’ve used this sort of forum, including one in Maine last month, to hear from willing witnesses.

‘Dual assassinations’

Family members and other representatives of Ruben Ray Martinez and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo of Texas, Renée Good and Alex Pretti of Minnesota, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero of Maine all testified.
The witnesses all described how, in addition to a complete lack of information and oversight after the shootings, the federal government spread falsehoods about the people killed.
Sean Murphy, an attorney representing the Guerrero family, told the panel, “The dehumanization of the victims of these crimes is despicable.”
“The patterns of dual assassinations — one of the body and then of the character — is disgusting, and there’s a pattern that if you’re not seeing it, it’s because you have your eyes closed,” Murphy said.
Ronaldo Salgado and Lorenzo Salgado Jr., whose father was shot and killed in July while driving to work, said the feds provided little information about what led to the shooting but instead made repeated false claims that were later walked back, including that their father had been the target of the operation and had weaponized his vehicle.
“DHS also claimed there may have been drugs in the vehicle, which, if anyone who knew my father would tell you, is absurd, and which testing later proved to be false, as we all knew it would,” Lorenzo Salgado Jr. said.
Stella Carlson, a community activist who filmed the shooting of Pretti in Minneapolis, told the lawmakers that she felt like she “witnessed two assassinations, the first was the literal assasination of Alex and the second was the attempted assassination of his character.”
Pretti, an ICU nurse for the Department of Veterans Affairs, was described by the Trump administration as a “domestic terrorist.” He had come to the aid of a woman pushed down by a federal officer before he was disarmed and shot in the back.
“We observed his murder with our own eyes, and the truth does not become less true because someone with great power tells a louder lie,” Carlson said. “When people are killed, and when the public is given false accounts of what happened, there must be accountability.”
ICE shot 23-year-old Ruben Ray Martinez in March 2025, making him the first U.S. citizen killed by ICE during the second Trump administration. As Blumenthal noted, however, “That fact was not disclosed to his family or to the public for nearly a year.”
His mother, Rachel Reyes, also told the panel about how video evidence and testimony from his lifelong best friend, who had been a passenger in the car at the time, contradicted the official account of the events that led to the shooting.
“Though the circumstances surrounding his death and these other victims are distinctly different, the pattern is the same: lives cut short by the same agency, agents without body cameras, no warnings, no attempt to de-escalate, excessive force followed by deflection and a lack of accountability after the fact,” Reyes said. “Other similarities are that these victims, despite being nonviolent community members with no criminal background, were disparaged and blamed to shift focus away from the officer’s misconduct.”
“What happened to my son is personal, but it should be a concern for us all,” she said.
As in the other instances, the government changed the official narrative of Guerrero’s shooting.
At first, Mullin told independent U.S. Sen. Angus King that Guerrero “weaponized” his vehicle before being shot by an ICE agent. But ICE later said he attempted to flee and “fearing for public safety” an agent shot him.

name: Mississippi Today
title: At northeast Mississippi summit, lived experience shapes conversations on addiction and recovery
description: In Tupelo, the annual Northeast Mississippi Mental Health & Substance Use Recovery Summit provides local counselors, social workers and teachers a way to fulfill their mandatory continuing education requirements without having to drive three hours to Jackson.
text:
During breaks between sessions at the Northeast Mississippi Mental Health & Substance Use Recovery Summit, Andy Newsom navigated through the vendor booths, shaking hands and asking about resources. New Orleans-raised Newsom, who stood out among attendees with his head-to-toe Jacksonville Jaguars outfit and colorful tattoos, already knew several of the treatment centers in attendance. One was his former employer, the North Mississippi State Hospital. 
That was a meaningful position, he told Mississippi Today, because it’s the same hospital where he finally “got clean.” 
“I’ve been in treatment 19 times,” Newsom said.  ”You would think I would’ve learned. But see, it took what it took.”
The final time he entered a treatment center, his mother checked him in. It was that “gift of desperation” that allowed him to slowly work toward recovery, Newsom said. After becoming fully sober on Nov. 8, 2017, he started working as a peer support counselor for youth and adults with substance use disorders. 
United Way of Northeast Mississippi President Patti Parker started the Health Alliance initiative in 2021, which organized its first summit a year later. The one-day event provides local counselors, social workers and teachers a way to fulfill their mandatory continuing education requirements without having to drive three hours to Jackson. 
Walking through the fifth annual summit at Tupelo’s Huntington Bank Conference Center, Tupelo-based counselor Theresa Triplett is grateful that the gathering exists. She earns most of her 15 hours of continuing education requirements a year through a conference in Biloxi, but she said she appreciates having a conference 10 minutes away from her workplace, versus several hours away. 
“We’re a one-of-kind conference in north Mississippi,” said Terry Baber, director of the Northeast Mississippi Health Alliance. 
Changing responses to addiction
Keynote speaker Christina Dent advocated for health-centered solutions for drug use instead of policies that push for incarceration. She founded the nonprofit organization End it For Good after her perspective on addiction was changed. She and her husband became foster parents in 2015 and then met the child’s birth mother. 
Christina Dent, founder of nonprofit education organization End it For Good, gave the keynote address on harm reduction for substance use disorders at the Northeast Mississippi Mental Health & Substance Use Recovery Summit in Tupelo Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
Before attendees seated over black tablecloths, Dent said she realized she had radically misunderstood how to treat addiction after seeing someone struggle with substance use.
“ This was me just with some different experiences and a different path to try to cope with those experiences,” she said.
At the summit, Dent also shared resources and therapies that are currently being studied. One was ibogaine, a psychoactive plant-based compound that some research suggests can rapidly reduce dependence on opioids. Dent said ibogaine helped her friend Juliana Mulligan end an intense opioid addiction after she accessed the treatment, currently illegal in the United States, at a clinic in Guatemala. Earlier in the day, Rep. Sam Creekmore, a Republican from New Albany, shared in his legislative update that Mississippi recently became the second state in the country to fund an ibogaine clinical trial. 
During the summit, participants also attended sessions on the complexity of suicide, disability and prevention, and recovering from sexual trauma, among others.
Whitney Watts, left, a community specialist at Friend of God Ministries, shares her journey of recovering from addiction in a conversation moderated by Lindsay Brett, right. Sept 22, 2026. Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
Ishaunna Gully, a consultant from the Jackson-based program Prevention Includes Everyone, was a first-time speaker at the summit. She shared her experiences growing up in Laurel and surviving the domestic violence that led to her becoming a wheelchair user. As her audience listened and reacted to her dramatic story, Gully talked about how mental health and substance use affected her family, from her parents to her romantic partners and herself. 
“ You see the chair, you see the paralysis. You know something happened, you don’t know what,” Gully told her audience. “But how many people walk around all day long, where something is happening within you?”
From conference rooms to community
In future conferences, Baber said he hopes to offer training with Narcan, the brand name of the medicine naloxone, that can reverse opioid overdoses within minutes. 
Baber said he became interested in counseling and treatment for substance use after his brother died from a stroke that may have been related to fentanyl. Now, he hopes to spread knowledge and reduce stigma for substance use disorders. 
Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
He hopes to see more families and members of the public at the summit, but he understands it’s hard to get off work. To reach more people, the Health Alliance plans to host its second “Recovery in the Park” from 2-5 p.m. at Ballard Park this Saturday. 
The family event will feature free food, a petting zoo and face painting, Baber said, and no one will know who is suffering from addiction and who isn’t. 
As a Narcan trainer at the community mental health center Communicare, Newsom goes wherever he can “get a foot in the door,” including into sheriff’s offices. Instead of being questioned about criminal activity, he helps train law enforcement officers in how to administer Narcan. 
“ I used to be the one getting Narcan,” he said. “Now I’m telling people about it.” 
Newsom said he’s made plenty of mistakes since entering recovery, spends more money than he should and has turned his spare bedroom into a shoe closet with nearly 400 pairs of tennis shoes. But he hasn’t gone back to heroin. 
Sporting the  Nike’s Air Max 90 shoes in the Jacksonville Jaguars’ teal and gold, he headed off to talk to the next vendor. 
This story was produced with support from the Sarah Yelena Haselhorst Fund for Health Journalism.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: White Stadium and the community engagement gap
description: There’s still time for White Stadium project planners to deliver on the principles of EJ Community Engagement and Outreach – improved levels of trust, transparency, and stronger pathways for ongoing collaboration.
text:
THE MASSACHUSETTS Supreme Judicial Court’s recent unanimous ruling in favor of the City of Boston did not just end the legal challenges to the White Stadium renovation project. It cemented the project’s many promised benefits, including a home for a prominent professional women’s soccer franchise while providing the community with significant access to a state-of-the-art athletic facility,  and substantial funds for Boston Public Schools athletics.  
The new White Stadium will also deliver much-needed substantial infrastructure upgrades in the Franklin Park neighborhood for stormwater management, public safety, and preservation of the tree canopy.  
Unfortunately, many residents in the surrounding neighborhoods of Roxbury, Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, and Mattapan are not celebrating the SJC’s White Stadium ruling. A significant reason was the decision to bypass what is known as the Environmental Justice Community Engagement and Outreach process. This is a legally required procedure for almost every large-scale infrastructure  proposal in a designated environmental justice area, according to the Massachusetts Environmental Policy Act. 
As a school facility, White Stadium can legally proceed without a full state-level environmental review, including EJ Community Engagement and Outreach. The project’s rightful exemption from full MEPA study allowed designers and planners to proceed without having to comply with the rigorous legal  components of EJ outreach. The decision to bypass a traditional process represents a missed opportunity for a collaborative journey between the City of Boston and local residents that delivers a White Stadium molded by a shared sense of place and unified sense of purpose.  
By opting out, city and project planners lost the chance to lessen mistrust and strengthen community bonds. It is widely understood that neighbors—even not-in-my-backyard folks—are best positioned to understand any project’s human needs and the impacts it will create based on their lived experience. Meaningful residential participation in the design and planning phases of a project goes a long way toward building lasting support for technical decisions affecting quality of life, equity, health, and economic vitality.  
At a minimum, the EJ Engagement and Outreach process offers substantial guidance for planners and engineers that allows projects to establish measurable, achievable goals that consider all stakeholder needs, in particular a community’s cultural and visual identity, accessibility, and health disparities. 
For the White Stadium project, the Franklin Park area exceeds every legal threshold to apply EJ standards. These include minority population percentages above 40 percent, disproportionate existing health and environmental burdens, and low-income households. 
Given the chance to participate in a rigorous EJ Engagement and Outreach process based on “meaningful” levels of involvement by all stakeholders, there is every reason to believe that the White Stadium redevelopment’s benefits would be even better that what has been delivered to date by finding ways to actively uplift residents.  
Instead, it is an unfortunate early legacy of the White Stadium project that a sizable portion of the community continues to express dissatisfaction based on a belief they were denied the opportunity to have a say in the future of their neighborhood and community.  
As things stand today, it will never be enough that the White Stadium project team and city have held more than 100 public and small-group meetings since the summer of 2023. The impressive monetary resources project leaders have touted as mitigation for game-day and construction-phase impacts will not wash away the disappointment and distrust. Many community stakeholders insist they were unseen, marginalized, and disproportionately burdened.  
Leaders at every level in the Commonwealth recognize and appreciate the benefits of embracing EJ Community Engagement and Outreach practices. This includes Mayor Michelle Wu’s administration, which has committed significant resources and time across Boston to foster widespread participation in other infrastructure project decision-making.  
There is no question that Mayor Wu supports the broad goal of identifying and delivering practical mitigation strategies for infrastructure and major real estate developments that are based on extensive community input. Every process that helps avoid, minimize, or mitigate disproportionately high and adverse human health and environmental effects associated with any particular project is a win for the city. 
In a perfect world, successful EJ Community Engagement and Public Outreach programs for infrastructure projects yield a new dynamic that redefines community relations with government. These processes drive project design that echoes community desires and secures local priorities, including economic equity, safety, environmental health, and mobility. Residents are given the chance to evolve from reactive players to involved partners invested in the future of their built environment.  
Historical skepticism toward public agencies is certainly understandable. The White Stadium engagement process certainly did not assuage that mistrust. Following formal project announcement in 2023, many opted out of stadium planning. Right or wrong, cynics felt the deal was done, engagement was a waste of time, and that nobody cares. 
But there’s still time for White Stadium project planners to deliver on the principles of EJ Community Engagement and Outreach – improved levels of trust, transparency, and stronger pathways for ongoing collaboration. The potential benefits—fewer transportation impacts, more impactful community investments, amplified public space enhancements—seem obvious. At a minimum, project engineers can volunteer to publish metrics that allow distrusting community leaders to monitor project commitments, environmental remediation, and neighborhood benefits during and after construction. 
Every infrastructure project wins when residents in environmental justice communities feel seen and heard. 
Scott Farmelant is the principal consultant and owner of Boston Strategic Communications. He served as lead author of the first-ever Massachusetts Department of Transportation Strategic Guidance for Environmental Justice Outreach Protocols, which was published in 2023.

name: Nevada Current
title: Buck attempts to erase social media record
description: Republican State Sen. Carrie Buck, who is challenging longtime U.S. Rep. Dina Titus, a Democrat, appears to be distancing herself from President Donald Trump’s agenda. In recent months, Buck has scrubbed social media posts in which she exalted tariffs and the One Big Beautiful Bill, and compared women who have abortions to Adolf Hitler.  Buck […]
text:
Screengrab from a National Republican Congressional Committee ad for Carry Buck.Republican State Sen. Carrie Buck, who is challenging longtime U.S. Rep. Dina Titus, a Democrat, appears to be distancing herself from President Donald Trump’s agenda. In recent months, Buck has scrubbed social media posts in which she exalted tariffs and the One Big Beautiful Bill, and compared women who have abortions to Adolf Hitler. 
Buck did not respond to requests for comment on whether her positions on those issues have changed. Her campaign website lists Trump among her endorsements, but makes no mention of his policies.
Last year on the Fourth of July, Buck praised the passage of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill on X.  “Today was such an awesome day! The BIG beautiful bill passed….and my boys are all together once again! … Thank you, Lord, for all our blessings.”
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) is projected by state officials to eliminate Medicaid coverage for roughly 70,000 to 100,000 Nevadans. Last year, the Joint Economic Committee Minority estimated just under 30,000 Nevadans in Congressional District 1, which Buck hopes to represent, could lose their health care coverage.  
The OBBBA capped the rate of a tax which may be assessed by states on private hospitals, known as the provider tax. The tax currently generates about $830 million a year in federal matching dollars for the state. The Nevada Hospital Association estimates that amount will be reduced by $300 million in fiscal year 2028, which begins next July, and by $507 million the following fiscal year.
A chunk of the matching funds— some 15% — is allocated to behavioral health services that facilitate access to mental health treatment. 



Projected cuts to provider tax funds in CD1, FY 2027

Sunrise Hospital and Medical Center Las Vegas, $4,445,117
Henderson Hospital Henderson, $4,421,911
St. Rose Dominican – Siena Henderson, $2,622,386
Desert Springs Hospital Medical Center Las Vegas, $585,496
St. Rose Dominican – DeLima Henderson, $372,524
Boulder City Hospital Boulder City, $308,156

Total: $12,755,590
Source: Third Way, GOP Medicaid Cuts Will Decimate Hospitals Nationwide, 7/8/25




Hospitals in CD1 are projected to lose just under $13 million, according to Third Way, a national think tank that advocates for moderate policies. 
Trump’s bill also put $328 million in clean energy investments and more than 7,200 jobs in the state at risk, according to the Clean Investment Monitor, a clean energy investment tracker created by Rhodium Group and MIT’s Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research.
Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, who is endorsed by Trump in his bid for reelection, says he persuaded the president to restore some of that money to a handful of solar projects in Nevada. 
Buck’s post hailing the OBBBA is no longer available. 
Buck also deleted a social media post endorsing Trump’s tariffs, which have raised prices for consumers and kept would-be tourists from traveling. 
In mid-March 2025, Buck asserted  on X that “It takes Trump’s policies to bring manufacturing jobs HOME. Made in America, baby! Just pointing out hypocrisy”.
Days earlier the Current reported that Trump’s tariffs were expected to put a damper on tourism, Nevada’s bread-and-butter industry. 
“I am gravely concerned that our tourism workers will face layoffs from the Trump tariffs,” Rep. Dina Titus, the Democrat incumbent Buck hopes to defeat, said at the time.  
The Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority reports visitation to Southern Nevada was down 7.5% last year, the first of Trump’s second term. It has yet to recover and remains essentially flat year-over-year. 
Since Trump took office for the second time, the average Nevada family has paid $3,300 more for goods and services, says a report from the Joint Economic Committee Minority.
By May of this year, Buck’s post from March 2025 praising tariffs was no longer available. 
A third post deleted by Buck equated abortion with Hitler’s attempted genocide of Jews and others. 
In the spring of 2023, explaining her vote against what would become the Question 6 ballot initiative, Buck posted on Facebook that abortion is akin to “ripping a baby limb from limb out of his/her mother,” and added “I think Hitler did that in his reign.” She urged Nevadans to vote against an amendment that would add the right to an abortion to the Nevada Constitution. 
The ballot measure, a backlash against Trump’s first term litmus test for Supreme Court nominees, passed with 64% of the vote and must be approved again in November to amend the Constitution. 
By May of this year, Buck had deleted the post. 
Buck’s social media scrub comes as Republicans, dragged down by the Trump agenda, face the possibility of losing control of the House of Representatives in November. 
A poll released Tuesday by the Economist and YouGov found “52% of likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their district, while only 38% would vote for the Republican candidate.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Three Clark County School Board seats are on the ballot this year
description: Voters will have the chance to reelect or replace three Clark County School Board District incumbents this November as public schools in Nevada face budget cuts and declining student enrollment. The Clark County School District (CCSD) Board of Trustees is a nonpartisan 11-member board responsible for governing the nation’s fifth-largest school district with[...]
text:
(Photo: Ronda Churchill/Nevada Current)Voters will have the chance to reelect or replace three Clark County School Board District incumbents this November as public schools in Nevada face budget cuts and declining student enrollment.
The Clark County School District (CCSD) Board of Trustees is a nonpartisan 11-member board responsible for governing the nation’s fifth-largest school district with over 300,000 students. Seven of those members are elected and work alongside four appointed members.
Their primary duties are hiring and monitoring the superintendent, establishing district policies, approving the annual budget, managing capital programs, and setting strategic goals to improve student achievement.
Trustees can serve for up to three four-year terms and receive a salary of $750 a month or $9,000 a year.
Earlier this month, CCSDannounced it must reduce its fall budget by $51.6 million, largely due to declining student enrollment and increasing employee costs. 
Enrollment for the 2026-2027 school year is more than 10,400 students lower than last year, a decline the district says amounts to more than $100 million in lost state funding.
Trustees will need to tackle those impacts while focusing on how to improve student achievement.
Clark County School Board District D
Brenda Zamora, the incumbent for District D who was elected in 2022 and previously served as the board’s vice president, is facing David Gomez, who has served on several school district commissions including zoning and facilities.
Brenda Zamora
Outside her role as a trustee, Zamora serves as a deputy director at Make It Work Nevada, a nonprofit focused on paid leave and childcare.
Gomez has a law degree, and works as a consultant and advisor.
Notable endorsements for Zamora include Culinary Union Local 226, SEIU Local 1107, AFL-CIO, the Education Support Employees Association, and the Nevada State Education Association. Assemblyman Jovan Jackson (D-LV) has also endorsed Zamora. 
Gomez has been endorsed by the Nevada Veterans Association, the Nevada Young Republicans, and Moms for Liberty. 
Zamora identifies as a Democrat. Gomez is registered as a Republican. 
Declining school enrollment is attributable at least in part to a declining birth rate and migration trends. 
But Zamora believes that lower enrollment in Clark County schools is also linked to the growing popularity of charter schools and homeschooling. In order to reverse that trend, Zamora said the district must address negative perceptions of CCSD schools. 
She pointed to the district’s specialized Career and Technical Academies (CTAs), many of which have long waitlists, as an example of where CCSD excels. 
“We are a big target for a lot of charter schools in the area. You drive down Bonanza, and there’s about four or five at this point. So our district is really suffering in my area specifically because of that, but our schools have really great programs,” Zamora said.
Addressing the current needs of students in the district would also help keep students in CCSD schools. For District D, Zamora said that would mean more bilingual educators, greater special education funding, stronger school safety, and expanding pre-K. 
David Gomez
The Clark County School District is facing a major budget shortfall, especially for schools with low enrollment. Zamora listed several solutions Clark County could explore including promoting open enrollment, and school consolidation or K-8 models. 
Zamora said she was proud of expanding transparency during her first term by bringing back trustee community engagement meetings, and spending more time visiting schools in her district. 
Gomez did not respond to requests for an interview from the Nevada Current. In an interview with Veterans in Politics, Gomez attributed the budget shortfall to mismanagement, and low enrollment to insufficiently attractive programs in public schools. Gomez suggested incorporating trade programs into more CCDS schools to attract enrollment.
Gomez also blamed low enrollment on CCSD policies, including the passage of a gender-identity policy in 2018 that gave principals guidelines for addressing issues like bathroom and locker room usage for trans and other gender diverse students.
Clark County School Board District F
Irene Bustamante Adams, the incumbent for District F who was elected in 2022 and serves as the board’s vice president, is facing first-time candidate Robert Hutchinson, the director of facilities for the Clark County School District.\
November’s general election will be the final match between Bustamante Adams and Hutchison. During the three way primary in June, Bustamante Adams received about 50% of the vote, while Hutchinson got nearly 33% of the vote. 
Irene Bustamante Adams
Outside her role as a trustee, Bustamante Adams works as deputy director and chief strategy officer at Workforce Connections, which is Southern Nevada’s Local Workforce Development Board. Bustamante Adams also previously served four terms as a Democrat in the Nevada State Assembly.
Notable endorsements for Bustamante Adams include the Clark County Education Association, AFL-CIO, the IBEW Local 357, and the Nevada Veterans Association. She was also endorsed by the Vegas Chamber and the Latin Chamber of Commerce. 
Hutchinson has been endorsed by Culinary Union Local 226, SEIU Local 1107, the Education Support Employees Association, Bartenders Local 165, and the Progressive Leadership Alliance of Nevada. He’s also endorsed by Hispanics in Politics. 
Both Bustamante Adams and Hutchinson identify as Democrats.  
Bustamante Adams highlights as key accomplishments from her first term on the Clark County School Board the hiring of Superintendent Jhone Ebert, adopting a governance model, and approving teacher contracts before the school year.
If reelected, Bustamante Adams said her goals will be improving student outcomes in literacy, mathematics, graduation and career readiness.
Low enrollment is a major contributor to the CCSD budget shortfall, said Bustamante Adams. She noted several steps CCSD can take to reverse some of the drop, including strengthening parent communication, multilingual engagement, and public awareness of alternative enrollment options.
Bustamante Adams pointed to open enrollment, formerly known as a “change of school assignment” (COSA), which allows CCSD parents to apply to send their children to other district schools that have open and available space. Bustamante Adams also hailed CCSD’s Career and Technical Academies (CTAs) — many of which have long enrollment waitlists.
“Parents want to be able to make a choice of what school their child goes to, and so we made that happen,” Bustamante Adams said. “We have large, very high-quality high schools in the district.”
The budget shortfall should be addressed by modernizing tax policy and changing budget-setting rules to improve long-term sustainability, said Bustamante Adams. 
“We need to look at modernizing our tax policy,” said Bustamante Adams. “We’re also leaving a lot of money on the table where we don’t tax or collect taxes for certain things that are new to the market, like digital platforms and some other things.” 
Hutchinson said if elected his top priorities would be school safety, student success, and educator empowerment. 
Robert Hutchinson
After decades working in the school district, Hutchinson said he has plenty of real operational experience from inside the district that can inform his decisions on the school board.
“I’m out there in the community, understanding real life problems. I understand what things are actually working and not working,” Hutchinson said. “I’m pretty embedded in our neighborhoods, and I want to bring that kind of community aspect into the board.”
Not every student wants to enter higher education, said Hutchinson, adding that Nevada falls behind when it comes to creating a pipeline for students who want to enter the workforce. He said expanding Career and Technical Academies (CTAs) who help retain students as enrollment drops in CCSD. 
Hutchinson attributed enrollment declines to lower birth rates, charter schools, homeschooling, and declining community trust. Hutchinson said CCSD must improve communication with parents and increase responsiveness to rebuild confidence in public education.
Declining enrollment in the Clark County School District could be mitigated by focusing on successful programs like the district’s career and technical education, said Hutchinson.
When it comes to budget shortfalls, Hutchinson said CCSD should start preventative planning rather than reactive cuts. He advocated for reducing central administrative excess and seeking more equitable state funding. 
“Back in 2008, I was personally caught up in a budget shortfall myself, and my position was cut. So I kind of know the anxiety that the frontline workers feel,” Hutchison said. “We can’t keep balancing these budgets on the books of our classrooms. We need to really start trimming some of those top-heavy central administrative things.”
Hutchinson said if elected, he would also prioritize expanding the Safe Routes to School program, adding that District F required better traffic management, including protected bike lanes, flashing beacons, and traffic monitoring near schools.
Clark County School Board District G
Linda Cavazos, the incumbent for District G who previously served as board president and vice president, is facing first-time candidate Paul Casey, an entertainment production businessman who also worked as a substitute teacher for the district at the elementary level for four years. 
Linda Cavazos
Cavazos is a part-time family therapist who worked in the district for 15 years and was appointed to the board in 2017, elected in 2018 and re-elected in 2022. If reelected, it will be Cavazos’ last term. 
Notable endorsements for Cavazos include Culinary Union Local 226, Make the Road Action Nevada, the Nevada State Education Association, the Southern Nevada Building Trades Unions, Hispanics in Politics, and Progressive Leadership Alliance of Nevada Action Fund. She is a registered Democrat. 
Casey was endorsed by the Clark County Republican Party, Nevada Veterans in Politics, and the Nevada Young Republicans. He is a registered Republican. 
Cavazos is known on the board for her vocal support of progressive positions, such as the district’s gender-identity policy and a policy requiring schools to distribute letters on the importance of safe gun storage. She said her ability to win reelection several times lie with her board experience and deep ties to the community. She considers herself one of the most accessible trustees. 
She attributed declining enrollment to lower birth rates, reduced migration into the state and parents choosing charter, private, or home schools. However, she said more detailed exit surveys are needed to identify the exact reasons.
“We need to try harder to reach out. Why are parents pulling their kids from CCSD? Why are they going to charters or private if they can afford it? Why are they going to homeschools? And then we need to fill in those gaps,” Cavazos said. 
Lack of equity in schools has driven students in lower performing schools to leave CCSD, said Cavazos, noting that students should have equal access to transportation, after-school programs, manageable class sizes, and other resources.
“We have some schools where their enrollment did not drop as drastically as other schools where it really dropped quite a bit. I think that to be able to make it more equitable, we have to see the challenges that they’re facing, and then how do we get them the resources,” Cavazos said. 
Data shows schools with better programs have retained students, Cavazos said, pointing to Career and Technical Academies (CTAs). She said comprehensive high schools need comparable opportunities to retain enrollment and broaden program access.
Cavazos said CCSD will have to embrace innovative solutions to address the $50 million budget shortfall facing CCSD, including having some support staff share a position.
“If those two people agree to share a position, they would end up with a half-time position, but they wouldn’t lose their job entirely,” Cavazos said. 
Paul Casey
Casey, who worked as a substitute teacher for the district, attributed the drop in enrollment to parent dissatisfaction. He said CCSD should retain enrollment by prioritizing foundational skills such as reading, writing, mathematics, and science. Casey said he believes education outcomes have been interrupted by politics. 
“One of the biggest issues that has reared its ugly head recently is politics, personal opinions of lifestyles, and that should be probably addressed by parents, not educators,” Casey said. 
In order to retain more students, Casey said he believes CCSD schools must expand technology education that can help students enter Nevada’s growing tech industry. 
Special education in CCSD should also be overhauled to improve student outcomes, said Casey. He advocated for more parent involvement in individualized Education Programs (IEPs), as well as more assistants and aids. 
“It’s hard to have individualized educational programs for them because the ratio of teacher to student is way past where it should be,” Casey said. 
Casey said he believes the budget shortfall is the result of mismanagement by CCSD. He proposed leasing CCSD properties to for-profit trade schools as a way to cover budget shortfalls, including schools that may need to consolidate in the future due to low enrollment. 
“If the programs are not effective, if they’re not producing desired results, they need to be red penned out, because that is the responsibility in the budget,” Casey said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Trinity Health layoffs expose the danger of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act
description: Recently, Trinity Health in Livonia, Michigan announced a mass layoff of 557 workers, citing federal cuts to Medicare and Medicaid as a direct catalyst for their decision. These devastating cuts are the result of congressional Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). The law makes historic cuts to Medicaid over the next decade, leaving states […]
text:
Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey MonitorRecently, Trinity Health in Livonia, Michigan announced a mass layoff of 557 workers, citing federal cuts to Medicare and Medicaid as a direct catalyst for their decision. These devastating cuts are the result of congressional Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). The law makes historic cuts to Medicaid over the next decade, leaving states with fewer federal resources and providers facing greater uncompensated care costs as millions of Americans are at risk of losing health coverage.
In Michigan, the OBBBA has already left 23 healthcare providers at risk, forcing them to cut services, prepare for closure, or shutter operations entirely. But despite this mounting crisis, U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers (R-White Lake) continues to praise the destructive legislation. Rogers claimed the OBBBA would protect Medicaid, but nonpartisan estimates tell a much darker story: between 171,000 and 355,000 Michiganders are projected to lose coverage thanks to the bill.
What’s more, Michigan’s Medicaid budget is set to drop by $1 billion by 2028 and plummet by a total of $10.8 billion by 2034. With over 221,000 Michigan residents already stripped of Medicaid, CHIP, or ACA coverage since the OBBBA’s passage, Rogers’ enthusiastic support for these cuts proves just how out of touch he is with his would-be constituents.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rogers’ celebration of the OBBBA aligns with his record. During his previous tenure in Congress, he voted 14 times to weaken Medicaid between 2003 and 2015. Just last year, he explicitly stated he would have voted to pass the OBBBA. Throughout his political career, Rogers has demonstrated a clear and consistent disregard for healthcare access in Michigan—and becoming a senator will not change his stance.
He isn’t alone. In fact, every member of Michigan’s Republican congressional delegation voted to pass the OBBBA, celebrating the policy as it moved forward. Rep. Tom Barrett (MI-07) declared he was “proud” to send the bill to the president’s desk; Rep. Bill Huizenga (MI-04) called it a “massive win;” and Rep. John James (MI-10) echoed the praise. Each of their votes represents a direct strike against the health and well-being of the communities these officials were elected to represent.
The recent layoffs at Trinity Health are not an isolated incident; they are the predictable consequence of a dangerous legislative agenda. Mike Rogers and Michigan’s congressional Republicans have made their priorities clear—and their enthusiastic support for the OBBBA and its cuts to healthcare funding represent a direct threat to a healthy Michigan.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey proposes two-month gas tax suspension
authors: Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
description: Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Minogue last week launched an ad saying he would suspend the gas tax "until prices stabilize."
text:
DAYS AFTER HER OPPONENT called for suspension of the gas tax, Gov. Maura Healey proposed a two-month gas tax holiday on Tuesday, saying she’ll put election season legislation before lawmakers to accomplish her goal. 
Healey will file the proposal in a supplemental budget, according to her office. House Speaker Ron Mariano on Monday called suspending the gas tax “fiscally irresponsible” because, he said, there is “no end to the war in sight,” referring to the war with Iran that began over the winter and has led to significantly higher gas and other prices. 
“This will offer some relief to people, for Massachusetts families driving to work and school every day, to our drivers and truckers out on the road, to our Uber and Lyft folks,” Healey said at a press conference on Tuesday. 
The governor blamed President Donald Trump for rising gas prices, citing the US war with Iran. 
“The price of gas has gone up 50 percent since this war, and we are paying for it every single day. People in America need relief, and as governor, I want to do what I can to give relief to people here in Massachusetts,” she said. 
Republican candidate for governor Mike Minogue last week launched an ad where he said he would suspend the gas tax “until prices stabilize.” 
Minogue’s ad said, “Massachusetts charges the gas tax whether you’re paying two bucks a gallon or five, whether you’re driving a semi or taking the kids to school. That’s why I’m proposing a gas tax holiday until prices stabilize. Maura Healey ignores the question. That doesn’t make Massachusetts more affordable, but families and working people in Massachusetts need relief now.”
Minogue’s campaign spokeswoman Elizabeth Hopkins told the News Service he envisions a gas tax holiday that would be triggered any time prices go above $4 per gallon and last “until prices drop back down.” Hopkins said Minogue would “also work to permanently eliminate the gas tax,” and anticipates “this money would be replaced following an audit of the budget. Mike anticipates finding 100s of millions of taxpayer dollars currently funding waste and fraud.”
The details of Healey’s planned gas tax holiday were not available after her press conference.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Small businesses slow to take up WA’s new electric truck vouchers
description: A line of work trucks sat running in the parking lot of Kent’s Pacific Raceways Monday, but there was hardly any engine noise and no diesel exhaust.  The vehicles, ranging from forklifts to delivery vans to semi trucks, were all electric models eligible for the Washington Zero-Emission Incentive Program, a new funding mechanism supplied by […]
text:
Kenworth electric heavy-duty trucks are among those available for the Washington Zero-Emission Program. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)A line of work trucks sat running in the parking lot of Kent’s Pacific Raceways Monday, but there was hardly any engine noise and no diesel exhaust. 
The vehicles, ranging from forklifts to delivery vans to semi trucks, were all electric models eligible for the Washington Zero-Emission Incentive Program, a new funding mechanism supplied by the state’s Climate Commitment Act designed to kickstart the state’s electric work truck market. 
When it comes to meeting its own greenhouse gas emissions, Washington is behind the curve on transitioning to electric vehicles. The transportation sector is the highest emitter in the state, accounting for 40% of total emissions, and will likely be the most difficult to decarbonize. 
“If we really want to meaningfully reduce our state’s GHG emissions, being able to deploy zero emission technologies on our streets, near our roads and communities, is one of the best ways to do that,” said Betz Mayer, incentive programs deputy director at Catalyst Mobility, a nonprofit implementing WAZIP that specializes in electrifying transportation.  
One major benefit of the incentive program is that by selling more electric work trucks, in future years they can be resold at a cheaper price, and become available for businesses that can’t afford to buy new, said Kelsey Nyland, director of communications at Clean & Prosperous, a nonprofit organization that promotes market-based clean energy.
Nearly five months after its launch, the program has been “pretty successful,” with roughly half of the $112 million in available vouchers requested, Mayer said. Some applicants have already received funding, while others are still awaiting approval. 
Vouchers for heavy-duty vehicles and agriculture and construction equipment have all been requested, but “where we’re really struggling is in our class 2b through 6 – that bucket of money is moving a lot slower than we originally anticipated,” said Mayer. 
Classes 2b through 6 include cargo vans and small work trucks. Less than 5% of vouchers of those available vouchers have been requested, according to agency data.
That’s because the trucking industry has spent years discussing the transition to electrify its fleet, while small business owners using cargo vans have not, said Mayer. And, they don’t have the same level of purchasing power. 
Johannes Ariens is optimistic about the program, but wants to see more funding for small businesses such as food truck owners, bakeries and florists. As the CEO of Range, Washington’s only car dealership exclusively selling zero-emission vehicles, he says smaller work trucks make up the majority of the market. 
But the barrier for small businesses is the upfront investment, he said. 
“My personal and maybe somewhat controversial opinion is that … a significant amount of [class 7 and 8 vehicle] vouchers will not come to fruition,” Ariens said, which include heavy duty and semi trucks. The product availability and the necessary infrastructure that’s required to operate them “are far more challenging to deploy.”
Meanwhile, there’s a “massive immediate market opportunity” for smaller work trucks, he added. 
Ariens called for a “drastic increase” in funding for vehicles in the classes 4 through 6 which include medium-duty commercial vehicles such as delivery trucks, utility vehicles and small buses. 
“The market for those trucks is much larger and the infrastructure is much simpler,” he said. 
WAZIP launched on April 29. During its six-month internal evaluation in October, program directors will reassess and reallocate the funding, said Mayer, which could potentially lead to more opportunities for small businesses.
“It’s still the same bucket of money, we’re just going to move it around a little bit,” Mayer added. “We’re going to set some new buckets to kind of help inspire investment.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: School’s back in session. Let’s talk mental health.
description: Mental illnesses among youth — and especially depression and anxiety — have increased over the past decade according to many studies. So it’s important for parents to learn the warning signs and what resources are available. Pay attention to changes – changes in how a child is eating, sleeping, performing in school and dealing with […]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)Mental illnesses among youth — and especially depression and anxiety — have increased over the past decade according to many studies. So it’s important for parents to learn the warning signs and what resources are available.
Pay attention to changes – changes in how a child is eating, sleeping, performing in school and dealing with friendships, along with changes in mood and interests (sports, music, art, etc.). A child may also complain of headaches or stomach aches. Parents should examine the intensity and length of time of these symptoms. Isolating in their room for a day or two is normal, but isolating for weeks is not. If you have concerns, parents should talk with their child’s physician and school social worker along with checking their insurance to see which mental health providers are in their network (try FastTrackerMN).
Taking off work to bring a child to therapy or navigating the mental health system can be difficult. Over the past 15 years Minnesota has believed that the best place to address children’s mental health is in the schools — going to where children already are eliminates many barriers to accessing treatment.
So how equipped are our schools to address mental health?
Children are in school a substantial part of the day. So it makes sense to have schools focus on mental health (which can also help students learn). There is a framework called multi-tiered systems of support. Not every student needs the same level of support but we need to have all the levels of support.
This commonly found schematic shows how the system should work for children and families.
Minnesota was the first state in the country to require teachers to receive continuing education on the early warning signs of mental illnesses in students. Later, suicide prevention education was added. Coaches who are licensed teachers receive this training, but they also receive additional training on eating disorders. 
Students should also understand mental health and mental illnesses. This fall, schools are required to educate students grades 4-12 about mental health and mental illnesses. There is a list of courses schools can use, but it’s important that when educating students on suicide prevention that evidence-based practices are used. All student IDs in Minnesota include 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and the local mental health crisis team number.
Many schools offer social-emotional learning,  especially in the early grades, which helps children manage their emotions and build healthy relationships. Social-emotional learning is also used in Minnesota to prevent and address bullying. Goldie Hawn’s program on meditation called MindUp is also popular in schools. 
Ask younger kids how they handle big feelings, and many talk about the breathing exercises they learned in school.
The Safe and Supportive Schools Act protects students from bullying, which is important because bullying can lead to students struggling with their mental health. The Minnesota Department of Education provides guidance to schools and parents, and students can contact the department if their concerns aren’t addressed.
School support personnel play an important role in helping students who may be struggling. This includes school social workers, school psychologists, nurses and and school counselors. It’s important to note that if the word “school” is before their profession, they are not necessarily licensed mental health professionals. So, while they may listen and try to help students who are struggling, they are not licensed to diagnose and treat. People often confuse school counselors with therapists, but school counselors are trained to focus more on academic counseling.
In some urban areas social workers in schools can often be a licensed clinical social worker. In these situations, students in special education on Medicaid can receive treatment from licensed social workers in the schools. Schools can then bill Medicaid for services and therapy.
Minnesota created a program called “school-linked or behavioral-linked” in 2006. Grants go to community mental health providers, which then co-locate in the schools, making it easier for students to access mental health care. Providers work closely with school support personnel and teachers, and there is a firewall between educational and health care records. Public and private insurance is billed for services, and the grant funds cover the costs for students who are under- or uninsured and to pay for activities not covered under insurance. It is not limited to students in special education. This extremely popular program covers about 86% of districts and 57% of school sites. Last year this program served 21,615 students. Here is a current map of this program.  
Full-Service community schools provide a wide range of resources and services to support the healthy development of students. This can include health and mental health care being provided at the school.
High schools are required to have plans to allow a student to meet with a mental health professional via telehealth at the school. This includes how to ask for a space to ensure privacy.
What if your child cannot attend school due to their symptoms? Missing school due to a child’s mental health symptoms or appointments/programs to treat a mental illness (including through telehealth) are valid excuses. A school may require a note from a physician or a licensed mental health professional. Some families have struggled with their child being labeled a truant for missing school due to their mental illness, but state law is clear.
Lastly, schools need resources to address suicide. Three national organizations have toolkits to assist schools in addressing this issue: Suicide Prevention Resource Center, American Foundation for Suicide Prevention and the Jed Foundation. How schools respond to a suicide is equally important to prevent a potential contagion.
As with any health care condition, early identification and treatment yields the best outcomes. Educate yourself on the warning signs and know that teachers and school personnel are also watching for those warning signs. There are resources available for your child and family. If you have questions, reach out to advocacy organizations such as NAMI Minnesota, Minnesota Association for Children’s Mental Health and PACER.
Minnesota has made great strides in building a mental health continuum in our schools. But we have more to do:

Fully fund school-linked mental health.
Increase funding for all school support personnel (too often we only focus on school counselors).
Ensure that mental health and suicide prevention education is evidence-based.
Enhance efforts to prevent and address bullying. 

To learn more about best practices around school mental health visit the National Center for School Mental Health and read their new report on this issue.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Rural Missouri families face longer drives, riskier births as maternity wards vanish
description: Melanie Pierce works with many pregnant women who know they’ll have a long drive ahead of them when labor starts. One of her jobs as a doula living in Mansfield, Missouri, is helping families answer a question that may not be as fraught for women who live closer to a delivery hospital: When is it […]
text:
Missouri also fares worse than the country overall. Nationwide, 35% of counties are considered maternity care deserts (Naomi O'Donnell/The Beacon).Melanie Pierce works with many pregnant women who know they’ll have a long drive ahead of them when labor starts.
One of her jobs as a doula living in Mansfield, Missouri, is helping families answer a question that may not be as fraught for women who live closer to a delivery hospital: When is it time to leave?
Pierce’s clients often call as contractions begin, describing what they’re feeling and asking if they should head to the hospital.
Across Missouri, this calculation is becoming more of a reality for many families as maternity care becomes increasingly concentrated outside of the state’s rural communities.
More than half of Missouri’s counties are now considered maternity care deserts, or counties with no labor and delivery unit and no obstetric doctors, according to a new March of Dimes report.
“That’s one in two counties,” said Honour Hill, the director of maternal and infant health initiatives at March of Dimes in Alabama. “That’s more than a lot of states. Even some of our states with even worse maternal and infant health outcomes.”
Nearly 140,000 Missouri women ages 15 to 44 live in counties that have no labor and delivery unit and no obstetric doctor, while more than 120,000 live more than 30 minutes from a hospital that has labor and delivery services.
Missouri also fares worse than the country overall. Nationwide, 35% of counties are considered maternity care deserts.
“Maternity care deserts are not just in rural areas, but a significant portion are,” Hill said. “So we’re seeing our rural moms and their families having to drive so much longer.”
 How did Missouri get here? 

Between 2010 and 2024, nine Missouri counties lost hospital-based obstetric services, researchers at the University of Minnesota Rural Health Research Center found.
But maternity care was already disappearing from many communities before researchers began tracking county-level changes.
“By 2010, when our data period started, a lot of places already lacked obstetrics,” said Emily Sheffield, a doctoral candidate and researcher at the University of Minnesota.
The problem isn’t limited to rural areas. Urban hospitals have also stopped delivering babies, including Research Medical Center in Kansas City last year. But researchers have found that rural hospitals are particularly likely to lack obstetric services.
Across the country, 718 hospitals stopped providing obstetric care between 2010 and 2024, either because labor and delivery units closed or the hospitals themselves shut down, a University of Minnesota analysis showed. By 2024, 57.5% of rural hospitals did not provide obstetric care, compared with 43.6% of urban hospitals.
For small rural hospitals, keeping labor and delivery units open is particularly difficult.
Obstetric care comes with high fixed costs, due to around-the-clock staffing requirements, dedicated labor and delivery space, anesthesia and the ability to perform C-sections — regardless of whether anyone is giving birth that day.
At the same time, rural hospitals generally have fewer births to spread those high fixed costs across. They also tend to have a higher proportion of patients covered by Medicaid, which reimburses hospitals less than commercial insurance.
“Rural hospitals already have lower patient volumes, just because they are located in areas with lower populations and a larger percentage of those patients are bringing those lower reimbursement rates,” Sheffield said.
In a survey published in 2022, rural hospital administrators told University of Minnesota researchers they generally needed at least 200 births each year for obstetric services to be financially viable.
The problem compounds as patients increasingly travel to larger hospitals for care. Fewer deliveries at a rural hospital can make it even more difficult to justify the cost.
Of course, closing a labor and delivery unit doesn’t mean people stop having babies. It just makes it more difficult to do so.
March of Dimes found that recent maternity ward closures increased the average travel times by 25 minutes for families living near the closure. Research also shows that the consequences go beyond a longer drive.
The Minnesota researchers found that in the year after rural counties lost hospital-based obstetrics, the risk of preterm birth and out-of-hospital birth increased, as did the risk of giving birth at a hospital that did not have a dedicated obstetric unit, Sheffield said.
The impacts were most pronounced in rural areas. Communities closer to urban areas and more hospitals could adjust more easily, data showed.
“That’s when we really start to see the risks of maternal and infant health outcomes go up,” Sheffield said, “because people don’t have access to the services that they need.”
In some of Missouri’s most rural communities, the nearest alternative is already more than an hour away.
March of Dimes estimates that women in Reynolds and Douglas counties face drive times of more than 60 minutes to reach the closest hospital that has a maternity ward.
Sarah Turnbow, the WIC coordinator at the Reynolds County Health Center, said families she works with typically travel 60 to 90 minutes to communities such as Farmington or Poplar Bluff for their prenatal and postpartum care.
“There are about four or five OBs who are serving our whole population,” Turnbow said.
But some routine care can now come to patients instead.
A mobile integrated health program operating in the area can send providers to patients’ homes for some prenatal and postpartum visits.
“As far as routine care and those types of things, it’s been very helpful,” Turnbow said. “I’m not quite sure the word has really gotten out as much as we would like it to have gotten out. It kind of still seems like a little bit of a foreign idea to a lot of our families here.”
 Bringing maternal healthcare to rural families across Missouri 

Missouri is trying to fill some of the gap by expanding the idea of mobile health units and bringing more services to patients, rather than making patients travel.
March of Dimes points to telehealth, mobile health services and better connections to obstetric providers to high-risk patients as ways to make some care more accessible in communities that don’t have local providers.
In Missouri, doulas are increasingly part of that effort.
The state recently awarded more than $730,000 to the Missouri Doula Association through the Rural Health Transformation Program to expand rural Missouri’s doula workforce.
The association is tasked with recruiting and training doulas and community health workers, building partnerships with rural health centers and helping workers navigate Medicaid billing, according to a press release from the state.
When the state approved Medicaid coverage for doula services, Pierce began learning the world of Medicaid billing and opened her books to Medicaid patients. But the transition hasn’t been seamless.
She said there are few doulas across most of the region, leaving providers like herself to cover wide geographic areas. Pierce lives in a town about an hour east of Springfield but works with clients as far away as Joplin, Branson and the Lake of the Ozarks.
Medicaid pays doulas a set amount for a prenatal or postpartum appointment lasting at least an hour, even if the visit lasts longer. Pierce also said she cannot combine multiple sessions into one longer appointment.
“The visits they pay for are only an hour long, and we can only cover so much within an hour,” Pierce said. “If it takes me an hour to drive to somebody, an hour to meet with them, and an hour to drive back home, I’m only being paid for one hour but it takes me three.”
The state recently added more doula visits for Medicaid patients to access, but Pierce said she still feels there are missing pieces for families who need her help the most.
“The insurance clients are the ones on Medicaid,” Pierce said. “They’re the ones who are really more in need… Those people wouldn’t have a doula if it wasn’t for Medicaid.”
Telehealth helps her bridge the gap for some families. Doulas don’t provide medical care, so much of the information and emotional support can be offered through virtual care.
“It’s not ideal,” Pierce said, “but it’s what we have to work with.”
Telehealth, mobile health units and doulas can help fill some of the gaps left by the absence of maternity care. But in Reynolds County, Turnbow said one of the most basic problems remains getting families to the care that has to happen somewhere else.
“There just aren’t really very many options,” Turnbow said. “There’s no taxi service, you’re not getting a Lyft here to go anywhere.”
For families in the area, getting time off work generally isn’t difficult, she said. Employers also have to travel for their health care.
“It helps that we’re all on the same boat here in this county,” Turnbow said.
More doctors practicing closer to Reynolds County would help, she said. So would transportation assistance and reducing some of the financial barriers that determine when and how families travel for their care.
“If we could have some jobs and some money and some cars and some doctors, that would be great,” she said.
